exp.15:5:
The explanation says that the border of the tribe of Ephraim reaches the Mediterranean Sea. Then it passes by Michmethah on the north side, and turns toward the east, as far as Taanath-shiloh. From there it continues east to Janohah. The border is the boundary or limit of the land. The sea is the Mediterranean, and the east is the direction toward the sunrise.

Here no one speaks as a character; this is the account in the book of Joshua, which describes how the promised land was divided among the tribes. Ephraim and Manasseh, sons of Joseph, received their inheritance together. These lists of places showed clearly where each family lived and helped to avoid conflicts. Today not all the places mentioned can be identified with certainty.

For today: God keeps his promises with concrete details. You can trust that he is concerned with your daily life, and that he also invites you to live with order, respect, and gratitude for what he has given you.
exp.13:3:
This verse explains how the tribes were counted when the land was divided. Joseph received two shares, because his sons Manasseh and Ephraim became two tribes. The Levites did not receive a territory of their own; they were given only cities to live in, together with the open land around them for their cattle and flocks.

The narrator of the book of Joshua gives this clarification. There were twelve tribes, but the Levites served God and received no land, so Joseph was divided into two and the number of portions remained complete. Everything was done as commanded through Moses.

Today we can learn that God cares for those who serve him, even when his provision looks different from that of others. Let us trust that he gives what is needed, and support with generosity those who devote themselves to teaching and serving in the church.
exp.8:9:
The explanation continues the previous phrase: the men say they heard of the fame of Jehovah and everything he did in Egypt, and also what he did to the two Amorite kings beyond the Jordan. Those kings were Sihon, of Heshbon, and Og, of Bashan, who lived in Ashtaroth.

The ones speaking are the Gibeonites, who present themselves to Joshua as travelers from distant lands. They mention only the distant victories, not those at Jericho and Ai, which were more recent and nearby. In this way they sustain their deception: they want a peace treaty with Israel and pretend not to be neighbors.

For today: what is said about God can sound good and still come with a hidden purpose. Before deciding, it is wise to pray and examine things calmly, as Joshua should have done.
exp.16:15:
Here the descendants of Joseph (the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh) say that the hill country is not enough for them. In addition, the Canaanites who live in the valleys have chariots of iron, that is, war chariots reinforced with iron. Beth-shean and Jezreel were towns and valley areas where they lived.

The sons of Joseph complain to Joshua because they received only one portion of land, even though they are a numerous people. Joshua answers them that they should clear the forest of the mountain and spread out. They use as an excuse their fear of the iron chariots. Joshua does not accept that excuse and encourages them to trust in their strength.

For today: sometimes we complain about what we lack, when God has already given us opportunities that require effort. Before making excuses for obstacles, we can take the step of faith and work with what we have.
exp.7:2:
This verse tells us that Joshua rose up with his whole army to attack the city of Ai. He chose thirty thousand valiant men and sent them out by night. The "people of war" are the soldiers, and "mighty men" means men who are brave and able for battle.

The narrator describes how Joshua obeys what God has just commanded him. Earlier, Israel had been defeated at Ai because of Achan's sin (chapter 7). Now God tells Joshua not to be afraid and gives him a plan: to set an ambush behind the city. The thirty thousand are to hide while Joshua draws the enemy out. Some scholars think this group is different from the five thousand mentioned in verse 12, and others see two accounts of the same plan.

When God encourages us not to fear, He also expects us to act with obedience and good order. Trusting Him does not mean standing still, but taking the steps He shows us.
exp.15:8:
This verse says that, besides the main territory the tribe of Ephraim received, some cities with their villages within the land belonging to Manasseh were also given to them. "Set apart" means they were separated or reserved for Ephraim. The "villages" were the small towns surrounding each city.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel divided the promised land among the tribes. Ephraim and Manasseh were sons of Joseph, and they received neighboring territories. Here the account describes Ephraim's boundaries and explains that their borders were mixed with those of Manasseh. The text does not say why this was done; the assigned territory probably was not enough, but that is an assumption. Soon after, it is mentioned that they did not drive out the Canaanites from Gezer.

For today: God divides with order, and also with generosity. We can learn to share what we have with others, without jealousy, and to finish with obedience what God has entrusted to us.
exp.6:21:
Joshua sends messengers who run to Achan's tent. There they find everything hidden, just as he had confessed: the cloak, the silver, and the bar of gold.

Israel had been defeated at Ai because Achan took things that God had set apart, after the victory at Jericho. Joshua does not rely only on Achan's word; he verifies the facts. That the spoil was hidden shows that the sin was committed in secret, although God saw everything.

For today: what we hide is not concealed before God, and sin in secret often harms others. Confessing in time, with sincerity, is better than hiding. God forgives the one who comes to Him with a humble heart.
exp.7:8:
This verse tells that Joshua sent away the group of chosen soldiers for the ambush. They went and hid between Beth-el and Ai, on the west side of Ai. "Ambush" is a hiding place used to surprise the enemy. Joshua, on the other hand, spent that night in the middle of the camp, with the people.

After the defeat at Ai, caused by the sin of Achan, God gave Joshua a new plan to take the city. Here the narrator shows that Joshua obeyed the instructions he had received. The earlier words are Joshua's to the men of the ambush, reminding them that God would deliver the city.

For today: when God gives us direction, obeying it with order and patience is part of faith. Joshua did not rush ahead or improvise; he also stayed with his people. Let us trust God and faithfully fulfill the place that is ours, even when no one sees it.
exp.5:14:
It says that on the seventh day the people of Israel got up very early, at dawn, and circled the city of Jericho the same way as on the previous days, but this time seven times.

The sentence about the trumpets and the camp is removed, since its quoted words do not appear in the verse. The word for camp and the explanation of the phrase about walking around the city are likewise removed, because the reader's verse already says plainly that they compassed the city.

The narrator of the book here tells how Israel obeyed the instructions God gave to Joshua for taking Jericho. For six days they marched in silence, once each day, with the ark of the LORD in front. This seventh day was different, and the account prepares the moment when God gives the city into their hands.

For today: sometimes God asks us to persevere in things that seem repetitive and without results. Obeying each day with patience, trusting that he keeps his word, is a real form of faith.
exp.12:3:
This verse continues the list of lands that still remained to be conquered. No one knows for certain where Mehara or this Aphek were located, and scholars continue to debate it.

God speaks to Joshua, who is now old. He reminds him that although Israel had won many victories, territories still remained unpossessed. Even so, he promises that he himself would drive them out before his people.

For today: sometimes we think we have already finished, but God shows us that there are still areas of our lives to surrender to him. Trust his promise and keep moving forward with faith and perseverance, without settling for what you have already achieved.
exp.7:12:
This verse describes how Israel's forces were positioned before the battle. The main body of the army camped north of Ai, and the hidden group was placed on the west side of the city. During that night, Joshua went down into the middle of the valley.

The explanation's note about two source-language words is not needed here, since the reader's verse uses different wording. The verse itself says "lay" and "liers in wait," so the hidden group is simply described as those lying in wait.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. He tells of Israel's second attempt against Ai, after the earlier defeat caused by Achan's sin. This time God had given Joshua a plan: prepare an ambush and feign a retreat. The details of the positions show a well-ordered plan. Some geographical details, such as the exact location of the places, are understood in different ways.

For today: trusting God does not remove the need for preparation. Joshua obeyed God's plan with order and care. Before an important decision, pray, ask for direction, and plan with diligence.
exp.20:25:
This verse sums up that the remaining families of the children of Kohath received ten cities in all, with their surrounding lands. The cities were places to live, and the open land around them was where they could keep their animals.

The book of Joshua tells how the promised land was divided. The Levites did not receive a territory of their own, because they served God in worship and in teaching. For that reason the other tribes gave them cities to live in, as God had commanded through Moses. Kohath was one of the Levite families, and this closes the list of what fell to him.

For today: God cares for those who serve others spiritually, and he does so through his people. Ask yourself how you can support, with generosity, your church and those who teach you the Word.
exp.15:9:
The explanation says that the tribe of Ephraim did not manage to drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer. These continued living among the Ephraimites to this day, that is, until the time the account was written. They served under tribute, meaning they paid taxes or worked for Israel. The word "Canaanites" is used here for the people who lived in the land before Israel.

It is part of the division of the land among the tribes. The narrator, who does not identify himself, honestly records a failure: God had commanded that these peoples be removed (Deuteronomy 7), but Ephraim was content with subjecting them. Judges 1:29 repeats this detail. Scholars debate when the phrase "to this day" was written, but the text points to incomplete obedience.

Today we can ask ourselves what things we have allowed to remain among us out of convenience, such as a habit or an attitude that God asks us to give up. Tolerating it seems useful or harmless, but over time it tends to grow. Let us ask God for the courage to obey him completely.
exp.7:18:
The explanation says that the Israelite soldiers hidden behind the city rose up quickly as soon as Joshua raised his spear. They ran toward Ai, which had been left open, took it, and at once set it on fire. An ambush is a group hidden in order to attack by surprise; quickly means with speed.

Here the book of Joshua tells the story. Earlier, Israel had failed at Ai because of the sin of Achan, and then God gave a new plan. God told Joshua to raise the spear as a sign, and he promised to hand the city over. The smoke told everyone that the plan was working.

Today we can learn to obey God promptly, when He shows us the step to take. The men in the ambush watched for the signal and did not delay. In the same way, we can pray with attentiveness and act without hesitation when we know what God asks of us.
exp.9:19:
This verse tells that Joshua and the Israelites kept attacking the enemy armies until they had almost wiped them out. A few survivors managed to escape and shut themselves inside fortified cities, that is, cities surrounded by walls for defense. The verse's "great slaughter" refers to a very large killing.

Here the book's narrator speaks. Five Amorite kings had attacked Gibeon, an ally of Israel, and Joshua confronted them. He had already ordered that the enemy be pursued and not allowed to enter their cities, because he trusted that God had given them into his hand. The text shows that the victory was completed, although some managed to flee. It is a war account from ancient Israel, and Christians read it in different ways.

For today: when God gives us strength to face a problem, it is good to finish what we have started with perseverance, without stopping halfway, trusting in his help and not only in our own effort.
exp.0:9:
This verse is a transition phrase. It says that Joshua gave an order to the "officers of the people." The word "commanded" means that he gave an instruction with authority. The officers were appointed leaders who helped organize and pass on the orders to the people. The sentence ends with a colon, because what Joshua said to them follows right after.

Joshua speaks here, the new leader of Israel after the death of Moses. God had just encouraged him to be courageous and to obey his law. Now Joshua begins to act: he takes the first practical step to prepare the people to cross the Jordan River and enter the promised land.

For today: when God encourages us and gives us his Word, the next step is to obey with concrete actions. Faith does not stay only in feelings; it gets moving, with order and trust in God.
exp.23:15:
The explanation says that the people of Israel answered firmly, "God forbid that we should forsake the Lord, to serve other gods", meaning that they did not even think of abandoning the Lord to serve other gods. The phrase "God forbid" means the same as "may it never happen". The letter "á" was an old spelling of "a", and this comment is not needed for the English reader.

Joshua, already an old man, had gathered the tribes at Shechem to renew the covenant. He asked them to choose whom they would serve, and declared that he and his house would serve the Lord. The people answer by recalling how God brought them out of Egypt, cared for them along the way, and gave them the land. Their answer grows out of what God had done for them. Later on, the history of Israel shows that they did not always keep this promise.

For today: deciding to follow God is not just a feeling of the moment. Remember how God has cared for you, and renew your commitment to Him in concrete things, such as prayer, obedience, and what you leave behind.
exp.7:3:
Joshua gives orders to the thirty thousand strong men he chose. He tells them to hide in an ambush behind the city of Ai. An ambush is a group of soldiers hidden in order to attack by surprise. Their instruction means they must stay close. Ready and alert is what it means to be prepared.

Joshua, the leader of Israel, is the one speaking. Earlier, Israel had been defeated at Ai because of Achan's sin. Now God gives them a new plan, and Joshua puts it into action. While he and the rest of the people draw the enemy out by pretending to flee, this group must wait for the right moment to act.

God often asks us for obedience and preparation, not just enthusiasm. Today we can live ready and alert: attentive, prepared, and close to the place where God has placed us, waiting for his timing without rushing ahead or wandering away from what he has asked of us.
exp.6:2:
The men who went to spy out the city of Ai returned to Joshua and gave him their advice: it was not necessary to send the whole army, since about two or three thousand men would be enough to win. They said Ai had few inhabitants, so it was not worth wearing out all the people.

The spies Joshua sent were coming from the victory at Jericho and felt confident. But they did not know that Achan had taken forbidden things and that God was displeased with Israel. They looked only at what was visible: the size of the city.

For today: let us not trust only our own calculations or past victories. Before facing a challenge, it is wise to pray and examine our hearts, because something hidden may be standing in the way.
exp.11:20:
The explanation says that Joshua and the Israelites defeated two more kings of Canaan: the king of Taanach and the king of Megiddo. The word "one" means that each of them counts as one more king in the list of the defeated. Taanach and Megiddo were important Canaanite cities in the north of the land.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Joshua chapter 12 summarizes Israel's victories west of the Jordan and totals thirty-one kings. The list is meant to show that God kept his promise to give the land to his people. Some details of those conquests are interpreted in different ways, but the purpose of the list is clear: to remember what God did.

For today: even though a list of names may seem dull, it teaches us to remember in detail the faithfulness of God. Make a list of the times He has helped you and give thanks to Him.
exp.21:23:
Here the men of Reuben and Gad explain why they built an altar beside the Jordan. They say they did it out of concern for the future: they feared that, in time, the children of the tribes on the western side would say to their own children, "What have you to do with the Lord God of Israel?" The old-style wording "for fear of this thing" means "out of concern that this would happen."

They speak as the tribes east of the Jordan, facing Israel, which had been alarmed, thinking the altar was an act of rebellion. They clarify that their intention was not to worship apart, but to leave a reminder that they, too, belonged to the people of God.

For today: let us make sure our children and the new generations know that they belong to God. Let us speak of our faith at home, with clarity and affection, so that they never feel far from Him.
exp.13:8:
Here Caleb recalls what Moses promised under oath. The phrase "the land whereon thy feet have trodden" is an old way of swearing an oath; it means "surely the land you walked on will be yours." The reader sees this in the verse as "the land whereon thy feet have trodden," so the phrase is simply what the verse says. The word "inheritance" in the verse refers to property that passes to your children forever. The reason is that Caleb wholly followed the Lord, that is, he was completely faithful to Him.

Caleb speaks at eighty-five years old, before Joshua in Gilgal. Forty-five years earlier, he was one of the twelve spies sent into Canaan. While the others discouraged the people, he trusted God. Now he asks for the region that Moses had promised him.

For today: God sees and remembers constant faithfulness, even when many years pass and others lose heart. Keep trusting Him and obeying Him in the small things of each day, without depending on the majority or on applause.
exp.17:21:
This verse is part of a list of towns that the tribe of Benjamin received. It names three places: Beth-arabah, Zemaraim, and Bethel. The spelling "Beth" is an older form of writing the name, and the verse itself uses the same spelling.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel divided the promised land. Here the narrator describes in detail what fell to Benjamin, lying between the tribes of Judah and Ephraim. This list shows that God kept his promise to give a land to his people, and that each family had its place. It is not known for certain where Zemaraim was.

For today: God pays attention to details and to each person. If he took care that every tribe had its place, he also cares for you. Trust that he has a place and a purpose for your life, even when it sometimes seems small to you.
exp.21:31:
This verse tells that Phinehas, son of the priest Eleazar, and the leaders who were with him returned from Gilead, where the tribes of Reuben and Gad lived, to Canaan, where the rest of the Israelites were. There they reported what had happened.

The leaders are the heads of the tribes, and they brought back the explanation they had received.

The tribes on the other side of the Jordan had built a large altar, and the rest of Israel feared it was an act of rebellion against God. Phinehas and the leaders went to ask for an account, listened to the explanation, and were satisfied. Now they carry the good news to their people, and so a war is avoided.

Today we can learn to ask and listen before judging. We often suspect the intentions of others without knowing their reasons. Speaking calmly and seeking the truth helps us care for unity and peace among brothers and sisters.
exp.14:34:
This verse is part of a list of towns. It names four places: Jerimot (in other versions, Jarmuth), Adullam, Socoh and Azekah. They were in the lowlands, the low hill country west of Judah. The word "villages" refers to the small settlements that surrounded each town.

The context is the division of the promised land among the tribes of Israel. The narrator of the book, whom tradition often links with Joshua (though this is not certain), lists the territories of Judah. This list shows that God was keeping his promise to Abraham. Later, the Bible tells that David took refuge in Adullam, and that Socoh and Azekah appear near the battle against Goliath.

For today: God notices details and ordinary places. No place or person escapes his attention. If today you feel you are in a small place, remember that God can use it for something important.
exp.18:23:
This verse says that the fifth portion of land went to the tribe of Asher, distributed according to their families. "Lot" is an old word for the drawing of lots used to decide which land each tribe would receive. "Inheritance" is the land received as an heritage.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel, now inside the promised land, divides it among its tribes. No character speaks here; the narrator simply records the order of the distribution. Earlier, Issachar was mentioned, and afterward the cities and borders of Asher are listed, near Mount Carmel and the coast. It shows that God was fulfilling the promise made to the patriarchs.

For today: God cares for every family and every detail, even those that seem like simple lists. We can trust that our share is in His hands, and live thankfully without comparing ourselves to others.
exp.17:6:
The explanation says that the Levites would not receive a territory of their own among the tribes, because their inheritance was to serve God as priests. It also notes that Gad, Reuben, and half the tribe of Manasseh had already received their land on the east side of the Jordan, given by Moses. "But" is the word in the verse that introduces this contrast, and "inheritance" is the word for what each tribe receives.

Joshua speaks at Shiloh, where the tabernacle was. Seven tribes still had not received their land, and he explains how to divide it into seven parts. He clarifies who already had their portion and who would not have territory, so that the distribution would be orderly and fair. Then lots would be cast before the Lord.

For today: our true wealth is not what we possess, but belonging to God and serving him. We can ask him to help us value his presence more than our possessions.
exp.18:10:
This verse describes the border of the tribe of Zebulun. "Border" means a limit or boundary. On the western side, the line goes up toward the sea (the Hebrew word can also simply mean "the west"), passes by Maralah and Dabbasheth, and reaches a stream near Jokneam. Today it is not known with certainty where some of these places were.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel divided the promised land among the tribes, by lot, after entering Canaan. Here the narrator lists in detail the boundaries of each inheritance, so that every family would know its portion.

God is concerned even with details, and gives each person a place and a task. Today we might ask ourselves: Do I faithfully care for what God has entrusted to me, without envying the portion of others?
exp.12:13:
This verse says that the tribe of Levi did not receive its own territory, as the other tribes did. Their inheritance was the sacrifices and offerings presented to the Lord. The word "but" in this verse is the plain modern form, and "gave" is the ordinary modern verb. The word "inheritance" means the portion of land that each tribe received as its share.

The narrator of the book tells how Moses divided the land east of the Jordan. Here he makes clear that the Levites were the exception. They served in worship and in teaching the law, and they lived from the offerings of the people. According to the text, God had already said this before, and they received cities to live in, though not territories of their own.

For today: our security does not depend on what we possess, but on God himself. We can ask him to teach us to trust his provision and to value his presence more than our possessions.
exp.0:17:
It says that if anyone rebels against Joshua's orders and does not obey his words, that person must die. And it closes by encouraging him: "be strong and of good courage." The phrase "whosoever he be that doth rebel" means "whoever would oppose," and "commandment" means "orders."

The speakers are the tribes of Israel, especially those who stayed east of the Jordan, and they are answering Joshua. God had just charged him with leading the people after Moses. They promise to obey him as they obeyed Moses. The death penalty reflects the law of that time, when Israel was a nation under a covenant with God. Their loyalty was a matter of life or death for everyone.

We do not use that punishment today, but we can learn to faithfully support those whom God places as leaders, praying for them and encouraging them to be brave. A word of encouragement can strengthen someone who carries a great responsibility.
exp.9:42:
The explanation says that Joshua and all the people of Israel returned to the camp at Gilgal. The word "returned" is the same idea as "turned back" or "went back" in the verse. After the battles in the south, they did not stay there, but went back to their base.

The book of Joshua is a narrative, so here it is not a character speaking, but the one telling the story. He has just recounted the victories over the kings of the south and affirms that God fought for Israel. Gilgal was the first camp after crossing the Jordan. Some scholars think this return was a brief rest, and others see it as a closing of the account. The text gives no further details.

After a great effort, it is healthy to return to a place of rest and to remember that God is the one who sustains the work. Pause, give thanks, and renew your strength.
exp.12:24:
This verse describes part of the territory that the tribe of Gad received, east of the Jordan River. It includes the city of Jazer, all the cities of Gilead, and half the land of the Ammonites, as far as Aroer, which is before Rabbah. "Coast" means the border or territory.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel divided the promised land. Here the account recalls what Moses had already given to Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh. About the exact location of some places, such as Aroer, scholars do not always agree. The list shows that God kept his promise to give an inheritance to every family.

For today: God is faithful and remembers the details of our lives, even the smallest ones. You can trust that what he promises, he fulfills. Today, give thanks for a specific blessing you have received and take responsible care of it.
exp.14:25:
This verse names three more cities: Amam, Shema, and Moladah. It is part of a long list of towns. It does not tell a story; it only names places. The names sound ancient because they come from Hebrew, and their spelling has been carried over from older English usage. Today no one knows for certain where each one was located, although Moladah appears later in other biblical texts as a city in the south.

There is no character speaking here. The book of Joshua recounts how Israel divided up the promised land. This passage lists the cities of the south that fell to the tribe of Judah, in the region called the Negev, near Beersheba. The list shows that God kept his promise to give a land to his people, and that each place was recorded.

For today: God pays attention to small things and forgets no detail. If even little-known towns were written down, you matter to God too. Trust that he keeps his promises, even when the details seem small to you.
exp.20:2:
The explanation says that the people of Israel, obeying what God had commanded, handed over to the Levites some cities from their own lands. The cities and their surrounding pasturelands are the points of interest here: the cities were places to live, and the pasturelands around them were grazing areas for livestock.

The heads of the Levite families went to speak with the priest Eleazar, with Joshua, and with the leaders of the tribes, at Shiloh. They reminded them that God, through Moses, had ordered that they be given places to live and pasture for their animals. The Levites did not receive a territory of their own like the other tribes, because their task was to serve God. For that reason they depended on the generosity of the whole people.

For today: when God shows us something, obeying it includes being generous toward those who serve others. We can gladly and honestly support those who teach and care for the spiritual life of our community.
exp.8:14:
This verse tells us that Joshua made a peace agreement with the Gibeonites and promised to let them live. The leaders of Israel, called "the princes of the congregation" in the older wording, also confirmed it with an oath. The sentence about the word for "made" can be rendered simply: Joshua entered into a formal agreement with them.

The Gibeonites were neighbors of Canaan, but they pretended to be travelers from a distant land. They used worn-out wineskins and old clothing as proof. Israel trusted appearances and did not ask counsel from the LORD, that is, they did not consult God. Three days later they discovered the deception, but they had already sworn an oath and could not take it back.

Before deciding something important, it is wise to pray and seek God's guidance, even when everything seems clear. What looks good on the outside can hide another reality, and haste can lead us into commitments that are hard to undo.
exp.3:4:
Joshua gives orders to twelve men to go to the middle of the Jordan River, in front of the ark of the Lord, which represented the presence of God. Each one must carry a stone on his shoulder, one for each tribe of Israel.

Joshua, the leader of Israel after Moses, is the one speaking. The people had just crossed the Jordan on dry ground, because God parted the waters. The twelve stones would serve as a memorial to remember this miracle, so that the children would ask questions and the parents would tell them what God had done.

Today we can do something similar: keep reminders of what God has done in our lives, such as a note, a date, or a testimony, and tell them to our children or to others, so that faith is passed on.
exp.6:8:
Joshua tells God that the Canaanites and all the inhabitants of the land will hear of the defeat of Israel. Then they will surround us and cut off our name from the earth. And he asks: "What wilt thou do unto thy great name?" To "cut off" means to wipe out or eliminate completely. To "surround" means to encircle. The "name" here means God's fame and honor.

Joshua speaks in anguish, face down on the ground, after Israel was defeated at Ai. He did not yet know that the cause was the sin of Achan, who had taken things set apart for God. His complaint is sincere and somewhat hasty, but he appeals to God's reputation. God answers that the problem lies within the people.

For today: when something goes wrong for you, bring it to God honestly, but also examine your own life. Sometimes the answer is not outside, but in something we need to correct with humility.
exp.5:4:
It says that when the priests blow a long blast on the ram's horn and the people hear that sound, everyone must shout with great force. Then the wall of Jericho will collapse, and each person will go straight ahead, without detours, toward the front. The "ram's horn" here is the horn of a ram, and the wall falling "flat" means it comes down right where it stands, collapsing to the ground. "With a great shout" means at the top of their lungs.

The one speaking is God, and Joshua passes on his instructions. Israel had just crossed the Jordan and faced a city with strong walls. God does not give them an ordinary military strategy, but a plan that demands obedience and trust. The victory would come from Him, not from their own strength.

For today: sometimes God asks us to take steps that seem illogical. We do not always see the result right away, but we can obey in faith, one day at a time, trusting that He keeps what He promises.
exp.18:14:
This verse says that the territory of Zebulun also included the cities of Kattath, Nahallal, Shimron, Idalah, and Bethlehem, twelve cities in all with their villages. "Includes" means the same as "takes in" or "comprises." The villages were small settlements around the cities. This Bethlehem is not the one in Judah, where Jesus was born, but another one in the north. Some believe it was in Galilee, though this is not entirely certain.

The book of Joshua tells how the promised land was divided among the tribes of Israel, by lot, before the Lord. Here the narrator records in detail only what fell to Zebulun. Such lists showed that God was keeping what he had promised to his people.

For today: God does not overlook the small. Even the names of little-known towns were written down. Trust that the place where he has put you matters, and be faithful there.
exp.23:29:
This verse tells where Joshua was buried: in the land that he himself had received as his inheritance, in a place called Timnath-serah, in the hill country of Ephraim, on the north side of the hill of Gaash. The explanation of the words "border" and "possession" has been left out here, since the verse itself already says "border of his inheritance."

The one telling this is the author of the book, who closes the story of Joshua. After sending the people away and renewing the covenant with God, Joshua dies at the age of 110. The Bible calls him "the servant of the LORD." His burial in his own inheritance shows that God kept the promise to give the land. The exact details of the place are little known, and it is not certain where the hill of Gaash is.

For today: a faithful life is remembered for its service to God, not for titles. Serve God faithfully where you are, and leave a good example for those who come after you.
exp.18:6:
This verse ends the list of cities that the tribe of Simeon received. It names four more: Ain, Rimmon, Ether, and Ashan, along with the villages that belonged to them. "Villages" are the small towns around a main city.

The one who tells the story is the author of the book of Joshua, who describes how Canaan was divided among the tribes by lot. Simeon did not receive a territory of its own, separate from the others. Its land was taken from the portion of Judah, because Judah had been given more than it needed. So Simeon was set down within the land of Judah. Some see here the fulfillment of Jacob's words about Simeon, that he would be scattered in Israel (Genesis 49:7), though this is an interpretation.

God cares for each person, even for those who seem small or are little mentioned. He also teaches us to share: Judah had more than enough and made room for its brother. Today we can ask ourselves what we have to spare to help someone.
exp.14:58:
This verse names three towns from the hill country of Judah: Maarath, Beth-anoth, and Eltekon. It says there were six towns in all, counting others that are not mentioned here, together with their villages, that is, the small settlements that depended on them.

It is part of a long list describing the land that fell to the tribe of Judah. The account is told by a narrator, and it is not known for certain who wrote these lists down. Their purpose is to show that God kept his promise to give the land to his people, with real places and clear boundaries.

For today: God does not forget small places or little-known people. If today you feel ordinary or unimportant, remember that God knows you by name. Serve him faithfully right where you are.
exp.17:17:
This verse continues describing the northern border of the land that the tribe of Benjamin received. It says the boundary passes by the side facing the northern open country and then goes down to the plain. The word for open country refers to flat, open land, and the word for border means the boundary or limit. Some scholars think the plain refers to the Arabah, the deep valley beside the Jordan, but not all of them are certain.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua details how the land was divided among the tribes of Israel after the conquest. Lots were cast before the Lord, and each family received a place with clear boundaries.

For today: God is concerned with the details of our lives, not only with the big things. Just as He made sure each tribe knew its inheritance, today we can trust that He knows our place and our task. Give thanks for what He has given you and care for it faithfully.
exp.14:46:
This verse continues the list of cities that were allotted to the tribe of Judah. It names Ashdod and Gaza, two cities of the Philistines, along with their towns and their villages. The border ran "unto the river of Egypt," which is usually understood as a stream on the southern border of Canaan. "The great sea" is the Mediterranean Sea, and "the border thereof" means the boundaries or the territory.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel received the promised land. Here the narrator describes in detail what belonged to Judah. Although the land was assigned, other texts suggest that not all of that territory was fully possessed. Scholars debate how far Judah actually controlled these Philistine cities.

For today: God keeps his promises, but sometimes we must walk in them with faith and perseverance. Ask him to help you not to settle for less than what he wants to give you.
exp.11:22:
This verse continues a list of defeated kings. It names the king of Dor, a town and region by the coast, and another king identified with the nations of Gilgal. The word "province" here means the area around Dor. The phrase "nations of Gilgal" may come from a Hebrew word that can mean "nations," or it may have been the name of a place. It is also not known for certain which Gilgal this is.

The narrator of the book of Joshua summarizes Israel's victories as they enter the promised land. The list reaches thirty-one kings, and its purpose is to show that God kept what he promised his people. Each name is a reminder of that faithfulness.

For today: God keeps his promises step by step, and he forgets no detail. Note the times he has helped you, even when they seem small, and give him thanks. This strengthens your confidence for what lies ahead.
exp.21:9:
This verse tells how the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half tribe of Manasseh, already on their way back to their lands east of the Jordan, stopped on the riverbank, on the Canaan side. There they built an altar that was very large and striking. The phrase about the borders means the edges of the land, the region along the frontier, and "to see to" means that it could be seen from far away.

Joshua had just sent them off with a blessing, after they had helped conquer the land. Here the narrator speaks, and does not yet explain why they built the altar. The other Israelites misunderstood it and thought it was an act of rebellion against God.

For today: before judging what others do, it is wise to ask and listen to their reasons. An action that looks wrong may have a good purpose.
exp.14:26:
This verse is part of a list of towns. It names three places in the tribe of Judah: Hazar-gaddah, Heshmon, and Beth-palet. Beyond what the text says, nothing more is known about them, and the exact location of Heshmon is not known for certain.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel received the promised land. Here the narrator describes the division of Judah's territory, and this section lists the towns of the south, in the region of the Negev, near Edom. They are recorded in detail to show that God kept his promise to Abraham and his descendants.

For today: God cares even for small and little-known places. If you sometimes feel insignificant, remember that God knows you by name and has a place for you. Trust that he keeps his promises, even in everyday life.
exp.9:20:
This verse says that all the people of Israel returned safe and sound to the camp where Joshua was, at Makkedah. No one dared to speak against them or threaten the Israelites. The phrase "move his tongue" means to say something against someone. It is a way of saying that no one could accuse them or do them harm.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua is speaking. Israel had just defeated five Amorite kings who attacked Gibeon. God had given them the victory, and the army returned without losing a single man. The enemy kings were hiding in a cave, and Joshua would order them brought out afterward.

For today: when God leads us through a struggle, we can rest in the knowledge that He cares for His own. Let us give thanks for His protection and trust that He goes before us.
exp.1:3:
It says that Rahab had already taken the two spies and hidden them. When the king's messengers arrived, she admitted that some men had indeed come to her house, but she claimed that she did not know where they were from. Old wording: the verse's "but I wist not" simply means "but I did not know," and the phrase "There came men unto me" is the same as saying "men had come to my house."

The Israelites had sent spies to Jericho before entering the land. The king of Jericho found out and demanded that Rahab hand them over. She speaks in order to protect them. The verses that follow show that she gave him a false trail. The Bible recounts this deception without expressly approving it; some see it as an act of faith in the middle of an extreme situation, and others debate whether it was right to lie.

Today we can learn that faith is shown through concrete and courageous actions. Rahab risked her life because she trusted the God of Israel. Let us ask for wisdom to obey God, even when it costs us, and to do so with honesty.
exp.2:16:
The explanation says that the priests who carried the ark of the covenant of the Lord stood firm in the middle of the Jordan River, on dry ground, while all the people finished crossing. It adds that "on dry ground" means on ground without water, and that the name of God is what the text uses for the Lord. So all of Israel crossed the river without getting wet.

The book of Joshua tells how the people, after years in the wilderness, finally entered the promised land. Joshua was the leader after the death of Moses. The account shows that God kept his word and was with Israel. The ark represented God's presence, and the river was swollen at the time of the harvest.

For today: sometimes God asks us to remain firm in the middle of difficulty, trusting in him, while others move forward or are blessed because of our faithfulness. Stand firm and trust, even if you cannot yet see the other side.
exp.17:15:
This verse describes the southern boundary of the territory of Benjamin. The line runs down to the end of the mountain that faces the valley of Hinnom, and in the valley of the giants (in Hebrew, "Rephaim") to the north. Then it passes through the valley of Hinnom, beside the city of the Jebusites (the ancient Jerusalem), toward the south, and reaches the spring of Rogel.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Joshua. He tells how the land was divided by lot among the tribes that still lacked their portion, at Shiloh. The boundaries were recorded in detail so that each family would know what its inheritance was.

For today: God cares about the details of your life. He has given you a specific place and task, so trust his care and live with gratitude and faithfulness where you are.
exp.18:8:
This verse tells us that the land of the tribe of Simeon was taken out of the territory that had first been given to Judah. The portion of Judah was too large for them, that is, more than they could use. For this reason the descendants of Simeon received their inheritance inside the territory of Judah. The phrase about the portion being too much is a rewording of the source's point that Judah's share was more than it needed.

The book of Joshua recounts how the promised land was divided among the tribes of Israel, and the narrator describes each portion. Here the list for Simeon is closed and the reason its land lies within Judah's is explained. This fits with the idea that the division was made by lot, and Judah had received more than it needed.

For today: Judah had more than was necessary and shared what was left over. We can ask whether what God has given us, whether time, money or space, can be opened up to help someone who needs it.
exp.8:4:
This verse describes how the Gibeonites looked: they wore old shoes and patched sandals, worn-out clothing, and bread that was dry and moldy. The word "clouted" in the verse refers to shoes that had been mended and patched. Everything was arranged to make it seem that they had come from a very long journey.

The narrator tells this after the Gibeonites heard what Joshua had done at Jericho and Ai. They were afraid and used cunning: they pretended to be envoys from a distant land in order to secure an alliance with Israel. The Bible says this was a deception, and that the Israelites did not consult the Lord before deciding (v. 14).

Today, this passage reminds us that appearances can deceive. Before making an important decision, it is wise to pray, ask for wisdom, and examine the facts carefully, without being led only by what seems convincing.
exp.7:14:
It says that Joshua and all the people of Israel pretended to be defeated. "Making themselves appear beaten" means they acted as if they had lost the battle, and so they ran toward the wilderness, drawing away from the men of Ai. It was not a real defeat but a strategy.

It is part of the account of the conquest of Ai. Earlier, Israel had failed there because of Achan's sin (chapter 7). Now God gives Joshua a plan: set an ambush and lure the enemy out of the city. The narrator tells how Joshua obeys the instructions God gave him, and the feigned retreat serves to draw everyone out of Ai.

Today we can learn that obeying God sometimes involves steps that do not seem logical or comfortable, such as retreating, waiting, or accepting that others may see us as weak. If God guides us, we can trust his plan even when we do not yet understand it.
exp.12:4:
This verse follows a list of territories that had not yet been conquered. It mentions the land of the Giblites (the area of Byblos, on the coast), and all of Lebanon toward the east, from Baal-gad, at the foot of Mount Hermon, to the entrance of Hamath. "Toward the sunrising" means toward the east.

God speaks to Joshua, who is now old. He reminds him that much land still remains to be possessed. Even so, he asks him to divide the inheritance among the tribes, and promises that he himself will drive out the peoples who live there. Some scholars think these boundaries show the full promise, although Israel did not occupy all of it.

God keeps his promises, but sometimes his work moves forward in stages. If there are goals you do not yet see fulfilled, keep obeying with patience and trust that God will finish what he has begun.
exp.9:25:
It says that Joshua struck down the five Amorite kings who had hidden in a cave, and hung their bodies on five trees, that is, on poles or trees. They stayed there until evening. The word "struck" here means that he beat them or put them to death.

The narrator tells of the end of a battle at Gibeon. God had given Israel the victory, and these kings had attacked their allies. Joshua acts as the leader of Israel in the conquest of Canaan, which the text presents as judgment on very corrupt peoples. Hanging the bodies was a public sign of total defeat. Afterward, according to the law, they were taken down at sunset (Deuteronomy 21:22-23). This passage is harsh, and Christians interpret it with care.

Today we do not imitate this violence. We can remember that God is just and that Christ calls us to love our enemies. Let us trust God to face our fears with courage, without hatred.
exp.14:21:
This verse continues a list of cities in the south of Judah. It names three: Kinah, Dimonah, and Adadah. Here "border" means the boundary or territory, and the phrase about the south refers to the southern side. Today it is not known with certainty where these places were exactly.

The text comes from the book of Joshua, which records how the promised land was divided among the tribes of Israel. This list served as a clear record of what fell to Judah, near the border with Edom. It showed that God was keeping what He had promised to His people.

For today: God does not overlook the details. Even small and little-known places were noted in His Word. This reminds us that He also knows your daily life, your simple steps, and your hidden places. Trust that nothing you go through is indifferent to Him.
exp.9:12:
It says that the sun and the moon stood still until Israel defeated its enemies. The phrase "hasted not to go down" refers to the sun delaying its setting, by nearly a whole day.

This is part of the account of the battle of Gibeon. Joshua had asked God for more time to defeat the Amorites, and the narrator comments on what happened. Scholars disagree about how it happened: a literal miracle involving the sun, an effect of light, or poetic language. The text emphasizes that "the LORD fought for Israel."

When you face something bigger than yourself, ask God with confidence, as Joshua did. He hears his children and can act in ways you do not expect. Do your part and leave the outcome in his hands.
exp.7:25:
The verse says that Joshua kept his arm stretched out, with the spear pointing toward Ai, and did not lower it until the destruction of the city was complete. The word "drew back" in the verse is the one to note here: it means he did not pull his hand back. The spear was a signal for the ambush that Israel had prepared.

It is an account of conquest. Joshua leads Israel against Ai after the earlier defeat caused by Achan's sin. Now they obey God with a strategy that He Himself had given them. The text tells, as ancient history often did, of judgment falling on a Canaanite city. This passage is difficult, and Christians read it in different ways without hiding its harshness.

For today: Joshua did not lower the spear until he had finished what he was given to do. Let us learn from his perseverance: we should not abandon halfway the task that God places before us.
exp.9:30:
Joshua and all Israel with him went from Libnah to Lachish. "Encamped against it" means that he set up camp in front of the city in order to lay siege to it, and "fought against it" means that he attacked it.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, recounting the campaign in the south of Canaan. Shortly before, five Amorite kings had joined together against Gibeon, an ally of Israel, and God gave victory to his people. The texts say that the LORD delivered the cities into the hand of Israel. These accounts of war are difficult, and Christians understand them in different ways.

For today: Joshua advanced step by step, city by city, without stopping halfway. When God gives us a task, we can continue with perseverance, one step at a time, trusting that he sustains our path.
exp.9:17:
Joshua gives a simple order: block the mouth of the cave with large stones and post guards at it. "Roll" means "to roll" as in the words "roll great stones," and the old form "á" is an older spelling of "to," which the verse above does not use. The five enemy kings had hidden there, and Joshua leaves them shut in for a time.

Joshua, the leader of Israel, speaks in the middle of a battle against the kings who had joined together against Gibeon. When he is told that the kings have been found, he does not stop to deal with them at that moment. He secures them and keeps pursuing the enemy army, trusting that God gives them the victory, as the following verses say.

For today: sometimes you must secure something and not get distracted, so that you can finish well what God has given you to do. Set wise limits on what hinders you, and keep moving forward with steadiness and trust in God.
exp.9:41:
This verse sums up the campaign in the south of Canaan. The phrase "took" means that Joshua conquered those kings and their territories, and "at one time" means in a single campaign, done quickly. The reason the text gives is that the Lord God of Israel fought for Israel.

The narrator of the book presents this as a summary of Joshua's victories. Israel was entering the promised land, and the account insists that the triumph came from God, not only from military strength. These war texts are difficult, and they are interpreted in several ways. Even so, the emphasis here is that God was keeping what he had promised to his people.

Today we can remember that we do not face our struggles alone. Doing what is ours to do with diligence is important, but we can rest in the fact that God works on our behalf, and give him the glory for what we accomplish.
exp.5:24:
This verse tells how Joshua spared Rahab the prostitute, her father's family, and everything she had. She remained living among the Israelites "even unto this day," meaning up to the time the account was written. The reason was that she hid the messengers whom Joshua sent to spy out Jericho. "Saved her life" means that he protected her, and "spy out" means to explore secretly.

This is the voice of the narrator, summarizing what happened after the fall of Jericho. Joshua kept the promise that the two spies had made to Rahab (Joshua 2). She had trusted in the God of Israel and risked her life for them. The New Testament remembers her for her faith (Hebrews 11:31).

Today, God looks at a person's faith and not at their past. If we trust in Him, He offers us a new beginning. We can also be faithful to our promises and welcome those who want to start over.
exp.12:6:
God tells Joshua to divide the land that still remained as an inheritance among the nine tribes and the half tribe of Manasseh. An inheritance is property that is received and then passed down to one's children. To divide the land means to share it out and distribute it.

The one speaking is the LORD. Joshua was already old, and much of the land still had to be conquered. Even so, God asks him to organize the distribution, because he promises that he himself will drive out the peoples who were still left. The other half of Manasseh, together with Reuben and Gad, had already received its portion east of the Jordan, according to what Moses had given them.

For today: God keeps his promises even when it seems that much of the road is still ahead. We can obey step by step what is in our hands and trust that he will do what we cannot.
exp.3:12:
This verse says that about forty thousand men ready for war crossed the Jordan and advanced toward the plains of Jericho, in the presence of God. "Prepared for war" means well equipped and ready to fight. "Plains" refers to an open area of flat land.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua speaks. He tells how the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh kept what they had promised Moses: to help their brothers conquer the land, even though they already had their inheritance on the other side of the Jordan. Some scholars think this number is literal; others think it is an approximate amount.

Today we can learn from their faithfulness. They kept their word and served others, even though they were not obligated to fight for their own sake. Ask yourself: is there a promise you made that you need to keep, or someone you can help without expecting anything in return?
exp.20:30:
This verse names two more towns of the tribe of Asher: Helkath and Rehob. Each is given along with its surrounding land, that is, the open fields around the town where the livestock grazed. Together with these two, Asher gives four towns.

The account is told by the narrator of the book of Joshua. Israel was already dividing the land, and the Levites did not receive a territory of their own, because their task was to serve God and teach his law. So the other tribes gave them towns to live in and pasture for their animals. These towns belonged to the families of the Gershonites.

For today: God cares for those who serve his people, and he often does so through us. We can support with generosity and gratitude those who teach and help in our church, so that they lack nothing they need.
exp.1:1:
Someone told the king of Jericho that some Israelites had come into the city during the night to spy out the land.

Here the text is not about a particular character. Rather, the account tells us what happened. Joshua had sent two men in secret, but they were noticed. The king grew alarmed because Israel was drawing near to the promised land. The text does not say who gave the warning, so it is better not to assume. What follows shows that Rahab hid them.

For today: even when plans seem to be in danger or discovered, God continues to work. We can do what is in front of us with courage and trust that He cares for His purpose, even when things turn out differently than we expected.
exp.2:1:
This verse says that, after three days of camping beside the Jordan, the officers of Israel went through the camp. The "officers" were leaders in charge of passing orders on to the people. The phrase "went through the camp" means they passed among all the tribes to let them know what was coming.

The narrator describes how Israel prepares to enter the promised land. Joshua had moved the people from Shittim to the banks of the Jordan. Now the officers carry the instructions: follow the ark of the covenant, which represented God's presence, and keep a distance so they could see the way clearly. It was a new road for them.

For today: when God leads us into something new, there is sometimes a time of waiting and preparation. Use that time to listen, to put your heart in order, and to look to God before taking the step. He guides better than we can see.
exp.3:20:
Joshua tells the Israelites that, in time to come, their children will ask them what those twelve stones mean. The old wording is easy to clear up: "in time to come" means "in the future," "ask" is "ask," and "mean" is "mean."

Joshua is the one speaking. The people had just crossed the Jordan River on dry ground and camped at Gilgal. There he set up the twelve stones taken from the river. He knew that, over time, people would forget what had happened, so the stones would serve as a visible reminder that would prompt questions and open the way to telling what God had done.

For today: think about which things in your home or your life can remind you of God's faithfulness, such as a journal, a photo, or a special date. And when children ask, tell them simply how God helped you.
exp.5:0:
The verse says that the city of Jericho was completely shut up. The word "but" is the usual meaning of that opening word, and the phrase "because of" can be read as "on account of" or "out of fear of." Nobody could go in or come out: the gates were firmly secured because the Israelites were nearby.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua is speaking. Israel had crossed the Jordan and stood before the first fortified city of Canaan. The text shows that Jericho was getting ready to defend itself. Right after this, God speaks to Joshua and promises him victory, although the plan God gives him is very different from a normal military strategy.

For today: we sometimes face walls that seem impassable, situations that look impossible. This passage invites us to trust that God can act where we see no way out, and to obey his instructions step by step, even when we do not fully understand them.
exp.12:29:
This verse says how far the territory went that Moses gave to the half tribe of Manasseh. It began at Mahanaim and covered all the region of Bashan, which had once been the kingdom of King Og. It also included the villages of Jair, which were sixty towns.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua is describing how the land east of the Jordan River was divided, a division Moses had already assigned before he died. Israel had defeated Og, and now the record is kept of which portion fell to each tribe. These details helped the people remember that the land was a gift from God, faithfully carried out.

For today: God keeps his promises with detail, even in what may seem small. We can trust that he cares for us, and remember with gratitude what he has already given us.
exp.14:37:
This verse is part of a list of towns. It names three places: Dilean, Mizpeh, and Joktheel. They are part of a group of cities named one after another, together with the ones that come before and after them. Today it is not known with certainty exactly where some of them were.

This is not a character speaking in a scene; it is the account in the book of Joshua, which describes how the promised land was divided among the tribes of Israel. This passage concerns the tribe of Judah, and these towns were in the low plain called the Shephelah. The list shows that God kept his promise to give a land to his people, and each place was given with care.

For today: God knows the small places and the names that almost no one remembers. If you feel overlooked, remember that He sees you and cares for you. Serve him faithfully wherever you are.
exp.12:26:
This verse closes the list of cities that the tribe of Gad received east of the Jordan. It names places in the valley (Beth-aram, Beth-nimrah, Succoth and Zaphon), which had previously been part of the kingdom of Sihon, the Amorite king in Heshbon. The land described here is flat, open ground, and the verse also points to the edge of the Sea of Chinnereth, which is the Sea of Galilee, as the farthest boundary, while the word "border" refers to the limit of the territory.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel divided the promised land. The narrator, whom tradition often associates with Joshua though this is not certain, recalls that Moses had already given these lands to Gad, Reuben and half the tribe of Manasseh. This detailed list shows that God kept His promise, with specific places and clear boundaries.

For today: God pays attention to details and fulfills what He promises. Although we sometimes take a long time to see results, we can trust His faithfulness and thank Him for the concrete blessings He has already given us.
exp.9:23:
What it says: Joshua brought out the five enemy kings from the cave and called all of Israel together. He told the commanders of the army to come near and put their feet on the necks of these kings, and they obeyed.

Context: Joshua, the leader of Israel, is speaking after a great victory at Gibeon. The kings had hidden in a cave. Putting a foot on the neck was an ancient gesture of complete victory and subjection. As the next verse shows, the purpose was to encourage the people: God would give them victory in the battles still to come.

For today: Remembering how God has helped us in the past strengthens our faith for the challenges ahead. When you face something difficult, think back to the times God sustained you, and move forward with courage and confidence in Him.
exp.14:61:
This verse closes the list of Judah's cities in the desert region. It names Nibshan, the city of Salt, and En-gedi, and says there were six cities with their villages, that is, the small towns that depended on them. These six include the ones named in the previous verse: Beth-arabah, Middin, and Secacah.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua speaks, dividing the promised land by tribes. This list shows that God kept his promise to give an inheritance to each family. The city of Salt is believed to have been near the Dead Sea, though its exact location is not certain. En-gedi was a well-known oasis. Right after this, the text admits a failure: Judah did not drive out the Jebusites from Jerusalem.

For today: God cares about small details and forgotten places. Be thankful for what he has given you, and do not leave unfinished what God has asked you to complete.
exp.18:36:
This verse is part of a list of towns. It names three more places that the tribe of Naphtali received: Kedesh, Edrei and En-hazor. They were towns within the territory assigned to that tribe, in the north of Canaan. Some ancient names are spelled differently today, such as Naphtali instead of Nephtalí.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel divided the promised land among the tribes. Here the narrator, whom tradition associates with Joshua though no one knows for certain who wrote the text, lists the towns of Naphtali in detail. This showed that God was keeping what he had promised to Abraham and his descendants. About the exact location of some of these places, scholars do not always agree.

For today: God pays attention to specifics, even to the names of small towns. If he keeps his promises with such detail, he also cares for your daily life. Trust that he does not forget you, and thank him for the specific blessings he has already given you.
exp.12:12:
This verse says that the Israelites did not drive out the people of Geshur and Maacah. These peoples continued living among Israel "until this day," that is, until the time when this account was written. The phrase "expelled" means to drive out, and "dwell" means to live.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua is describing the lands east of the Jordan, which Moses had already distributed. Although great territories had been conquered, the text acknowledges that one task was left unfinished. It does not explain why they were not driven out, so it is best not to invent reasons. Later in the Bible, this coexistence is shown to have had consequences.

For today: God calls us to obey him completely, not only in part. Think of something you have left half-done, perhaps a habit or a decision, and ask God for strength to finish it faithfully.
exp.5:23:
It says the Israelites burned Jericho and everything inside it. The only things they did not burn were the silver, the gold, and the objects of bronze and iron, which they put into the treasury of the house of the Lord.

This is the account of the narrator of the book of Joshua. God had commanded that Jericho be set apart for Him, that is, devoted and not taken as plunder (Joshua 6:17-19). That is why they burned the city, and the metals were dedicated to the treasury of the sanctuary. Rahab and her family were rescued, as had been promised to them, because she had protected the spies.

For today: God deserves the first and the best. We can ask ourselves what we should give to Him honestly and gratefully, without keeping what does not belong to us.
exp.20:31:
This verse says that the tribe of Naphtali gave three cities to the Levites: Kedesh in Galilee, Hammoth-dor, and Kartan. Kedesh was also a city of refuge for those who had killed someone, that is, a place where a person who had killed by accident could flee and be safe. The word "suburbs" in the verse refers to the pasture lands that surrounded each city.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel divided the promised land. The Levites did not receive a territory of their own, but cities within each tribe, so that they could live among the people and teach them God's law. This passage speaks of the cities given to the Gershonites, a Levite family. The cities of refuge, according to the law of Moses, protected the one who had killed without intent until justice could be done.

For today: God made sure there were places of mercy and teaching within reach of everyone. We can ask ourselves how we might be a safe refuge for others in our own surroundings, with patience, justice, and compassion.
exp.16:12:
It says that when the Israelites grew stronger, they forced the Canaanites to work for them and pay them tribute, that is, to give them service or payments. But they did not drive them out of the land, as God had commanded.

The narrator of the book of Joshua explains what happened with the tribe of Manasseh. They could not drive the Canaanites out of several cities. Here it is noticed that, now with more strength, they preferred to profit from them instead of obeying completely. Later the sons of Joseph complain that their territory is small, although they had not finished taking what they already had.

For today: sometimes we tolerate a sin or bad habit because it is useful or comfortable to us. God invites us not to make a deal with that, but to leave it behind entirely, trusting in his strength and not only in our own.
exp.11:16:
It says that among the kings Israel defeated in Canaan were the king of Tappuah and the king of Hepher. It is part of a short list: each "one more" means one more king defeated. The ancient names are written in the old-style spelling (Tappua, Hepher).

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua speaks. After recounting the conquests, he summarizes in a list the 31 kings defeated west of the Jordan. His purpose is to record that God kept his promise to give the land to Israel. About the exact location of some cities, scholars do not always agree.

For today: God pays attention to the specific and remembers every step of his work. We can note the times he helped us, even when they seem small, like a list of gratitude. That strengthens faith when new battles come.
exp.0:2:
God tells Joshua that he has already given him every place where the sole of his foot treads. The phrase "the sole of your foot shall tread upon" is an older way of saying "every place that you set foot on." The phrase "as I said unto Moses" shows that God is repeating a promise he had already made before.

The speaker is God, just after the death of Moses. Joshua is the new leader and is getting ready to cross the Jordan into the promised land. God encourages him by reminding him that his word still stands, even though the previous leader is no longer there. In the text, the giving depends on the people moving forward and taking possession, since the promise is received by walking.

For today: God keeps what he promises, but he often asks us to take steps of faith. Think of something God has shown you in his Word and take one concrete step of obedience today, trusting that he goes with you.
exp.7:26:
After defeating the city of Ai, the Israelites kept the livestock and the goods that were in it. The spoils are the valuable things taken from those who have been defeated. "But" is the word used here in place of "however," and "according to" means "in agreement with."

The narrator of the book of Joshua is speaking here. Earlier, at Jericho, God had forbidden taking plunder, and Achan disobeyed and brought defeat (chapter 7). Now, after that sin was dealt with, God himself allows them to take the plunder of Ai. This war is a difficult episode; the text presents it as obedience to a divine command in a very particular time and context.

For today: God knows what is good in every moment, and obeying him well means listening to his instructions, not using what someone else received as an excuse. Ask him for wisdom to do what is right with what you have.
exp.16:5:
This verse says that the five daughters of Manasseh received an inheritance of land along with the sons of their tribe. Also, the region of Gilead was left to the rest of Manasseh's descendants.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua speaks, summarizing how the land was divided. The daughters of Zelophehad had asked Eleazar and Joshua to carry out what the LORD had commanded Moses. Their father had no sons, and they claimed their right. This verse shows that the promise was fulfilled.

God sees and honors those who respectfully ask for what he has already promised. We can approach him with confidence, and we should also take care that no one among us is left without space or justice, especially those who might easily go unnoticed.
exp.20:7:
It says that the children of Israel gave to the Levites these cities, together with their pasture lands around them (this is what "suburbs" means), by casting lots. They did so just as the Lord had commanded through Moses.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel settled in the promised land. The Levites, who served God, did not receive a territory of their own like the other tribes. For that reason they were given cities within the lands of the other tribes. The narrator, whose identity is not known for certain, emphasizes that the division was made in obedience to what was commanded in Numbers 35.

Today we can learn to care for those who devote themselves to serving God and others. One practical way is to support your pastor or your church with generosity, prayer, and concrete help, thus fulfilling with gratitude what God asks.
exp.14:62:
This verse says that the descendants of Judah were not able to drive the Jebusites out of Jerusalem. "Drive out" here means to remove completely, to clear them away entirely. That is why the Jebusites kept living in the city alongside the people of Judah, down to this very day, meaning down to the time when the book was written.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel received the promised land. Here the narrator closes the list of Judah's cities with a note of failure. He does not fully explain the reason. Later, in the time of King David, Jerusalem was taken (2 Samuel 5). Who wrote this note and exactly when is not known for certain.

For today: even after great victories, some area may remain unconquered in our lives, such as a habit or a fear. Let us be honest about that, ask God for help, and not let what is unfinished become a settled custom.
exp.22:12:
It says that if the people mix with the nations that remained in the land, God will no longer drive those nations out from before them. Those nations would become a trap, a stumbling block, a whip at their sides and thorns in their eyes. In the end, the people themselves would lose the good land.

Joshua, now old, speaks in his farewell to Israel. He reminds them that God has kept all his promises. For that reason he warns them with seriousness: if they turn away from God and join with the peoples who worshiped other gods, they will suffer the consequences.

For today: the friendships and alliances we accept can draw us closer to God or pull us away from Him. Let us ask Him for wisdom to love everyone without letting anything separate us from Him.
exp.14:29:
This verse is part of a list of towns. It names three places: Eltolad, Chesil, and Hormah. They belong to the towns in the far south of Judah, near the Negev. Today it is not known with certainty where each one was. Hormah appears in other passages, and its name is connected with something devoted to destruction.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Joshua, who describes how the promised land was divided among the tribes. Here the inheritance of Judah is laid out in detail. These lists served to show that God kept his promise to Abraham and to his descendants, giving them specific places to live.

For today: God pays attention to the small and the concrete. No place or person escapes his notice. Trust that he cares for the details of your life too, even when they seem unimportant.
exp.0:15:
The men of the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh answer Joshua that they will do all he commands them and will go wherever he sends them. The explanation's note about the old spellings of certain words is omitted, since those spellings do not appear in the verse your reader sees.

Moses had given them land east of the Jordan. Joshua, Israel's new leader, reminds them that their families and livestock could remain there, but that the strong men had to cross over armed to help their brothers conquer their land. They agree, and they ask that God be with Joshua as He was with Moses.

Today, this answer invites us to cooperate with others without thinking only of our own rest. If we have already received a blessing, we can help others who are still waiting for theirs, in the family, the church, or the workplace, with willingness and good spirit.
exp.6:25:
It says that Israel raised a great heap of stones over Achan, and that the heap was still there when the book was written, "unto this day." Then the Lord's anger turned away. That is why the place was called the Valley of Achor, a name that sounds like the Hebrew word for "trouble" or "bring disaster."

The narrator tells the end of Achan's story. At Jericho he took things that God had set apart for Himself, and Israel lost at Ai. After this hidden sin was removed, the relationship with God was restored. This punishment was severe, and it is understood within Israel's covenant at that time.

For today: hidden sin harms us and others. If there is something you are hiding, confess it to God today with sincerity. He forgives and restores those who come to Him with humility (1 John 1:9).
exp.23:0:
Joshua gathers all the tribes of Israel at Shechem. He calls for the elders, the heads or leaders, the judges, and the officers, that is, the leaders of the people. Everyone presents themselves before God, which shows that the gathering was a solemn and serious act, done in the presence of the Lord.

Joshua is now an old man, and the promised land had already been divided among the tribes. Before he dies, he gathers the people to remind them of what God has done and to ask them for a decision of faithfulness. Shechem was a place with much history for Israel, tied to Abraham and to earlier promises. Soon Joshua will speak in God's name.

For today: before making important decisions, pause to present yourself before God. Remembering what He has done for you helps you answer Him with honesty and firmness.
exp.13:1:
This verse says that the land was divided among nine and a half tribes by lot, just as God had commanded through Moses. "By lot" means that lots were cast, a way of deciding without human favoritism.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel settled in Canaan. Here the narrator explains that Eleazar, Joshua, and the heads of the tribes made the division following what Moses had commanded earlier. The other two and a half tribes had already received their land east of the Jordan. The Levites received no territory, but cities in which to live.

For today: God cares that each person receives their place and their portion. We can trust what He gives us, without envying what belongs to others, and serve with gratitude where He has placed us.
exp.23:22:
The explanation says the people must put away from their lives the "foreign gods," that is, the idols or strange gods, and give their heart fully to the LORD, the God of Israel. The word "incline" that appears in the verse means to direct or bend the heart toward Him. It is not enough to say that one serves Him; one must act.
