Joshua, now an old man, speaks at the assembly in Shechem. The people had just promised to serve the LORD, but Joshua knew that some still kept idols. So he asks them for a concrete change, not only words. Afterward they renew the covenant.

Today we can ask ourselves what things in our hearts occupy the place that belongs to God: money, success, a relationship, or a habit. Choose one and, with God's help, remove it or set limits on it this week, and set aside time to pray.
exp.17:5:
Joshua asks the tribes to take the land that had not yet been divided, to map it, and to describe it in seven parts. Afterward they are to bring that description to Joshua.

Joshua, the leader of Israel, speaks at Shiloh, where the tabernacle stood. Seven tribes had not yet received their inheritance, and it seems they had delayed in taking it. Joshua organizes the work in order: first to explore and describe, then to divide before the Lord.

For today: before deciding something important, do your part with effort and order, and then place it in God's hands through prayer. Planning well and trusting Him are not opposites; they walk together.
exp.6:0:
This verse says that the people of Israel were unfaithful to God regarding the "devoted thing," that is, what God had set apart for destruction and that could not be taken. "Transgression" means betraying or breaking a command. A man named Achan, of the tribe of Judah, took something from that forbidden spoil. That is why the anger of the Lord burned against Israel.

The narrator tells this after the fall of Jericho. God had commanded that everything in Jericho be devoted to him. Although only one man disobeyed, the text says that "the children of Israel" committed the wrong, since the people acted as one united community before God. What follows shows that Israel did not yet know of this hidden sin.

For today: hidden disobedience is never only private; it can affect others. Examine your life honestly, confess to God what you have kept silent, and obey him in the small things.
exp.23:11:
God says that he sent "hornets" ahead of Israel. With that, God drove out the two kings of the Amorites. He makes clear that it was not by Israel's sword or bow.

God himself speaks, through Joshua, at the assembly in Shechem. Joshua reviews everything God did for his people, from Abraham through the conquest. He wants Israel to remember that the victory was a gift, so that they would decide to serve the LORD with their whole heart.

For today: think of an achievement or blessing you have received and acknowledge how much of it was God's work and not only yours. Thank him and respond with a faithful and grateful life.
exp.8:8:
The Gibeonites tell Joshua that they have come from a very distant country. They say they have done so because of the name of the Lord, the God of Israel, because they have heard of his deeds in Egypt. The name of God is given in the verse as "the Lord thy God," and the word "name" here refers to his reputation or renown.

The people of Gibeon, who knew that Israel was coming to take the land of Canaan, wanted to save their lives. So they made up the story that they had come from far away, in order to secure an alliance. Part of what they say is true: they had indeed heard of the works of God. But they lie about their origin, since they lived nearby. Joshua and the leaders did not seek the counsel of God before deciding (v. 14).

Today, it is not enough for something to sound pious or convincing. Before making important decisions, it is wise to pray, to seek God's guidance, and to examine calmly what we are told, even when it seems reasonable.
exp.3:2:
God tells Joshua that the twelve chosen men should take twelve stones from the middle of the Jordan River, right where the priests carrying the ark had stood. They are to carry the stones with them and set them down in the place where they will spend the night.

The LORD speaks to Joshua when the whole people had already crossed the Jordan on dry ground. God wants a memorial of that miracle to be set up. Each tribe contributes one stone, so everyone takes part. Later in the text, it explains that the stones would serve as a sign so that the children would ask what they meant.

For today: do not let the works of God in your life be forgotten. Write down or count regularly what He has done, and share it with your family, so that His faithfulness may inspire trust in the generations to come.
exp.5:12:
This verse describes the order of the march around Jericho. Seven priests went ahead carrying trumpets made from rams' horns, and they kept blowing them without stopping. In front were the armed men, and behind the ark of the Lord came the rest of the people. Everyone walked in order, and the sound never stopped.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua speaks. He tells what Israel did in following God's instructions to take Jericho. It was the second day of the march: one circuit each day, with the people silent while the trumpets sounded. The ark represented God's presence, which is why it was placed at the center of everything.

For today: sometimes God asks us to obey day after day, even when we do not yet see results. Walk with steadiness and trust, putting God at the center of what you do, even when the plan seems strange to you.
exp.11:12:
This verse is part of a list of defeated Canaanite kings. It says that the king of Debir was defeated, and also the king of Geder.

Joshua 12 summarizes Israel's victories under the leadership of Moses and Joshua. The narrator goes over the cities conquered when they entered the promised land. It is an account that reminds us that God kept his promise to his people. About Geder, it is not known with certainty where it was located, and scholars do not agree.

For today: God pays attention to every detail and every victory, even to names that seem small. It is worth remembering and giving thanks for what He has done in your life, even the simple things, because in this way your trust in his faithfulness grows.
exp.5:20:
This verse tells how, after the walls of Jericho fell, the Israelites killed all the inhabitants and the animals of the city. The words "young" and "old" are the terms used for each group, and "donkey" is the animal the verse lists alongside the ox and the sheep. The phrase "with the edge of the sword" means with the sword, leaving no survivors.

It is part of the account of the conquest of Canaan. The narrator presents this as the fulfillment of a command from God, in which the city is set apart for complete destruction. God said he was doing this because of the wickedness of those peoples (Deuteronomy 9:4-5). It is a difficult text, and scholars debate whether the language is literal or exaggerated. Even so, Rahab and her family were saved because they trusted in the God of Israel.

Today it reminds us that God is just and also merciful. We can draw near to him with humility, as Rahab did, trusting in his grace, and never use this passage to justify present-day violence.
exp.8:21:
Joshua calls in the Gibeonites and confronts them with a question: why did they deceive them? They had said they lived very far away, but in reality they lived very close, right in the middle of Israel.

Joshua speaks as the leader of Israel. The Gibeonites, fearing they would be destroyed, pretended to come from a distant country in order to make a covenant. Israel made an oath without seeking God's counsel (v. 14). By the time they discovered the lie, they were already bound by their word. For that reason Joshua keeps his promise and spares their lives, but he assigns them to serve in the worship of the sanctuary.

For today: before making important decisions, it is wise to pray and ask God for direction, without being guided only by appearances. And when we make mistakes, it is good to accept the consequences honestly and keep what we have promised.
exp.9:18:
Joshua orders the Israelites not to stop, but to keep pursuing their enemies and strike them from behind, at the rear, the ones who are at the end of the flight. This way they will not let them take refuge in their cities. The reason is that God has already handed them over into Israel's hands.

Joshua, the leader of Israel, is speaking to his soldiers. The five enemy kings were already shut up in a cave, but the battle was not yet over. Joshua wants them to finish the task and trust God's promise. This passage describes an ancient war at a particular moment in history, and it should be read within that context.

Today, we are not talking about war, but about perseverance. When God has given us a victory or an opportunity, it is not wise to ease off halfway. If you are overcoming a bad habit or finishing an important task, move forward with confidence and do not stop before the time is right.
exp.1:16:
The Israelite spies tell Rahab that they will be free from the oath she made them swear. The freedom they describe, however, depends on certain conditions, which they lay out in the verses that follow.

The two spies sent by Joshua to Jericho are the ones speaking. Rahab hid them and risked her life, and they promised to protect her and her family. Now they make clear that their promise has conditions: the red cord in the window and the whole family staying inside the house.

For today: keeping what we have promised is important, but so is making the conditions of a commitment clear. Be honest and clear when you promise, and faithful when you keep your word. Rahab also trusted and obeyed, which reminds us that faith is shown through actions.
exp.14:53:
This verse closes a list of towns in the hill country of Judah. It names Humtah, Kirjath-arba (which is Hebron), and Zior, and says there are nine cities with their villages, that is, with the small settlements that surrounded them. The phrase "Kirjath-arba" means "the city of Arba," and it was the older name of Hebron.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua speaks. He describes how the promised land was divided among the tribes of Israel, and this passage lists the territories of Judah. These lists show that God kept his promise to give an inheritance to his people. Hebron also recalls Caleb, to whom that area was given (Joshua 14:13-14).

For today: God pays attention to the details and does not forget anyone. Even if your life seems small or unnoticed, he faithfully keeps his promises. Trust that he cares for you, and thank him for what he has already given you.
exp.14:6:
This verse describes a stretch of the northern border of the tribe of Judah. The line goes up toward Debir from the valley of Achor, looks northward toward Gilgal (opposite the ascent of Adummim, on the south side of the river), passes by the waters of En-shemesh, and ends at the spring of Rogel.

The word "border" means the boundary or limit, and "south" is what is meant by the direction described as the south side.

It is part of Joshua's account of dividing the promised land among the tribes. The narrator lists the landmarks in detail so that each family could know clearly what its inheritance was. Some of these places are hard to locate today with certainty.

For today: God is concerned with the concrete details of our lives. He fulfilled his promise with real boundaries and real names. You can trust that he also cares for what he has given you, and live thankful within what he has entrusted to you.
exp.21:12:
This verse says that the people of Israel sent a group of representatives to the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half tribe of Manasseh, who lived in the land of Gilead, on the other side of the Jordan. The leader of the commission was Phinehas, son of the priest Eleazar. The name appears in the King James Version as Phinehas.

The account is told by the author of Joshua. The tribes of the east had built an altar beside the Jordan, and the rest of Israel thought it was an act of rebellion against God. They gathered at Shiloh, ready to fight, but first they decided to send a delegation to ask questions. Afterward it is made clear that the altar was a witness, not a place for sacrifices.

Before judging or attacking someone for what we have heard, it is wise to speak with that person face to face and with respect. Often rumors show us only part of the story, and dialogue can prevent great harm.
exp.14:59:
This verse names two more cities of the tribe of Judah: Kirjath-baal, which is also called Kirjath-jearim, and Rabbah. Each had its villages, that is, the small towns that depended on it. About the exact location of Rabbah there is no certainty.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel received the promised land. Here the narrator lists, district by district, what fell to Judah. These lists made clear who lived where and confirmed that God was keeping his promise. Kirjath-jearim appears later in the Bible as the place where the ark of the covenant stayed (1 Samuel 7:1-2).

For today: God pays attention to details and to places that seem small. Your daily life, your neighborhood, and your work do not go unnoticed by him. Today, faithfully do one simple task, trusting that God sees it.
exp.20:42:
This verse says that God kept his promise. He had sworn to Israel's ancestors (Abraham, Isaac and Jacob) that he would give them a land, and now the people received it, took possession of it, and lived in it. The word "gave" is spelled one way in the older text, and "possessed it" means they took it as their own.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel entered Canaan after leaving Egypt and wandering in the wilderness. Here the narrator, who is not named in the text, summarizes the division of the land, just after listing the cities of the Levites. He emphasizes that God was faithful. Some scholars note that other passages mention territories not yet fully conquered, and they explain this in different ways; this verse stresses above all the faithfulness of God.

For today: when waiting drags on, remember that God keeps what he promises, even if in his own time. Write down his promises and the times he has answered you, and trust him again.
exp.15:0:
The territory assigned by lot to the descendants of Joseph (the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh) began at the Jordan River, near Jericho. It continued eastward to the waters of Jericho, and then climbed through the wilderness toward the mountain of Bethel. The word "lot" here refers to the portion of land that fell to them when the lots were cast. "Went out" means that this was the starting point of their border.

This passage is not about a single character; the book of Joshua tells how Israel divided the promised land. After the conquest, each tribe received its inheritance, and its boundaries were described in detail. Scholars believe these lists helped each family know clearly what belonged to them. Some place names are hard to locate today.

God keeps his promises with detail, even in the practical things. You can trust that he also cares for your daily life. Just as each tribe received its place, be thankful for what God has given you and look after it faithfully, without envying what belongs to others.
exp.8:0:
This verse tells us that the kings of the peoples who lived west of the Jordan River heard about what had happened. They were kings of the hill country, of the lowlands, and of the whole coast of the Great Sea (the Mediterranean), all the way to Lebanon. Six peoples are named: the Hittites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Israel had already entered the promised land, and the news of the fall of Jericho and Ai had spread through the region. The verses that follow show the reaction: these kings joined together to fight against Joshua and Israel.

For today: when God acts, not everyone responds the same way. Some join together to resist, and others look for another way. Ask yourself how you respond to what God is doing: with fear, with stubbornness, or with humble trust.
exp.9:10:
This verse tells how the enemy armies were fleeing from Israel down the descent of Beth-horon, and how God hurled huge stones from heaven, which seem to be hailstones, all the way to Azekah. More people died from the hailstones than were killed by Israel's swords. The phrase "with the sword" means by the blade of a weapon, and "the LORD" is the name of God.

The book of Joshua recounts the battle of Gibeon. Israel had promised to protect the Gibeonites, and five Amorite kings attacked them. Joshua marched up all night from Gilgal and caught them by surprise. The narrator is the author of the book, and presents the victory as the work of God more than of the soldiers.

For today: do your part with effort, like Joshua who marched all night, but trust that the outcome is in God's hands. He can help you in ways you do not expect.
exp.12:21:
This verse tells us that the Israelites killed Balaam, the son of Beor, a soothsayer, along with other enemies, with the sword. Balaam was a man who claimed to know the future through forbidden spiritual means.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua is reviewing the lands that Moses divided east of the Jordan, in the territory of Reuben. Balaam is mentioned because he was connected with Midian. According to Numbers 31:8, he died there, and Numbers 31:16 says that his counsel led Israel into sin at Peor. The Bible does not give more detail about how he was connected to those lands.

For today: God takes seriously any counsel that turns us away from Him, even when it sounds spiritual or convenient. Let us ask for wisdom to examine the voices we hear, and hold on to what agrees with the Word.
exp.3:5:
This verse says that the twelve stones would be a "sign," that is, a visible reminder. When the children of the Israelites asked in the future what those stones meant, the parents would have an opportunity to explain it to them.

Joshua speaks to the twelve men, one from each tribe. Israel had just crossed the Jordan River on dry ground, after God stopped the waters in front of the ark of the covenant. God wanted that miracle not to be forgotten, and for every generation to know what he had done for his people.

For today: God invites us to remember his faithfulness and to tell it. We can create simple signs at home, such as a journal of answered prayers or a family conversation, so that the younger ones hear how God has helped us.
exp.13:9:
He says that Caleb acknowledges that the Lord kept him alive for forty-five years, just as he had promised. Those years passed from the time the Lord spoke this word to Moses, when Israel was still wandering in the wilderness. Now Caleb is eighty-five years old.

The speaker is Caleb, addressing Joshua, at Gilgal. He had been one of the twelve spies sent into Canaan. While others discouraged the people, he kept trusting God. Moses had promised him an inheritance in the land he had walked through. Now, as the land is being divided, Caleb asks that this promise be fulfilled.

For today: God is faithful to his promises, even when they take years to be fulfilled. We can wait with patience, keep obeying, and remember how God has cared for us along the way, so that we can trust him with greater firmness.
exp.14:30:
This verse names three more towns in the list of Judah's territory in the south: Ziklag, Madmannah, and Sansannah. They are part of the twenty-nine towns of the far south, along with their villages. In this older version, the name "Madmannah" is spelled with a double n, but it is the same place that is written Madmannah today.

Here no one is speaking. The narrator of the book of Joshua describes how the promised land was divided among the tribes, as God had commanded. These lists served to record what each tribe received. Scholars do not always agree about the exact location of some of these towns. Later on, Ziklag appears in the story of David, who lived there.

For today: God keeps his promises with concrete details and remembers every place and every person. If he cared about the names of small towns, he also cares about your daily life. Trust that his promises still stand, even when you cannot see everything at once.
exp.17:22:
This verse continues a list of towns that fell to the tribe of Benjamin. It names three places: Avim, Parah, and Ophrah. The form "Ophra" is the old spelling of "Ofra," so the place is the same one this verse calls Ophrah. Its exact location is not completely certain; it is thought to have been in the hill country north of Jerusalem, but scholars do not fully agree.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel received the promised land. Here the narrator, who is not certainly identified, records the division by tribes and families. This list of names served as a kind of title deed: it made clear what belonged to each group, to prevent disputes and to remind them that the land was a gift from God, fulfilling his promise to their ancestors.

For today: God pays attention to places and people that seem small to us. If He remembers the names of little-known towns, He also knows you. Trust that your life and your place do not go unnoticed by Him.
exp.5:1:
This verse shows God speaking to Joshua. He says: "See, I have already given Jericho into your hand, along with its king and its mighty men." He speaks of it as something already done, even though it is not yet visible.

Here the Lord, the God of Israel, is speaking. Joshua is the new leader of the people after Moses. Jericho had its gates tightly shut out of fear of Israel, so it seemed impossible to conquer. God encourages him before giving him instructions, which are very different from a normal attack: march around the city.

For today: when you face something that seems closed off and impossible, remember that God can go ahead of you. Trust his promise and obey step by step, even when his instructions do not seem logical to you.
exp.9:32:
This verse tells how Horam, king of Gezer, came with his army to help the city of Lachish, which was under attack. Joshua defeated him and his people, and not one of them was left. The word "smote" means that he struck them down in battle.

It is part of the account of Israel's campaign in the south of Canaan, after several kings had joined together against them. The narrator presents these victories as the work of God, who had promised the land to Israel. These are texts about ancient warfare, and they are difficult to read. Christians understand them in different ways, and it is wise to read them with humility, without using them to justify violence today.

For today: the passage reminds us that God keeps his promises, even when the road is hard. We can trust that he sustains our lives, and we can seek peace with others, following Christ.
exp.7:20:
This verse tells that Joshua and the Israelites saw the smoke rising from the city of Ai. That smoke was the sign that the ambush had already taken the city. Then they turned around and attacked the men of Ai.

It is part of the account of the conquest. The narrator tells how Israel defeated Ai with an ambush strategy that God himself had indicated to Joshua (8:1-2). Earlier, Israel had failed there because of Achan's sin (ch. 7). Now, with the matter resolved, God gives them the victory. These accounts of war are difficult, and they are read within the ancient history of Israel.

For today: when God guides us, it is wise to obey his directions and wait for the right sign, without rushing ahead. It also reminds us that, after acknowledging a mistake, God can restore us and give us a fresh start.
exp.21:6:
This verse tells us that Moses had already given the half of the tribe of Manasseh its land in Bashan, east of the Jordan. To the other half, Joshua gave its inheritance to the west, among the rest of their Israelite brothers. When Joshua sent those from the east back to their dwellings (that is, to their homes), he first blessed them.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Joshua. The tribes of the east had helped conquer Canaan, just as they had promised. Now Joshua sends them off with his blessing and with a reminder to love God and obey him. The two groups of Manasseh were separated by the river, but they still remained one people.

For today: even though life may separate us by distance or by different paths, we can bless others and keep our unity. A word of encouragement when we part can strengthen bonds that last a long time.
exp.12:25:
This verse continues the list of the boundaries of the territory received by the tribe of Gad. It names places that marked its border: Heshbon, Ramath-mizpeh, Betonim, Mahanaim, and the border of Debir. The word "border" here means a boundary or limit. "Ramath-mizpeh" is an old place name, the same site called Ramath-mizpeh.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua reviews how the land east of the Jordan was divided. That region had already been given by Moses to Gad, Reuben, and the half tribe of Manasseh. Names and boundaries are recorded so that each family would know what its inheritance was. The exact location of some of these sites is uncertain today.

For today: God attends to the details of the life of his people. If he remembered every city and border, he also remembers you and what he has entrusted to you. Receive with gratitude what God gives you, and care for it faithfully.
exp.19:2:
This verse says that someone who kills a person by accident, without knowing it and without intending it, may flee to a city of refuge. The word "unawares" in the verse means without knowing or without warning, and "unwittingly" means without intending it. The one who must avenge the death, sometimes called the avenger of blood, is the close relative of the dead person.

God speaks to Joshua and asks that the people set apart those cities, just as he had commanded earlier through Moses. They were already in the promised land. God wanted to protect the innocent from unjust revenge, and at the same time to take seriously the value of human life. Afterward, the elders of the city would hear the case.

For today: before judging or punishing, let us seek the truth. God calls us to distinguish between a mistake and a deliberate wrong, and to deal with mercy and justice toward the one who has erred.
exp.9:4:
Five Amorite kings joined together, gathered their armies, and surrounded the city of Gibeon to attack it. The phrase "encamped before" means they set up their military camp against it. The Amorites were one of the peoples living in Canaan. The kings were from Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon.

The one who had called the kings together was Adoni-zedek, king of Jerusalem. He was alarmed because Gibeon had made peace with Joshua and Israel, and that weakened the whole region. That is why they wanted to punish the Gibeonites. Afterward, Gibeon asked Joshua for help, and he went up to defend them.

For today: sometimes making the right decision, such as seeking peace with God and with his people, brings opposition from those who feel threatened. When that happens, you are not alone. Ask God and your community for help, as Gibeon did, and act with confidence.
exp.20:8:
This verse says that the tribes of Judah and Simeon gave the Levites certain cities, and that these are named right after.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Joshua, who describes how Israel divided the land. The Levites did not receive a territory of their own, because their task was to serve God. So each tribe gave them cities from its inheritance, as the Lord had commanded through Moses. This verse opens the list of the cities given by Judah and Simeon, and the first lot fell to the sons of Aaron.

For today: what God gives us is not only for ourselves. We can share generously, with our time, money, or gifts, to support those who serve and teach in the church.
exp.23:12:
It says God gave the Israelites a land they did not work for, with cities they did not build, and that they now eat from vineyards and olive groves they did not plant. The word "dwell" in the verse is what the explanation calls "moráis," and it is used the same way as the word "dwell" in this verse, and the explanation's note about "eat" means that they enjoy the fruit of those vineyards and groves.

God speaks through Joshua, who is now old and gathers the people at Shechem. He reminds them how he helped them defeat their enemies, not by their own strength. He wants them to see that everything they have is a gift from him, so that they will answer him with sincere faithfulness.

For today: think about what you enjoy without having earned it alone, such as your family, your health, or your faith. Recognizing that it comes from God leads us to give thanks and to serve him with all our heart, not out of obligation.
exp.8:16:
This verse tells how the children of Israel set out from where they had been and, on the third day, came to the cities of the Gibeonites. There were four of them: Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth, and Kirjath-jearim. The phrase about setting out simply means they got moving on their journey.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. The Gibeonites had deceived Joshua, pretending to be travelers from a distant land in order to secure a treaty of peace. The Israelites had not consulted God before deciding. When they discovered that these were their neighbors, they had already sworn an oath in the name of the LORD and were bound to keep their word.

For today: before making important decisions, do not rely only on what you see or on what others tell you. Pray, ask God for direction, and seek wise counsel. A hasty decision can bring consequences that cannot easily be undone.
exp.18:24:
This verse names four places that were part of the territory of the tribe of Asher: Helkath, Hali, Beten, and Achshaph. The word "border" means the territory or area that fell to the tribe. The form "was" appears here in its older wording. Today it is not known with certainty where exactly these cities were.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua speaks. After Israel entered the promised land, the land was divided by lot among the tribes. This passage tells that the fifth lot fell to Asher. The list of names and boundaries shows that God fulfilled his promise to give his people an inheritance.

For today: God cares even for details that seem small to us. If he remembered each city of each tribe, he also knows your situation and your place. Trust that he has an inheritance and a purpose for you, and thank him for what he has given you.
exp.14:14:
This verse tells that Caleb, after driving out the three sons of Anak in Hebron, went up from there against the inhabitants of Debir. It is explained that this city was formerly called Kirjath-sepher. "Went up" means that he marched toward that area, which lay in higher ground. The name Kirjath-sepher is usually understood as "city of the book," although its exact meaning is not entirely certain.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel received the promised land. Here the narrator describes the inheritance of Caleb, a man who had trusted God since his youth. He was given Hebron according to what the LORD had commanded, and from there he continued the conquest with courage.

For today: God keeps his promises, but often he calls us to take the next step. Caleb did not settle for one victory; he kept moving forward. Ask yourself what step of faith you can take today, trusting that God goes with you.
exp.23:7:
He says that God brought Israel into the land of the Amorites, who lived on the other side of the Jordan River, that is, on the east side. They fought against Israel, but God handed them over into their hands. So the Israelites took that land, and God says that he destroyed them before them. The Amorites were a people who lived in Canaan and the neighboring regions.

Joshua speaks, passing on the words of God at the great assembly in Shechem, at the end of his life. He is reminding the people of everything God did for them, from Egypt to the promised land. He does this so that they will renew their commitment to serve the Lord alone.

For today: when you remember how God helped you in past struggles, your confidence grows. Write down today one help you received from God and give thanks for it, and let that memory encourage you to obey him faithfully.
exp.6:4:
This verse tells of Israel's defeat at Ai. The men of Ai killed about thirty-six Israelites, chased them from the city gate down to Shebarim, and beat them on the way down the slope. "Smote" means they struck them down and killed them, and "wherefore" introduces the result: the hearts of the people melted and became like water, which describes a fear that drained away all their strength.

This is the narrator's account. Israel had come from the victory at Jericho, and the spies, confident, advised sending only about three thousand men. But they had not consulted God. The chapter explains that Israel had sinned (Achan took what was forbidden), and that is why God was not with them in that battle. The exact location of Shebarim is not known with certainty.

For today: let us not trust in our own security. Before deciding, let us seek God in prayer and examine our hearts. And if we fail, let us turn to Him as Joshua did, with humility.
exp.1:6:
This verse tells how the men sent by the king of Jericho went out to chase the two Israelite spies. They followed the road that leads to the Jordan River, as far as the shallow crossing places where one could cross on foot. As soon as they had gone out, they shut the gate of the city.

Here the narrator is speaking. Earlier, Rahab had deceived the pursuers by telling them the spies had already left, when in fact she had hidden them on the roof, among stalks of flax. The pursuers believed her words and set out. Some scholars debate how to judge her lie; what the text emphasizes is her faith in the God of Israel.

For today: sometimes God works quietly and through unexpected people. If you feel that your faith is small, remember that God can use a simple act of courage to carry out his plans.
exp.10:3:
This verse tells how the northern kings of Canaan went out to war with all their armies. There were so many soldiers that they are compared to the sand on the seashore, that is, a multitude impossible to count. They also brought very many horses and chariots of war. The word "much people" in the verse simply means a great number.

The narrator of the book describes how Jabin, king of Hazor, gathered several cities together against Israel. The Israelites had already entered the promised land under the leadership of Joshua, and these kings wanted to stop them. Chariots and horses were the most feared military technology of that time. Even so, the following verse shows God telling Joshua not to be afraid.

For today: sometimes problems look enormous, like an endless army. God does not promise that there will be no difficulties, but He does invite us to trust Him and not to let fear dominate us. Before acting, we can pray and remember that He is greater.
exp.23:16:
The verse says that the people remember what God did for them. The Lord brought them out of Egypt, a place of slavery. God performed great signs before their eyes and cared for them throughout the entire journey, even among other peoples.

The people of Israel are speaking, answering Joshua. He had challenged them at Shechem to choose whom they would serve, and he declared that he and his house would serve the Lord. The people respond with this reminder of God's faithfulness. Shortly afterward, Joshua warns them that serving God is no light matter, and he invites them to think about it seriously.

For today: before making decisions of faith, remember how God has cared for you. Writing down three moments when you felt his help can strengthen your trust and your commitment to follow him each day.
exp.23:14:
If it seems bad to the Israelites to serve the Lord, they must choose today whom they will serve: the gods their ancestors served beyond the river Euphrates, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land they live. Joshua declares that he and his household will serve the Lord.

Joshua, now an old man, gathers the tribes at Shechem before he dies. He reminds them of what God has done for them, and asks them for a clear decision. The people answer that they will not abandon the Lord, for He brought them out of Egypt and cared for them.

Serving God is a personal decision that must be renewed. It is not enough to inherit the family's faith; it must be chosen again each day. Think about what competes for your loyalty today, and simply decide to serve God in your home.
exp.4:8:
Here God tells Joshua that on that day he removed from his people "the reproach of Egypt," that is, the shame or disgrace they had been carrying. For this reason the place was called Gilgal, a name that sounds like the Hebrew word for "to roll." The phrase "to this day" shows that the name was still in use when the book was written.

The words are spoken by the LORD, after Joshua had circumcised the new generation born in the wilderness. They had already crossed the Jordan and were about to begin the conquest. It is not known with certainty which shame is meant: some think of slavery, others of the taunts of the Egyptians, or of the years of disobedience in the wilderness.

For today: God knows how to take away our shame and give us a fresh start. If you are carrying a past that weighs on you, bring it to him with confidence and walk forward in obedience.
exp.5:13:
This verse tells us that on the second day the people did the same thing as on the first: they circled the city once and returned to the camp. In this way they repeated the same thing for six days.

The word "camp" is the place where the army stayed. The trumpets were made from ram's horns.

This is part of the account of the fall of Jericho. The one telling the story is not a character but the author of the book, who describes how Israel obeyed the instructions God gave to Joshua. The people were to march in silence, with the ark at the front, without attacking. The text does not explain why God chose this method, but it shows that the victory depended on Him and not on military strength.

For today: sometimes obeying God means continuing faithfully even when we do not yet see results. You can persevere in prayer, in your honest work, or in caring for your family, trusting that God is at work even in days that seem repetitive and unchanged.
exp.23:19:
It says that if the people turn away from the Lord and serve foreign gods, God will turn against them. He will punish them and destroy them, even after doing so much good for them. "Hurt" here means to do harm or send evil, and "consume" means to bring them to an end.

Joshua, now an old man, speaks at the assembly in Shechem. Israel had just promised to serve the Lord, remembering how God rescued them and gave them the land. Joshua confronts them so that they do not speak lightly. He reminds them that God is holy and jealous, meaning that He does not share His place with other gods. He wants their decision to be sincere, not merely emotional.

For today: let us not take God's goodness for granted or serve Him halfheartedly. Examine what things are taking the place of God in your heart, such as money or pride, and return to Him with sincerity and humility.
exp.2:5:
Joshua orders the priests to take up the ark of the covenant and walk at the front of the people. They obey and carry it ahead of them. The phrase "pass over before" means to go first, and "ark of the covenant" was the sacred chest that symbolized God's presence and his agreement with Israel.

Joshua speaks as the new leader after the death of Moses. Israel is about to cross the Jordan River into the promised land, a road they had never traveled. The priests go ahead so that everyone can see that God is leading them. The people were to keep their distance and consecrate themselves, because God would do wonders.

For today: when you face an unfamiliar road, let God go first. Before you take your steps, seek his guidance in prayer and in his Word, and obey with confidence, even though you do not yet see how everything will be resolved.
exp.13:0:
This verse says that in Canaan the Israelites received their inheritance, that is, the land that was given to them as their possession. Three kinds of leaders shared in dividing it: Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the heads of the families of each tribe. The word translated "inherited" here refers to the portion of land that fell to each tribe.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel entered the promised land. The narrator begins here to explain how the division was carried out west of the Jordan. This fulfilled the promise God had made to Abraham and to his descendants. The verses that follow say that lots were used, following what God had commanded through Moses.

For today: God keeps his promises, sometimes after a long time. Also, the division was done with order and with several leaders, not with just one. We can learn to serve as a team, with justice and openness, in the family, the church, or the workplace.
exp.18:32:
It says that the boundary of the tribe of Naphtali began at Heleph, passed by Allon to Zaanannim, Adami-nekeb and Jabneel, reached as far as Lakum, and ended at the Jordan River. The word "border" means the limit or boundary line. Some scholars think that "Allon to Zaanannim" refers to a large oak or tree, but the exact location of several of these places is not known with certainty.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel received the promised land. Here the narrator describes the sixth portion, divided by lot among the tribes. The written boundaries served so that each family would know what its inheritance was, and to record that God was keeping his promise.

For today: God cares about the details of each person's life. If he took care that every family had its place, you can also trust that he does not forget you. Give thanks today for what he has given you, and look after it faithfully.
exp.6:22:
This verse tells how the messengers brought out of Achan's tent the cloak, the silver, and the gold that had been hidden. Then they took them to Joshua and all Israel, and laid them out before the Lord.

Before this, Achan had confessed that he coveted and took things that God had commanded to be set apart from the conquest of Jericho. Because of that sin, Israel had been defeated at Ai. Joshua sent messengers, and they confirmed the confession. The narrator describes how what had been hidden came into the open, and judgment would follow.

For today: what we hide does not stay hidden before God. It is better to confess in time and let Him cleanse us, rather than let a secret sin grow until it ends up harming others too.
exp.18:13:
This verse continues describing the border of the tribe of Zebulun. It says that the boundary curves around toward the north, passes by a place called Hannathon, and ends in the valley of Jiphthah-el. The word "border" means the line or limit of a territory, and "compasseth" means goes around or curves about. Today it is not known with certainty where all these places were.

Joshua is the book where the promised land is divided among the tribes of Israel. The narrator records the boundaries in detail because each family needed to know what belonged to it. It was a sign that God was keeping what he had promised to their ancestors.

For today: God pays attention to details, even those that may seem dull to us. If he cared for every boundary of his people, he also cares for the small things in your life. Trust that your inheritance, what he has given you, is not overlooked by him.
exp.7:17:
Here God orders Joshua to raise his spear toward the city of Ai, and he promises to hand it over to him. Joshua obeys and raises it. The word "ambush" refers to a group of soldiers hidden in place, and "option" means a possibility or resource.

The Lord speaks to Joshua. Israel had been defeated before at Ai because of Achan's sin. Now, with the sin dealt with, God gives a strategy: to pretend to flee in order to draw the men out of the city. The raised spear was the signal for those who were hidden to enter and take it. Scholars do not agree on all the military details of the account.

God often gives us promises together with specific steps. Joshua not only listened, he also obeyed with a simple gesture. Today, trusting God means taking the step he shows us, even when it seems small, and waiting in faith for him to fulfill what he promised.
exp.14:12:
Here it is told that Caleb, son of Jephunneh, received a portion within the territory of the tribe of Judah. This was done following the command that God had given to Joshua. The city he received was Kiriath-arba, which means "the city of Arba," and it is the same city that was later called Hebron. Arba was known as the father of Anak, whose descendants are mentioned later on.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Joshua, who describes the division of the promised land. After listing the boundaries of Judah, the text pauses on Caleb. Here we are reminded that God fulfilled a promise made to this faithful man (see Numbers 14:24 and Joshua 14:6-14).

For today: God sees faithful perseverance and keeps his promises in his own time. We can follow him with steadiness, even when the answer takes years.
exp.9:13:
It says there was never a day like that, either before or after, when God listened in such a way to the voice of a man. The reason is that the Lord was fighting for Israel. Where the explanation quotes an old spelling, I'll simply note the phrase "listened to the voice" means that God did what Joshua asked.

The one telling this account is the author of the book of Joshua, who summarizes what happened in the battle of Gibeon. Joshua had asked that the sun and the moon stand still while Israel defeated the Amorites. Scholars debate exactly how to understand that miracle, but the text insists that the victory came from God.

For today: pray with courage about what God has already entrusted to you, but remember that the final victory belongs to the Lord. Do your part in faith, and trust that He fights alongside you.
exp.10:15:
This verse sums up how far Joshua's conquest reached. It names several areas of Canaan: the hills, the south country (the Negev, which is the "region of the south," that is, the south), the land of Goshen (an area in southern Canaan, different from the one in Egypt), the lowlands (low hills), the plains, and the mountains of Israel with their valleys.

The narrator of the book tells us that Joshua completed what God had commanded through Moses. The text stresses Joshua's obedience. These wars are hard to read; scholars explain them in different ways, and it is good to read them within the whole biblical story, where God keeps his promise to Israel.

For today: Joshua's faithfulness reminds us that God values steady obedience, even in long and difficult tasks. We can ask him for strength to keep carrying out, step by step, what he has entrusted to us.
exp.9:8:
It says that Joshua attacked his enemies by surprise. To manage this, he marched all night from Gilgal, Israel's camp. The phrase "came unto them suddenly" means that he arrived all at once, when they did not expect him. The word "went up" is used because the road from Gilgal to Gibeon went uphill.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. The Gibeonites had made an alliance with Israel, and five Amorite kings attacked them for that reason. Gibeon asked for help, and Joshua went. God had already told him not to fear, because he would give them the victory. So Joshua acts with effort, but trusting in God's promise.

For today: trusting God does not mean sitting still. When God gives you a promise or a task, do your part with diligence, even when it is hard, and leave the outcome in his hands.
exp.0:12:
The explanation says that Joshua asks certain tribes to remember what Moses commanded them. Moses had told them that God was giving them that land east of the Jordan.

Joshua, the new leader of Israel, speaks just before crossing the river into Canaan. He speaks to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and half the tribe of Manasseh, who already had their inheritance on the east side. He reminds them of their promise: to leave their families there and cross over armed to help their brothers until they too received rest.

For today: what God has given us is not only for us to enjoy. If you have stability or peace today, ask yourself whom you can help who is still in the struggle, and faithfully keep your commitment.
exp.18:42:
This part of the list says that Elon, Timnah and Ekron were towns within the inheritance of the tribe of Dan. The word translated as "territory" in this sense refers to the assigned area or boundary, and "inheritance" is the land received as an heritage.

The text is part of the account of how Israel divided the promised land in the time of Joshua. The narrator lists the places in detail to show that God was keeping his promise to each tribe. Later, the Bible tells that Dan had difficulty occupying all of its territory. Ekron and Timnah appear afterward in areas connected with the Philistines.

For today: God keeps his promises, but sometimes he asks us to walk in faith to take possession of what he has already given us. Trust his word, be steadfast, and do not lose heart when the road meets opposition.
exp.20:39:
This verse says that the descendants of Merari, one of the three main groups of the Levites, received twelve cities in all. These were the cities that were left to be divided. The word "cities" here stands for towns or settlements, and "by their lot" refers to the drawing of lots by which they were allotted, and the grazing lands around each city are part of what was given with it.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua, who keeps the record of how the promised land was divided, speaks. The Levites did not receive a territory of their own, because their inheritance was to serve God. So they lived in cities spread among all the tribes, until the total reached forty-eight. In this way they could teach and serve the whole people.

For today: God cares for those who serve him and places them in the midst of his people. Ask yourself where he has placed you to serve, and give generously to those who teach and care for your community.
exp.3:7:
This verse tells how the Israelites obeyed Joshua. They took twelve stones from the middle of the Jordan River, one for each tribe, just as the Lord had commanded. They carried them with them to the place where they would camp and set them down there.

Israel had just crossed the Jordan on dry ground, when the waters stopped before the ark of the covenant. God told Joshua to raise these stones as a sign. That way, when the children later asked what they meant, their parents would tell them what God had done. The text indicates that the stones would serve as a memorial forever.

God knows we forget his works quickly. Today we can do something similar: write in a notebook the prayers God has answered and the moments when God helped us. Then tell them to our children, to other relatives, or to friends, so that faith is passed from one generation to the next.
exp.19:5:
It says that the person who killed someone unintentionally had to stay in the city of refuge until he presented himself for trial before the congregation (the "assembly" being the gathering of the people). He had to remain there until the death of the high priest of that time. Afterward he could return to his own house and his own city. "Unintentionally" means by mistake, without intent.

God speaks to Joshua so that Israel sets apart cities of refuge, as he had commanded earlier through Moses. His purpose was to protect the one who caused an accidental death from revenge by the relative of the one who died, and at the same time to take seriously the value of life. Why the death of the high priest marked the end is something interpreted in various ways; the Bible does not explain it in detail.

Today it reminds us that God joins justice and mercy. We can seek that wrongs be dealt with truth and fairness, without vengeance, and offer others a path of restoration.
exp.23:3:
It says that God gave Abraham a son, Isaac, and that Isaac in turn had Jacob and Esau. To Esau he gave the mount Seir to possess, that is, to live there as his own. Jacob and his children, by contrast, went down into Egypt.

Joshua speaks to the gathered people at Shechem, near the end of his life. In God's name, he goes over the history of Israel from Abraham onward. He wants to remind them that everything began through God's initiative, not because of their merit, so that they may decide whom they will serve.

For today: remember that everything you have, and your own story, begins with God's grace. Today, give thanks to him for something specific that he has given you without your having earned it.
exp.21:19:
This verse recalls Achan, son of Zerah, who disobeyed God by taking things that had been set apart for destruction. The word "accursed" in the verse names those devoted things. Breaking faith with God's command is what the verse calls a trespass, and God's judgment is its consequence. Because of one man's sin, all of Israel suffered, and Achan did not die alone.

Phinehas, the priest, speaks along with the leaders of Israel. The eastern tribes had built an altar by the Jordan, and the others thought they were rebelling against God. So they remind them of what happened with Achan. Later it became clear that the altar was a witness and not a rebellion, although this was not yet known.

For today: our decisions affect others, for good or for harm. It is wise to live honestly before God, and also to ask calmly and humbly before judging others, because sometimes we do not know their reasons.
exp.18:35:
This verse is part of a list of towns. It names three: Adamah, Ramah, and Hazor, which are added to others from the same group. These were towns that formed part of the territory of the tribe of Naphtali.

Here no character is speaking in a speech; the book of Joshua recounts how the promised land was divided among the tribes of Israel. These lists show that God kept his promise to give an inheritance to every family. It is not known with certainty where each town was located, and scholars debate some of the locations.

God knows the names and places of his people, even those that seem small to us. Today you can remember that your life, your family, and your place of work do not go unnoticed by him. Trust that he has given you a place and a task, and serve him faithfully where you are.
exp.9:3:
Adonizedec, king of Jerusalem, asks four other kings for help. He says to them: "Come up to me and help me, so that we may attack Gibeon." The reason is that Gibeon made a peace agreement with Joshua and with the Israelites. The sentence that explains the old words is removed, since those words do not appear in the verse you are reading.

Adonizedec speaks out of fear. Gibeon was a large and strong city, and its alliance with Israel made him feel threatened. For this reason he gathers the Amorite kings to punish Gibeon. This sets the scene for Gibeon's request for help from Joshua.

For today: fear sometimes leads us to attack someone who chose to do what is right or to seek peace. Instead of reacting with anger or pressure, we can stop, examine what frightens us, and hand it over to God. He takes care of those who take refuge in Him.
exp.14:13:
It says that Caleb drove out of Hebron three descendants of Anak: Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai. The verse says he "drove thence" them, meaning he drove them out of there, removing them from the land. The "children of Anak" were a people of great stature who had frightened Israel forty years earlier.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua speaks. Caleb received Hebron as his inheritance, in keeping with what the LORD had promised. He is the same Caleb who, as one of the twelve spies, trusted that God would give them that land. Now, already an old man, he takes it in faith. Some think that "children of Anak" refers to three families or clans, not only to three persons; the text does not make this clear.

For today: God keeps His promises, and sometimes it takes years. Like Caleb, trust Him and go forward with courage, even in the face of the giants that once frightened you.
exp.1:11:
Rahab asks the two Israelite spies to swear to her by Jehovah that, just as she was kind to them by hiding them, they will also show kindness to her father's family. "I pray you" means "I beg you," "kindness" here is loyal goodness, and "sure sign" is a reliable proof that they will keep their word.

Rahab, a woman of Jericho, speaks with the spies that Joshua sent. She had heard how God acted on behalf of Israel and recognized that Jehovah is God of heaven and earth. For this reason she risked her life, and now she asks for protection for her family when the conquest arrives.

Today we can learn that true faith shows itself in actions and also cares for loved ones. If God has touched our hearts, let us pray and act with courage so that others too may find his mercy.
exp.5:2:
God gives Joshua a simple instruction: all the men of war must go around the city of Jericho once a day for six days. The word translated "compass" in the verse means to go around or make a circuit about something. They are not asked to attack, but to walk around the walls.

The LORD speaks to Joshua. Jericho was completely shut up, and no one went in or out. Before giving the plan, God assures him that he has already handed the city over. The victory comes from God, and Israel's part is to obey a method that, by human standards, seems strange.

For today: sometimes God asks us for small, steady steps of obedience, even when we do not yet see results. Trust his promise, stay faithful each day, and do not lose heart at how slow the process seems. He works in what appears quiet.
exp.1:13:
The two spies promise Rahab that they will give their lives for hers and her family's, on one condition: that she not tell anyone what they are doing. They say that when God gives them the land, they will treat her with kindness and faithfulness, that is, with goodness and loyalty.

The Israelite spies had arrived in Jericho, and Rahab hid them, risking her own life. She asked them to swear by the Lord that they would save her family, since she had heard that God was with Israel. Here the men respond with a solemn pledge.

For today: keep what you promise, especially when someone has trusted you or helped you. And guard the secrets entrusted to you, because loyalty and discretion are what allow others to trust you.
exp.13:11:
Caleb asks Joshua for the hill country of Hebron, which God had promised him years earlier. He acknowledges that the Anakim live there, a people of great stature, in large and well-fortified cities. He says "if so be the Lord will be with me," and this does not express doubt about the promise, but humility and dependence on God. The phrase "I shall be able to drive them out" means to force those inhabitants out of the land.

Caleb speaks at eighty-five years of age. Forty-five years earlier, Moses sent him to explore the land, and he trusted God when others were afraid. Now, with the land already divided, he asks for what God promised him. Joshua blesses him and gives him Hebron.

For today: faith does not expect everything to be easy. Caleb faced giants without denying them, but he trusted God. Ask God with courage and humility for what He has placed on your heart, and walk with Him even when there are obstacles.
exp.9:37:
The verse says that Joshua, together with all the people of Israel, turned back to the city of Debir and attacked it. The word "fought against it" stands for the same action: they made war on the city. It is part of a series of military campaigns in the south of Canaan.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua speaks, summarizing how Israel took the promised land, city by city, after the victory over an alliance of kings. The text presents these conquests as the fulfillment of what God had commanded. The war passages of the Old Testament are harsh, and scholars debate how to understand them and how literal their language of total destruction is.

Joshua advanced steadily, without stopping halfway. In the same way, when God gives us a task, we can persevere step by step, trusting that he sustains what he has entrusted to us.
exp.3:3:
This verse tells us that Joshua gathered the twelve men who had already been chosen, one from each tribe of Israel. "Gathered" means he called them together, and "chosen beforehand" means he had appointed them earlier.

The people were crossing the Jordan River to enter the promised land. God had held back the waters, and the priests carrying the ark stood firm in the middle of the riverbed. Joshua, the leader of Israel, brings these representatives together to take twelve stones, which would be a reminder of the miracle for the generations to come.

For today: God wants us to remember what he has done for us. We can create our own reminders, such as a journal or a conversation with family, to tell others how God helped us.
exp.23:27:
It says that Joshua sent the whole people of Israel away, so that each family returned to the land that had fallen to them as their inheritance. Here "sent away" means he let them go, and "inheritance" is the land each tribe and family received as their own property.

The narrator is the author of the book. Joshua, now old, had just gathered Israel at Shechem to renew the covenant with God. The people had promised to serve only the Lord, and Joshua set up a stone as a witness to that commitment. This verse closes the assembly, and each person goes back to their daily life.

For today: the promises we make to God are kept in ordinary life. After a special moment at church or in prayer, the real test is in the home, at work, and in the family. There we can live out faithfully what we promised.
exp.20:17:
It says that, from the tribe of Benjamin, the Levites who were descendants of Aaron also received Anathoth and Almon, each with its open land around it, that is, the pasture grounds around the town for their animals. With these two, Benjamin gave four cities: Gibeon, Geba, Anathoth and Almon.

Context: the account in Joshua lists how Israel, now in the promised land, carried out what God had commanded through Moses: giving cities to the Levites, who did not receive a territory of their own. This way they would live spread among all the people, serving and teaching. Here the cities of the priests, the sons of Aaron, are counted: thirteen in total.

For today: God cares for those who serve others, and the people are called to support them generously. Think about who teaches or serves you in the faith, and how you can support them with gratitude, prayer or practical help.
exp.12:5:
It says that God himself will drive out the peoples who live in the hill country, from Lebanon to Misrephoth-maim, a place to the north; the name means something like "burning waters" or "smelting places." To uproot means to pull up by the roots, that is, to remove those peoples from the land. A lot was a drawing used to divide up the territory, and an inheritance is land received as a family's share. Joshua only had to divide it.

God speaks to Joshua, who is already old and still has much land left to take. God encourages him: He will do the difficult work, and Joshua must do his part and divide the land among the tribes. There are different views on how to understand the conquests, but the text emphasizes that the promise depends on God.

For today: do not wait to have everything resolved before you obey. Faithfully do what God places in your hands today, and trust that He will fulfill what He has promised, even in what you do not yet see.
exp.18:2:
This verse continues the list of towns that the tribe of Simeon received: Hazar-shual, Balah, and Azem. These are names of places in the south of Canaan. Hazar-shual seems to mean "the encampment or village of the fox," though this is an interpretation. Today it is not known for certain where all these places were. "Inheritance" means the land received as a portion.

The account comes from the book of Joshua, which tells how the promised land was divided among the tribes of Israel by lot. Simeon's portion lay within the territory of Judah; that is, it shared space with another tribe. The list of names shows that God kept his promise to Abraham with concrete details, place by place.

For today: God remembers the small things. Even though these towns may seem unfamiliar to us, he included them in his plan. You can trust that he also sees you and cares for the details of your life, even those that seem unimportant.
exp.18:46:
The tribe of Dan did not have enough territory; that is, the land allotted to them was not sufficient for them, or they could not fully occupy it. So they went up, attacked the city of Leshem, defeated it with the sword (with violence, killing its inhabitants), took it, lived there, and gave the city the name Dan, after their ancestor.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua is listing the division of the land among the tribes. This note appears at the end of the list for Dan. Why they lacked territory is not explained here; some think they failed to drive out the peoples in their assigned area (Judges 1:34). In Judges 18 the city is called Laish.

For today: when what we receive seems insufficient, it is wise to seek God in prayer and trust, rather than acting only on impulse. And before moving forward, let us ask whether our steps respect what God has given and commanded.
exp.18:45:
It says that the tribe of Dan was also given the towns of Me-jarkon and Rakkon, along with the territory that lies opposite Japho, a port on the Mediterranean Sea. The word "border" means territory or boundary.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua speaks, listing in detail how the promised land was divided among the tribes of Israel. This list shows that God fulfilled what He had promised to His people. The verses that follow tell that Dan lacked territory, perhaps because it could not take all that had been assigned, and so it conquered Leshem. The Bible does not explain every detail of that situation.

For today: God cares for each person, even in details that seem small, like a name in a list. Trust that He sees you and keeps His promises, and also take steps of faith to receive what He has given you.
exp.11:13:
This verse is part of a list of defeated Canaanite kings. It says that the king of Hormah was defeated, and also the king of Arad. The word "one" in the verse only serves as a count: each name adds to the total of thirty-one kings.

Joshua 12 is a summary of the book. The narrator, whom tradition associates with Joshua, reviews the victories of the people of Israel as they conquered the promised land. Hormah and Arad were in the south, near the Negev desert. Before this, Numbers 21 tells of a clash with the king of Arad. The list is meant to remind readers that God kept what he promised his people.

For today: God attends to the details and forgets none of his works. Learn to remember with gratitude the times he helped you, even when they seem small. Making a list of those blessings can strengthen your faith.
exp.23:13:
After all that God has done for Israel, the people are to hold him in reverence and serve him with a sincere and faithful heart. The word translated "sincerity" means complete honesty, with no double-mindedness. The phrase "beyond the river" means on the other side of the river, that is, the Euphrates. He also calls them to put away the false gods that their ancestors worshiped there and in Egypt.

Joshua, now an old man, is speaking at the assembly in Shechem. He has just reminded them how God gave them victories, land, and cities that they did not win or build. For this reason he asks them to renew their commitment to God. They will answer that they will not abandon him.

For today: God is not content with a faith made only of words. Ask yourself what thing in your life is occupying the place that belongs to him, and give it over to him with sincerity. Do it today, giving thanks for what he has already given you.
exp.18:37:
This verse closes the list of cities that fell to the tribe of Naphtali: Iron, Migdal-el, Horem, Beth-anath and Beth-shemesh. In all they total nineteen cities, together with their villages, that is, the small towns around each city that depended on it.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel divided the promised land, tribe by tribe, by casting lots. The account is told by a narrator, not by a person speaking in the first person. Its purpose was to record that God kept what he had promised his people. Some of these places cannot be located with certainty today.

For today: God attends to details and knows each person by name and place. You can trust that your life is also in his hands, even when you feel small or unseen. Today, give thanks for something specific that he has given you.
exp.23:24:
This verse tells us that Joshua made a covenant with the people that very day, at Shechem. "Covenant" means a solemn agreement between God and his people. "Statute and ordinance" refers to clear rules for living according to God's will.

Joshua was already an old man, and he had gathered the tribes of Israel. He reminded them of what God had done for them and challenged them to choose whom they would serve. The people promised to serve the LORD and obey him. Then Joshua put that commitment in writing and firmly established it, so that it would not remain only in emotional words.

For today: saying that we love God is a good beginning, but we need concrete decisions. Think of one specific step of obedience, such as removing something that takes God's place in your heart, and write it down to remember it.
exp.16:7:
This verse explains how a border area between two tribes was divided. The land around Tappuah belonged to Manasseh, but the town of Tappuah itself, which lay on the boundary, belonged to the children of Ephraim. The boundary line is what the verse is describing, and the translated words are "border," "was," and "belonged," which appear in the verse above.

The speaker here is the narrator of the book of Joshua, who describes how Israel received the promised land. Manasseh and Ephraim were descendants of the sons of Joseph. The boundaries were recorded in detail to avoid disputes. Some towns of Ephraim lay within the territory of Manasseh, and scholars do not explain with certainty all the reasons for that arrangement.

For today: God cares about details and order. We can learn to respect boundaries and to share with others, even when things are not perfectly separated.
exp.7:28:
This verse tells how Joshua hanged the king of Ai on a wooden pole, that is, on a tree or stake, until evening. When the sun went down, he ordered the body taken down and thrown at the entrance of the city. There they set over it a large heap of stones, which remains there to this day, meaning up to the time the book was written.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not Joshua. The conquest of Ai follows the earlier defeat caused by the sin of Achan. Taking the body down before night fell fulfills what Deuteronomy 21:22-23 commanded, that a body should not be left hanging from one day to the next. The heap of stones served as a memorial.

For today: God takes obedience seriously, even in the details. We can ask ourselves what instruction from his Word we are putting off for later, and obey it simply and on time.
exp.11:8:
This verse begins a list of the Canaanite kings whom Israel defeated under the leadership of Joshua. Two appear here: the king of Jericho and the king of Ai, a city that was beside Bethel. Each is counted as "one," as in an official tally. The word "struck" means that they were defeated in battle.

The book of Joshua summarizes here the conquests west of the Jordan. The narrator is the author of the book, who is not named; some believe he used writings from Joshua. It is a record meant to help people remember that God kept his promise to give the land to his people. Jericho and Ai are mentioned first because they were the first cities conquered when entering Canaan.

For today: God keeps what he promises, and it is worth keeping track of his works. Write down with gratitude the times when he has helped you, so that your faith is strengthened when new challenges come.
exp.20:28:
This verse ends the list of the cities that the tribe of Issachar gave to the Levites: Jarmuth and En-gannim, with their suburbs. The suburbs were the open lands around each town, used for livestock. Four cities are named here, along with Kishion and Daberath.

The account in Joshua tells how Israel divided the land. The Levites did not receive a territory of their own, because they served God in worship and in teaching. For this reason, each tribe gave them cities in which to live. These cities belonged to the family of Gershon. Some of the names appear a little differently in 1 Chronicles 6, and the reason is not known for certain.

Today, God cares for those who serve, often through his people. We can ask ourselves how to support, with generosity and gratitude, those who teach and care for our faith.
exp.14:2:
This verse follows the southern boundary line of the territory of Judah. The explanation of "south" is that it is the direction the boundary runs. The border went up by the ascent of Akrabbim, passed through the wilderness of Zin, and reached Kadesh-barnea. Then it continued toward Hezron, went up to Addar, and turned around toward Karkaa. Some of these places cannot be located with certainty today.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel divided the promised land by lot, tribe by tribe. Here the limits of Judah, the largest tribe, are described. These clear boundaries prevented disputes and showed that God kept what he had promised to his people.

Today we can learn that God is a God of order and faithfulness, who keeps his promises even in the details. You can trust that he knows your place and your calling. Give thanks for what he has given you and care for it faithfully.
exp.6:19:
Here Achan answers Joshua and openly admits his guilt: "Indeed I have sinned against the Lord God of Israel." Achan says "thus and thus I have done" to announce that he is about to describe in detail what he did. "Answered" here means that he replied to Joshua's request.

Achan speaks; he was of the tribe of Judah. Israel had been defeated at Ai because someone took things that God had set apart under the ban at Jericho. Through a process of selection, Achan was singled out. Joshua called him "my son" and asked him to tell the truth. Achan confesses, though he does so only after he had already been discovered.

For today: do not wait for others to discover your fault. Confessing honestly and without hiding anything to God opens the way to truth and restoration.
exp.4:10:
This verse tells that, on the day after celebrating the Passover, the people of Israel ate for the first time what the land of Canaan produced: unleavened cakes, that is, made without yeast, and fresh ears of grain roasted in the fire, which were tender young grains of cereal.

The one who tells the account is the author of the book of Joshua, who is not named. Israel had just crossed the Jordan and was camped at Gilgal. They had carried out the circumcision and the Passover, remembering the deliverance from Egypt. This food marks the end of one stage: the day after, the manna ceased and provision from the promised land began.

God cares for us in every stage, even though the form of his provision changes. Give thanks for what He gives you today, without clinging to what has already passed.
exp.21:27:
This verse says that the tribes east of the Jordan, namely Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh, got ahead of a possible accusation. If someone one day told their descendants that they did not belong to God's people, they would show the altar and say: "This is a copy of the altar of the Lord. It was not made for offering burnt offerings or sacrifices, but as a witness between us and you."

The speakers are the group of tribes that built a large altar beside the Jordan. The other tribes believed it was an act of rebellion and prepared for war. They explain that their intention was to keep a shared faith with their children and with the children of their brothers.

Today we can take care that our actions are not misunderstood. Clarifying our intentions with humility and listening before judging helps prevent divisions among brothers and sisters.
exp.3:10:
This says that when the whole people of Israel had finished crossing the Jordan River, the ark of the Lord (the sacred chest that symbolized God's presence) also crossed, carried by the priests. They did it "in the presence of the people," that is, while everyone was watching.

The context: it is not a character speaking, but the narrator of the book of Joshua. It tells how God held back the waters so that Israel could enter the promised land. The priests with the ark stood firm in the middle of the river until everyone had passed. Only then did they cross themselves, and so the people saw that God kept His promise to the very end.

For today: God does not leave you halfway across. When you face a difficult change, trust that His presence holds you up until you have finished passing through. And then, like Israel, remember and tell what He has done for you.
exp.0:10:
Joshua orders the officers to go through the camp and tell the people to prepare provisions, that is, food for the journey. The word "prepare" in the verse is the same idea as the explanation's own meaning: get ready. Within three days they would cross the Jordan River to enter and take possession of the land that God was giving them.

Joshua has just taken command after the death of Moses. God had told him to be strong and courageous, and not to be afraid. Now Joshua responds with concrete actions. Some scholars debate how these "three days" fit with other texts in the book, but the meaning is clear: the time to move forward was near.

God had promised the land, but the people had to get ready and move forward in faith. Trusting God does not mean doing nothing. Today we might ask ourselves: what practical step is mine to take in order to prepare for what God places before me?
exp.20:20:
It says that to the Levites of the family of Kohath who were not priests they gave Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim, and also Gezer, each with its surrounding pasturelands. A city is what is meant by the word for a fortified settlement. The surrounding lands are the grazing fields around the town, for the livestock. The word for those who kill here refers to someone who killed without meaning to, and who could flee to that city to be protected until he was judged.

This chapter is a historical account from the book of Joshua. It tells how, after dividing the land, Israel gave cities to the Levites, because they did not receive a territory of their own. Shechem was one of the cities of refuge, where justice was mixed with mercy.

For today: God cares for those who serve and also for those who need protection. We can imitate that mercy by being a safe place for someone going through a hard time, without giving up truth or justice.
exp.18:33:
The boundary of the tribe of Naphtali is described here. From there the line turns westward toward Aznoth-tabor, passes Hukkok, and touches Zebulun on the south.
