To the west it borders Asher, and toward the east it reaches the Jordan. The mention of Judah at that place is hard to explain, and scholars understand it in several ways.

The narrator of the book of Joshua tells how the promised land was divided by lot among the tribes of Israel. This was the fulfillment of God's promise to the patriarchs, and the boundaries helped prevent conflicts between the tribes.

For today: God cares even about the details of your life. Trust the place and the responsibilities he has given you, and live them out with gratitude and without envying others.
exp.21:7:
Joshua tells the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh to go back home. They return with great wealth: livestock, silver, gold, bronze, iron, and many clothes. He also asks them to share with their brothers what they took from their enemies. The spoil of war is what is gained in battle. "Tents" here means their homes.

Joshua speaks as the leader of Israel. These tribes had helped conquer Canaan, on the other side of the Jordan, and they had done what Moses asked of them. Now he sends them off with a blessing. His command to share the plunder with those who stayed behind to guard their families and flocks can be understood as an act of justice and unity among the tribes.

What God gives us is not only for ourselves. If we have received blessings, we can share them with those who supported us or are in need. Sharing strengthens unity and gratitude.
exp.20:0:
This verse tells how the heads of the Levite families came near to three authorities: Eleazar the priest, Joshua the son of Nun, and the heads of the other tribes of Israel. The phrase "heads of the fathers" means the leaders of the households or clans. The Levites were the descendants of Levi, set apart to serve God.

The passage is not speaking of one particular person here, but is telling the story as a whole. Israel was already dividing the land of Canaan, and the Levites had not received their own territory as the other tribes had. According to the next verse, they gathered at Shiloh to remind everyone that God, through Moses, had commanded that cities be given to them to live in, with pasture lands for their animals.

For today: when God has promised something, we can ask for it with respect and good order, without demanding it in anger. And those of us who have resources can take care of those who serve others.
exp.21:26:
It says that the altar was not built for offering sacrifices, but as a visible sign. It would serve as proof for them, for the other Israelites, and for future generations that they too can worship the Lord. The "peace offerings" are the fellowship or peace offerings. The "burnt offerings" are offerings burned up entirely. So, in the future, no one could say to their children, "You have no part in the Lord."

The speakers are the tribes of Reuben and Gad (together with the half-tribe of Manasseh), who lived east of the Jordan. The other tribes believed they had built a rival altar and were preparing for war. They explain that their intention was to keep the unity of faith, not to separate themselves.

For today: let us make sure our children know that they belong to God. Let us talk about faith at home and avoid letting distances or differences build walls between brothers and sisters.
exp.22:8:
It says that God has driven out from before Israel great and powerful nations. Until that day, no enemy had been able to stand against them. "Driven out" means expelled or pushed back, and "stand before your face" means to resist them or face them.

Joshua, now an old man, speaks to the leaders of Israel before he dies. He reminds them of what God did in the conquest of Canaan. His purpose is to encourage them to remain faithful to God and not to mix with the gods of the peoples who still remained in the land.

For today: when you face something that seems bigger than you, remember the times God has sustained you in the past. That grateful remembrance strengthens trust and keeps us close to Him, instead of looking for support in other things.
exp.14:16:
It says that Othniel, son of Kenaz and brother of Caleb, captured the city of Debir, which had previously been called Kiriath-sepher. Since Caleb had promised, Othniel received Achsah, Caleb's daughter, as his wife. The phrase "took it" means that he captured the city, and "gave him Achsah his daughter to wife" means that he handed her over to him as his wife.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua speaks, describing how each tribe received its territory. Caleb, of the tribe of Judah, offered his daughter as a prize to whoever would capture that city. Some understand that Othniel was Caleb's nephew, and others see him as a close relative; the text is brief and allows both readings.

For today: Othniel acted with courage and dared to undertake what others had not. Let us ask God for the courage to faithfully carry out the difficult tasks he sets before us, trusting that he keeps his promises.
exp.4:7:
This verse says that, when they had finished circumcising all the men of the people, they stayed in the camp without moving until they were healed. The word "healed" here means that their wounds were made whole. "Circumcising" is the rite that marked a male as part of God's covenant with Israel.

Here the narrator tells what happened at Gilgal, right after crossing the Jordan. The generation that came out of Egypt had died in the wilderness for not obeying God, and their sons had not been circumcised. Before moving forward into the conquest, the people renewed their sign of the covenant. Some scholars note that the moment was a vulnerable one, and yet Israel obeyed.

For today: before we rush toward great goals, it is wise to stop and renew our relationship with God. Resting, healing, and returning to what is essential is not wasted time; it is preparing us to walk with Him.
exp.4:12:
Joshua is near Jericho, the city Israel must conquer. He lifts up his eyes and sees a man standing in front of him with a sword drawn in his hand, ready to fight. Joshua approaches with courage and asks him whether he is for Israel or for their enemies.

The narrator tells this moment right after the Passover and the end of the manna. Israel is already in the promised land and the battle is near. From the answer that follows, this figure presents himself as the Commander of the army of the LORD. Many understand him to be an angel; others, an appearance of the Lord himself. The Bible does not fully clarify this.

For today: before asking that God be on our side, let us ask ourselves whether we are on his side. He is not an ally at our service; he is the Lord whom we must obey and worship.
exp.8:17:
It says that Israel did not kill the Gibeonites, because the leaders had sworn an oath to them in the name of the Lord, the God of Israel. Even so, the people complained against those leaders, since they felt they had been deceived.

The narrator tells what happened after they discovered that the Gibeonites did not come from far away, as they had pretended, but lived nearby. The leaders had not asked the Lord before making the covenant (v. 14). Even so, they decided to keep their word, because the oath had been made before God.

Keeping our word is a way of honoring God, even when it costs us or when we have decided in haste. Before promising something, it is good to pray and ask for wisdom, so that we do not act only on what we see.
exp.12:16:
This verse continues the list of cities that were given to the tribe of Reuben east of the Jordan. It names Heshbon with the towns around it on the plain, along with Dibon, Bamoth-baal, and Beth-baal-meon. It is a description of territory, not a direct teaching.

The narrator describes how Moses divided these lands before he died. Now Joshua is old and must divide the rest of the promised land. This list reminds the reader that God kept his promise and that each tribe received its inheritance. Some of these places had names tied to the worship of Baal, which shows that they were lands once inhabited by other peoples.

God takes an interest in the details of his people's lives: each family had a place with its own name. You can trust that God keeps what he promises, and that he also knows you and cares for you personally.
exp.10:5:
In this verse, God tells Joshua not to be afraid. He promises that the next day, at this same time, the enemies will be defeated before Israel. He also commands Joshua to hamstring the horses, that is, to cut the sinews of their hind legs so they become useless for war, and to burn the chariots.

The LORD speaks to Joshua. A great alliance of Canaanite kings, with a huge army and many horses and chariots, gathered together by the waters of Merom to attack Israel. Joshua had human reasons to feel fear. God gives him encouragement and a clear promise. The command to disable the horses and chariots was probably meant to keep Israel from trusting in weapons, and instead to trust in God.

For today: when you face something that seems bigger than you, remember that God invites you to trust in Him and not in your own resources. Hand your fear over to Him in prayer, and take the next step with faith.
exp.4:2:
This verse says that Joshua obeyed God's command: he made sharp knives and circumcised the Israelite males who had been born in the wilderness. "Foreskins" refers to the skin that is cut away in circumcision. That is why the place received that name, which the King James Version renders as "the hill of the foreskins."

"Circumcise the second time" does not mean repeating the operation on the same men, but doing it again with the new generation.

The narrator of the book speaks here, telling what Joshua did. Israel had just crossed the Jordan, and the neighboring kings were filled with fear. Even so, God first asked for the sign of the covenant to be renewed. Those who had been born in the wilderness had not received it.

Today we can learn that, before moving on to new battles, it is wise to put our relationship with God back in order. Simple obedience, even when it seems uncomfortable, prepares us for what lies ahead.
exp.11:9:
This verse is part of a list of defeated Canaanite kings. It says that the king of Jerusalem was one, and the king of Hebron, one. Each "one" simply counts one more king in the series. Jerusalem is Jerusalem, and Hebron was an important city in the mountainous region of Judah.

The book of Joshua presents this list as a summary, after recounting Israel's conquests under Joshua's leadership. The narrator, who is not identified with certainty, wants to record that God fulfilled his promise to give the land to his people. The names of the cities function as a record of what God did. Some scholars think the list seeks to show the full extent of the victory.

For today: God remembers the details, even the names that seem small. You can write in a notebook the times God has answered your prayers or cared for you. Remembering his works one by one strengthens your confidence when difficult days come.
exp.12:8:
This verse describes part of the territory east of the Jordan River. It runs from Aroer, on the bank of the Arnon stream, includes the city that is in the middle of the stream, and all the plain of Medeba, as far as Dibon. It is a list of places, like a map in words.

God speaks to Joshua, who is now old, and tells him to divide the land that remains among the nine tribes and the half tribe of Manasseh. The tribes of Reuben and Gad, and the other half of Manasseh, had already received their share through Moses. These boundaries remind the reader of what had already been given and what was still left to be taken.

For today: God takes an interest in concrete details and keeps his promises with real places and names. We can trust that he also cares for the details of our lives. Today, write down a promise of God and ask him to help you wait for it faithfully.
exp.12:32:
This verse says that Moses did not give land to the tribe of Levi. Instead of a territory, their inheritance was the Lord God of Israel himself, just as he had promised them. The word "inheritance" means the portion or possession that each tribe received. "But" introduces the contrast with the other tribes, and "gave" is the verb for what Moses did.

The narrator of the book of Joshua summarizes how Moses distributed the lands east of the Jordan to the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh. Here he makes clear that the Levites were different: they were devoted to the service of worship and to teaching the law, and they lived from the offerings and in cities assigned to them among the other tribes. God himself was their portion.

For today: we often look for security in money, work, or possessions. This text invites us to place our trust first in God, who cares for those who serve him. Ask yourself today: what holds the most important place in my heart?
exp.17:12:
This verse continues to describe the northern border of the territory of Benjamin. From the wilderness of Beth-aven, the line runs toward Luz, which is the same as Bethel, on its south side. Then it goes down to Ataroth-adar, toward the hill that lies on the south side of the lower Beth-horon.

The book tells how Israel divided the promised land among the tribes, and here the portion of Benjamin is set out in detail. That inheritance lay between Judah and the sons of Joseph (Ephraim and Manasseh). The text does not focus on any particular person; it is a record of places, written so that each family could know clearly what had been given to them.

For today: God cares about what is concrete and orderly. He keeps his promises with real places and clear boundaries. So we can trust that he attends to the details of your life, and also learn to value and care gratefully for what he has given you.
exp.8:23:
The Gibeonites explain to Joshua why they deceived him. They say they had heard that the Lord, the God of Israel, had commanded his servant Moses to give them all the land and to destroy all its inhabitants. That is why they were very afraid for their lives and acted as they did.

The people of Gibeon speak here. They had pretended to be travelers from a distant land in order to make a peace agreement with Israel. When the deception was discovered, Joshua confronted them. They admit that they recognized the power of God, although their fear led them to lie. Israel had sworn the covenant and kept it, and the Gibeonites were left as servants of the sanctuary.

For today: recognizing God is not enough if only fear moves us. He wants us to seek him with sincerity and truth, not with deception. And when we fail, we can come to him honestly, trusting in his mercy.
exp.21:14:
Joshua 22:15 tells us that Phinehas and the ten leaders came to the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half tribe of Manasseh, in the land of Gilead. There they spoke with them. The words "they spake with them" simply mean "they spoke with them and said."

After the eastern tribes built an altar beside the Jordan, the rest of Israel thought they had rebelled against God. Before going to war, they sent a delegation made up of leaders from each tribe. They intended to ask for an explanation, because they feared that the whole people would suffer punishment, as had happened at Peor.

Before accusing or judging someone, it is wise to go and speak with them face to face. Listening first can prevent conflict and protect unity, without setting aside a love for the truth.
exp.16:10:
This verse says that the tribe of Manasseh received some cities that lay within the territories of Issachar and Asher: Beth-shean, Ibleam, Dor, Endor, Taanach, and Megiddo, each with its villages. "Villages" are the small towns around a city. The phrase "three countries" is hard; some believe it means three regions or districts, and others think it refers to the area of Dor. It is not known for certain.

It is part of the account of the division of the promised land, after the conquest under Joshua. The author describes the boundaries of each tribe, and here shows that Manasseh had strong and important cities outside its main area. What follows explains that they were not able to drive out the Canaanites who lived there.

For today: God gives us promises and blessings, but sometimes we do not fully live them out because of fear or because we settle for less. Ask him for the courage to obey him completely, without leaving areas of your life half-done.
exp.1:14:
Rahab lets the two Israelite spies down through a window with a cord. Her house was built against the city wall, that is, it was part of the wall itself, and the phrase "she lived on the wall" means that her house was built on top of the wall or joined into it.

Here the book's narrator speaks. Rahab had already hidden the spies from the king of Jericho. They had promised to protect her family because she had acknowledged the God of Israel. Now she acts to save them, and that promise is upheld by a faith shown in deeds.

For today: true faith shows itself when we act with courage and obedience, even when we do not understand everything. Think of one concrete step of trust in God that you can take today, even if it seems small.
exp.1:7:
This verse tells us that, before the two Israelite spies went to lie down to sleep, Rahab went up on the roof, the flat roof of the house, to speak with them. The roof is the flat top of the house, and the verse itself says she "came up unto them upon the roof."

The narrator speaks, and then Rahab speaks. The king of Jericho's men had already gone out to look for the spies toward the Jordan, and the city gate was shut. Rahab had hidden the spies among the stalks of flax. Now that there is a quiet moment, she confesses to them what she believes about the God of Israel.

For today: Rahab took advantage of a quiet moment to speak about her faith. We can ask God to help us speak honestly and boldly about what we believe when the opportunity comes, even when our situation is difficult.
exp.23:5:
This verse recalls that God brought Israel's ancestors out of Egypt. When they came to the sea, which is today called the Red Sea (though some scholars debate the exact place of the crossing), the Egyptians pursued them with chariots and horsemen, that is, with soldiers on horseback.

Here God himself speaks, through Joshua, before all the tribes gathered at Shechem. Joshua reviews the history of God's faithfulness in order to bring the people to a decision: to serve the LORD alone. He reminds them that the deliverance was the work of God, not of their own doing.

For today: when you face a problem that seems to be catching up with you from behind, remember what God has already done for you. Recalling his past help strengthens trust and encourages us to obey him with gratitude.
exp.11:2:
This verse continues to describe the territory of King Sihon, east of the Jordan. It runs from the plain (the Jordan valley) to the Sea of Chinneroth, which is the Sea of Galilee, and toward the sea of the plain, the Salt Sea, which is the Dead Sea. It mentions the road to Beth-jeshimoth and, to the south, the slopes of Mount Pisgah.

It is part of the account in the book of Joshua, which summarizes Israel's victories over the kings east of the Jordan, under the leadership of Moses. The text does not cite a speaker; it is the narrator who lists the boundaries to remind us that God kept what he had promised.

For today: God remembers his promises in detail, down to the exact places. Note the times God has been faithful to you and give him thanks; that strengthens your confidence for what comes next.
exp.17:11:
This verse describes the northern border of the territory allotted to the tribe of Benjamin. The line begins at the Jordan River, goes up on the north side of Jericho, then runs westward through the hill country, and ends at the wilderness of Beth-aven.

The narrator here is the writer of the book of Joshua. After entering the promised land, Joshua cast lots at Shiloh, before the Lord, to divide the land among the tribes that remained. Benjamin received an area between Judah and the sons of Joseph (Ephraim and Manasseh). The boundaries are recorded in detail so that each family would know what its inheritance was.

For today: God cares about the details of our lives. Just as each family received its place, we can trust that He knows where He has put us, and live with gratitude and faithfulness in what He has entrusted to us.
exp.22:5:
It says that the Israelites were to be very determined in carrying out everything written in the book of the law of Moses. The word "courageous" means being brave and steadfast. The phrase "to the right hand or to the left" means neither to the right nor to the left: not turning away from the path God had marked out.

Joshua speaks as an old man, near the end of his life. He gathers the leaders of Israel after the conquest and the division of the land. He reminds them that God has been faithful, and he warns them that, in order to keep enjoying the land, they must remain loyal to Him and not mix with the gods of the peoples who remained.

For today: obedience to God requires decision and perseverance. You might choose a fixed time each day to read the Bible and ask God for help in putting into practice what you read, without looking for shortcuts or excuses.
exp.9:14:
The explanation says that Joshua and all the people of Israel returned to the camp at Gilgal. The word "returned" here means going back to the camp.

The narrator tells this right after the great victory at Gibeon, when God made the day last longer. Gilgal had been Israel's base since they entered the land. Some scholars note that this phrase is repeated in verse 43, and that some ancient manuscripts do not include it here, because the pursuit continues afterward. For that reason it is understood in several ways: as an early summary or as a later return.

For today: after a great achievement or an answer from God, do not stay in the excitement. Go back to your usual place with humility and gratitude, remembering that God is the one who fought for you.
exp.9:24:
Joshua speaks to his fighting men and tells them not to be afraid or lose heart. He asks them to be strong and courageous, because God will do the same to all the enemies they are still facing.

Joshua speaks after the victory over five kings who had hidden in a cave. Placing their feet on the necks of the defeated was a gesture of complete victory, common in that time. Joshua wanted the soldiers to remember that God had given them the victory and that they could trust Him for the battles still ahead. Some scholars see here a symbolic act of encouragement rather than of cruelty.

Today, when you remember how God helped you through past difficulties, let that memory give you courage to face what comes next. His faithfulness of yesterday supports your confidence for tomorrow.
exp.8:10:
Here the Gibeonites tell how their leaders and all their people said to them that they should take food for the journey, go to meet the Israelites, and present themselves as their servants. They asked to make an alliance, that is, a covenant of peace.

The speakers are the Gibeonites, who lived nearby, in Canaan. They had heard what God had done for Israel and were afraid. To save their lives, they pretended to come from very far away. The Bible shows that they lied, and Joshua did not consult God before making a covenant with them (v. 14).

For today: before making an important decision, even when everything seems convincing, stop and pray, asking God for direction. Appearances can deceive, and God's wisdom protects us from mistakes that are later hard to correct.
exp.10:16:
The verse marks the boundaries of Joshua's victories: from Mount Halak, in the south, to Baal-gad, at the foot of Mount Hermon, in the north. "Struck" means that he defeated them in battle. Joshua captured the kings of that region and put them to death. Scholars are not sure of the exact location of these places.

The account is told by a narrator who summarizes the conquest of Canaan. Its emphasis is that Joshua obeyed everything that God had commanded Moses. The text presents this as a unique moment in the history of Israel, not as a model for using violence today.

For today: Joshua obeyed without leaving anything half-done. We can ask God for help to obey him completely in what he has already shown us, even in small things.
exp.13:7:
Caleb says that the other spies who went up with him to explore the land "made the heart of the people melt," that is, they discouraged them and took away their courage. By contrast, he "wholly followed" the Lord, meaning he was faithful to him completely and without doubting. The words "but" and "however," used in the verse, both mean "but."

Caleb, now 85 years old, speaks before Joshua at Gilgal. He recalls what happened at Kadesh-barnea (Numbers 13–14): ten spies gave a fearful report, and only he and Joshua trusted that God would give them the victory. Now he asks for the land that Moses promised him because of his faithfulness.

For today: when the people around you are carried away by fear or doubt, you can keep trusting God firmly. Ask him for the courage to be steadfast, and do not let the discouragement of others decide your faith.
exp.9:16:
This verse tells that someone brought word to Joshua that the five enemy kings had been found. They were hiding in a cave in Makkedah, a place in Canaan. The phrase "It was told" means that they gave him the news, and the word "found" means discovered.

Here it is not God or Joshua who speaks, but an unnamed messenger who carries the news. Israel had just won a great battle at Gibeon, and the kings who had joined together against them fled. Joshua immediately gives an order: close the cave with stones and post guards, so that they can keep pursuing the rest of the enemy. He trusted that God had already given them the victory.

For today: when God gives you an advantage, do not stop halfway. Act with order and keep moving forward, trusting that He sustains what He has begun.
exp.10:9:
It says that Joshua, after defeating the allied kings in the north, turned back and conquered the city of Hazor. He struck down its king with the sword (the phrase rendered "with the edge of the sword" means with the blade of the sword). The text explains that Hazor had been the head before, that is, the most important city and leader of those kingdoms in the north of Canaan.

This is part of the account of the conquest of Canaan. The narrator tells how Israel defeated a coalition led by the king of Hazor. The text says that Joshua was carrying out what Moses had commanded. These war passages are difficult, and scholars interpret them in several ways; they should be read within their historical context and within the whole of the Bible.

God is faithful to his promises, and obedience to him matters. Today, instead of fighting with weapons, we can face with prayer and courage whatever dominates us, without leaving unfinished what God asks of us.
exp.20:10:
This verse tells that the priests descended from Aaron were given the city of Arba, which is also called Hebron, in the hill country of Judah. Along with the city they received its pasture lands, which were the grazing grounds around it, where they could keep their animals.

The book of Joshua is a narrative, not a discourse. Here the narrator explains how Israel distributed cities to the Levites, since they did not receive a territory of their own as the other tribes did. The first to receive them were the sons of Aaron. Hebron was also a city of refuge, and its surrounding fields had earlier been given to Caleb.

God cares for those who serve him, and he also cares that everyone has a place. We can support with generosity those who devote themselves to serving in the church, and trust that God provides for us.
exp.7:29:
Joshua builds an altar to the Lord, the God of Israel, on Mount Ebal. The word "built" means that he raised it up or constructed it. The words "to the Lord" simply mean "for the Lord."

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Joshua. Israel had just been defeated at Ai because of Achan's sin, and then they captured the city. Now, instead of pressing ahead on their own, Joshua carries out what Moses had commanded (Deuteronomy 27): worshiping God at Ebal, with an altar of uncut stones, offerings, and the reading of the law. Worship comes first, then the conquest.

For today: after a victory, don't just rush past. Stop to give thanks to God and return to his Word. One good way is to set aside a moment this week to thank him and read a passage from the Bible.
exp.10:0:
This verse says that King Jabin, who ruled the city of Hazor, learned what was happening and sent messengers to other kings: Jobab of Madon, the king of Shimron, and the king of Achshaph. He wanted to gather them together. "When he heard this" means "when he heard this news."

Here it is not God or a prophet who speaks, but the narrator of the book. Jabin had heard of Israel's victories in the land of Canaan, such as the defeat of the kings of the south in the previous chapter. For that reason he sought to form an alliance of northern cities to face Israel.

For today: when faced with something we cannot control, we can react with fear and pride, looking for human allies, or we can seek God with humility. Before deciding, it is good to ask ourselves whether we are resisting what God is doing.
exp.20:18:
This verse sums up how many cities the priests, the descendants of Aaron, received: thirteen.

The book of Joshua tells how the promised land was divided. The Levites did not receive a territory of their own like the other tribes, so they were given cities within the other tribes. Here the narrator closes the list of the priests' cities, which were in Judah, Simeon and Benjamin. In this way they would live near the people to teach them and serve them.

God cares for those who serve others, and he also wants the people to have near them those who will teach them his Word. Today we can support our pastors and teachers with generosity and prayer, and seek to stay close to God's teaching in our daily lives.
exp.18:48:
It says that when they had finished dividing the land among the tribes, the children of Israel also gave an inheritance to Joshua, the son of Nun, among them. Where the verse says "inheritance," the word refers to a portion of land received as an inheritance. The "coasts" are the borders or boundaries of each territory.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. He wants to show that Joshua, the leader who brought the people through, received his share last, after all the others. According to the next verse, they gave him the city he asked for, and this was done according to the word of the LORD.

For today: Joshua served others first and received his share at the end. We can learn to serve with humility, without demanding our own first, trusting that God keeps his promises in his own time.
exp.21:3:
Joshua tells the tribes on the other side of the Jordan that they may now return home. God has already given rest to their brothers, that is, peace and a secure place in the promised land, just as he had said. "Tents" here means their homes, and "possessions" are the lands that Moses assigned to them east of the river.

Joshua, the leader of Israel after Moses, is speaking. Reuben, Gad, and the half tribe of Manasseh had helped conquer Canaan alongside the other tribes, as they had promised. Now the main war is over, and Joshua acknowledges their faithfulness before sending them off with a blessing.

For today: keeping a promise to the end is one way of loving God and others. But it is also necessary to keep obeying when the task is finished, because faithfulness is not only for a season.
exp.12:22:
This verse says that the border of the tribe of Reuben was the river Jordan. That was the inheritance their families received: the cities with their villages, which are the small towns and nearby settlements. "Territory" means boundary or land, and the phrase about dividing it according to their families means the land was shared out by clans.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua is summarizing the division of the lands east of the Jordan, which Moses had already given before he died. That land was taken after defeating Sihon, the Amorite king. The text also recalls the end of Balaam, who had led Israel into sin.

For today: God takes care that every family has a place, and he does so with great attention to detail. We can trust that he knows our particular situation. Be thankful for what he has already given you, and look after it faithfully.
exp.22:9:
One man among you could chase off a thousand enemies, with God's help. The reason is that the Lord himself was fighting for them, just as he had promised. "Shall chase" means that he would drive the enemy back and pursue them as they fled.

Joshua is speaking here, now old and near the end of his life. He gathers the leaders of Israel and reminds them of the victories God gave them in conquering Canaan. He also reminds them that they must remain faithful to the Lord. God's promise in the law, as in Deuteronomy 32:30, foretold this help. But the passage that follows warns that they would lose that strength if they turned away from him.

For today: when you face something that is beyond you, do not trust only in your own strength. Trust in God and stay close to him, obeying him day by day.
exp.10:11:
It says that Joshua conquered the cities of the kings of northern Canaan, took their kings, and struck them down with the edge of the sword, that is, with the sword. The phrase about destroying them speaks of total destruction, which in the Bible is called being devoted to destruction. It also says that this was done as Moses the servant of the Lord had commanded.

It is part of the historical account in the book of Joshua, which tells of the conquest of Canaan. The narrator emphasizes that Joshua obeyed orders given earlier through Moses (Deuteronomy 20:16-18). Interpreters debate the scope of these words: some see a judgment of God on very corrupt peoples, and others note that the language of ancient warfare was often exaggerated. It is a difficult passage, and it is best read with humility.

For today: let us learn from Joshua to obey God fully, without leaving unfinished what He asks of us, and let us seek with sincerity the peace that Christ taught.
exp.19:1:
God tells Joshua to speak to the people of Israel. He instructs them to set apart, or choose, the cities of refuge that He had already spoken about through Moses. The explanation of what this means is that they were to set apart these cities for themselves, and they were safe places within the promised land.

God speaks, and Joshua is the one who passes on the message. Israel was already dividing up the land. God wanted anyone who caused a death without intending it to be able to flee to one of these cities and not become the victim of a hasty revenge. There he would be heard by the elders and protected until his case was clarified.

God cares for justice and also for mercy. Today we can be people who do not act out of anger or on rumors, but who listen first, protect the vulnerable, and offer a safe place. And we remember that in Christ we have our true refuge.
exp.20:5:
This verse says that the descendants of Gershon, one of the groups of the Levites, received thirteen cities. Those cities were in the territory of four tribes: Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, in the region of Bashan. The word "cities" here means towns or villages, and the phrase "by lot" means that they were divided by casting lots, a way of leaving the decision in God's hands.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua speaks. He tells how what God commanded through Moses was fulfilled: the Levites did not receive a land of their own like the other tribes, but cities spread among all Israel, to serve and to teach the people.

For today: God cares for those who serve others, and he also wants his people to support them. We can ask ourselves how we might support, through prayer, time, or concrete help, those who serve in our church.
exp.1:20:
Rahab agrees to the terms the two Israelite spies set for her. They leave, and she ties the scarlet cord (a red cord) to the window. She let them go, and scarlet is an intense red.

Rahab speaks with the spies that Joshua sent to Jericho. She hid them and helped them escape, and in return they promised to protect her family when the conquest came. The red cord would be the sign on her house. Some Christians see in it a symbol of the blood of Christ, but the text does not say so, so this is a possible reading and not a certain claim.

For today: Rahab believed and acted right away, without waiting to see everything clearly. If God has shown you something, take a concrete step of obedience or trust today, even a small one.
exp.1:0:
This verse tells that Joshua, son of Nun, secretly sent two men from Shittim, a place east of the Jordan. He asked them to look over the land, especially Jericho. Here "look over" means to explore and observe. The spies came to the house of Rahab, a woman who made her living as a prostitute, and they stayed there. "Stayed there" means they spent the night.

The narrator recounts what Joshua did, the new leader of Israel after the death of Moses. The people were about to cross the Jordan to enter the promised land. Joshua wanted information before moving forward. Scholars do not agree on why the spies chose that house; the Bible does not explain it.

For today: trusting God does not remove the need to plan wisely. And God can work through people no one would expect, like Rahab.
exp.9:6:
This verse tells that Joshua set out from Gilgal with his whole army to go to the aid of Gibeon. The men ready to fight are the people of war, and the strongest and most capable soldiers are the mighty men of valour. The text says Joshua "ascended" because Gilgal lay in a low area and Gibeon was in a higher place.

The narrator relates that five Amorite kings attacked Gibeon, a city that had made peace with Israel. The Gibeonites asked Joshua for help. He answered at once, keeping the covenant he had made with them. Shortly afterward God encouraged him not to be afraid.

For today: when someone who depends on you needs help, act promptly and faithfully to your word. Do it with courage, trusting that God goes before you and sustains what he has called you to do.
exp.10:7:
God said he had handed the northern kings over to Israel. The Israelites defeated them and chased them as far as great Sidon (a coastal city), as far as the place called "hot waters" (Misrephoth-maim, whose exact location is not known for certain), and as far as the valley of Mizpeh to the east. Striking them meant beating them or defeating them in battle.

This is part of Joshua's account of the conquest of Canaan. A large alliance of kings, with many horses and chariots, gathered against Israel beside the waters of Merom. God had told Joshua not to be afraid. The text presents the victory as the work of God, not only of the army. This passage is difficult because of its violence, and Christians interpret it in different ways.

For today: when you face something that seems bigger than you, remember that God can give you calm and guidance. Trust Him, obey what He shows you, and do not despair over what you see.
exp.10:12:
It says that Israel did not burn the cities that stood on their hills (cabezos are hills or mounds). Only Hazor was burned.

The narrator of the book describes Joshua's campaign in northern Canaan. Hazor was the most important city of those kingdoms, and that is why it was the only one set on fire. The others were taken, but they were left standing. The text says this fulfilled what God commanded through Moses. It is a hard passage, and scholars debate how much of the language of "destroy" is literal and how much is the typical style of war chronicles of that time.

For today: this verse shows obedience with precision, adding nothing and taking nothing away. Ask God to help you follow his instructions with care and humility, and not to use these ancient accounts to justify present-day violence.
exp.5:25:
Joshua makes the people swear that no one will rebuild the city of Jericho. Whoever tries it will be cursed before God. The verse says Joshua "adjured" them, which means he made them promise under oath. The curse says that whoever lays the foundation will lose his firstborn, and whoever sets up the gates will lose his youngest son.

Joshua speaks as the leader of Israel, just after Jericho was destroyed and burned. He probably wanted the city to stand as a reminder that the victory was the work of God. Later, 1 Kings 16:34 tells that Hiel of Bethel rebuilt it and lost his sons, although scholars debate how that connection should be understood.

For today: let us remember with gratitude what God has done for us, and not rebuild in our lives what He has torn down, such as old habits that used to harm us.
exp.14:22:
This verse names only three more cities of the tribe of Judah: Kedesh, Hazor, and Ithnan. The "and" linking them is the ordinary word for "and," so the sentence needs no special comment. These names belong to a long list of towns in the south of Judah, near the border with Edom. We do not know with certainty where each place was; scholars debate their location.

Here there is no character speaking in the first person. The book of Joshua tells how Israel received the promised land. The narrator lists in detail the cities of each tribe, to record that God kept his promise and so that each family would know what its inheritance was.

For today: God cares even for the details that seem small to us. Though these names may sound unfamiliar, he remembered them and placed them in his Word. You are not overlooked by him either; trust that he knows your place and your need.
exp.7:30:
The explanation says that Joshua built an altar on Mount Ebal following what Moses had commanded. It was made of whole stones, that is, unhewn, with no iron tool ever touching them. On it they offered burnt offerings, which were burned completely for God, and peace offerings, which expressed thankfulness and fellowship with Him.

The narrator of the book tells how Israel, after the defeat at Ai, renewed its covenant with God. Moses had given these instructions in Deuteronomy 27, and Joshua carries them out to the letter. First they worship, and then they hear the law and the blessings.

For today: before moving forward with your own plans, set aside time to give thanks and to put yourself in obedience before God. Obeying what He has already said in His Word, simply and without additions, is a real way of worshiping Him.
exp.20:21:
This verse closes the list of the four cities that the tribe of Ephraim gave to the Levites of the family of Kohath: Shechem, Gezer, Kibzaim and Beth-horon. The pasture lands around each city are the fields where their flocks grazed, and the cities are the towns that held them.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua speaks. He tells how Israel carried out what God had commanded through Moses: the Levites did not receive a territory of their own, but cities scattered among all the tribes. In this way they would live close to the people to teach them God's law and serve them.

For today: God cares for those who serve others, and His people should care for them too. We can ask ourselves how to support our pastor, teacher or missionary, through prayer, practical help or generosity, so that they can devote themselves to serving.
exp.16:2:
This verse tells us that Zelophehad, a descendant of Manasseh, had no sons, but only five daughters: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah. His whole family line is named, going back from Manasseh to him, to show where they came from. Zelophehad is the name that is usually written this way today.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua speaks, as the promised land is being divided among the tribes. Normally the inheritance passed to the sons, so these women risked being left without land. For that reason, in the text that follows, they come before Eleazar, Joshua, and the leaders, and remind them that God had already commanded Moses to give them an inheritance. And it was granted to them.

For today: God sees those whom others overlook. If there is a just need, we can bring it forward with respect and trust in what God has said in his Word.
exp.22:0:
This verse tells us that a long time passed after the Lord had given Israel rest from the enemies around them. At that point Joshua was already old, "advanced in years," meaning of very great age.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Joshua had led Israel after Moses so they could enter the promised land. Now, as an older man, he is about to gather the leaders of the people to give them a final message. The text does not say exactly how many years passed, only that there were many.

For today: when God gives you a time of peace, do not waste it. Use it to remember what He has done, to thank Him, and to encourage others to keep trusting Him, as Joshua did.
exp.22:7:
This verse says the people must hold firmly to the Lord their God and stay close to Him, just as they have done until now. The word "cleave" is an old way of saying "cling to," "stay joined to," or "remain close." It is the idea of holding on to someone with loyalty.

Here Joshua speaks as an old man, shortly before his death. He gathers Israel's leaders to say farewell and encourage them. He reminds them that God has given them victories, and he warns them not to mix with the gods of the nations that still remained in the land. Their faithfulness in the past is the basis for asking them to continue in the same way.

For today: it is not enough to have started well in faith. Each day we can choose to draw near to God through prayer, reading His Word, and obedience, and so remain steady when other things try to take His place.
exp.19:6:
This verse says that the Israelites set apart three cities west of the Jordan to serve as places of refuge: Kedesh, in the region of Galilee, in the hill country of Naphtali; Shechem, in the hill country of Ephraim; and Kiriath-arba, which is Hebron, in the hill country of Judah. The word "appointed" means that they chose these cities and set them apart for this purpose.

Here the account in Joshua tells how the instructions that God gave to Israel were carried out. These cities protected anyone who had killed someone without intending to. In this way, the avenger of blood, the relative who sought to take revenge, could not kill him without a judgment. The cities were spread across the land so that they would be within reach of everyone.

For today: God cares for both justice and mercy. We can imitate him by avoiding hasty revenge and by making sure people are heard before we judge them.
exp.17:3:
Joshua asks the people to choose three men from each tribe that still had no land. They would be sent to go through the territory and describe it in writing, divided according to the shares each tribe would receive. Then they were to return to Joshua with that report. "Inheritance" means the portions of land each tribe would receive. "Return to me" means "come back to me."

Joshua, leader of Israel, speaks at Shiloh. Seven tribes had still not taken their portion, and he gently rebukes them for their slowness. His response is an orderly plan: first to know the land, and then to divide it before God.

For today: when God gives us a promise or a task, it is not enough to wait. We can take concrete steps, make a plan, and ask others for help. Today you can choose one small step and begin with prayer.
exp.0:14:
Here Joshua tells the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh that their families may stay in the lands east of the Jordan. But their fighting men must cross over and help their brothers until they too have been given rest and have taken possession of their own land. "Rest" means peace and safety from enemies. The phrase "on this side Jordan toward the sunrising" means the east side of the river. After they have helped, they will return to their inheritance.

Joshua speaks as the new leader of Israel after the death of Moses. He reminds them of a promise they made earlier: to help the other tribes conquer Canaan. He wants them to keep their word and for Israel to move forward together.

For today: if God has given us rest or blessing, it is not meant only for us to enjoy alone. We can use it to support others who are still struggling, through practical help, time, or prayer.
exp.14:31:
This verse closes the list of cities in the southern part of Judah, in the region of the Negev. It names four places: Lebaoth, Shilhim, Ain, and Rimmon. It says that in total there were twenty-nine cities, each with its villages, that is, the small towns that depended on them.

The book of Joshua is an account that describes how the promised land was divided among the tribes of Israel. Here the portion received by the tribe of Judah is laid out in detail. Some of the numbers in the list do not match the names easily, and scholars explain this in several ways, so it is wise to be cautious.

For today: God keeps his promises even in the details. Names that seem unimportant to us now were real homes for people whom God cared for. Trust that he also knows your everyday life, even the small things, and remains faithful to you.
exp.14:44:
This verse names the city of Ekron, which belonged to the tribe of Judah. It says that it was given along with its surrounding towns and villages. In other words, Ekron was the center of a region with several places around it.

Here no particular person speaks. It is part of a long list describing how the promised land was divided among the tribes of Israel after the conquest, under the leadership of Joshua. Its purpose was to leave a clear record of the borders and cities of Judah, so that no one would doubt what God had given them. Later, Ekron appears as a Philistine city, and the Bible does not always make clear how long Judah controlled it.

For today: God cares about the details, even about the small places that almost no one remembers. You matter to Him too, even when you feel little noticed. Trust that He keeps His promises faithfully, step by step.
exp.13:5:
These verses tell how men of the tribe of Judah came to Joshua, who was at Gilgal, the camp of Israel. Caleb, son of Jephunneh, spoke on their behalf. He reminded Joshua of what God had said to Moses, the man of God (a man who belonged to God and spoke on His behalf), at Kadesh-barnea. That word from God concerned Caleb and Joshua.

Caleb speaks because the people were dividing up the promised land. He had been one of the twelve spies sent into Canaan, and together with Joshua he trusted God when others were afraid. Now he comes forward to claim the promise God made to him years earlier. Some understand the word for his family background as a family or clan; the evidence about this is not entirely clear.

For today: God does not forget His promises, even when many years pass. Keep trusting and obeying with patience, and do not hesitate to remind God in prayer of what He Himself has said.
exp.19:3:
The person who fled to one of the cities of refuge had to reach the gate of the city, which was the place where decisions were made and justice was carried out. There he would tell his case before the elders, that is, the leaders of the place. They would receive him and give him a place to live. "Taking refuge" means seeking protection. "Declare his cause" means he would explain what had happened.

God speaks to Joshua and asks him to tell the people to set apart the cities of refuge, which had been announced earlier through Moses. They were for the one who killed someone without meaning to, and so he was protected from the revenge of the dead person's relative while his case was examined with justice.

Today we can learn that God joins justice with mercy. We can listen patiently before judging and offer a safe place to someone who is in trouble.
exp.6:10:
This verse says that Israel, as a people, has disobeyed God. They broke the covenant when they took things that God had set apart. "Accursed thing" means something devoted to God for destruction, which no one was to take. To "steal" is to take what belongs to another, and "stuff" refers to their belongings or baggage. Moreover, they hid the items among their own possessions, as if nothing had happened.

God speaks, answering Joshua, who had fallen face down and was distressed after the defeat at Ai. God explains that the cause was not a lack of power, but the hidden sin of someone among the people. The text presents that sin as the fault of all Israel, because it affected the people's relationship with God.

For today: hidden sin does not disappear by being concealed. We can ask God to examine us, confess honestly what we have kept back, and let it go. His forgiveness and nearness return when we act with honesty.
exp.15:7:
This verse finishes describing the border of the tribe of Ephraim. From Tappuah, the border runs west to the river Kanah and ends at the sea. The word "border" means the boundary or edge of the land, and "inheritance" is the land received as a possession. This land is said to belong to the children of Ephraim according to their families.

It is part of the account in Joshua, where the promised land is divided among the tribes of Israel. The writer lists places in careful detail, like an official record. This shows that God was keeping what he had promised to the patriarchs. The verses that follow say that Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites from Gezer, so their obedience was left incomplete.

For today: God gives what he promises, but he hopes we will receive it with faith and complete obedience. Think about which area of your life you have left unfinished, and ask him for help to finish it, without letting what is still undone keep living with you.
exp.8:1:
It says that all those kings came together "as one," that is, in a single group, and "with one accord," meaning with one shared decision: to fight against Joshua and the people of Israel.

The narrator is telling the story here; no single person is speaking. The kings of the nations of Canaan had heard about Israel's victories, such as the one at Jericho and the one at Ai. Those peoples had rivalries among themselves, but their fear of Israel united them. By contrast, the people of Gibeon chose a different path: deception, in search of peace.

For today: this reminds us that people can join together with strength to oppose God or his work. We should not be surprised by this. Rather, let us seek unity in what is good, and ask God for wisdom before acting out of fear or haste.
exp.10:10:
"With the edge of the sword" means with the sword, and "utterly destroying" here means destroying completely.

The account describes Joshua's victory over an alliance of kings from the north of Canaan, of which Hazor was the chief city. The text stresses that Joshua was obeying what the LORD had commanded through Moses. It is a hard passage, and many readers interpret it as judgment on peoples whom the Bible presents as deeply corrupt, while others debate the literal scope of the language of total destruction.

For today: the passage invites us to take God's holiness and obedience seriously, without forgetting that in Christ the mission of God's people is no longer the sword, but love, service, and the proclamation of peace.
exp.10:13:
The verse tells that, after defeating the cities of northern Canaan, the Israelites kept the plunder and the livestock for themselves. But the inhabitants they put to the sword, killing them until none were left alive. The phrase "put to the sword" means they were killed by the sword, and "plunder" means the goods taken from the enemy.

The narrator of the book recounts Joshua's campaign against a coalition of Canaanite kings. He insists that Joshua obeyed what God had commanded Moses. This passage is difficult, and scholars interpret it in several ways: as God's judgment on very corrupt peoples, as typical war language of the time, which sometimes exaggerated, or as a reality that remains painful to read.

For today: we do not use this text to justify violence. We learn that obeying God requires fully attending to what He says, without taking away or adding to it. Today that obedience is lived out in love, justice, and mercy, as Jesus taught.
exp.9:36:
The verse tells how Israel took the city of Hebron and put it to the sword, that is, to the edge of the sword. Its king and the people of its villages were killed, and no one was left alive. The text says they did just as they had done earlier with Eglon. The word "destroyed" here translates a Hebrew word meaning to set something apart for God through its total elimination.

This is part of the account of Joshua's campaign in the south of Canaan, after defeating a coalition of kings. The text presents these conquests as the fulfillment of what God had commanded Israel. Many scholars point out that the language of "leaving none" was typical of war accounts from that period and may be exaggerated. Others take it literally. Believers have debated for centuries how to understand these harsh passages.

Today we can learn that God takes sin seriously and that his judgment is real. This invites us to live with humility, grateful for the mercy we receive in Christ.
exp.12:1:
This verse begins a list of the land that had not yet been taken. It mentions "all the borders of the Philistines," that is, the whole territory of the Philistines, who lived along the coast, and "all Geshuri," another region in the area, probably to the south, near them. The words "borders" and "remaineth" mean "boundaries" and "still to be taken."

The one speaking is God, addressing Joshua, who was already old. Israel had won many battles, but important areas remained. God does not rebuke Joshua; He shows him clearly what is still needed so that the land could be divided among the tribes and the work could continue.

For today: we can thank God for what He has already done in us, while still recognizing that there are areas of our lives where He wants to keep working. With humility and trust, let us keep moving forward step by step.
exp.21:29:
This verse tells us that Phinehas the priest, the leaders of the people, and the heads of the tribes heard the explanation given by Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh. The words "princes" and "heads of the thousands" refer to the leaders, and the phrase "heads of the thousands" means those in charge of each group. When they heard them, they were satisfied and at peace.

The tribes on the other side of the Jordan had built a great altar, and the rest of Israel thought they had rebelled against God. So Phinehas and the leaders went to call them to account. The tribes explained that the altar was not meant for sacrifices, but as a reminder that they too belonged to the Lord. The narrator shows that the explanation cleared up the misunderstanding.

For today: before judging someone's intentions, ask and listen calmly. Many quarrels are avoided when we speak with humility and seek the truth.
exp.18:34:
This verse gives a list of fortified cities (with walls and defenses) that belonged to the tribe of Naphtali: Ziddim, Zer, Hammath, Rakkath, and Chinnereth. The names appear in an older form of spelling, such as the one that gives the city of Chinnereth. Some of these cities were near the Sea of Galilee, although not all of the places can be located with certainty today.

The book of Joshua tells how the promised land was divided among the tribes of Israel. Here the narrator, whose identity is not known for certain, describes the borders and cities of Naphtali. This detailed list showed that God was keeping his promise to Abraham to give a land to his people.

God is concerned with the specific details of our lives: places, names, and particulars. If he cared for every city of his people, he also cares for your home, your work, and your family. Trust that nothing that belongs to you is too small for him.
exp.6:5:
This verse shows Joshua and the leaders of Israel in deep grief. They tore their clothes, threw themselves to the ground with their faces down before the ark of the Lord (the sacred chest that represented God's presence), and put dust on their heads. They stayed like this all day, until evening. These were common gestures of mourning and humiliation in that culture.

Israel had just been defeated at Ai, a small city, and about thirty-six men had died. The people were left discouraged. Joshua does not speak yet here, but he acts as a leader who brings his anguish before God. Later he will ask very sincere questions, even with complaint. The chapter explains that the cause was the hidden sin of Achan.

For today: when something goes wrong, the first step is to seek God with humility and honesty. Bringing him our pain is good, but it is also wise to ask him to show us if there is something we need to correct.
exp.9:21:
Joshua gives an order to his men: they are to open the mouth of the cave and bring out to him the five kings who were hiding there. "Bring them out" is an older way of saying the same thing as the verse's "bring out." These kings were the kings of Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish and Eglon.

The speaker is Joshua, the leader of Israel. The five kings had joined together against Israel, lost the battle, and fled into a cave at Makkedah. Earlier, Joshua had ordered the entrance sealed with large stones. Now, with the victory almost secured, he has them brought out. What follows in the text is a symbolic act: placing their feet on their necks, a sign of complete victory.

For today: God gives us victories, but we must finish what we begin with faith and courage. Let us not leave hidden what we must face; with God's help, let us bring it into the light and resolve it.
exp.6:12:
God tells Joshua to get up and prepare the people. "Sanctify" here means setting oneself apart and making oneself clean to come before God. "Accursed thing" refers to something devoted to God for destruction, which no one could take for himself. God says there is an accursed thing among them, and that they will not be able to withstand their enemies until it is removed.

God is speaking in response to Joshua after the defeat at Ai. According to the context, someone took part of the spoil from Jericho, which God had forbidden, and hid it. That is why all of Israel suffered the consequences. God makes this clear before pointing out the guilty person the next day.

For today: hidden sin is never only private, and it takes away our peace and strength. Instead of making excuses, let us ask God to show us what we need to let go of, confess it, and set it aside with sincerity.
exp.16:13:
The children of Joseph, that is, the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, make a complaint to Joshua. They say they received only one lot (the land that fell to them by drawing lots) and one portion, even though they are a numerous people and God has blessed them. The word translated "inheritance" in the source means the land received as an inheritance.

The speakers are Joseph's descendants, and they speak with Joshua, their leader. They lacked land, and they had not succeeded in driving the Canaanites out of their cities. Some understand their complaint as a fair claim; others see it as an excuse for not making an effort. Joshua answers them that, if they are so many, they should clear the wooded hill country and settle it.

For today: before we complain about what we lack, let us consider whether we are using with courage and effort what God has already given us. Blessing does not remove our responsibility to act.
exp.11:3:
This verse continues the list of kings defeated east of the Jordan. It speaks of the territories of Og, king of Bashan, who was of the remnant of the giants, that is, of the Rephaim, an ancient people whom the Bible describes as very tall. Og lived in Ashtaroth and in Edrei, two cities of Bashan. The word "coast" here means the borders or territory.

The book of Joshua summarizes here the victories Israel won under Moses, before crossing the Jordan. Tradition attributes much of the book to Joshua, although no one knows for certain who wrote it. The list reminds us that God had already given real victories and that those lands were handed over to Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh.

For today: when you face something that seems like a giant, remember the times God has already helped you. Remembering his faithfulness strengthens confidence for the next step.
exp.9:33:
After defeating Lachish, Joshua and all the people of Israel went on to Eglon. There they encamped against the city, that is, they set up their camp in front of it, and they attacked it.

The narrator of the book describes how Israel advanced through the land of Canaan, city by city, under the leadership of Joshua. The text presents these victories as the fulfillment of God's promises to his people. These accounts of war are difficult, and believers have interpreted them in different ways. Even so, the passage shows that Israel did not stop halfway.

For today: when you finish a difficult task, do not stop there. God often guides us step by step. Keep going with perseverance and trust that He accompanies you in what comes next.
exp.16:0:
The verse tells us that a portion of land also fell by lot to the tribe of Manasseh, because he was the firstborn of Joseph. Machir, the firstborn of Manasseh and the father of Gilead, was a man of war, and for that reason he received Gilead and Bashan, lands lying east of the Jordan.

The author of the book of Joshua, who recounts how the promised land was divided among the tribes of Israel, is the one speaking. Manasseh was divided into two parts: one east of the Jordan and one west of it. Here the text explains why one part already had land, and it clarifies who Machir was within the family. Exactly who wrote the book is not known with certainty.

For today: God keeps his promises and does not forget anyone in his distribution. Today you can trust that he sees your place and your effort, and be thankful for what he has given you without comparing yourself to others.
exp.16:6:
This verse describes the border of the tribe of Manasseh in the promised land. It ran from Asher to Michmethah, a place facing Shechem, and then continued to the right, that is, toward the south, where the people of Tappuah lived. The word "border" here means the limit or boundary line, and the old spelling "went" is simply the ordinary word "went" in modern English.

Here the book of Joshua tells how the land was divided among the tribes of Israel after the conquest. The text has no speaker; it is a description of boundaries. These details made clear what each family was to receive and helped prevent conflicts. Some of the exact places are hard to locate today, and scholars do not agree on everything.

For today: God cares about the details and about the place he gives each person. You can trust that your inheritance, your family, your work, and your calling are under his care, and live them out with gratitude and order.
exp.18:21:
The explanation says that the territory of the tribe of Issachar reached as far as Mount Tabor, and also included Shahazimah and Beth-shemesh. Its border ended at the Jordan River. In all there were sixteen cities with their villages. The word "boundary" here means the limit or edge of the land, and the "villages" are the smaller towns around each city.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel divided the promised land after entering Canaan. Here the narrator, whose identity is not known with certainty, summarizes the inheritance of Issachar, which was assigned by lot among the tribes. This list reminds readers that God kept his promise to give land to each family. Today it is not known exactly where some of these places were.

God remembers every tribe and every family, even those that almost no one mentions. Today you can trust that he also knows you by name. Give thanks for what he has given you, and faithfully care for that portion of land: your home, your work, and your community.
exp.4:11:
This verse says that the manna stopped falling the very day after Israel ate the produce of the land of Canaan. From then on there was no more manna, and the people fed on the harvests of that year.

The book of Joshua tells what happened after forty years in the wilderness. The narrator is the one speaking. Israel had just crossed the Jordan, camped at Gilgal, and kept the Passover. God had given them manna during all that time, and now that stage came to an end because they already had food in the promised land.

For today: God cares for us at every stage, even though the way he does so changes. Let us learn to be thankful for what he gives today, without clinging to yesterday, and to trust that he continues to provide.
exp.20:35:
The verse says that to the Levites descended from Merari, cities were also given in the territory of the tribe of Reuben: Bezer and Jahazah, each with its surrounding lands. The surrounding lands are the pasturelands around each city, where the Levites could keep their livestock.

The book of Joshua recounts here the distribution of 48 cities for the Levites, just as God had commanded through Moses. This tribe did not receive an inheritance of its own land, because its service was the worship of God. For that reason they would live scattered among all the tribes. Some versions include here four cities, with Jahaz and Kedemoth, although the text in this edition shows variations.

Today we can learn to generously care for those who serve God in our community, making sure they lack nothing necessary to live.
exp.14:50:
This verse ends a list of towns in the hill country of Judah. It names Goshen, Holon and Giloh, and says there were eleven cities "with their villages," that is, with the smaller settlements that depended on them. This Goshen is not the one in Egypt; it is another place in the south of Canaan. Some names on the list are hard to locate today.

The narrator is the author of the book of Joshua, which records how the promised land was divided among the tribes. Here he describes the inheritance of Judah, and the list serves as an official record. It showed that God was keeping what he had promised to Abraham and his descendants, giving them a specific place to live.

For today: God pays attention to the small. No town or village was left without a name in his plan. If you feel unimportant, remember that God knows you by name and cares for the details of your life.
exp.8:22:
Joshua tells the Gibeonites that they are now under a curse, that is, under a consequence for having lied. "Ye" is "you," and "cursed" here means condemned to a penalty. They will never stop being servants: there will always be some among them who cut wood and draw water for the sanctuary, "the house of my God."

Joshua speaks after discovering that the Gibeonites had pretended to be people from distant lands in order to make a peace agreement. Israel's leaders had already sworn not to harm them, so they did not kill them, but they put them to service. The Gibeonites explained that they acted out of fear of dying. Some think their service was also a way of welcoming them into the worship of God, though the text does not detail this.

For today: lies bring consequences, and our promises matter even when we have been deceived. Before deciding, consult God and seek his direction, without rushing because of appearances.
exp.3:18:
What it says: The people of Israel came up out of the Jordan River on the tenth day of the first month, which was the first month of the Hebrew calendar. Then they camped at a place called Gilgal, east of the city of Jericho. "They pitched camp" means they set up their camp.

Context: The narrator of the book tells how God opened the way through the Jordan to enter the promised land. When the priests carrying the ark came up out of the riverbed, the waters flowed again. Gilgal would be their first camp in Canaan, and there Joshua set up twelve stones as a reminder for future generations. Some scholars think this was a starting point for the battles that followed, but the text does not put it that way.

For today: God helps us cross difficult moments, and He also wants us to remember what He has done. Write down or tell someone about a time when God sustained you, so that your faith and your family's faith may be strengthened.
exp.18:29:
This verse ends the list of cities that fell to the tribe of Asher. It says that their territory also included Ummah, Aphek and Rehob, and that in total there were twenty-two cities with their villages. "Embraces" means that the territory surrounded or included them. The villages were the small towns near each city.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel received the promised land. Here the narrator, whom tradition usually associates with Joshua though this is not known for certain, records in detail the division of the land by lot among the tribes. This list serves as a record: each family knew what belonged to it through God's promise. Some place names are hard to locate today.

God keeps His promises even in the small details. If He remembers every city and village, He also knows your everyday life. Trust that what He has given you has a purpose, and care with gratitude for your portion in your family, work and church.
exp.21:33:
They say that the tribes of Reuben and Gad gave the altar a name: "Ed," which means "witness" or "testimony." The reason is that this altar would be a sign between them that the Lord is God. It should be noted that in the original Hebrew text the name appears without further explanation, and some older versions add one.

The narrator tells how a misunderstanding came to an end. The tribes on the east side of the Jordan built a large altar, and the other tribes thought they had rebelled against God. Phinehas and the leaders went to ask, listened to their explanation, and were satisfied. The altar was not for sacrifices but a reminder for future generations: they too belonged to God's people.

Today, before judging the actions of others, it is wise to ask and to listen. And we can also look for simple ways for our lives and our homes to bear witness that the Lord is God.
exp.19:7:
This verse names the three cities of refuge east of the Jordan River. Bezer was in the wilderness, on the plain of the tribe of Reuben; Ramoth was in the region of Gilead, in the territory of Gad; and Golan was in the region of Bashan, in the territory of Manasseh. To "assigned" means that they set these cities apart or designated them for this purpose. A "mistake" here means an error made without evil intent.

The narrator of the book of Joshua tells how Israel carried out what God commanded through Moses. Earlier, they had designated three cities west of the Jordan, and here he completes the six. They were spread across the land so that anyone who killed another person by accident could reach one quickly and receive a fair hearing, without becoming a victim of revenge.

For today: God cares for justice and mercy at the same time. We can imitate him by being patient before we judge, distinguishing between a mistake and a wrongdoing, and offering refuge and a second chance to someone who has made an error.
exp.6:20:
Achan describes what he saw among the plunder from Jericho: a fine garment from Babylon, two hundred shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing about fifty shekels. The bar of gold is the word that the translation calls a wedge of gold, a solid piece of gold. He says he coveted them, took them, and hid them in the ground inside his tent.

He is speaking to Joshua after Israel was defeated at Ai. God had commanded that everything from Jericho be set apart for Him, and Achan disobeyed. Joshua asked him to tell the truth, and here he makes his confession. Notice the sequence: he saw, he coveted, he took, and he hid.

For today: sin often begins with a look that turns into desire. When you feel drawn to something and know it is not rightfully yours, do not hide it. Bring it to God in prayer soon and, if needed, tell someone you trust.
exp.14:17:
As Achsah was on her way to her new home, Othniel encouraged her to ask her father for a field to plant. She got down from the donkey, and Caleb asked her, "What do you want?" The phrase about getting down is rendered in the verse as "lighted off her ass," and the question matches the verse's "What wouldest thou?"

Caleb, one of the faithful spies, had promised his daughter to whoever conquered Kiriath-sepher. Othniel succeeded and married Achsah. Before they began their life together, she approached her father with respect to ask for something more: the land he had given her was dry, and she needed water. Then Caleb gave her springs. Some think Othniel encouraged her out of prudence; the text gives no further details.

For today: do not be afraid to ask God for what you need, with humility and trust. He is a generous Father, and sometimes one blessing needs another in order to bear fruit.
exp.1:8:
Rahab, a woman of Jericho, tells the two Israelite spies that she knows the Lord has given them the land. She says that fear of Israel has fallen on everyone, and that all the people of the land have lost their courage and strength because of them.

Rahab speaks after hiding the spies on the roof of her house. Before they went to sleep, she wanted to explain why she was helping them. She had heard how God dried up the Red Sea and how Israel defeated the kings Sihon and Og. From that news she concluded that the God of Israel is the true God.

For today: Rahab did not see God with her own eyes, but she believed what she heard about Him and acted on it. We can ask ourselves what we have heard about God and whether we respond with faith and concrete obedience.
exp.21:32:
It says that the explanation the Israelites on the Canaan side received seemed good to them, and they praised God. The phrase "the thing pleased" means the matter was pleasing to them. So they gave up going to war against the tribes of Reuben and Gad, and did not destroy the land where those tribes lived.

The tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh had built a great altar beside the Jordan. The other Israelites thought it was an act of rebellion against God and prepared to fight. But Phinehas and the leaders went to speak with them, and they learned that the altar was not for sacrifices, but a reminder that they too belonged to the Lord. The narrator tells here of the peaceful end of the conflict.

For today: before judging or fighting, let us talk calmly and listen. Many times a misunderstanding is resolved through humility and dialogue.
exp.3:23:
The explanation says that God had the Jordan dried up so that all the nations would know that his hand is mighty. It also seeks that his people respect and honor him always. Here the sense of "fear" is not being afraid, but holding God in reverence, taking him seriously and living in obedience.

Joshua speaks to the people of Israel after crossing the Jordan to enter the promised land. He had ordered twelve stones to be raised as a memorial. When the children asked what they meant, the parents would tell what God had done. In this way the miracle would not be forgotten, and it would be joined to the story of the Red Sea.
