Today we can tell our children, friends, or family how God has helped us. And we can remember his works with gratitude, so that we trust in him and live with respect every day.
exp.11:10:
It says that Israel also defeated the king of Jarmuth and the king of Lachish. It is part of a short list of defeated Canaanite kings. The word "one" only counts one more in the list, as if it said "one more." Jarmuth and Lachish were cities in the lowland region of Judah, southwest of Jerusalem.

The narrator of the book gives a summary of the conquests under Joshua, after the death of Moses. Earlier, in chapter 10, these kings joined forces against Gibeon and were defeated. The list reminds us that God kept his promise to give the land to Israel. Who wrote the book is not known for certain; tradition links it to Joshua, but some think it had later editors.

For today: remember with gratitude what God has done in our lives. Just as Israel recorded each victory, we can keep a record of the times God helped us, so that we trust Him in new trials.
exp.12:31:
This verse sums up what Moses gave as an inheritance to the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh. Those lands lay east of the Jordan River, across from the city of Jericho, on the plains of Moab. An inheritance means the portion of land that is received and passed down to one's children.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel received the promised land. Here the narrator makes a closing note: before dividing the land west of the Jordan, he recalls what Moses had already given on the east side. God had guided that distribution, and the text that follows points out that the Levites received no land, because God himself was their inheritance.

For today: God keeps what he promises, even when years pass. We can trust that he knows how to give us what we need, and be thankful for what we have received without comparing our portion with that of others.
exp.9:7:
God tells Joshua not to be afraid of the enemy armies. The phrase "I have delivered them into your hand" means that God has already given them the victory. The phrase "no one will stand before you" means that no one will be able to resist him or hold firm against him. The name "the Lord" is used for God here.

God speaks with Joshua, the leader of Israel. The Gibeonites, with whom Israel had made a covenant, asked for help because five Amorite kings were attacking them. Joshua went up from Gilgal during the night, and God confirmed that he should not fear. Afterward, the account tells how God threw the enemies into confusion and Israel won.

For today: when you do your duty and face something that frightens you, turn to God before you act. His promise does not remove the need to act with courage, but it gives you peace to take the next step.
exp.14:52:
This verse is part of a list of towns in the tribe of Judah: Janum, Beth-tappuah, and Aphekah. It is a small group within a longer list of cities in the hill country. The names are written the way they appear in the verse you are reading.

The book of Joshua shows how the promised land was divided among the tribes of Israel. Here the narrator describes the territories of Judah in detail. These lists show that God kept his promise to Abraham and his descendants. About the exact location of some places, such as Janum, scholars are not entirely certain.

For today: God pays attention to the small things. Even though these towns may seem like nothing more than names, each one was part of his promise fulfilled. If you feel unimportant today, remember that God knows you and includes you in his plans.
exp.5:15:
On the seventh time, when the priests blew the trumpets, Joshua told the people to shout. The "rams' horns" are trumpets made from ram's horn, and the command to shout means to let out a loud cry. The reason is that God had already given them Jericho.

Joshua, the leader of Israel after Moses, is the one speaking. For six days the people went around the city once each day; on the seventh day they went around it seven times, just as God had directed. Joshua does not announce a hope but a promise that God has already given. He then recalls that the city was set apart as devoted to God, and that Rahab would be spared.

For today: obeying God in simple things, even when we do not understand the method, is trusting his promise. Let us persevere in faith, for he fulfills what he says.
exp.3:11:
This verse says that the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh crossed the Jordan with their weapons, at the front of the rest of Israel, just as Moses had instructed them. "Armed" means ready to fight.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. These tribes had already received land east of the Jordan, but they had promised to help their brothers conquer Canaan before returning to their homes (Numbers 32). Now they keep that promise. The following text mentions about forty thousand armed men, and it is not certain how that number should be understood or whether it includes every man from these tribes.

For today: keeping what we have promised, even when we already have our own comfort, is a way of showing love. Think of an unfinished commitment to your family, your church, or a friend, and carry it out faithfully.
exp.5:5:
Joshua calls the priests and gives them instructions: some carry the ark of the covenant, and seven of them carry seven trumpets made from rams' horns, walking in front of the ark of the Lord.

Joshua speaks here as the leader of Israel after Moses. He has just received from God the plan for taking Jericho, a walled city. He passes on faithfully what God commanded, and the priests stand at the center of the march, because the victory would come from God and not from weapons.

For today: God sometimes asks us for simple steps that do not seem logical. Obeying with trust, even without understanding the whole plan, is a way of saying that he guides our lives.
exp.9:40:
The verse sums up how far Joshua's military campaign reached in southern Canaan. The word "smote" simply means that he defeated them. Kadesh-barnea was in the south, near the desert, and Gaza was to the southwest, by the sea. The "country of Goshen" here is a region in southern Canaan, different from the Goshen of Egypt. Gibeon was north of that area. It is like tracing a map of the victory.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel entered the promised land after the death of Moses. The narrator presents these victories as the fulfillment of God's promise and command. These texts are difficult because of their harshness, and Christians interpret them in different ways. Many note that the Bible sees them as a unique moment in Israel's history, not as a model for us.

What we can apply is this: God keeps his promises, even when it takes generations. Trust his faithfulness today, and not your own strength.
exp.8:7:
The men of Gibeon answer Joshua by saying that they are his servants, meaning that they place themselves under his authority. Then Joshua asks them a direct question: who are you, and where do you come from? The sentence explaining the old spelling and the word "Hivites" is removed because those words do not appear in the verse your reader sees.

The Gibeonites knew that Israel was taking over the land, and to save their lives they pretended to have come from very far away. These deceivers are the first to speak, and Joshua answers with caution. However, the account shows that Israel did not consult the LORD before deciding (v. 14), and that led them into error.

For today: before making an important decision, it is not enough to ask questions and trust appearances. Let us pray and seek God's guidance, for He sees what we cannot see.
exp.12:19:
This verse is part of a list of cities: Beth-peor, Ashdoth-pisgah and Beth-jeshimoth. They were towns east of the Jordan River, near Mount Pisgah and the northern end of the Dead Sea. These are ancient names, written here in the form shown in the verse.

The book of Joshua lists the territories that fell to the tribe of Reuben, distributed from the time of Moses. The account is told by the author of the book, and its purpose is to record that God kept his promise to give land to his people. Beth-peor, moreover, lies near the place where Israel fell into sin with Baal-peor (Numbers 25), so the place has a solemn history.

For today: God notices the details and keeps what he promises, even in what seems small. You can trust that he also cares for your life with that same care. And remember that a place of failure can become a place of grace and a new beginning.
exp.12:10:
This verse follows a list of territories east of the Jordan. It mentions Gilead, the lands of the Geshurites and the Maachathites, all of Mount Hermon, and all of Bashan as far as Salcah. These are areas that Moses had already assigned to the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh. The word "borders" in this verse means the boundaries or territories.

Here the biblical account recalls what God had already given to Israel. Joshua is now old, and much land still remained to be conquered. Before dividing the rest, the text reviews what has already been received. The next verse makes clear that the Geshurites and Maachathites were not driven out, and they continued to live among the Israelites.

For today: before looking at what is still lacking, it is good to remember with gratitude what God has already given us. It is also worth checking whether we have left any task unfinished that God asked of us.
exp.9:22:
This verse tells us that the Israelites did what Joshua commanded. They brought out of the cave the five enemy kings: the kings of Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon.

The five kings had hidden in a cave near Makkedah when they fled from the battle against Israel. Joshua had ordered the entrance sealed with stones and guarded until the pursuit was finished. Now he gives the order to open it. The account presents this as a victory that God gave to his people, and in the next verse Joshua encourages everyone not to be afraid.

For today: when you face a great problem, remember that God has helped his people before. Obey step by step what you know is right, and trust that He sustains you, even when the challenge seems impossible.
exp.23:8:
Balak, king of Moab and son of Zippor, rose up against Israel. He sent for Balaam, son of Beor, to put a curse on them. The explanation of the word "arose" in the verse: it is the same as "rose up," and "cursed" means "put a curse on." Although the verse says "warred," in Numbers his attack was mainly spiritual: he wanted Israel to be cursed.

Joshua speaks, in the name of God, before the tribes gathered at Shechem. He reminds them what God did for them: he delivered them, guided them, and gave them victories. He wants them to remember this with gratitude before they decide whom they will serve.

Today: sometimes we do not see the threats that God holds back on our behalf. Remembering his past care helps us trust him and serve him with gratitude and faithfulness.
exp.2:10:
It says that the ark of the covenant, which represents God's presence, is going to cross the Jordan River ahead of the people. The word "lord" in the older wording is an old word that means "Lord and owner," and here God is presented as the one who rules over all the earth. The word "passeth" speaks of something that is already set in motion, even though the miracle has not yet happened.

It is Joshua, the leader of Israel after Moses, who is speaking. The people are about to enter the promised land, but the Jordan blocks their way. Joshua tells them that God himself goes before them, so that they will know that the living God is among them and that they will face the peoples of Canaan with his help.

For today: when you face a "river" that seems impossible to cross, remember that God does not send you alone. He goes ahead. Trust his guidance and take the next step of obedience, even though you do not yet see how the way will open.
exp.14:47:
This verse begins a list of towns in the hill country of Judah. It names three: Shamir, Jattir, and Socoh (which is now written Soco). "Hamlets" and "villages" are small settlements. Where Shamir was located is not known for certain.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel received the promised land. Here the account describes in detail what fell to the tribe of Judah, distributed by lot. The verses before spoke of the coastal region; now the list climbs into the mountains. Later on, Jattir would be a city for the Levites. Lists like these show that God kept His promise to give an inheritance to His people.

For today: God does not forget any place or any person, not even the small towns. If you feel overlooked, remember that God knows you by name. Be faithful where He has placed you.
exp.15:2:
The boundary of the territory of Joseph's descendants goes down again toward the west, passing the border of the Japhletites, then down to Beth-horon the lower, and on to Gezer, and it ends at the Mediterranean Sea. "Goeth down" means "goes down," "coast" is the border or edge, and "the sea" is the Mediterranean Sea.

It is part of the description of how the promised land was divided by lot. The narrator of the book records the boundaries of Ephraim and Manasseh, the descendants of Joseph. No one particular person speaks; it is a geographical list. It served so that each family would know clearly what God had given them. Some of the places are hard to locate today with certainty.

God cares about the details of our lives, even those that seem small. Just as each family received its place, today you can trust that God has given you a place and a task. Take care with gratitude of what he has entrusted to you.
exp.20:40:
The explanation says that the Levites received forty-eight cities in total within the territory of the other tribes of Israel. Each of these cities came with the open lands around it, where they could keep their livestock.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua speaks (tradition often links the book to Joshua, though this is not certain). The Levites did not receive a territory of their own, because their inheritance was to serve God. For this reason cities were distributed among all the tribes, so that they would be close to the whole people to teach them and care for them.

God looked after those who served him and placed them in the midst of his people. Today we can gratefully support those who teach and serve in our church. And if we serve, let us stay close to people, not separated from them.
exp.23:4:
It says that God sent Moses and Aaron as his messengers, that he punished Egypt with the plagues he brought upon the people of that land, and that afterward he brought his people out of there.

Joshua speaks in Shechem, near the end of his life, gathering the tribes of Israel. In God's name, he reminds them of their history from Abraham onward. He wants them to see that everything they had was the work of God, not their own, so that they would be encouraged to choose to serve him faithfully.

For today: take time to remember the times God helped you or rescued you, perhaps by writing them down in a notebook. Remembering his past faithfulness strengthens your trust and your gratitude, and helps you follow him with determination in what lies ahead.
exp.14:42:
This verse only names three more towns: Jiphtah, Ashnah, and Nezib. They are part of a long list of cities. In the old text some of the names are spelled differently from how we see them today (the name in this verse is written Jiphtah, not Jiftá). They were located in the lowlands, the Shephelah, west of Judah. Their exact location today is not entirely certain.

Here there is no character speaking in a scene; it is Joshua's account of the division of the promised land. Each tribe receives its territory, and this list of towns belongs to Judah. The names functioned as a record, almost like a deed of property, showing that God was keeping his promise to Abraham and to his people.

For today: God remembers places and people that may seem small or unimportant to us. If today you feel forgotten or little noticed, remember that he knows you by name. You can live with confidence and serve faithfully where you are.
exp.14:45:
This verse describes the western boundary of the territory of the tribe of Judah. It says that the land extended from Ekron to the Mediterranean Sea, and included all the cities near Ashdod, along with their villages.

This appears in the long list of cities that Joshua distributed among the tribes of Israel. The narrator tells how the promised land was assigned to Judah according to its clans. Ekron, Ashdod, and Gaza were Philistine cities, and the text does not make clear how much of that area Judah actually came to control; the book of Judges shows that many areas were not fully conquered.

For today: God keeps his promises with concrete details, but it is our part to move forward with faith and perseverance. Think about which promise of God you need to keep believing in and working toward, even though you do not yet see it fully fulfilled.
exp.14:23:
This verse names three more towns: Ziph, Telem, and Baaloth. They are part of a long list of places in the southern part of Judah, near the Negev desert. The spellings "Ziph" and "Baaloth" are older forms of writing these names.

The one telling the story here is not a character; the account is given by the narrator of the book of Joshua. After conquering the land, Israel divided it among the tribes. This list shows which towns the tribe of Judah received. We do not know much about these places, and some cannot be located with certainty today.

God keeps His promises down to the details. To Him, no place or person is insignificant, even when the world forgets them. If today you feel small or little noticed, remember that God knows you by name and has a place prepared for you. Trust His faithfulness, including in the everyday things.
exp.14:1:
The explanation says that the southern border of Judah's territory began at the shore of the Salt Sea, which is the Dead Sea. There was a bay or inlet of water that reached into the land and pointed southward, which is the part the verse describes.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel divided the promised land after entering it. The narrator describes in detail the boundaries that fell to the tribe of Judah, according to the lot that was cast. That precision showed that the land was a real gift, with specific places, just as God had promised his people.

For today: God is interested in the concrete and the everyday. Just as he gave each tribe a defined place, he also has a place and a task for you. Today you might thank him for what he has already given you and care for it faithfully, without living by comparing yourself to others.
exp.1:21:
The two spies left Jericho and went up to the mountain. They stayed there hidden for three days, until the men chasing them stopped searching and returned. The pursuers searched the whole road, but they did not find them.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua speaks. Joshua had sent two men to explore the land, and Rahab, a woman from Jericho, hid them and helped them escape. They gave her their promise of protection, and she tied the red cord in the window as a sign. After waiting, the spies returned to Joshua to report to him.

For today: God takes care of us even in times of waiting and uncertainty. The spies did not move forward at once; they waited wisely in the place of shelter. When you have to wait, do not think that God has forgotten you. He may be protecting you while the danger passes.
exp.14:10:
This passage describes the northern boundary of the land of Judah. The line runs toward Ekron, curves around Shicron, passes the hill of Baalah, reaches Jabneel, and ends at the sea, which is the Mediterranean. The word "border" means a boundary or frontier, and "went out" means that the line reaches or ends at that point. Some of these places cannot be located with complete certainty today.

The book of Joshua is the one narrating, and it recounts how Israel divided the land among the tribes. After the conquest, each tribe received its territory according to its families. These detailed boundaries show that God's promise to Abraham was being fulfilled in a concrete way. Right after this, the text mentions Caleb and his inheritance in Hebron.

For today: God cares about the details of our lives, not only about what is general. If he kept his promise with real places and real boundaries, we can trust that he will fulfill what he has promised, and we can give thanks for what he has already given us.
exp.17:7:
The explanation says that the chosen men set out, and that Joshua ordered them to walk through the land that was still left to be divided, to map it or describe it in writing, and to come back with their report. To "describe" means to trace or record the land in detail. Casting lots was a way of deciding the division, and "come again" means "return."

Joshua speaks at Shiloh, where the tabernacle stood. Seven tribes had not yet received their territory and were slow to take it. Joshua organizes the work in an orderly way: first to know the land, then to divide it before the Lord. In this way the inheritance was understood to come from God, not from human preference. Scholars do not agree on exactly how the lots worked.

For today: before receiving what God gives us, it is wise to prepare ourselves with diligence. Let us take concrete steps, plan with wisdom, and place the outcome in God's hands, trusting that He knows how to share things well.
exp.8:12:
Here some men say that their wineskins, which were new when they filled them, are now torn. They also say that their clothes and their sandals are worn out from the very long journey. "Filled" is the word used for the wineskins being full, and "wineskins" are leather bags for holding liquid.

The speakers are a group of Gibeonites, inhabitants of Canaan. They feared Israel after the victories over Jericho and Ai, so they pretended to come from very far away in order to make an agreement. They presented false evidence: dry bread, torn wineskins, and old clothing. Israel allowed itself to be convinced by appearances.

For today: appearances can persuade us, but they do not always tell the truth. Before making an important decision, it is wise to pray and seek God's direction, as the Israelites did not do when they failed to ask the mouth of the Lord.
exp.10:1:
This verse continues a list of kings whom Jabin, king of Hazor, summoned. It names those who lived to the north, in the mountains, in the plain south of Chinneroth (the Sea of Galilee), in the lowlands, and in the region of Dor by the sea to the west. The word "south" in that phrase refers to the direction toward the Negev and the southern lands, as opposed to the north mentioned earlier.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel entered the promised land. Here it is not God or Joshua who speaks, but the narrator. Jabin hears of Israel's victories and gathers a great alliance of peoples from the north to stop them. It is a human attempt to resist what God was doing.

For today: when you feel that the forces against you are many and well organized, remember that God is not measured by the size of the threats. Trust his promise, take the next step with faith, and ask him for the courage to obey him.
exp.21:30:
Phinehas, the son of the priest Eleazar, tells the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh that he now understands God is with them. The reason is that they did not commit an act of unfaithfulness against the Lord by building the altar. Because of this, he says, they have saved the children of Israel from God's punishment.

The tribes on the other side of the Jordan built a large altar, and the rest of Israel thought it was an act of rebellion and prepared for war. Phinehas went with the leaders to ask them about it. They explained that the altar was not for sacrifices, but a reminder that they too belonged to God's people. Phinehas was convinced.

Before condemning someone, it is wise to ask and to listen. We often judge by appearances and get it wrong. Speaking with humility and honesty can prevent conflict and protect unity among brothers.
exp.18:26:
The explanation says that the border of the tribe of Asher, on reaching the coast, turned eastward, "toward the sunrise," to Beth-dagon. Then it touched the territory of Zebulun and the valley of Iphtah-el to the north, passed Beth-emek and Neiel, and went out to Cabul on the left hand. "Turneth" means returning or doubling back, and "on the left hand" indicates that the line lay toward the north.

It is part of the division of the promised land under Joshua. The account describes in detail the boundaries of Asher, the tribe that received this portion. Some of these places are hard to locate today, and scholars do not agree on all of them.

For today: God attends to the details and gives each person their place. You can trust that he also has a place and a purpose for you. Give thanks for what he has given you, and live faithfully within your own "boundaries."
exp.23:18:
Joshua tells the people that they cannot serve the Lord, because God is holy and jealous. "Jealous" here does not mean bad envy, but that God wants exclusive loyalty, as in a marriage covenant. "Transgressions" are acts of disobedience, and "will not forgive" means that he will not simply overlook them.

Joshua, now an old man, gathers the tribes at Shechem to renew the covenant. After hearing the people promise faithfulness, he answers them with firmness. He does not want them to commit lightly. Some understand that he wants them to measure their own strength carefully and depend on the grace of God; others read it as a serious warning.

For today: do not serve God with careless promises or by trusting in your own strength. Acknowledge your need for forgiveness and ask God to help you be faithful to him each day.
exp.14:48:
This verse names two cities in the hill country of Judah: Dannah and Kirjath-sannah. The text makes clear that Kirjath-sannah is another name for Debir. Being called by more than one name was common for a place.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel received the promised land. In this chapter the cities of the tribe of Judah are divided out, and the account lists them in detail. There is no speech here, only a list. Debir also appears in Joshua 15:15-17, where Othniel captured it. Scholars debate exactly who wrote these lists.

For today: God pays attention to specific places and people, not only to general things. Remember that every detail of your life matters to Him, and give thanks for the promises He has kept with you.
exp.1:2:
The king of Jericho sends a message to Rahab. He demands that she hand over the men who came into her house, because he knows they are spies from Israel. The words "bring forth" mean "hand them over." The word "speedily" in the next verse means "quickly."

The speaker is the king of Jericho, alarmed because Israel is drawing near. Someone had warned him that the spies had arrived at night. Rahab was a prostitute, that is, a woman who made her living from prostitution, and her house was near the wall, which perhaps gave the men a place of refuge. The king presses her with authority, but she had already hidden the men, for she had decided to trust the God of Israel.

For today: sometimes the pressure of authorities or of other people pushes us to stay silent about what we believe. Rahab reminds us that God can use anyone who trusts in Him, regardless of their past, and that faith calls us to brave decisions.
exp.7:1:
God tells Joshua to do to Ai and its king just what he did to Jericho and its king. This time, however, the people may keep the plunder (what was in the city) and the livestock. He also orders him to set an ambush, that is, to hide troops behind the city so they can attack by surprise.

The LORD speaks, encouraging Joshua after the defeat at Ai, which came because of the sin of Achan, who had taken what was forbidden from Jericho. Now, with the sin dealt with, God restores confidence and gives a concrete plan. The victory comes from God, but He asks Joshua to use strategy and obedience.

For today: after a failure, God can lift us up again. But He also expects us to act with wisdom and planning, trusting in Him while we do our part responsibly.
exp.14:43:
The verse names three more cities: Keilah, Achzib, and Mareshah. With them the group of nine cities is completed, together with their villages, that is, the smaller towns that depended on each city. Here "Achzib" is an old name for a place, not the city of the same name in the north.

No one speaks in this passage. It is the narrator of the book of Joshua, who lists how the promised land was divided among the tribes of Israel. These cities belonged to Judah, in the lowland area to the west. The list serves to record that God kept his promise and that each family knew what its inheritance was.

For today: God does not overlook details or the humble. Even the most modest villages appear in his Word. This reminds us that you too have a place, and that God keeps his promises even in everyday things.
exp.3:13:
That day the Lord raised Joshua up in the eyes of all Israel, after they had crossed the Jordan, and the people held him in deep respect. The explanation of what they did is this: they viewed him with the same authority they had given Moses. Here the narrator of the book is speaking. The people had just crossed the Jordan on dry ground, and the men of Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh kept their promise to go with their brothers into battle. In this way God confirmed Joshua as the successor of Moses. The Bible does not say that Joshua sought this honor; it was God who exalted him.

For today: if God has given you a responsibility, do not depend on winning applause. Serve him faithfully, and trust that he knows how to confirm those he calls, in his own time and in his own way.
exp.21:15:
This verse records the accusation made by the leaders of Israel. They ask the tribes on the other side of the Jordan what offense this is. Breaking faith with God, meaning being unfaithful, is what they are charging, and "rebelling" means rising up against God. They think that building an altar is turning away from following the Lord.

Phinehas speaks with ten leaders, one from each tribe, sent by the whole assembly gathered at Shiloh. Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh had built an altar beside the Jordan. The others feared it was false worship and that God would punish the whole people. It is then made clear that the altar was only a witness, not a place for sacrifices.

Before condemning anyone, it is wise to ask and to listen. We can guard our faithfulness to God without rushing to assume the worst about other believers.
exp.7:34:
This verse says that Joshua read the whole law that Moses had commanded, leaving nothing out. The reading was done aloud, before all the people: men, women, children, and also the foreigners who lived among them. The word "congregation" in the verse refers to the assembly or gathering of the people.

The book of Joshua recounts this moment after the conquest of Ai. Israel gathered between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, as Moses had ordered in Deuteronomy, to renew the covenant with God. Joshua, as their leader, read the blessings and the curses of the law. He wanted everyone, without exception, to know what God asked and what He promised.

Today we can learn that God's Word is for the whole family and for everyone. We can set aside time to read it at home, with our children or with friends, without skipping the difficult parts, and let it shape our lives.
exp.4:14:
This verse tells how the Prince of the army of the Lord commands Joshua to take off his sandals, because the place where he was standing was holy. The sandals here are the shoes on his feet, and "holy" means set apart for God. Joshua obeyed without arguing.

Joshua was near Jericho, about to begin the conquest. He met an armed man and asked him whose side he was on. The man answered that he came as commander of the army of the Lord. Joshua fell to the ground and worshiped him, and the visitor did not correct him. For this reason many believe it was a special appearance of God, though some understand him to be a powerful angel. The command recalls Moses before the burning bush (Exodus 3:5).

Before we ask God to be on our side, it is wise to ask ourselves whether we are on His side. Today we can approach Him with humility and reverence, and obey promptly, as Joshua did.
exp.18:50:
This verse closes the great division of the promised land. It says that Eleazar the priest, Joshua, and the heads of the families gave the inheritances to each tribe, casting lots at Shiloh, before the Lord, at the entrance of the tent of meeting. The inheritances were the portions of land, and the tent of meeting was the sacred tent where God was present with his people.

The book of Joshua tells this as a narrator. After the conquest, Israel was to settle according to God's promises. It was done at Shiloh, where the tabernacle stood, to show that the land was a gift from God and not a human arrangement.

For today: before deciding something important, place yourself before God in prayer. Recognize that what you have is a gift from him, and manage what he has entrusted to you with gratitude and justice.
exp.18:16:
This verse says that the fourth lot fell to the tribe of Issachar. The "lot" was a drawing of lots, like casting lots to divide the land. "According to their families" means that each clan within the tribe received its share.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel divided the promised land. Here the narrator describes the division after finishing with Zebulun. It was done by lot, and the Bible presents this as a way of recognizing that God was deciding. Then comes the list of the cities of Issachar.

For today: God cares for every family and every person, and has a place for you. Instead of envying what others receive, we can trust that God is faithful and be thankful for what he has given us, using it responsibly.
exp.14:24:
This verse is part of a list of towns. It mentions Hazor-hadattah and Kerioth-hezron, which is also called Hazor. Some believe these are three different places, and others believe they are two. The Hebrew text allows both readings, so there is no complete certainty. We do not know exactly where they were.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel received the promised land. Here the narrator describes the territory that fell to the tribe of Judah, in the southern region. The writer wanted to leave an exact record that God kept what he had promised his people.

For today: God pays attention to the details, even to names that seem unimportant to us. If he kept his word even in places so small, you can trust that he also cares for your daily life and keeps his promises to you.
exp.23:25:
It says that Joshua wrote the words of the covenant in the book of the law of God. Then he took a large stone and set it up under an oak tree (a large tree, like a holm oak or an oak) near the sanctuary of the Lord. The name of God is the Lord, and the sanctuary is the holy place where he was worshiped.

Joshua is already old and is at Shechem, near the end of his life. The people had just promised to serve and obey God. Joshua renews the covenant and leaves a record of it, with a written text and a stone, which he calls a witness, so that the people would remember their promise and not break it.

For today: our promises to God should not stay as words spoken in the moment. We can leave reminders, such as writing a commitment in a journal or in your Bible, so that we can return to it when we feel weak.
exp.7:9:
Joshua got up very early in the morning and counted the people, organizing them for the battle. Then Joshua went up toward the city of Ai, accompanied by the elders, who were the leaders of Israel, and he went at the head of the people.

The biblical account speaks here. Israel had been defeated earlier at Ai because of the sin of Achan, but that problem had already been dealt with. Now God gave Joshua a clear plan, with an ambush. Joshua obeys without delay and marches at the front together with the leaders.

For today: when God shows you the way, act promptly and in an orderly manner. Obeying early, and setting an example if you have responsibility over others, helps everyone move forward with confidence.
exp.13:6:
Caleb recalls that he was forty years old when Moses, the servant of the Lord, sent him from Kadesh-barnea to spy out the land of Canaan. The word "espy out" here means to examine or explore the land. When he returned, Caleb spoke honestly about what he felt and thought, hiding nothing and not changing his report to please the people.

Caleb speaks before Joshua at Gilgal, when the promised land was being divided. About forty-five years have passed since that journey. Caleb asks for the mountain that God promised him, and to make his request he recalls that he was faithful when the other spies were filled with fear and discouraged the people.

For today: speak the truth honestly and follow God even when most people are afraid. Speaking with a sincere heart and trusting God's promises may cost you something, but He does not forget the one who is faithful to Him.
exp.20:11:
This verse says that the fields around the city of Hebron, along with its villages, were not given to the Levites but to Caleb, son of Jephunneh, as his possession. The comments about the old word forms and the meaning of the quoted words are not included here, since they refer to wording that does not appear in your verse.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua is listing the cities given to the Levites. Hebron was a city of refuge and was given to the priests to live in. But the farmland had already been promised to Caleb because of his faithfulness to God (Joshua 14:13-14). In this way both promises were honored.

For today: God keeps his promises with order and faithfulness, and he forgets no one. We can trust that what he has promised is not lost, and learn to live faithfully even when his reward takes a long time to arrive.
exp.3:6:
This verse tells the Israelite parents what they were to answer when their children asked about the stones. They would reply that the waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and that the stones would be a memorial for ever. The reply itself carries the meaning: the stones stand as a reminder.

Joshua, leader of Israel, is speaking just as the people were crossing the Jordan into the promised land. He commanded that twelve stones be taken, one for each tribe, so that future generations would ask what they meant and the story of what God had done would be told. God guided the crossing, and the ark represented his presence.

For today: let us not let the works of God be forgotten. We can tell our children and others how God helped us, perhaps through a journal, a photograph, or an object that reminds us of his faithfulness.
exp.23:9:
God says that he would not listen to Balaam. Instead of letting Balaam curse Israel, he made him bless them again and again, and so he rescued them from Balaam's power. "Rather" here means "on the contrary," and "again and again" refers to several blessings in a row.

Joshua speaks on God's behalf to the tribes gathered at Shechem. He reminds them of what God did for them from Abraham to the conquest. Balak, king of Moab, hired Balaam to curse Israel, but God turned his words into a blessing (Numbers 22–24). Joshua wants the people to see that God cared for them even from threats they never saw, and that this is why they deserve their faithfulness.

Today we can remember that God protects us many times without our knowing it. When someone speaks badly of you or you feel threatened, rest in the fact that God has the last word. And respond with gratitude and obedience.
exp.20:23:
This verse ends the list of the cities that the tribe of Dan gave to the Levites: Aijalon and Gath-rimmon, with their suburbs. The suburbs were the open lands around each town, used as pasture for the livestock. Cities here means the towns themselves. With these two, Dan's total comes to four cities.

The speaker is the narrator of the book of Joshua, who records the division of the land. The Levites did not receive a territory of their own like the other tribes, but cities scattered among all of them, to live and serve among the people. These cities went to the families of Kohath. The name Gath-rimmon appears again in the next verse, this time in Manasseh. Some think these are two different places with the same name, and others think a mistake was made in copying. It is not certain.

God made sure that those who taught his Word were near everyone. Today we can support, respect, and pray for those who teach us the faith.
exp.9:31:
The explanation says that God gave the city of Lachish into Israel's hands. Joshua took it on the second day of fighting. "Smote it with the edge of the sword" means they attacked it with the sword, and "all the souls that were therein" refers to its inhabitants. It is compared with what had happened earlier at Libnah.

It is part of the account of the campaign in the south of Canaan. Here the narrator of the book speaks, presenting these events as the work of God and not only of Israel. These conquests are understood within the story of Israel entering the promised land and of God's judgment on peoples of that region. It is a hard text, and Christians read it with reverence and care, in the light of the whole Bible.

For today: trust that God is faithful to his promises, even when the road is long and difficult. Move forward step by step, without claiming the credit for yourself, and give thanks to him.
exp.18:49:
This verse tells us that Joshua received the city he asked for: Timnath-serah, in the hill country of Ephraim. There he rebuilt it and settled down to live. "Inheritance" means the land a person receives as their own property, and "rebuilt" means he built it up again, like someone repairing a city that had fallen into ruin.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Joshua. He records that Joshua was the last to receive his share, after all the other tribes had already received theirs. The city was given to him "according to the word of the Lord," that is, in line with what God had commanded. This shows that Joshua did not take anything on his own authority.

For today: Joshua served others first and asked for his own portion afterward. We can trust that God cares for us while we serve, and we can work with humility and diligence in whatever he gives us.
exp.20:24:
This verse says that the half tribe of Manasseh gave the Levites two cities: Tanach and Gath-rimmon, each with its suburbs. "Cities" are the towns themselves, and the "suburbs" are the pasture lands around them, where the Levites could keep their livestock.

The book of Joshua tells how the land was divided. The Levites did not receive a territory of their own, because their task was to serve God and teach the people. So each tribe gave them cities, as God had commanded through Moses. Gath-rimmon also appears in the list for Dan, and it is not known for certain why it is repeated. Some think it was a variation introduced when the text was copied, and others think they are different places with the same name.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are caring generously for those who serve in our church. God wants his people to share what they have so that no one who serves him is left without support.
exp.4:3:
This verse explains why Joshua circumcised the people. The generation that came out of Egypt, especially the men of war, had already died in the wilderness. The explanation of the foreskin and of the word "consumed" is left out, since those words do not appear in the verse your reader sees.

The narrator of the book gives this explanation. God had commanded Joshua to circumcise the children of Israel, who were born in the wilderness and had not received this sign of the covenant. They were about to live in the promised land. Their earlier generation had died for not obeying God, and now a new generation had to renew its commitment.

For today: God does not stand on what others did before us. Each person needs their own surrender to Him. Today we can ask Him to renew our heart and to obey Him in something specific, without relying only on the faith of our parents.
exp.6:15:
Joshua got up early in the morning and had all of Israel come forward, tribe by tribe. The phrase "had come forward" can also be understood as "brought near" or "presented." "Was taken" means that God pointed to that tribe, in this case the tribe of Judah.

Israel had just been defeated at Ai, and God explained that someone had taken things that were to be destroyed and had broken the covenant. Joshua, as the leader, obeys and begins the search for the guilty person. The text does not say with certainty how the selection was made; many think it was by casting lots, but the passage does not give the details.

For today: hidden sin does affect others, but God sees it, and He gives us the opportunity to return to Him. We should not wait until we are found out; let us confess today what we know is wrong, trusting in His forgiveness.
exp.14:5:
This verse follows the line of the northern boundary of the territory of the tribe of Judah. The border goes up to Beth-hogla, passes by the north of Beth-arabah, and reaches the "stone of Bohan", a boundary marker. The word "border" here means the limit or edge of a territory. Bohan was a son of Reuben, but it is not known with certainty when or why that stone came to bear his name.

This is not the speech of one particular character; it is the account in Joshua, which describes how God divided the promised land among the tribes. Clear boundaries prevented disputes and showed that God was keeping what He had promised to Israel. Each family knew what belonged to it.

For today: God is interested in the concrete and the orderly. Give thanks for what He has entrusted to you, whether your home, your work or your service, and care for it faithfully, without envying what belongs to others.
exp.17:2:
Joshua asks the Israelites: "How long are you going to keep being slack about going to take the land that the Lord God has given you?" The word "slack" means careless, lazy, or slow to act. "Possess" means to take possession of something that already belonged to them. "Lord" is the name of God, and "your fathers" refers to the ancestors of Israel.

Joshua, the leader of Israel, speaks at Shiloh, where the tabernacle was. The land was already under control, but seven tribes had not yet received their portion. Joshua confronts them firmly and then proposes a practical plan: send men to survey the land and describe it so it can be divided.

God often gives us promises or blessings that require us to take concrete steps. Ask yourself: is there something God has already put within your reach that you have left for later? Today you can take a small and real step.
exp.7:22:
The explanation says that the Israelites captured the king of Ai without killing him at that moment, and brought him to Joshua. "They took him alive" means they seized him while he was still living. The phrase "they brought him" is a plain way of saying "they brought him to Joshua."

The book of Joshua tells how Israel entered the promised land. Here no single character speaks; the narrator recounts the victory over Ai, after Israel had earlier failed because of Achan's sin. This time they followed the ambush plan God had given them. Bringing the king before Joshua shows that the leader of the enemy people was placed under control. The text does not explain why they let him live for a while; afterward he was put to death (v. 29).

For today: this passage reminds us that when we obey God with order and humility, after having corrected our mistakes, He can give us a fresh start. Think about what step of obedience you still have pending and what you can do today.
exp.20:27:
This verse is part of a list of towns. The tribe of Issachar gives two towns to the Levites of the family of Gershon: Kishon and Dabareh.

The commentary explains the words "suburbs" and "villages" in the verse, but I've left those out of the translation, so the explanation here is simply that the land around each town was used for grazing animals.

The book of Joshua tells here how the promised land was divided. The Levites did not receive a territory of their own, because their task was to serve God and teach his law. For that reason, the other tribes gave them towns to live in, according to what God had commanded through Moses. The narrator simply records, in detail, that this was carried out.

For today: God cares for those who dedicate themselves to serving him, and he often does so through his people. We can ask ourselves how we might support, with generosity and gratitude, the pastors, teachers, and missionaries who walk with us in the faith.
exp.20:41:
This verse says that each of the Levites' cities was a separate place, with its own pasturelands around the city, used for cattle and flocks. This was the same in all forty-eight cities.

It is part of the account in the book of Joshua. The narrator, who is not named, tells how Israel divided the land. The Levites did not receive a territory of their own, but cities within the lands of all the tribes. In this way they were close to all the people to teach and serve them. Then the text emphasizes that God kept his promise.

For today: God cares even for the details of those who serve him, giving them a home and provision. We can support with generosity those who serve in our church, and trust that God also provides for us while we serve him.
exp.1:17:
The explanation says that when the Israelites enter the land, Rahab must tie a cord of red thread in the window through which she let them down. She must also gather her whole family into her house: her father, her mother, her brothers, and her father's relatives. The word for the cord is a deep, bright red dye, and the phrase about letting them down means she lowered them with a rope.

The two spies sent by Joshua speak here. Rahab hid them and helped them escape from Jericho, and they promised protection to her and her family. The red cord was the sign to recognize her house. The verses that follow explain that whoever stayed inside would be safe, and that she was not to reveal the plan.

For today: Rahab had to trust and obey specific instructions, even though they were simple. We can learn to believe God's promises and to act on them, also thinking of the good of our family.
exp.14:20:
This verse begins a list of cities that fell to the tribe of Judah. They were the ones in the far south, near the border with Edom. The three first names are Kabzeel, Eder, and Jagur.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua is describing how the promised land was divided. Earlier, the story of Achsah was told, who asked her father Caleb for springs of water. Now the text moves on to list the towns of Judah by region. For several of these cities we do not know for certain where they were, so scholars do not always agree.

For today: God pays attention to the details and forgets no place and no person. If you feel small or little noticed today, remember that your name and your story matter to Him.
exp.6:17:
It says that Joshua had the men brought near, one by one, from the house of Zabdi, and that in this way Achan, of the tribe of Judah, was singled out. The sentence about the old word and the phrase "was taken" is removed, since the reader's verse does not contain those words.

Israel had been defeated at Ai because someone took things that God had commanded to be set apart at Jericho. Joshua, as leader, follows the process by tribe, family, household and person. The Bible does not explain in detail how the selection was carried out; many think of the use of lots, but the text does not specify this. The result was that Achan was exposed.

Today it reminds us that hidden sin is not only a private matter, for it can harm others. It is better to confess it in time, with humility, than to wait until it comes to light.
exp.23:10:
This verse recalls that Israel crossed the Jordan River and came to Jericho. The people of that city fought against them, and so did other peoples of Canaan: the Amorites, Perizzites, Canaanites, Hittites, Girgashites, Hivites, and Jebusites. But God says, "I delivered them into your hand." The word "delivered" here means that God gave them the victory.

God speaks through Joshua near the end of his life, at an assembly in Shechem. Joshua reviews Israel's history to show that every victory was the work of God. With this he calls them to decide whether they will serve Him alone.

For today: when you look back on your achievements or the battles you have overcome, do not forget to thank God. Remembering His faithfulness in the past helps you trust Him in the present and serve Him with humility and gratitude.
exp.5:22:
The two young men who had spied out the land went into Rahab's house and brought her out along with her father, her mother, her brothers, all her belongings, and all her family. They left them outside the camp of Israel.

It is part of the account of the fall of Jericho. The narrator tells how Joshua kept the promise the spies had made to Rahab, who had hidden them (Joshua 2). She was kept outside the camp for a time, and the following text says that afterward she lived among the Israelites. Some scholars see in this a process of purification or of incorporation into the people, but the text does not explain it in detail.

God is faithful to His promises, and He also honors the faith of the one who trusts in Him, regardless of her past. We can keep our word and, at the same time, believe that God gives a new opportunity to everyone.
exp.17:1:
This verse says that seven tribes of Israel were still left who had not yet been given their inheritance. The word "but" is what the verse uses to show the contrast, "remained" means they were still pending, and "given their portion" refers to giving them their share of the land.

The account is told by the narrator of the book. Israel had already gathered at Shiloh, where they set up the tabernacle, and the land was under control. But seven tribes had not yet moved to take what was theirs. So Joshua asks them how much longer they will wait, and orders them to send men to walk through the territory and describe it.

For today: God has already given us many blessings, but sometimes we leave them unused out of discouragement or comfort. Ask yourself what concrete step you can take this week to live out what God has already offered you.
exp.17:10:
It says that the tribe of Benjamin received its portion of the land by lot, distributed by families. "Lot" here is not meaningless chance, but the method for assigning the inheritance. The boundary of Benjamin's territory lay in the middle: between Judah to the south and the children of Joseph (Ephraim and Manasseh) to the north.

The author of the book tells how Joshua divided the land at Shiloh, where the tabernacle stood. After men had gone through the territory and described it in writing, Joshua cast the lots before the LORD. This showed that God, and not human favoritism, decided each inheritance. Many believe Benjamin lay between two large tribes, though the text gives no further reason.

For today: trust that God knows where to place us. Sometimes our place, work, or situation seems small or narrow, but it may be the place where He wants us to live faithfully and with gratitude. Ask Him for wisdom to care well for what has been given to you.
exp.8:20:
The explanation says that Israel's leaders decided to let the Gibeonites live, but they put them to work as woodcutters and water carriers, that is, those who chop the wood and draw the water. The "princes" are the leaders or heads of the people, and the "assembly" is the whole gathered nation of Israel.

The leaders of Israel are the ones speaking. The Gibeonites had deceived them, pretending to come from a distant land in order to make a peace covenant. The leaders had not consulted God, and they had sworn in the name of the LORD. When they discovered the deception, they did not want to break their word, so that punishment would not fall on them. So they looked for a solution: they spared their lives, but gave them lowly service in worship.

Today: let us think and pray before we commit ourselves, because our promises carry weight. And if we make a mistake, let us accept the consequences honestly and seek God's guidance.
exp.0:5:
God tells Joshua to take courage and be strong. He promises that Joshua will be the one to divide the land among the people of Israel as their inheritance. That land is the one God solemnly promised to their ancestors.

God speaks with Joshua after the death of Moses. Joshua now must lead the people into the promised land. It was an enormous task and a frightening one. That is why God reminds him of his faithfulness: he had already made a promise and would keep it. In addition, he assures him that he will be with him, as he was with Moses.

For today: when you face a responsibility that frightens you, remember that God is faithful to his word. Take the next step with courage, trusting that he is with you.
exp.10:19:
This verse says that the Canaanite cities fought against Israel because the LORD allowed their hearts to become hardened. "Hardened" here means that he made them firm in their stubbornness. "Uprooted" means pulled up by the roots, removed. "Mercy" here means compassion or forgiveness. This is said to fulfill what God had commanded Moses.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Joshua, and no one knows for certain who he was. It recounts the conquest of Canaan. Earlier it is said that only Gibeon made peace with Israel. Many believe God was acting as judge over peoples steeped in great wickedness (Genesis 15:16; Deuteronomy 9:5). Others point out that the Bible also speaks of hardening as something they themselves did. It is a difficult theme, and Christians explain it in different ways.

For today: When a passage of Scripture raises questions for us, let us not set it aside. Let us keep reading, compare it with the whole Bible, and trust that God is just and also full of mercy. And let us not harden our hearts when He calls us.
exp.22:14:
This verse says that God keeps his promises, both the good ones and the warnings. Just as everything good that God promised has already come to them, so the evil he announced will also come upon them if they disobey him. The phrase about being destroyed from off the good land means being removed from the promised land.

Joshua, now an old man, speaks shortly before he dies. He sends Israel off by reminding them that God has been faithful. His warning is clear: if they worship other gods and break the covenant, they will lose the land.

For today: God can be trusted both in what he promises and in what he warns. Remembering how faithful he has been to you can encourage you to obey him sincerely and to put nothing in his place.
exp.23:1:
Joshua speaks to all the people on behalf of God. He reminds them that their ancestors lived "on the other side of the flood," that is, beyond the Euphrates River. There lived Terah, the father of Abraham and Nachor, and all of them "served other gods," that is, they worshiped idols.

Joshua is now old and gathers Israel at Shechem, near the end of his life. Before asking them to decide whom they will serve, he goes over God's history with them. He begins at the beginning: they were not a special people on their own merit, since they came from an idolatrous family, and God called them by his grace.

For today: remembering where God brought us from keeps us from pride and fills us with gratitude. Everything good we have began with his initiative, not with our merits.
exp.7:23:
This verse tells of the end of the battle against Ai. The Israelites finished putting to death the soldiers of Ai who had been chasing them out in the open country, and all of them fell by the sword, that is, they died in combat. Then they returned to the city and destroyed it too. The phrase about the open country refers to unpopulated ground, not a place of sand.

It is part of the historical account of the conquest of Canaan. The narrator does not speak about himself but tells how Joshua followed the plan God gave him with an ambush. Earlier, Israel had failed because of the sin of Achan (chapter 7). Here it is shown that God restores his support to them. These passages are difficult, and believers understand them in different ways.

For today: this account reminds us that obedience to God matters, and that hidden sin brings consequences. We can ask him to show us what we need to correct so that we walk with confidence and a clear conscience.
exp.18:20:
This verse continues the list of towns given to the tribe of Issachar: Remeth, En-gannim, En-haddah, and Beth-pazzez. The word "En" means "spring" or "fountain," so several of the names suggest places with water. The exact meaning of some of the names is uncertain.

The narrator of the book of Joshua describes how the promised land was divided among the tribes. According to the chapter, the division was made by lot, at Shiloh, before the Lord. This list shows that God kept his promise to Israel and that each family received a specific place to live.

For today: God pays attention to details and does not forget anyone. Even though these names may seem distant to us, they remind us that He keeps what He promises. Today you can trust that He also cares for your daily life, even in the small things.
exp.16:14:
Joshua answers the tribe of Joseph with a touch of irony: if you are such a numerous people, go up to the forest, cut down the trees, and make room for yourselves there.

The Perizzites are mentioned as the people living in that forest land, and the giants refers to the Rephaim, the ancient inhabitants of the region. The phrase "too narrow" means that the mountain country does not offer enough room.

The sons of Joseph, that is Ephraim and Manasseh, complained that they had received only one portion of land. Joshua reminds them that if they were so many, they could work and conquer more territory. They were afraid of the Canaanites who had iron chariots, and for that reason they preferred to ask for more instead of fighting.

Today, we sometimes complain about what we lack, when God has already given us ability and opportunities. Before demanding more, let us ask ourselves what we can do with what we already have, trusting that God walks with us in the effort.
exp.18:27:
This verse continues describing the border of the tribe of Asher. It says the boundary takes in several towns: Hebron (a different place from the famous Hebron of Judah; some versions read "Abdon"), Rehob, Hammon and Kanah, and it reaches as far as great Sidon, an important coastal city in the north. Where the text says the territory "takes in" these places, it means the land includes or surrounds them.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel divided the promised land among the twelve tribes. Here the narrator, following the division made by lot at Shiloh, records the boundaries of Asher in careful detail. We do not know for certain where each town mentioned was located; scholars debate some of the locations. What is clear is that the land was given according to the promise God made to Abraham and his descendants.

God cares about the concrete details of our lives, even about what may look like a simple list. He keeps his promises with care, place by place. Today we can trust that what God promises, he fulfills, even when the path seems long and made up of small steps.
exp.21:28:
This verse says that the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh would never want to rebel against God or stop following him. They say that the altar they built was not for offering burnt offerings (sacrifices that were completely burned), meat offerings (grain offerings), or any other sacrifices. The only altar for those was God's altar, which stood before the tabernacle (the tent of worship).

These tribes, who lived east of the Jordan River, were speaking. The other tribes believed they had committed idolatry and were preparing for war. They explain that the altar was only a reminder, a witness, so that their descendants would never be shut out from God's people.

Today this passage teaches us to explain our intentions with humility and to listen before we accuse. Many conflicts among believers are resolved when we speak with clarity and keep God at the center.
exp.6:13:
The explanation says that the next morning the people were to present themselves before God in order: first by tribes, then by families, then by households, and at last each man one by one. God himself would point out, at each step, who was responsible. Coming near is the meaning of the act described, and the choosing or pointing-out is what God would do. How that selection was made is not explained here; many think it was by lot, but the text does not make this clear.

God speaks through Joshua. Israel had been defeated at Ai because someone had taken for himself things that God commanded to be destroyed at Jericho, the devoted things set apart for destruction. God requires that the hidden sin be brought into the light so that fellowship with his people can be restored.

For today: hidden sin harms the whole community and hinders our relationship with God. Rather than waiting to be found out, we can ask him to examine our heart, confess honestly, and put away what displeases him.
exp.0:8:
God commands Joshua to be strong and courageous. The phrase "see that I command you" is the same as saying "look, I am commanding you." "Dismayed" means losing heart or giving up. The reason is simple: the Lord your God will be with him wherever he goes.

God himself is speaking. Moses had died, and Joshua now had to lead Israel into the promised land. The task was enormous and frightening. That is why God reminds him to meditate on his law and obey it. After hearing this, Joshua gives orders to the people to prepare to cross the Jordan.

For today: when you face a change or a responsibility that frightens you, do not rely only on your own strength. Set aside time each day to read the Bible and to pray. In this way you will remember that God is with you, and you will be able to take the next step with courage, even while you still feel fear.
exp.16:11:
This verse says that the tribe of Manasseh could not drive out the people of certain cities. The Canaanites were determined to stay in that land and did not leave. The explanation of the words "drive out" and "but" as meaning "rather" or "on the contrary" is set aside here, since those words do not appear in the verse you are reading.

The book of Joshua tells how the promised land was divided among the tribes. Here the narrator explains that Manasseh received cities that were still occupied. The verses that follow say that when Israel grew strong, it put the Canaanites to work for them, but did not drive them out. Afterward, the tribe complained that its portion was small. Some think there was a lack of faith or obedience; the text only shows the result.

For today: sometimes we leave unresolved what God asked us to face, and then it stays with us. Let us ask him for the strength to obey him completely, without settling for less.
exp.22:1:
Joshua gathers all of Israel: the elders, the leaders (the heads of the tribes), the judges, and the officers (those who helped keep order). He tells them that he is now old and has lived many years.

It is Joshua speaking, the leader who succeeded Moses. A long time has passed since God gave Israel rest from their enemies. He feels that his life is nearing its end, and so he gathers the leaders to leave them a final message. He is going to remind them of what God has done and ask them to remain faithful to him.

For today: do not wait until the last days of your life to encourage others to trust God. Take every opportunity today to remind your family and friends of the good things God has done, and to live in a way that makes them want to follow him too.
exp.12:11:
This verse says that the territory of King Og, in the region of Bashan, was also conquered. Og ruled from two cities, Ashtaroth and Edrei, and he was one of the last survivors of the giants, an ancient people whom the Bible describes as very tall. Moses defeated them and drove them out of that land.

The book of Joshua here recalls the earlier victories before dividing the land among the tribes. The account is narrative, not a speech. What Moses won on the east side of the Jordan was already given to Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh. The verses that follow admit that not every people was driven out, such as the Geshurites and the Maacathites.

For today: God finishes what he begins, even when years pass and leaders change. We can trust that he sustains his work, and be thankful for what others planted before us.
exp.6:24:
Joshua asks Achan, "Why hast thou troubled us?", that is, "why did you bring this disaster upon us?". Then he says that the Lord shall trouble him that day. Then all Israel stoned the guilty ones and burned their belongings. "Troubled" here means bringing ruin or serious trouble.

Israel had lost a battle against Ai because Achan took plunder that God had commanded to be destroyed and hid it in his tent. Joshua speaks as the leader of the people, and the punishment fell on Achan and his household. The text does not explain in detail the role of the children, and interpreters understand it in different ways. What is clear is that one person's hidden sin affected the whole community.

For today: no hidden sin is only private. If something in your life is not right before God, confess it soon, before it harms others.
exp.13:2:
This verse explains that Moses had already given land to two and a half tribes (Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh) on the other side of the Jordan River. He did not give the Levites a share of land as he gave the other tribes. The word "inheritance" means the portion of land that each tribe received as its possession.

The narrator of the book of Joshua explains how Canaan was divided. There were twelve tribes, but Joseph was split into two (Manasseh and Ephraim), and the Levites were set apart. So the remaining nine and a half tribes received their land by lot. The Levites received cities to live in, since their service to God was their special portion (Joshua 13:33).

Today we can remember that God cares for each person in a different way. Others may receive things you do not have, but God knows how to give you what you need for your calling. Trust in his provision and avoid comparing yourself with others.
exp.2:6:
Here God speaks to Joshua and promises that from that day on he will begin to exalt him before all the people. The purpose is that the Israelites will see that God is with Joshua just as He was with Moses.

The Lord is the one speaking. Moses had already died, and Joshua was the new leader. They were about to cross the Jordan River to enter the promised land. The people needed to trust him, and God would back him with a powerful sign: the crossing of the river, which is told right after.

God does not ask Joshua to assert himself on his own; it is God who affirms him. If God has given you a new task, you can obey with humility and confidence, knowing that his presence is what sustains your path.
exp.17:9:
This verse tells how Joshua cast lots before the Lord at Shiloh to divide the land that was still left among the tribes of Israel. Casting lots was a way of deciding something by chance, and here it was used to assign each tribe its territory, which was called its share.

The one acting is Joshua, the leader of Israel after Moses. Seven tribes had not yet received their inheritance. So Joshua sent men to travel through the land and describe it in seven parts, and then he divided those parts. Shiloh was the place where the tabernacle stood, so everything was done in the presence of the Lord. The Bible does not explain in detail how the lots were cast.

For today: when something must be shared or a decision must be made that affects others, do it with prayer, order and justice, recognizing that God is the one who gives every blessing. In this way envy is avoided and we trust in his care.
exp.21:10:
This verse tells us that the rest of Israel heard that the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half tribe of Manasseh had built an altar near the Jordan River. It says "over against the land of Canaan," meaning facing it, and "at the passage of the children of Israel," meaning at the place where people cross over. Only a report reached them.

The narrator describes what happened when those tribes returned to their lands east of the Jordan, after helping to conquer Canaan. The other Israelites thought it was a rival altar, and that would have been rebellion, because worship was to be carried out at Shiloh, where the tabernacle stood. The explanation that follows shows that the real purpose was something else.

Today, before judging someone by what we hear, it is wise to ask and to listen. A rumor can give a wrong idea, and speaking calmly helps protect unity.
exp.8:26:
It says that Joshua made the Gibeonites woodcutters and water carriers for the people of Israel and for the altar of the Lord, in the place that God would choose. The phrase "made them" is the same as "put them" or "appointed them." "Jehovah" is the name of God. "Even unto this day" shows that when the book was written, they were still doing this service.

The Gibeonites had deceived Israel. They pretended to come from a distant land to make a peace treaty, and Joshua swore to it without asking God. When Israel discovered the deception, they did not kill them because of the oath they had made. The Gibeonites accepted whatever Joshua decided. So Joshua let them live, but in humble service, tied to worship.

For today: let us think before we commit ourselves and seek God's guidance. Even so, we see that God can use our mistakes and give a place in his house to those who come near to him.
exp.6:16:
Joshua brought Israel near by tribes, then by families, and then by men. First the tribe of Judah was singled out, then the family of the Zarhites, and then a man named Zabdi. The word "brought near" means to bring forward or make present. "Was taken" means that he was pointed out as the guilty one.

The people had just been defeated at Ai. God told Joshua that someone had taken things that were to be destroyed, and this affected the whole nation. Here Joshua follows the process God commanded to find the one responsible. The Bible does not explain in detail how this selection was made; many think of lots, but the text does not specify.

For today: hidden sin is never only private, because it harms others. God sees what is hidden, but He does so with the purpose of cleansing and restoring. It is better to confess in time, before what is hidden comes to light.
exp.10:8:
Joshua obeyed God after the battle. "Houghed" means cutting the tendons of the back legs of the horses so they could no longer be used for war. He also burned the chariots, which were the great weapon of those armies.

The author of the book tells how Israel defeated a coalition of Canaanite kings at the waters of Merom. Those kings had many horses and chariots, and this frightened Israel. God had already told Joshua not to be afraid and that he would do this to the horses and chariots (Joshua 11:6). It was a command for that particular war, and Christians have debated how to understand these accounts.

Today, we can learn not to place our trust in resources, power, or human security, but in God. Ask yourself: what "chariots" give me a false sense of security? Obeying God fully, even when we do not understand everything, is a way of trusting him.
exp.10:14:
This verse says that Joshua fully obeyed what the Lord had commanded Moses. The chain is clear: the Lord commanded Moses, Moses commanded Joshua, and Joshua carried it out. The phrase "he left nothing undone" means he did not skip anything or change it.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, who summarizes the military campaign in northern Canaan. Earlier, orders are mentioned such as destroying the peoples of the land (Deuteronomy 20:16-17) and burning only Hazor. It is a difficult passage because of its violence. Christians understand it in different ways, but the text stresses that Joshua acted according to the word he had received, not on his own initiative.

Today we can learn to obey God faithfully in what he has already shown us in his Word, without trimming what makes us uncomfortable or adding what suits us. Let us start with one concrete step of obedience this week.
exp.23:17:
It says that God drove out from before the people all the nations that lived in Canaan, including the Amorites, who were the inhabitants of that land. Therefore the people declare that they too will serve the Lord, because he is their God. The sentence that explains what "serve" means is left out here, since the reader's verse does not use that word in that form. The phrase "drove out" is what the verse itself says.

Here the people of Israel speak, answering Joshua, who is already an old man. He gathered them at Shechem and challenged them to choose whom they would serve. They remember what God did: he brought them out of Egypt, cared for them along the way, and gave them the land. Still, Joshua answers them seriously, for he knows that it is easy to promise and hard to keep the promise.

For today: remembering what God has done for us strengthens our faith. But gratitude alone is not enough; each day we must decide to follow him sincerely, asking him for help to be faithful.
exp.12:15:
It says that the territory of the tribe of Reuben began at Aroer, on the bank of the Arnon stream, included a city in the middle of the stream, and all the plain (the open flat high ground) up to Medeba. "Boundary" means the edge or limit of an area.

This is part of Joshua's account of how the land was divided. It recalls what Moses had already given to Reuben east of the Jordan. The narrator lists boundaries and cities in detail, and just before this he notes that Levi received no territory, since their inheritance was to serve God. It is not known with certainty where each of the places mentioned was.

For today: God keeps his promises with concrete details, and each person receives a place and a task. Instead of comparing what you have with what others have, thank God for your present portion and work it faithfully.
exp.15:4:
This verse describes the boundary of the territory that fell to the tribe of Ephraim, according to their families. It speaks of the eastern side, which ran from Ataroth-addar to Beth-horon the upper.

"Border" means the boundary or edge of a territory, and "inheritance" is the land they received as a family's property.

It is part of Joshua's account of how the promised land was divided after the conquest. No character is speaking; the author describes in detail the borders of the tribes of Joseph, Ephraim, and Manasseh. These details helped each family know what its portion was. Some of the places are hard to locate today with exactness.
