For today: God cares for the details of the life of his people. If he kept every boundary of every family in mind, he also knows your particular situation. Trust that what he has given you is enough, and look after it with gratitude.
exp.1:19:
It says that if Rahab tells others about what the two spies are doing, that is, their secret mission, then they will be free from the oath they made to her. The word that means to report or reveal is not used here; instead, the explanation's sense is simply that telling others would break the agreement. The phrase for being released from an obligation means freed from the duty they had taken on. To make someone swear an oath is the sense of the last term.

The two Israelite spies, sent by Joshua to Jericho, speak here. Rahab hid them and risked her life, and they promised to save her and her family when Israel conquered the city. Now they explain the conditions: the red cord in the window as a sign, the family gathered in her house, and total silence about the mission. Her faith in the God of Israel is seen in her action.

For today: important promises carry responsibilities. If God offers us salvation or entrusts something to us, we must respond with faithfulness and trust. We can also learn to keep what we promise, and to expect others to keep what they have agreed to.
exp.0:11:
This verse says that Joshua addressed a special group: the tribes of Reuben, of Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh. The word "spake" simply means "said to them," and the old-style "to" in the verse is just the ordinary word "to" in modern English. It is an introductory phrase; what Joshua says to them comes in the following verses.

Joshua was already the leader of Israel after the death of Moses, and he was preparing the people to cross the Jordan River. These three tribes had already received their land east of the river, but Moses had asked them to join their brothers in conquering the rest. Joshua reminds them of that promise.

For today: keep what we have promised, even when we already have our own peace. We can ask ourselves whom we still ought to help, and support others generously until they too can rest.
exp.10:4:
This verse tells how several kings from the north of Canaan joined together and gathered their camps and troops by the waters of Merom. Their purpose was to fight against Israel. Their joining together meant they formed an alliance, and their gathering of armies means they brought their forces together, camped in one place.

The account is told by the author of the book of Joshua. Israel had already entered the promised land and had won victories. Jabin, king of Hazor, called this coalition together out of fear of losing his territory. The text emphasizes that they were very many, with horses and chariots, which was something very frightening. But right after, in the next verse, God tells Joshua not to be afraid.

For today: sometimes our problems gather together and seem bigger than we are. This passage encourages us not to measure everything by what we see, but to remember that God can give us peace and direction even in the face of what overwhelms us.
exp.14:28:
This verse is part of a list of towns. It names three places: Baalah, Iim, and Azem. The old wording is limited. The word "and" appears in the verse as "and," so the list simply joins the names with "and." Baalah also appears under other names in other texts, and it is thought to be the same as Balah or Bilhah, though this is not entirely certain.

Here there is no character speaking in a speech. The book of Joshua tells how Israel received the promised land, and the account lists the towns that fell to the tribe of Judah, in the southern region near Edom. This list shows that God kept his promise to give land to his people, with real and specific places.

For today: God remembers the details, even about small places that almost no one knows. You can trust that he also cares for the details of your life. Thank him today for a promise kept, even if it seems small to you.
exp.20:13:
This verse is part of a list of cities. It says that Jattir and Eshtemoa, together with their suburbs, were given to the priests. The "suburbs" were the pasturelands around a city, where livestock could be raised.

The book of Joshua tells how the promised land was divided. Here the narrator describes the cities given to the Levites, the descendants of Aaron, because the tribe of Levi did not receive a territory of its own. They would live among the other tribes to serve and teach the people. These cities are located in the territory of Judah.

God cared for those who served him, and the people were to do the same. Today we can ask ourselves whom we should support with generosity: our church, a pastor, or a missionary. Supporting those who serve is a way of giving thanks to God.
exp.2:2:
The officers tell the people that when they see the ark of the covenant of the Lord carried by the Levitical priests, they are to break camp and follow it. The sentences that explained the old wording have been left out, since the phrases they discussed do not appear in the verse you are reading. The ark represented God's presence with his people.

Israel is camped by the Jordan, about to enter the promised land. The officers speak on Joshua's orders, giving instructions before the river crossing. They had never been along that way before, so they needed a sure guide. The verses that follow call for keeping a distance from the ark and preparing spiritually.

For today: when we do not know the way, we do not need to see the whole future. We can seek God in his Word and in prayer, and follow with confidence the step he shows us, letting him go ahead.
exp.18:11:
The explanation says that the border of the tribe of Zebulun turned at Sarid and continued eastward, "toward the sunrising," that is, toward the east. It reached Chisloth-tabor, and from there went out to Daberath and went up to Japhia. These are place names that mark the line of the territory.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel divided the promised land after the conquest. Here the narrator describes, by lot, what fell to each tribe; this is the third lot, for Zebulun. The very detailed boundaries show that each family received a specific place. Some sites cannot be located with complete certainty today.

God cares for the details of his people's lives. If he took care to give each family a place with a name and boundaries, he also knows your particular situation. Today you can entrust to him your home, your work, and your plans, thankful for what he has given you.
exp.0:1:
God tells Joshua that Moses, his servant, is dead. For that reason he orders him to get up and cross the Jordan River together with all the people, toward the land he is giving them. The sentence that explained the old wording is removed, since the verse itself uses the words "is dead" and "go over," which the explanation was clarifying.

The LORD speaks right after Moses' death. Joshua had been Moses' assistant, and now he had to take up the leadership. The people had been waiting for years to enter the promised land. God does not let grief stop his plan, and he reminds Joshua that the land is a gift from him.

Today, when a season ends or we lose someone important, God invites us to move forward with confidence. We can grieve and remember with gratitude, but we can also take the next step, knowing that God continues to guide and to fulfill what he promises.
exp.21:2:
Joshua tells the tribes on the far side of the Jordan that they did not abandon their brothers during all that long time of war. They also kept carefully what God had commanded them.

Joshua, the leader of Israel, speaks to Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh. They had received their land east of the Jordan, but they had promised to help the other tribes conquer Canaan. Now that the other tribes have rest, Joshua acknowledges their loyalty before sending them home.

For today: Speaking sincere words of recognition for the faithfulness of others strengthens unity. This week, thank someone who has stood beside you with steadfastness, and ask God that your loyalty toward others would grow out of obeying Him.
exp.4:0:
The explanation says that when the kings of the Amorites (who lived west of the Jordan, in the hill country) and the kings of the Canaanites (who lived near the sea) heard that God had dried up the Jordan River so that Israel could cross, they were overcome with fear. Their hearts melted, meaning they lost their courage, and they had no fight left in them.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua is speaking. Israel had just entered the promised land after crossing the Jordan in a miraculous way. The text shows that God was already at work before the first battle. Right after this comes the circumcision of the people, an act of obedience and of commitment to the covenant.

For today: when you face something that seems enormous, remember that God can work even in places where you cannot see Him at work. Trust Him and obey Him step by step.
exp.17:0:
The whole nation of Israel gathered together at Shiloh and set up the tabernacle there, the sacred tent where God met with them. The explanation for why it is called the tabernacle of the congregation is that it held the tablets of the law. The land already being under their control, with the main enemies defeated, is what this verse means.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Israel had already conquered much of Canaan, and Shiloh, in the region of Ephraim, had become a center of worship. However, the text that follows shows that seven tribes had not yet received their inheritance, and Joshua rebukes them for their delay.

For today: God gives us blessings and promises, but sometimes we leave them unused out of laziness or fear. Before moving forward, the people gathered to worship. We can put God first and then take concrete steps to live out what He has already given us.
exp.7:4:
Here Joshua explains the battle plan against the city of Ai. He and the people who are with him will approach the city. When the men of Ai come out to fight, as they did the first time, Joshua and his men will pretend to flee.

Joshua speaks to the thirty thousand men who are preparing the ambush. Earlier, Israel had been defeated at Ai because of Achan's sin (chapter 7). Now, with the people restored, God gives Joshua a strategy. The retreat is part of the plan, not a real defeat.

For today: sometimes God asks us for patience and humility, even when it seems like a step backward. When we follow his guidance, a move that appears to lose ground can be part of his path toward victory. Trust and obey with wisdom.
exp.14:11:
This verse closes the description of the borders of the tribe of Judah. It says that the western border was "the great sea," that is, the Mediterranean Sea. The phrase "round about" in the verse means the land on every side, and "according to their families" means that the land was divided according to the clans of the tribe.

Here it is not a character who speaks; it is the account in the book of Joshua, which records in detail how the promised land was divided. After the conquest, each tribe received its territory with clear boundaries. Then the text turns to Caleb, who received his share at Hebron as God had commanded.

For today: God keeps his promises and cares about the concrete details of life. You can trust that He also has a place and a purpose for you, and learn to be thankful for what He has given you, without envying what belongs to others.
exp.18:22:
This verse closes the description of the territory that fell to the tribe of Issachar. It says that this land was their inheritance, the property they received from God, divided according to their families. It also mentions that it included cities with their villages, that is, small towns around the main cities. The phrase "according to their families" means that each clan received its own share.

The narrator of the book of Joshua explains how Israel divided the promised land after entering Canaan. The land was assigned by lot, and this was the fourth portion, for Issachar. This record shows that God kept what he had promised to the people's ancestors. Then the account continues with the tribe of Asher.

For today: God cares for each person and each family, even in the details. If today your life seems small or unimportant, remember that God knows you and gives you a place. Give thanks for what he has given you and take care of it faithfully.
exp.20:44:
It says that God did not leave unfulfilled any of the good promises he made to the people of Israel. Everything came to pass. The phrase "not one word failed" means that no promise fell short. The phrase "stood before them" means that no one could stand against them.

The text is written by the narrator of the book of Joshua, who looks back after dividing the land among the tribes. He wants to remind us that Israel was already living in the land God had sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Other passages in the book show that territories still remained to be conquered, so the emphasis is on God's faithfulness, not on everything being finished.

Today you can remember how God has been faithful to you in the past. Write down three things in which you have seen him keep his word, and trust that he will remain faithful in what you are still waiting for.
exp.21:16:
Here the question is asked: was the sin of Peor too small a thing, the sin from which we still have not fully been cleansed, and because of which so many people died among God's people? The words "evil" and "death" here refer to a serious sin and a mass death, and "the whole congregation" means all the people of Israel.

The speakers are the leaders of the tribes on the western side of the Jordan, sent with Phinehas. They see that the tribes on the other side of the Jordan built an altar, and they fear it is a rebellion. They remember the sin of Peor (Numbers 25), when many joined in idol worship and a punishment fell on everyone. Later it became known that the altar was a witness, not a place for sacrifices. Even so, they acted out of fear that the sin of some would bring harm to all.

For today: before judging someone, ask questions and listen with humility. Guard your faithfulness to God, but seek the truth with patience and love.
exp.8:18:
This verse says that the leaders of Israel answered all the people that they could not harm the Gibeonites. They had sworn an oath in the name of the LORD, the God of Israel. "Princes" means the heads or leaders of the tribes. "Congregation" is the whole people gathered together. "Touch" here means to harm them.

The leaders speak because the people were complaining. The Gibeonites had deceived them, pretending to come from a distant land, and the Israelites made a covenant with them without consulting God. When the people discovered that they lived nearby, they grew angry, but the leaders argued for keeping the oath made in God's name.

For today: our word carries weight before God. It is wise to think and pray before promising something, and once we have promised, to strive to be faithful, even when it has become uncomfortable.
exp.11:1:
This verse introduces Sihon, king of the Amorites. He lived in Heshbon and ruled over a territory that stretched from Aroer, on the bank of the Arnon, to the Jabbok river. That was the border with the Ammonites. He also ruled half of Gilead.

The text is part of a list of kings defeated by Israel east of the Jordan. Who wrote the book is a matter of debate, but the account summarizes what God had done for his people. The geographic details show that those victories were real and that God kept his promise.

Today we can learn to remember with gratitude what God has already done in our lives. Write down a few occasions when he helped or sustained you. That remembrance strengthens trust when you face a new challenge.
exp.12:7:
This verse says that the other half of the tribe of Manasseh, together with Reuben and Gad, had already received their share. Moses gave it to them on the east side of the Jordan, while he was still alive. "Inheritance" refers to the portion of land received as a family property. "The servant of the Lord" is a title of honor for Moses.

God speaks to Joshua, who is now old. There is still much land to be conquered, but God orders him to divide it among the nine and a half tribes that had not yet received their portion. This verse explains why: the other two and a half tribes already had theirs. God promises to drive out the peoples who remain.

For today: God keeps what he promises, even when it takes time, and he distributes with order. We can trust that he has a place and a purpose for each person, without comparing ourselves to others.
exp.9:2:
This verse says that Adoni-zedek, king of Jerusalem, sent messengers to four other kings: Hoham of Hebron, Piram of Jarmuth, Japhia of Lachish, and Debir of Eglon. The names of the cities here are Jerusalem, Jarmuth, and Lachish. "Sent unto" means that he sent a message.

The one speaking is the narrator, who tells what Adoni-zedek did. He was afraid, because Israel had already defeated Jericho and Ai, and now Gibeon, a large and strong city, had made peace with Israel. So he looked for allies to attack Gibeon and teach a lesson to those who had switched sides.

For today: fear can lead us to react with anger and gather forces against others, instead of asking what God is doing. Before joining a fight, it is wise to stop, pray, and examine whether we are resisting God.
exp.7:15:
All the people of Ai gathered to chase the Israelites. They pursued Joshua so eagerly that they were drawn away from their city. The point is that they were pulled out of it and left without protection. The word "drawn away" in the verse above conveys this.

This is part of the account of the second battle against Ai. Earlier, Israel had been defeated there because of Achan's sin. Now God gives Joshua a plan: an ambush. Joshua and his people pretend to flee, and the king of Ai, confident after the earlier victory, does not know that soldiers are hidden behind the city. The narrator shows how overconfidence leads to downfall.

For today: trusting in ourselves can leave us unprotected. Before taking a step, it is wise to stop and seek God's guidance instead of relying only on our past successes.
exp.10:2:
This verse continues the list of peoples whom Jabin, king of Hazor, called on for help. It names the Canaanites to the east and to the west, and the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, and Jebusites who lived in the mountains. It also mentions the Hivites, at the foot of Mount Hermon, in the land of Mizpah.

It is part of the account in the book of Joshua. The author describes how the kings of northern Canaan formed a great alliance when they learned of Israel's victories. Their purpose was to stop Joshua and the people. The text stresses that they were many and well armed.

When problems seem enormous and the forces against us gather together, let us remember that God is not intimidated by the number of His opponents. In the next chapter, He encourages Joshua not to be afraid. We can trust God calmly and obey Him step by step.
exp.7:21:
It says that the men of Ai were trapped. The Israelites who had entered the city came out against them, and the rest of the Israelites were waiting for them on the other side. So the men of Ai were caught in the middle, as if between two pincers, and not one of them escaped. The word "possibility" in the previous verse means chance or way out.

This is part of the account of the conquest of Ai. Earlier, Israel had failed because of the sin of Achan (Joshua 7). After they repented, God gave Joshua a plan: an ambush. The narrator tells how it was carried out. It is a harsh passage, and many read it within God's judgment on the nations of Canaan, within the ancient history of Israel.

For today: when God corrects and restores, he can also guide with wisdom. After failing, do not stay defeated: acknowledge your mistake, obey step by step, and trust in his direction.
exp.18:31:
This verse says that the sixth lot for dividing the land fell to the tribe of Naphtali, and that the division was made according to their families. "Lot" here does not mean chance, but the drawing by which each tribe was assigned its portion. The "inheritance" was the land they received as their share.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel divided the promised land. The narrator records the tribes one by one, and just before this he had finished with Asher. The division was done by lot because the Israelites believed God directed the outcome. Afterward, the text describes the boundaries of Naphtali's territory. Some of the details of those places are hard to locate today, and scholars do not agree on everything.

God keeps his promises with care and attention to each family. If today you feel that your place is small or little noticed, remember that God knows you and has a place for you. Trust in his care and serve faithfully where you are.
exp.18:41:
The verse says that the tribe of Dan also received the towns of Shaalabbin, Ajalon, and Jethlah. It is part of a list of places that made up their inheritance. In the King James wording, "lot" is the portion of land given out by casting lots, and "border" is the territory or boundary. Very little is known about Jethlah, and its exact location is uncertain.

The text is narrated, not spoken by a character. Joshua 13 to 21 tells how the promised land was divided among the tribes of Israel, and here the seventh portion, that of Dan, is described. These lists showed that God was keeping his promise to Abraham to give that land to his descendants. The names serve as a record of what each family received.

For today: God pays attention to the concrete and to every detail of his people, even in small places. You can trust that he also cares for your everyday life. Thank him today for something specific he has given you, however modest it may seem.
exp.6:14:
God says that whoever is found with what was set apart for destruction will be burned, along with everything that belongs to him. The reason is that he broke the covenant with the Lord and did something shameful in Israel.

God speaks to Joshua after Israel's defeat at Ai. He had commanded that the spoils of Jericho be dedicated to Him, and someone took them. That is why Israel could not win. God orders the people to consecrate themselves and to search out the guilty one by tribes, families, and men. The punishment was severe because the sin was hidden, but it harmed the whole community.

For today: a hidden sin is never only private. Ask God to examine your heart, confess what He shows you, and do not wait for it to come to light.
exp.0:3:
This verse describes the borders of the land that God promises to Israel. It runs from the wilderness in the south and Lebanon in the north, to the river Euphrates in the east, including the land of the Hittites, and reaches the great sea to the west, the Mediterranean.

God speaks to Joshua after the death of Moses. Joshua must lead the people across the Jordan. God reminds him of his promise and gives him courage for the task. Scholars debate whether Israel ever came to occupy that whole extent, or whether it was a promise fulfilled only in part, for example in the times of David and Solomon.

For today: when God calls you to something great, trust first in his promise and his presence, not in your own strength. Take the next step with courage, knowing that he goes with you.
exp.2:12:
It says that when the priests who carry the ark of the Lord set their feet in the waters of the Jordan, the river will be cut off. The water coming down from above will stop and pile up.

Joshua speaks here to the people of Israel, before they cross the Jordan to enter the promised land. The river was overflowing, because it was harvest time. God shows them that He goes before them, and that the whole earth belongs to Him. The ark stood for his presence among them.

For today: sometimes God asks us to take the first step before we see the way opened. The priests got their feet wet first. We can obey with confidence in what God asks of us today, knowing that He goes ahead.
exp.1:23:
The two spies tell Joshua that the Lord has already given them the whole land of Canaan. They also report that all the inhabitants of the country are fainthearted, full of fear and without courage, because of the Israelites. The phrase "given into our hands" means that God has already placed the land in their power.

The two men are the ones Joshua had sent secretly to Jericho. There Rahab protected them and told them that the people trembled when they heard what God had done for Israel, as at the Red Sea. On their return, the spies report to Joshua. Their conclusion is based not only on what they saw, but on God's faithfulness to his promise.

When God has promised something, we can face challenges with humble confidence. This does not mean that everything will be easy, but that God goes before us. Before taking a difficult step, pray, remember how God has helped you before, and move forward in faith.
exp.5:6:
Here Joshua gives the order to begin the march around Jericho. He says that the people must move forward and go around the city, and that the armed men must go ahead of the ark of the Lord. The word "compass" means to go around in a circle, and the ark was the sacred chest that represented God's presence with his people.

Joshua speaks here as the leader who succeeded Moses. He does so after receiving instructions from God to take Jericho. It is an unusual plan: this is not a normal attack, but obedience taken one step at a time. The soldiers go at the front, but they follow the ark, that is, God.

For today: sometimes God asks us to take a step of obedience without explaining the whole path. We can move forward with confidence, putting his presence first, even when the plan seems strange to us.
exp.21:13:
This verse says that, together with Phinehas the priest, ten leaders were sent: one from each family house of the tribes of Israel. "Prince" here means leader or chief. Each one was the head of his family among the people. That is, these were not just anyone, but men with authority and responsibility.

The account is told by the narrator of the book of Joshua. The tribes on the west side heard that the tribes on the east side had built an altar by the Jordan, and they feared that they had rebelled against God. Before fighting, they sent a representative delegation to ask for an explanation. The text says nothing more about how they were chosen.

For today: when something troubles us about other believers, it is wise to proceed calmly, in a sensible group, and with a willingness to listen. Speaking first and respectfully can prevent a serious conflict caused by a misunderstanding.
exp.6:6:
Joshua cries out to God in grief and complaint. He asks why God brought the people across the Jordan if he was going to let the Amorites destroy them. He says it would have been better to have stayed on the other side of the Jordan.

Joshua, the leader of Israel, speaks after the defeat at Ai. About thirty-six men died, and the people were left afraid. Joshua falls face down before the ark with the elders. His complaint is sincere, although later God shows him that the cause of the defeat was sin hidden among the people.

For today: when something goes wrong, we can speak to God honestly, even in the middle of pain. But we should also listen, ask him for light, and be willing to examine our hearts, instead of accusing him.
exp.4:6:
This verse says that Joshua circumcised the children of the Israelites who had died in the wilderness. Those children had taken the place of their parents, but they had never received circumcision during the journey. The sentence explaining the first quoted word is removed, and the phrase "by the way" is simply rendered as the journey itself, referring to the years in the wilderness.

Here the narrator of the book explains why Joshua did this before entering the promised land. Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham. The previous generation had disobeyed, and now the new people were renewing their commitment to God. The Bible does not explain in detail why it had not been done earlier.

For today: before moving on to the new things God gives us, it is good to stop and renew our commitment to Him, with an obedient heart and not merely with outward customs.
exp.5:16:
It says that Jericho would be "anathema" to the Lord, that is, totally given over to God to be destroyed, along with everything in it. Only Rahab, the harlot (a woman who sold her body), would live together with those who were in her house, because she hid the messengers, that is, the spies that Israel sent.

Joshua speaks to the people just before the city falls, after the seventh circuit. He explains that Jericho belongs to God and that they must not take anything for themselves. Rahab is the exception, because she protected the spies. Scholars understand the severity of the devoting to destruction in various ways, but the text presents it as an act of judgment and total obedience.

For today: God honors humble faith, regardless of a person's past. Rahab received mercy for acting in faith. Today we can trust that God welcomes whoever comes to Him with sincerity.
exp.16:16:
Joshua answers the tribe of Joseph, made up of Ephraim and Manasseh. He tells them that they are a numerous and strong people, and that for this reason they will not receive only one portion of land, but more. The word "lot" refers to the land divided by casting lots, that is, a portion of land.

Joshua speaks because they had complained that their territory was too small. At the same time, they were afraid of the Canaanites of the valley, who had chariots of iron. Joshua does not give them an excuse, but a challenge: to take the forested mountain and drive out the enemies. Some think there is some irony in his answer, but the text does not say so clearly.

For today: sometimes we complain that we lack space or opportunity, when God has given us strength to work and move forward. Ask for his help, and take the step before you, even if it takes effort.
exp.21:18:
Here it is said that if the children of Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh thought their land east of the Jordan was unclean (impure for worship), they could move to the land where the tabernacle stood and live with the rest of Israel. What they must not do was rebel by building another altar apart from the altar of God. The sentence about the phrase that means "in addition to" or "apart from" is removed because that wording is not in the verse your reader sees.

The speakers are the leaders of the western tribes, with Phinehas the priest. They saw a great altar by the Jordan and believed it was an act of rebellion. They feared that the sin of some would bring punishment on all, as had happened with Peor and with Achan. Later it would be made clear that the altar was only a witness, not meant for sacrifices.

For today: before judging someone, let us speak with them and listen. But let us also take sin seriously, because it affects the whole community.
exp.3:19:
This verse says that Joshua set up a memorial with twelve stones at Gilgal. The stones had been taken from the Jordan River, from the place where the priests had stood with the ark.

It is part of the account of Israel crossing the Jordan to enter the promised land. The author of the book tells the story, and Joshua is the leader of the people. The stones were a reminder, as the following verses show: when their children asked what they meant, the parents would tell them that God dried up the river so that Israel could pass. Gilgal lies to the east of Jericho.

For today: God wants us to remember what he has done for us and to tell others about it. Think of a help God has given you and find a simple way to keep it in mind, such as writing it in a notebook, and share it with your family.
exp.9:27:
That day Joshua captured the city of Makkedah. The phrase about putting it to the sword means that he attacked it with the sword. Its king and all its inhabitants died, and no one was left alive. What happened to the king of Makkedah was the same as what happened to the king of Jericho.

The narrator of the book describes Joshua's campaign in southern Canaan, right after defeating the alliance of five kings who attacked Gibeon. The book presents these conquests as the fulfillment of God's promise to Israel and as judgment on peoples whom God had already warned. Many scholars debate how literally the language of total destruction should be read, since the Bible itself shows that some peoples continued to live there.

Today we do not use violence to serve God, since Jesus called us to love even our enemies. We can still learn that God keeps what he promises and that he takes justice seriously. Trust his faithfulness with humility.
exp.8:24:
The Gibeonites say to Joshua: "We are in your hand. Do with us whatever seems good and right to you." In this way they fully surrender themselves to his decision. The phrase "here we are" in the original is simply the wording "we are here," and it is translated as part of this verse.

Hold on: the second part of that paragraph is needed. Here is the complete translation:

The Gibeonites say to Joshua: "We are in your hand. Do with us whatever seems good and right to you." In this way they fully surrender themselves to his decision.

The people of Gibeon had deceived Israel by pretending to be travelers from distant lands, and Joshua made a covenant with them. When the deception was discovered, Joshua confronted them. They confessed that they feared for their lives, because they knew what God had promised to Israel. Here they speak humbly, without defending themselves, and accept whatever Joshua decides.

For today: when we fail or act wrongly, the wisest course is to acknowledge it with humility and place ourselves in God's hands, who is just and merciful. The Gibeonites, although they had lied, sought refuge in the God of Israel, and their lives were preserved.
exp.12:23:
This verse says that Moses gave land to the tribe of Gad, giving each family of the children of Gad its share. "Gave" is the word "dio," and "according to their families" means that the inheritance was divided among the family groups of the tribe.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua speaks. Israel was about to enter the promised land, and the text reviews what Moses had already distributed, east of the Jordan. Gad, Reuben, and half the tribe of Manasseh received their territory there. The verses that follow list the cities and borders of Gad. For the Israelites, the land was a promise fulfilled by God, and recording it prevented future disputes.

For today: God cares for each family, not only for the crowds. We can thank him for what he has given us and manage it with order and honesty, without envying what belongs to others.
exp.10:21:
This verse says that the Anakims, a people known for the strength and height of their men, were no longer left in the part of the land that the Israelites occupied. They survived only in three Philistine cities: Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod. The word "left" here means that they remained or survived.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel entered Canaan. The narrator summarizes that Joshua removed the Anakims from the mountains. Earlier, the spies had feared these men (Numbers 13). Later, Caleb received Hebron and drove the Anakims out of there (Joshua 14–15). Gath, the city of Goliath, was among the cities where they remained.

For today: God keeps his promises, even when the obstacle seems enormous. What once caused fear can be faced with faith and obedience, one step at a time, trusting that God goes before us.
exp.11:5:
This verse says that Moses, called "the servant of the Lord," and the people of Israel defeated the kings Sihon and Og. Then Moses gave those lands east of the Jordan to the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh. "Smote" means they defeated them in battle, and "gave" is what the verse uses for handing over the land.

The author of the book of Joshua makes a summary here of Israel's victories. First he reviews what happened east of the Jordan, under Moses, and then what happened west of it, under Joshua. This reminds us that the land was a gift from God, fulfilled little by little.

For today: remembering with gratitude what God has already done gives us confidence for what lies ahead. You can write down the times God has helped you and thank him, without forgetting that every good thing is a gift from him.
exp.12:30:
This verse says that half of the territory of Gilead, along with the cities of Ashtaroth and Edrei, which had once been part of the kingdom of King Og in Bashan, was given to the descendants of Machir, son of Manasseh. Each family received its share.

The narrator of the book of Joshua summarizes how Moses divided the lands east of the Jordan, before Israel entered Canaan. Those lands had been taken by defeating Og. Machir and his clan were known as warriors, and so it is fitting that they received this region. Afterward the text reminds us that the tribe of Levi received no land, because God himself was their inheritance.

For today: God keeps his promises with attention to detail, and every person matters in his plan. We can trust that he cares for our family and our needs. We can also be thankful for what we have received, knowing that the most valuable thing is to have God himself.
exp.14:36:
This verse is part of a list of towns. It names three more cities: Zenan, Hadashah, and Migdal-gad. They belong to a group of cities in the tribe of Judah, in the low country or plain to the west, called the Shephelah. There are no hard words here; they are simply the old names of places, and today it is not known for certain where all of them were.

Here no character is speaking. The book of Joshua tells how the promised land was divided among the tribes. This list of towns shows that God's promise to Israel became real in concrete places. The author records each name to keep a record of Judah's inheritance.

For today: God pays attention to details and keeps his promises, even in small things. If today you feel forgotten or unimportant, remember that God knows your name and your place, just as he did not overlook these small towns.
exp.20:33:
This verse says that the descendants of Merari, one of the Levite families who had not yet received cities, were given towns in the tribe of Zebulun: Jokneam and Kartah. The "suburbs" are the open lands around each town, used for livestock and pasture.

The speaker is the narrator of the book of Joshua. He tells how Israel gave cities to the Levites, because they did not receive a territory of their own like the other tribes. They would live scattered among all the people to teach the law and serve in worship. Some biblical lists of these cities differ a little, and the reason is not known for certain.

Today we can care for and support those who serve in the church, and remember that serving God is lived out close to people, in everyday life.
exp.5:18:
This verse says that all the gold, silver, and objects of bronze and iron found in Jericho were to be set apart for God. They were not to be plunder for the soldiers, but were to go into the Lord's treasury, the place where offerings for God's service were kept.

The one speaking is Joshua, instructing the people before the fall of Jericho. It was the first city conquered in Canaan, so it functioned as a firstfruits belonging to God. That is why he warns them not to take anything set apart for destruction, so that they would not bring trouble on the camp.

For today: the first and best of what God gives us belongs to Him. We can be honest and generous, returning to Him with gratitude a part of our time, money, and talents.
exp.17:25:
This verse continues a list of towns belonging to the tribe of Benjamin. It names three: Mizpah, Chephirah (spelled "Chephirah" here), and Mozah. They were small villages, and here only their names appear. An inheritance was the land a family received and passed on to its children.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel divided the promised land. This passage describes the portion that fell to Benjamin, according to the families of the tribe. It is not known with certainty who wrote this list, but its purpose is to record that God kept what he had promised his people, even in the smallest places.

God does not overlook the details or the people who are little known. If today you feel passed over, remember that he sees your place and your life. Trust that he cares for you, and give thanks for what he has given you.
exp.5:8:
This verse describes the order of the march around Jericho. First came the armed men, then the priests blowing the trumpets (which were horns made from rams' horns), and at the end the rest of the people, following behind the ark. Everyone kept walking, and the horns kept sounding without stopping.

The narrator tells what happened when Joshua gave the instructions of God for taking Jericho. The ark of the covenant represented the presence of the Lord, and that is why it held a central place. God was asking them to obey a plan that did not look like an ordinary war strategy. What Joshua commands next is to keep silent until the order to shout.

For today: sometimes God asks us to take steps of obedience even when we do not understand the whole plan. You can walk with confidence, putting his presence first and moving forward patiently in what he is showing you today.
exp.11:17:
This verse follows a list of defeated kings. It names two more: the king of Aphek and the king of Lasharon. The word "one" in the verse stands for one more victory, and each one is counted as it is listed. The location of Lasharon is not certain, and some scholars think the original text may say something different.

The book of Joshua summarizes here Israel's conquests west of the Jordan. The one who recounts them, traditionally Joshua or those who continued his writing, wants to show that God kept his promise to give the land to his people. That is why he names each victory one by one, even in a long and simple list.

Today, this text reminds us that God is faithful in the details too. Your life may not have great feats, but you can write down the small help God has given you and thank him for each one. Remembering them strengthens confidence for what lies ahead.
exp.18:15:
This verse closes the description of the territory that fell to the tribe of Zebulun. "Inheritance" means the land received as a portion handed down to them. "According to their families" means the land was divided according to the clans of the tribe. The "villages" were the small towns around each city.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel divided the promised land. The narrator is not a character who speaks, but the one who records the division made by lot, under the direction of Joshua. Shortly before, twelve cities with their villages are mentioned. They are listed to show that God kept his promise and that each tribe knew what its share was.

For today: God cares for each family and gives it a place. Instead of comparing what you have with what others have, thank God for what he has given you and care for it faithfully, whether it is your home, your work, or your community.
exp.11:14:
This verse is part of a list of Canaanite kings. It says that Joshua and the Israelites defeated the king of Libnah and the king of Adullam. The word "one" in the verse means one more: each king counts as one victory. In total the list adds up to thirty-one kings.

The narrator is the author of the book of Joshua; tradition attributes it in part to Joshua, though this is not certain. After recounting the battles, he summarizes all the conquests west of the Jordan. His purpose is to remind Israel that God kept his promise to give them the land. These cities appear in earlier accounts in the book.

For today: God cares for the details and remembers every name. We can remember the small helps he has given us, write them down, and thank him, so that we trust him more when we face new challenges.
exp.3:16:
Joshua carries out God's command and tells the priests who were carrying the ark to come up out of the Jordan River. "Ark of the testimony" refers to the sacred chest where the tablets of the law were kept.

God had just spoken to Joshua, and he repeats the order exactly as he received it. The people had already crossed the river on dry ground, and the priests had stood in the middle of the riverbed while everyone passed. When they came out, the waters flowed back, as the text that follows says.

For today: this verse teaches us to obey God step by step, both when moving forward and when pausing. Joshua did not go ahead or change the instruction. We can ask God to help us wait for his signal and to act simply when he shows us the moment.
exp.18:1:
This verse begins the list of towns that the tribe of Simeon received. It says that they had as their inheritance Beersheba, Sheba, and Moladah. "Inheritance" means the land that was given to them as their own. "Had" means the same as "received." Some translators and scholars note that "Sheba" does not appear in other parallel lists, so it could be a variant of the name or a copying error; there is no certainty.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua speaks, recording how the promised land was divided among the tribes. The lot of Simeon fell within the territory of Judah, in the south. This fulfills what was said earlier about Simeon, and the Bible does not explain it in more detail.

For today: God keeps his promises with detail, and each person has a place that matters to him. You can trust that God does not forget you, even when your part seems small or hidden. Serve faithfully where he has placed you.
exp.0:13:
It says that the families and livestock of these tribes would stay on the eastern side of the Jordan, in the land Moses had given them. But the brave and strong men would cross the river with their weapons, at the front of their brothers, to help them. The word "cattle" refers to the livestock, and "armed" means ready for war.

Joshua speaks to Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh. They had already received their land in the time of Moses, on the condition that they would accompany the other tribes in the conquest. Joshua reminds them of that promise before they enter Canaan.

For today: when God gives us rest or blessing, it is not so that we may simply stay comfortable, but so that we can help others who are still struggling. We can ask ourselves whom we might accompany with our time, strength, or resources.
exp.23:30:
It says that the people of Israel worshiped and obeyed God while Joshua lived, and also while the elders lived who outlived Joshua. Those elders had seen with their own eyes the mighty works of God on Israel's behalf. "Served" means that they remained faithful to him and obeyed him. "The Lord" is the name of God.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, summarizing Joshua's life right after recounting his death. Joshua had led Israel into the promised land and had called them to serve God alone. The text shows that the people's faithfulness depended greatly on those who remembered what God had done. The book of Judges later tells that another generation did not know him (Judges 2:10).

For today: let us not allow faith to fade with time. Let us remember what God has done in our lives and tell it to our children and friends, so that they too may come to know him.
exp.11:7:
This verse describes the places where Joshua and the Israelites defeated their enemies: mountains, valleys, plains, hillsides, the wilderness, and the south. The hillsides, the sloping sides of the hills, are named along with the other terrain, and the south is the region toward the Negev. It also names the peoples who lived there: the Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites.

The author of the book gives here a summary of the conquests. Earlier he mentions what was achieved under Moses east of the Jordan, and now he summarizes what was achieved under Joshua west of it. Then comes the list of the kings who were defeated. It recalls that God had kept his promise to give the land to Israel. Who wrote the book is not known for certain.

For today: God keeps what he promises, even when the road passes through mountains, valleys, and deserts. When you face a difficult season, remember the times God has been faithful and trust that he will continue to be.
exp.6:7:
Joshua is distressed and speaks to God. He cries out "O Lord" as an expression of grief and bewilderment. He asks what he can say now that Israel has turned their backs, that is, has fled defeated before their enemies.

Joshua speaks after the defeat at Ai. Israel expected to win, but they lost, and some soldiers died. He tears his clothes and falls prostrate before the ark as a sign of mourning. He is concerned for the people and for the good name of God. Then God explains to him that there was sin in the camp, since someone had taken forbidden things.

When something goes wrong for us, we can bring it to God with sincerity, as Joshua did. But it is also wise to ask him whether there is something we should correct, and to be willing to obey.
exp.21:20:
This verse only presents the moment when the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half tribe of Manasseh begin to answer. They speak to "the heads of the thousands of Israel," that is, the leaders and representatives of the people who had come to call them to account. The word "answered" shows that now it is their turn to give their explanation.

These tribes lived on the east side of the Jordan River, and they had built a large altar beside the river. The other tribes thought this was an act of rebellion against God, and they prepared for war. Before fighting, they sent envoys to ask questions. Now the accused respond, and in the verses that follow they explain their true intentions.

For today: before judging someone by what it appears they have done, it is wise to ask and to listen. And if we are accused, we can answer with calm, with humility, and with honesty before God.
exp.7:5:
Here Joshua explains the battle plan against the city of Ai. He says that the men of Ai will come out to chase them, until they are far from the city. They will think that Israel is fleeing as in the first battle. Then Joshua and his people will pretend to flee.

The one speaking is Joshua, the leader of Israel. In the first battle against Ai, Israel had been defeated because of Achan's sin (ch. 7). Now God gives a different strategy: an ambush. The deception serves to draw the soldiers of the city out, so that another group can enter. Some readers wonder about the ethics of this kind of deception in war; the text presents it as a command from God.

Today we can learn that, after a failure, God can still guide us. It is good to turn back to Him, correct whatever needs correcting, and follow His direction with humility and obedience.
exp.20:37:
This verse says that the tribe of Gad handed over several cities to the Levites. Two are named here: Ramoth, in the region of Gilead, and Mahanaim. Ramoth was also a city of refuge for someone who had killed another person without meaning to. The pasturelands around the city, where the Levites could keep their livestock, are its suburbs.

It is part of a list of cities that Israel gave to the Levites, who did not receive a territory of their own as the other tribes did. The account of Joshua lists these places to show that what God had commanded through Moses was fulfilled. Here it speaks of the sons of Merari, one of the Levite families.

For today: God cared for those who served others and also for the one who needed protection. We can ask ourselves whom we can offer help and refuge to, and whom we should support, such as those who serve in our church.
exp.4:4:
This verse explains that the men who came out of Egypt were circumcised, but those who were born later, during the years in the wilderness, were not. Being circumcised means the circumcision had been performed on them, the sign of God's covenant with Abraham. Those who had not received it were uncircumcised.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua speaks. He explains why Joshua, just as they were entering the promised land, circumcised a whole new generation. The previous generation had died for not obeying God. The children now had to receive the sign of the covenant before beginning their life in the land. The Bible does not detail why it was not done on the journey.

For today: God takes care that each generation lives its own relationship with Him. The faith of our parents is not enough; today you can choose to obey Him with a willing heart.
exp.5:10:
This verse tells that the ark of the Lord went around the city one time, on the first day. Afterward, the people returned to the camp, which is called here "camp," and they spent the night there. The "trumpets" were horns made from rams' horns.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Joshua. He describes how Israel obeyed God's instructions to take Jericho. Joshua had told the people to keep completely silent until the moment to shout. The daily march was simple and repetitive and did not seem like a battle plan, but it showed that the victory depended on God.

For today: sometimes God asks us to take small, steady steps, even when we do not yet see results. Obey what God shows you today, rest at night, and trust that He is still at work.
exp.18:7:
This verse says that, in addition to the cities already named, the tribe of Simeon also received the villages that surrounded them, as far as a place called Baalath-beer, which was also known as Ramath of the South. The phrase "of the south" in this version refers to the southern region. The word "inheritance" means the land received as a family's portion, and "families" refers to the clans within the tribe.

This is part of the account of how Joshua divided the promised land among the tribes of Israel by casting lots. The text is a closing list: it summarizes what fell to Simeon. The following passage explains that Simeon's territory came out of the portion of Judah, because Judah had received more than it needed.

For today: God cares for each person, even in details that seem small. Let us learn to share generously, as Judah did, and to trust that God gives us what we need.
exp.13:14:
This verse explains that the city of Hebron used to be called Kiriath-arba, that is, "the city of Arba." Arba was a very great and respected man among the Anakim, a people of great stature. It then says that the land had rest from war.

The narrator of the book of Joshua explains here why Hebron had that other name. He has just told how Joshua blessed Caleb and gave him Hebron as an inheritance, because Caleb followed God faithfully. Caleb had conquered that area, where the Anakim lived, and afterward a time of calm came. It is not known for certain how long that rest lasted.

For today: steady faithfulness to God, even in the face of "giants," brings fruit and rest. Follow God today in the small things, and trust that He will sustain you through the long battles.
exp.12:9:
This verse continues a list of the territories east of the Jordan River. It says that all the cities of Sihon, king of the Amorites, who ruled from Heshbon, also belonged to that region, and that his kingdom reached as far as the border of the Ammonites. The word "borders" in this verse means the boundaries or limits of the land.

The book of Joshua describes how the promised land was divided. Here the account recalls what Moses had already given to the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh. When Joshua was already old, God reminded him that land still remained to be conquered and that it had to be divided. The text marks the boundaries carefully, and this emphasizes that the inheritance was real and concrete.

For today: God keeps his promises with detail and leaves nothing to chance. We can trust that he remembers what he has promised us, even when it takes time to be seen. Give thanks today for a promise you have already seen fulfilled.
exp.17:14:
This verse describes the southern boundary of the tribe of Benjamin. The line starts at the edge of Kiriath-jearim, runs westward, and reaches the spring of the waters of Nephtoah. "South" means the southern side, and "boundary" means the border or limit. Scholars believe Nephtoah was near Jerusalem, though its exact location is debated.

Joshua speaks to the people when they are already living in the promised land. Seven tribes had not yet received their inheritance, so he sent men to survey and describe the land so that it could be divided by lot. These details about borders show that God was keeping his promise with order and care.

For today: God attends to the details of your life, even the ones that seem small. Trust that he gives you a place and a purpose, and receive with gratitude what he has given you.
exp.21:5:
This verse says that Joshua blessed the men of the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh, and sent them away. They went to their tents, that is, to their homes, on the other side of the Jordan River.

Joshua speaks after years of war for the conquest of Canaan. These tribes had helped their brothers until God gave them rest. Now they had kept their promise and could return home. Before sending them away, Joshua encouraged them to love God, obey Him, and serve Him with all their heart.

For today: when you finish a task or say goodbye to someone, do it with a blessing. Ask God to care for that person and to help them remain faithful to Him in their daily life.
exp.23:31:
This verse tells that the Israelites buried in Shechem the bones of Joseph, which they had brought up from Egypt. They placed them in a piece of ground that Jacob had bought from the sons of Hamor for a hundred pieces of silver (some understand this to have been a coin or unit of value, and it is not known with certainty). That ground became the inheritance of Joseph's descendants.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, closing the account of Joshua. Joseph had asked that his bones be carried to the promised land (Genesis 50:25). Centuries passed, but it was fulfilled. Joshua had already died, and the account shows that God is faithful to his promises.

For today: God keeps what he promises, even when it takes a long time. Joseph trusted in a promise he did not see fulfilled in his lifetime. We can keep trusting God and keep our commitments faithfully, even when the results come later.
exp.18:4:
This verse is part of a list of towns. It names three places: Ziklag, Beth-marcaboth, and Hazar-susah. The last two names probably mean "chariot house" and "horse village," though scholars are not entirely certain. The "villages" are the smaller settlements around each town.

The narrator of the book describes how Joshua divided the promised land among the tribes of Israel. Here the subject is the tribe of Simeon, which received its inheritance within the territory of Judah (Joshua 19:1). The list shows that God kept his promise to give a land to his people, with specific and real places.

For today: God does not forget the details of our lives. Just as he took care to give each family its place, he invites us to trust that he knows our needs. Give thanks today for what he has given you, even if it seems small.
exp.18:30:
This verse closes the description of the territory that fell to the tribe of Asher. The inheritance is the land they received as their share, and the villages are the smaller settlements near each city. The verse sums up that each family of Asher had its place, with its cities and their villages.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel divided the promised land after entering it. The narrator goes tribe by tribe, and Asher was the next-to-last to receive its portion, just before Naphtali. The list of borders and cities, though it may seem dull, shows that God fulfilled what he had promised to Abraham and his descendants.

For today: God keeps his promises with careful attention to detail, even when they take a long time. You can trust that he does not forget you, and be thankful for what he has already given you, faithfully caring for the place and the responsibilities that have been entrusted to you.
exp.16:4:
This verse says that the tribe of Manasseh received ten portions of land west of the Jordan, in addition to Gilead and Bashan, which lie on the other side of the river. "Portions" are the shares that were distributed by casting lots, and "in addition to" is the meaning of the phrase here. The ten portions are explained this way: five sons of Manasseh and five daughters of Zelophehad received an inheritance.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua speaks, while Israel divides the promised land. The daughters of Zelophehad had asked for their inheritance because their father had no sons. According to the text, God had already commanded Moses that they be given it, and Joshua carried it out.

God cares for those who might be left forgotten. Today we can imitate that care, defending with justice those who are overlooked, and trust that God keeps what he promises.
exp.11:21:
This verse is part of a list of defeated Canaanite kings. It mentions the king of Kedesh and the king of Jokneam, which was beside Mount Carmel. The word "one" only indicates that each of them counts as one more king on the list. Kedesh and Jokneam were cities in the north and center of Canaan.

The book of Joshua presents here a summary of Israel's victories. The author, whom tradition usually credits to Joshua although this is not certain, reviews the kings defeated east and west of the Jordan. He ends by saying there were thirty-one kings. The list is meant to remind readers that God kept his promise to give the land to his people.

For today: God does not overlook the details of what he does. It is worth noting and remembering his works in your life, even the small ones, as if you were making your own list of gratitude. That strengthens your faith when difficult days arrive.
exp.20:43:
It says that God gave Israel rest on every side, just as he had sworn to their ancestors that he would. No enemy was able to stand against them, because the Lord had handed them over to them. The rewrite for "gave them rest" is that God granted them peace and quiet. The phrase "stood before them" means that no one was able to resist them. The word "pasture lands" referred to the grazing fields around the cities.

This is part of the account in the book of Joshua, probably written by a narrator who summarizes what happened after the land was divided. The cities of the Levites have just been mentioned. The author wants to emphasize that God was faithful to the promise made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The verse that follows confirms this: not one of his good words failed.

For today: God keeps what he promises, even though sometimes he takes longer than we expect. We can rest in his faithfulness and remember the times he has sustained us, so that we can trust him in what we are still waiting for.
exp.3:1:
God tells Joshua to choose twelve men from the people, one for each tribe of Israel. The word "Take" here means "choose" or "pick out." The word "tribe" refers to each of the large family groups descended from the sons of Jacob.

The Lord speaks and gives the command to Joshua, the leader who followed Moses. The people had just crossed the Jordan River, which according to the account was opened to let them pass. God wants each tribe to take part in setting up a reminder of what happened. The verses that follow explain that there would be twelve stones taken from the river.

For today: God values everyone taking part in remembering his works. We can do the same by writing down or sharing with our families and our church the times God has helped us, so that our faith and the faith of others may be strengthened.
exp.5:7:
As soon as Joshua had finished giving his instructions, this verse tells us, seven priests began to walk ahead of the ark of the Lord. They carried seven trumpets made of rams' horns and kept blowing them as they went. Behind them came the ark of the covenant, the sacred chest that represented God's presence with his people.

Joshua, the leader of Israel after Moses, speaks to the priests and to the people. They are standing before Jericho, a walled city. God had given them an unusual plan to conquer it, and Joshua passes it on step by step. Here we see the people beginning to carry it out.

For today: sometimes God asks us to obey even when his way seems strange or hard to understand. We can take the next step with confidence, knowing that he goes before us and that his presence is our security.
exp.7:6:
Here Joshua gives instructions to a group of soldiers who are hidden. An ambush is a place where people wait in secret to attack by surprise. He tells them that when the city of Ai comes out chasing the others, they must rise up and take it. He adds that God himself will deliver it into their hands.

Joshua speaks after the defeat at Ai, which was caused by the sin of Achan (chapter 7). Now God gives them a specific strategy: pretending to flee in order to draw the enemy out of the city. The promise does not cancel the plan; God gives the victory and also directs the steps of the people.

For today: trust that God is at work, but do not use that as an excuse for not preparing yourself. Pray, seek his guidance, plan with wisdom, and act in obedience, knowing that the final outcome is in his hands.
exp.21:17:
Here the tribes on the other side of the Jordan are told: "Today you are turning away from following the Lord. If today you rebel against Him, tomorrow His anger will fall on all of Israel." The word "airará" means that He will be angry. "Congregation" refers to the whole people gathered together.

The speakers are representatives of the tribes on the west side, led by the priest Phinehas. They had heard that Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh had built an altar near the Jordan, and they thought it was an act of rebellion. They remembered the sin at Peor and the sin of Achan, where one person's wrong affected many. Later it became clear that the altar was a witness, not a place for sacrifices.

For today: before judging someone, let us seek to understand their reasons with humility. But let us also take seriously that our decisions can affect others, and let us guard our faithfulness to God in community.
exp.8:5:
This verse tells that some men came to the Israelite camp at Gilgal. They spoke to Joshua and to the Israelites, saying that they came from a very distant land, and they asked them to make a covenant, that is, a binding agreement of peace.

The ones speaking are the Gibeonites, here called Hivites. They had heard what God had done to Jericho and Ai, and they were afraid. So they pretended to be travelers from far away, with worn-out clothing and dry bread. Their plan was to deceive Israel in order to save their lives.

For today: before making an important decision, let us not rely only on appearances or on persuasive words. Let us pray, seek God's guidance, and ask for wisdom. The Israelites did not consult the Lord, and that brought consequences.
exp.14:32:
This verse begins the list of towns of Judah in the lowlands, that is, the low land and hills lying between the mountains and the coast. It names three settlements: Eshtaol, Zoreah, and Ashnah. The word "villages" in the verse before refers to the small towns that surrounded each city.

The book's narrator describes how the promised land was divided among the tribes under the direction of Joshua. These lists show that God's promises to Israel were fulfilled in real and specific places. Later on, Eshtaol and Zoreah are also connected with the tribe of Dan and with the story of Samson, though the details of that connection are explained in different ways.

For today: God does not forget small places or little-known names. If your life seems ordinary and without fame, trust that God keeps his promises there too, in everyday life, and be faithful where he has placed you.
exp.18:3:
This verse is part of a list of towns. It names three more places that the tribe of Simeon received: Heltolad, Bethul, and Hormah. Today it is not known with certainty where all of them were. Heltolad also appears as Eltolad, and Bethul is probably called Bethuel in another passage. Hormah is mentioned in other accounts, where it is connected with the destruction of the Canaanite cities.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua speaks, recording how the promised land was divided among the tribes. The inheritance of Simeon lay within the territory of Judah, which is why its towns are in the south. This list shows that God kept his promise and that each family received its place.

For today: even though these may seem to be only names, God remembers each person and every detail. You can trust that your life does not go unnoticed by him. Today, give thanks for something specific that God has given you.
exp.11:11:
This verse follows a list of defeated kings. It mentions the king of Eglon and the king of Gezer. The word "one" here means "one more": each king is counted as one of those who were defeated.

Joshua 12 is a summary of the account. It reviews Israel's victories over the kings of Canaan, first east and then west of the Jordan. Tradition attributes the book to Joshua or to writers close to him, although this is not known with certainty. The list serves to remember that God kept his promise to give the land to his people. Even so, some cities, such as Gezer, were not fully conquered afterward.

For today: remember the times God helped you, even if they seem small. Writing them down, as this list does, strengthens your trust in him for the challenges ahead.
exp.4:13:
Joshua asks the armed man whether he is on their side or on the side of their enemies, and he answers "Nay": he has not come to take a side, but as commander of the army of the Lord. Joshua falls with his face to the ground and worships, and asks: "What saith my lord unto his servant?" The word "worshipped" means that he bowed down in deep reverence.

Israel had just entered Canaan and stood before Jericho. Joshua, the leader, needed direction for the battle. Many believe this visitor is the Lord himself or a very powerful angel, since he accepts the worship and says the place is holy. Interpreters do not fully agree about his identity.

Before we ask God to bless our plans, we should ask ourselves whether we are on his side. We can come near to him with humility and a willingness to listen: "What do you say, Lord, to your servant?"
exp.6:23:
Here it is told that Joshua and all the people took Achan, son of Zerah, along with what he had stolen: the silver, the robe, and the wedge of gold, which was a bar or ingot of gold. They also brought his family, his animals, his tent, and all his possessions to the valley of Achor.

The narrator recounts what happened after Israel was defeated at Ai. God had commanded that what was captured at Jericho be set apart for Him, but Achan took part of that spoil and hid it. His sin affected the whole people. Some scholars debate whether his family took part in the punishment through complicity or because of the customs of the time; the text does not fully explain this.

For today: hidden sin is never only private, because it almost always harms others. Today we can confess in time what we conceal, trusting that God offers forgiveness and restoration before the consequences grow.
exp.21:8:
This verse tells how the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half tribe of Manasseh left Shiloh, where the tabernacle stood, and returned to Gilead, the land across the Jordan that belonged to them. "Returned" means they turned back and went home, and "possession" refers to the land they had received as their inheritance.

The narrator continues the account after Joshua had blessed them and sent them away. They had helped their brothers conquer Canaan, just as Moses had commanded. Now they were doing their part and going home. The next verse sets up a conflict over the altar they built.

For today: fulfilling what was promised and returning home with gratitude is good, but we should also take care that our actions do not cause misunderstanding among brothers. It is wise to act with clarity and seek unity.
exp.18:25:
This verse continues the list of towns that made up the territory of the tribe of Asher. It names three places: Alammelech, Amad and Misheal. Then it says that the boundary reached Carmel, toward the west, and Shihor-libnath. This last one is a place whose exact location is not known with certainty; some believe it was a stream or river near the coast.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua describes how Israel divided the land by lot, once a large part of Canaan had been conquered. Each tribe received its portion according to what God had promised to their ancestors. These lists made clear who lived where and gave order and security to each family.

For today: God cares for the details of our lives, and each person has a place and a task. We can give thanks for what He has given us and manage it faithfully, without envying the portion of others.
exp.8:15:
This verse says that three days after making the covenant with the Gibeonites, the Israelites learned the truth: these people did not come from distant lands, but were their neighbors and lived right in the midst of them. The word "league" means a pact or agreement, and "they heard that they were their neighbours" means they found out who these people really were.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua speaks. The Gibeonites had deceived Israel with old clothes and dry bread, pretending to come from far away. Israel had acted without consulting God, and then the leaders swore an oath in the name of the LORD. That is why, although they discovered the deception, they did not kill them.

For today: before making important decisions, it is wise to stop and pray and ask God for direction, rather than relying only on what we see or on what seems reasonable. And when we make mistakes, we can act with honesty and keep our word.
exp.3:21:
This verse says that parents were to tell their children what God did: Israel crossed the Jordan River on dry ground. The word "declare" in the verse means "explain" or "make known." "On dry ground" means on land without water.

Joshua, the leader of Israel, speaks after crossing the Jordan on the way to the promised land. He had set up twelve stones at Gilgal as a memorial. He knew the children would ask what they meant, and he wanted the answer to be a testimony of what God did. The text compares this to the Red Sea.

Today, we can tell younger people how God has helped us. A simple conversation at home, with memories of answered prayers, can encourage their faith and teach them to trust God.
exp.14:55:
This verse continues a list of towns belonging to the tribe of Judah in the hill country. It names three places: Jezreel, Jokdeam and Zanoah. This Jezreel is not the famous valley in the north, but a small town of Judah.

No one is speaking here in a sermon; this is the account in Joshua that records how the promised land was divided. Each tribe received its territory, with lists of towns and villages. These lists probably served so that each family would know where to live. Of many of these places we know little today, and their exact location is uncertain.

God keeps his promises even in the details. To him, no place or person is insignificant. If you feel little noticed, remember that God knows your name and your place, and cares for you faithfully.
exp.18:47:
This verse closes the list of the land that the tribe of Dan received. "Inheritance" means the portion of land that is received as a family possession, and "villages" are the small towns that surrounded each city. "According to their families" means that the land was divided according to the clans of the tribe.

The account comes from the book of Joshua, which describes how Canaan was divided among the tribes. Before this closing statement, it is told that Dan lacked territory, and so some went up to conquer Leshem and gave it the name Dan. Many understand that the tribe did not fully manage to take the land that had fallen to it, though the text gives no further details about why.

For today: God gives each person a portion, but we need faith and effort to live it out. Instead of complaining about what is missing, we can ask Him for wisdom and act with confidence in what He has entrusted to us.
exp.14:35:
This verse ends a list of towns in the lowlands (the Shephelah) that fell to the tribe of Judah. It names Sharaim, Adithaim, Gederah, and Gederothaim, and says there are fourteen towns "with their villages," that is, with the small settlements that depended on them. Some scholars note that the names in the list add up to fifteen rather than fourteen, and the reason is debated; it may be a repeated name or a variant in the text.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua records how the promised land was divided among the tribes after the conquest. These lists showed that God was keeping what he had promised to Abraham and his descendants. They also helped each family know what its inheritance was.

For today: God pays attention to places and to people who seem small. Even a town without fame was part of his plan. Trust that your simple life also has a place and a purpose before him.
exp.12:18:
This verse continues a list of cities east of the Jordan River. It names Kirjathaim, Sibmah, and Zareth-shahar, which was "in the mount of the valley," meaning in a region of hills above a valley. These are place names, and today no one knows exactly where each one was.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel divided the land. Here the account recalls the territory that Moses had already given to the tribe of Reuben, taken from the kingdom of Sihon, the Amorite king. The writer notes even the small towns to make clear that every region had its owner and that God kept what he had promised.

For today: God pays attention to details and to what seems small. If he cared for towns that almost no one remembers, he also cares for your everyday life. Trust that his promises are kept, even when they take time, and thank him today for something specific he has given you.
exp.3:22:
This verse says that God dried up the waters of the Jordan River so the people could cross over, just as He had done earlier at the Red Sea.

Joshua is speaking to the Israelites after they crossed the Jordan. He had commanded them to set up twelve stones as a reminder. He wanted that when their children asked what they meant, the parents would tell them what God had done. In this way he linked this miracle with the one at the Red Sea and showed that it was the same faithful God.

For today: let us not allow the memory of what God has done to be lost. Tell your family how God has helped you in the past. That strengthens their faith and also your own trust in Him for tomorrow.
exp.1:4:
Rahab tells the king's messengers that the two men left when the city gate was being shut, at dusk. She says she does not know where they went and advises them to pursue quickly so they can catch them.
