Speaking is Rahab, a woman of Jericho. The king knew that two Israelite spies were in her house. She had already hidden them on the roof, so she gives false information to lead the pursuers away. Earlier she had acknowledged that the God of Israel is the true God (2:9-11). The Bible records what she did, but it does not say that lying is ideal; many believers understand this in different ways.

For today: Rahab's faith led her to take a risk for God's people. Let us ask God for courage and wisdom to act in faith, always striving to do so with honesty and trust in Him.
exp.17:4:
The explanation says that the land not yet divided would be split into seven parts. Judah would remain in its territory to the south, and the descendants of Joseph (Ephraim and Manasseh) in theirs, to the north. The words "boundary" and "toward the south" are the two terms the explanation clarifies: "boundary" means territory or border, and "toward the south" means in the direction of the south.

Joshua speaks to a people who were already in the promised land, but who had stalled. Seven tribes had not yet taken their inheritance. So Joshua confronts them: how long would they remain negligent? He asks them to send men to survey and describe the land, so that it could then be divided by lot before God.

God sometimes gives us promises that we must take up with action rather than passivity. Ask yourself what blessing or responsibility you have left pending through neglect or fear. Take a concrete step today, with prayer and order, and trust that God goes before you.
exp.11:19:
This verse is part of a list of Canaanite kings defeated by Israel. It names the king of Shimron-meron and the king of Achshaph, and each one is introduced with the same word, which in the count means "one more." They were rulers of city-states in northern Canaan.

The book of Joshua summarizes here the conquests west of the Jordan, about thirty-one kings in all. The narrator is not a character who speaks but the author of the book, who makes an inventory to remember what God did for his people. The list is repetitive on purpose: each name counts as a specific victory.

For today: God pays attention to the specific. Just as this list does not overlook a single name, we can keep a record of the times God has helped us, one by one. Writing down those answers, even the small ones, strengthens gratitude and trust when the next challenge comes.
exp.20:34:
This verse names two more towns, Dimnah and Nahalal, which the tribe of Zebulun gave to the Levites. Together with Jokneam and Kartah, they make four cities.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel divided the land. The Levites, who served God in worship and teaching, did not receive a territory of their own. So the other tribes gave them cities to live in, according to what God had commanded through Moses. Here the cities of the sons of Merari are listed.

For today: God cares for those who serve him, and he does so in part through his people. Think about how you can generously support your pastor, your church, or a missionary, with offerings, time, or concrete help.
exp.1:12:
Rahab asks the two Israelite spies to promise that they will spare the lives of her whole family: her father, her mother, her brothers and sisters, and everything that belongs to them. She asks that they be rescued from death.

Rahab, a woman of Jericho, speaks here. She hid the spies and declared that the God of Israel is God in heaven above and on the earth below. Because she showed mercy to them, she now asks them to show mercy to her family, before the city is taken.

For today: when we trust God, we can also think of those we love and pray for them. Rahab's faith was not only personal; she sought the good of her family. Today you can bring your loved ones before God, and care for them through concrete acts of love.
exp.3:15:
God gives Joshua a command to tell the priests who carry the ark of the testimony to come up out of the Jordan River. The explanation of the word "testimony" is that it refers to the tablets of the law kept inside the ark, which bore witness to God's covenant with his people. The word "command" is the verb for "order," and "come up" means to come out of the river.

God speaks to Joshua. The people had already crossed the Jordan on dry ground, and the priests were still standing in the middle of the riverbed with the ark. God is the one who gives the signal to finish the crossing. As soon as they come out, the waters return to their place, showing that the miracle depended on God's presence and word.

For today: God guides every step, not only the beginning. Just as the priests waited for his order before moving, we can learn to wait for his direction with patience and obey when he indicates, trusting that his care sustains us all the way.
exp.21:21:
The explanation of Joshua 22:22 opens with a solemn declaration. The men repeat the name of God, "The Lord God of gods," to say that God knows their intentions, and that Israel will also know them. They say that if they built the altar out of rebellion or transgression, meaning deliberately betraying or disobeying God, then God should not save them that day.

The tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh speak here. They lived east of the Jordan and had built a large altar. The rest of Israel thought it was an act of rebellion and prepared for war, remembering the sin of Achan. They respond with an oath, to show that their intention was sincere. Then they explain that the altar would be a witness, not a place for sacrifices.

Before judging the intentions of others, it is wise to ask and to listen. And when we are accused, we can speak with humility and sincerity, knowing that God knows our hearts.
exp.20:16:
From the tribe of Benjamin, the cities of Gibeon and Geba were given to the Levites, together with their surrounding pasturelands. Such lands were the open fields around each city, where the Levites could keep their livestock.

This is part of Joshua's account of how cities were distributed to the Levites, since they did not receive a territory of their own like the other tribes. These cities belonged to the priests descended from Aaron. They were within Benjamin, near Judah, and together they numbered thirteen. The narrator shows that Israel did what God had commanded Moses.

For today: God cares for those who serve him, and his people have the responsibility to support them. We can ask ourselves how we sustain, with generosity and gratitude, those who teach and serve in our church.
exp.9:35:
This verse tells how Joshua and all the people of Israel left Eglon and went up toward Hebron, a city in the hill country. The word "went up" is used because Hebron stands on higher ground. They attacked it.

It is part of the account of Joshua's campaign in southern Canaan. The narrator tells how Israel advanced from city to city after defeating a coalition of kings. Readers have held different views about the conquests and their severity. The text stresses that Joshua did not act alone, but with all Israel with him, as one united people.

For today: God often leads us step by step, not all at once. Faithfully finish the task before you and move on to the next, without ceasing to walk in unity with your brothers and sisters.
exp.14:9:
Here the northern border of the land of Judah is described. The line runs from Baalah (also called Kiriath-jearim), goes westward to mount Seir, passes along the north side of mount Jearim, which is Chesalon, goes down to Beth-shemesh, and continues on to Timnah. The word "border" means the boundary or limit of an area. The phrase "turns" means that the line changes direction and curves around.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel received the promised land. The account has no speaker addressing the reader directly; it is a record of the boundaries assigned to the tribe of Judah. The places are listed so that each family could know clearly what its inheritance was. Today it is not known with certainty where each point was.

God keeps his promises with concrete details, not only with general ideas. We can trust that he also cares about the details of your life. Today, give thanks for a specific blessing you have received, and recognize that it comes from his faithfulness.
exp.7:7:
It says that when the Israelites enter the city of Ai, they must set it on fire. Joshua reminds them that this is not his own idea: it is what God commanded. "You shall set the city on fire" means "they will set the city on fire." "See, I have commanded you" is a firm way of saying: "Do not forget, I have already commanded you."

Joshua, the leader of Israel, speaks to the men who will hide in the ambush. Earlier Israel had failed at Ai because of Achan's disobedience. Now God gives a plan, and Joshua insists that it be followed just as it was given, without adding or taking away anything. It should be remembered that this takes place in the conquest of Canaan, a difficult subject that should be read within that historical moment.

For today: when God shows us something clearly in his Word, it is good to obey it fully and on time, without changing it to suit ourselves or leaving it half done.
exp.18:28:
This verse continues describing the border of the tribe of Asher. The boundary turns toward Hebron, reaches Tyre, which was a well-walled city (a "strong" city means fortified), then turns back toward Hosah and ends at the Mediterranean Sea, in the area of Achzib. "Turneth" means "turns around" or "changes direction."

Here there is no one giving a speech. The book of Joshua, whose author is not named with certainty, recounts how Israel divided the promised land among the tribes. This list of boundaries and cities made clear what territory belonged to Asher. Some places are hard to locate today, and scholars do not always agree.

For today: God keeps his promises with detail and cares about what is concrete. Just as each family received its share, you can trust that God has also given you a place and a task. Give thanks for what you have received and care for it faithfully.
exp.3:17:
It says that when the priests who carried the ark of the covenant came up out of the riverbed and their feet touched dry ground, the water flowed back and ran as it had before. The phrase "returned to their place" means the river went back into its channel, and "over all its banks" means it was overflowing, as was normal in that season.

The narrator describes what happened after Joshua, at God's command, told the priests to come up out of the Jordan. Israel had just crossed the river on foot, on dry ground. The water stopped while the ark stood in the middle, and it returned when they came out. In this way it was made clear that the miracle came from God, not from chance.

For today: God remains faithful in difficult moments. When you face a "river" that seems impossible to cross, take the step of obedience that God shows you, trusting that he goes with you. And afterward, remember what he has done for you.
exp.14:60:
This verse is part of a list of towns. It names four places in the desert area: Beth-arabah, Middin, Secacah (and then, in the next verse, Nibshan, the City of Salt, and Engedi). "Desert" here refers to a dry region near the Dead Sea, not a completely empty place.

No one speaks in a dialogue; the narrator of the book describes how the land was divided among the tribes. This list corresponds to the tribe of Judah. Its purpose is to record what God gave them, fulfilling his promise to Israel. Many of these places are little known today, and not all of them can be located with certainty.

For today: God remembers places and details that seem small to us. If He cared for every town in the desert, He also cares for your everyday life, even the dry or difficult areas. Trust that nothing of yours goes unnoticed by Him.
exp.14:39:
This verse is part of a list of towns. It names three places: Cabbon, Lahmam, and Kithlish. They were villages in the lowlands of Judah. Today no one knows for certain exactly where they stood, and scholars do not agree on all of their locations.

Here there is no speaker; the book of Joshua tells how Israel received the promised land. This section describes what fell to the tribe of Judah. Each town is recorded with care to show that God kept his promise to Abraham and to his descendants, and so that each family would know what its inheritance was.

For today: God pays attention to the small things and does not forget names or places. If he took care over every detail of this inheritance, he also cares for your daily life. Trust that he keeps his promises, even in what seems unimportant.
exp.23:2:
God says that he took Abraham from the other side of the river (the Euphrates River, as it is commonly understood) and led him through all the land of Canaan. He also says that he multiplied Abraham's descendants and gave him Isaac.

Joshua gathers all Israel at Shechem, before God, shortly before his death. He speaks on behalf of God and reviews the history of the people. He begins by reminding them that their ancestors served other gods. In this way he shows them that everything began through God's initiative, not through human merit. With this, he prepares them to decide whom they will serve.

For today: remember that God sought you first. Your faith did not begin only with your own effort, but with his grace. Thank him for this today and respond with a faithful and grateful life.
exp.20:32:
This verse sums up the account of the cities given to the Gershonites, one of the families of the Levites. In all there were thirteen cities, each with its open land around it, the pasture grounds where they could keep their animals.

Here no character is speaking; this is the record of the book of Joshua. The Levites did not receive a territory of their own like the other tribes, so God commanded that they be given cities within the land of all the tribes. In this way they would live spread among the people, to teach them and to serve them.

For today: those who serve God need the support of the community, and the community needs their service. Think about how you can generously support those who teach and care for you spiritually.
exp.22:6:
It says that, while living among the peoples who still remained in the land, Israel was not to mention the names of their gods, nor make oaths by them, nor serve them, nor bow down before them. The words "come not among" mean "mix with" or "join with"; "mention" means naming them with respect or devotion.

Joshua, now an old man, speaks to Israel's leaders before he dies. He knows that Canaanite nations still remain among them. He reminds them that God gave them the victory, but the greatest danger now is not war, but that their hearts will slowly turn away under the influence of those cultures.

Today we can ask ourselves which things around us compete with God for our loyalty. One practical step is to be careful about what we admire, repeat, and obey each day, so that Jesus remains first in our decisions.
exp.1:15:
She tells the two Israelite spies to go up into the hills and stay hidden there for three days. In this way the men who were searching for them would not find them. When the pursuers went back to the city, the spies could continue on their way in safety. The sentence about the old wording is removed here, since the phrases it explains do not appear in the verse you are reading.

The speaker is Rahab, a woman of Jericho. She had hidden the spies sent by Joshua, and the king of Jericho sent men to look for them. She took a risk because she believed that the God of Israel was the true God. Now she helps them escape, and they promise to protect her and her family.

For today: faith sometimes leads us to act with wisdom and courage, not only to feel confident. We can ask God for guidance and take practical, careful steps to do what is right.
exp.12:20:
This verse lists the territory that Moses conquered east of the Jordan. It includes the cities of the plain (the lowland) and the whole kingdom of Sihon, the Amorite king who ruled from Heshbon. "Struck down" means that he defeated him. It also mentions five Midianite leaders: Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur, and Reba, described as the dukes of Sihon.

The author of the book of Joshua describes how the land was divided among the tribes. Here the inheritance of Reuben is in view. The victories of Moses are recalled to show that God fulfilled what He had promised. It is not known with certainty how those Midianite leaders were related to Sihon; perhaps they were allies or were under his rule.

For today: God keeps His promises, sometimes through other people and at different stages. Remembering what He has already done gives us confidence and gratitude, and encourages us to faithfully care for what He has given us.
exp.17:18:
This verse finishes describing the southern border of the tribe of Benjamin. The line passes along the north side of Beth-hoglah and reaches the north bay of the Salt Sea, that is, the northern end of the Dead Sea, where the Jordan River flows into it.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel divided the promised land among the tribes. Here the narrator describes Benjamin's inheritance in detail, so that each family would know its portion and there would be no disputes. It is the fulfillment of the promise God made to their ancestors.

For today: God is a God of order and faithfulness, who keeps his promises down to the details. We can trust that he also cares for our lives, and live thankful and content with what he has given us, without envying what belongs to others.
exp.9:34:
The explanation says that Joshua and the Israelites captured the city of Eglon that same day. "They put them to the sword" means they killed them with the sword. "Everything that breathed" refers to the people of the city, as had happened before at Lachish.

The narrator of the book describes Israel's campaign in southern Canaan, after five kings attacked Gibeon. Israel understood this as God's judgment on very corrupt peoples, under the command of "devoted to destruction," or total destruction. Some scholars believe that the language of "nothing was left" is partly exaggerated, as was common in accounts of war in that period.

Today, this passage reminds us that God is holy and just, but also patient. Let us give thanks for his mercy in Christ, and never use this text to justify violence.
exp.3:9:
What it says: The priests who carried the ark stood still in the middle of the Jordan River until everything that God had commanded Joshua to tell the people was finished. This was the same thing Moses had already ordered. Meanwhile, the people hurried and crossed the river.

Context: The narrator of the book tells how Israel entered the promised land. God had stopped the waters of the Jordan when the priests stepped into the river with the ark, a sign of his presence. They were to remain firm until everyone had passed. Afterward, twelve stones are mentioned as a reminder of the miracle. The text does not say how long the crossing lasted.

For today: God sometimes asks us to stand firm in obedience while others move forward because of it. Keep faithfully doing what He entrusted to you, even when your task seems quiet, because your steadiness can help others arrive safely.
exp.11:18:
Joshua and the Israelites defeated the king of Madon and the king of Hazor. Each one appears as "one", that is, one more in a list of defeated kings. Madon and Hazor were cities in the north of Canaan.

This chapter is a summary of the book of Joshua. The narrator lists the kings that Israel defeated west of the Jordan, after the conquest of the land. The list does not count battles, but records what God gave them. Some scholars think the repeated "one" is meant to stress that there were many and that none was left unmentioned.

For today: God remembers every detail of what he does for his people. It is worth keeping your own "list" of thanksgiving: noting the times God helped you, even when they seem small, so you can recall his faithfulness when a new difficulty comes.
exp.4:1:
God tells Joshua to make sharp knives, that is, of flint or a sharp cutting edge, and to circumcise the Israelites again. "The second time" does not mean repeating the operation on the same people, but doing it again with this new generation. The foreskin refers to the skin that is cut away in circumcision.

The Lord speaks to Joshua just after they have crossed the Jordan. The enemy kings were terrified. The men who had come out of Egypt had died in the wilderness, and those born along the way had not been circumcised. Circumcision was the sign of the covenant with God. Before fighting, the people had to renew their identity with Him.

For today: before undertaking great tasks, it is good to review our relationship with God. His favor does not depend only on our strength, but on living as His people, with sincere obedience.
exp.2:3:
The explanation says the people were to keep a distance of about two thousand cubits behind the ark of the covenant, without coming close to it. In this way they could see the route well and know where to go, because they had never passed that way before. A cubit measured roughly half a meter, so the distance would be nearly a kilometer.

The words of the officers of Israel are conveyed here, passing on Joshua's instructions. The people were about to cross the Jordan River to enter the promised land. The ark, which represented God's presence, would go at the front. The distance also suggests reverence for what is holy, although the text gives no further explanation.

When you face something new and unknown, let God go ahead of you. Give space to his guidance, and walk with confidence and reverence, step by step.
exp.11:4:
This verse describes how far the territory of Og, king of Bashan, extended. "Ruled" means governed or held power. His kingdom included Mount Hermon, Salcah, all of Bashan, and half of Gilead.

The book of Joshua here gives a summary of the kings that Israel defeated. This passage recalls the victories east of the Jordan under Moses, whose lands were given to Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh. Exactly who wrote this summary is not known for certain. Its purpose is to show that God kept what He promised.

For today: take time to remember what God has already done in your life. Writing down, with names and details, His answers and His care will help you trust Him with greater gratitude when you face new challenges.
exp.14:0:
This verse says that the tribe of Judah received its share of the promised land, distributed by lot, according to its families. Its territory reached to the border with Edom and to the wilderness of Zin in the south. "Lot" here means the portion assigned by drawing lots. "South" is the direction the verse describes. "Border" is the boundary or edge of the territory.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel received the land after entering Canaan. The narrator describes in detail the boundaries of Judah, the first tribe to receive its territory in this section. We do not know for certain who wrote the book, but the text aims to show that God kept his promise to Abraham and to his descendants.

For today: God knows how to give you a place and a concrete portion. Instead of comparing your life with that of others, trust in what he has entrusted to you and be faithful in that space, whether it is your family, your work, or your community.
exp.16:8:
This verse describes the boundary between the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh. The border goes down to the brook Kanah, on the south side. Some cities of Ephraim lay within the territory of Manasseh. The border of Manasseh ran along the north side of the brook and ended at the sea (the Mediterranean).

The book of Joshua tells how Israel divided the promised land. Here, in careful detail, the portions of the sons of Joseph are recorded: Ephraim and Manasseh. It is not a speech but a report of the division. The exact boundaries cannot always be located today with certainty.

For today: God cares for the details and gives each one their place. We can give thanks for what He has given us, respect the limits of others, and cooperate with those who share our path, like these sister tribes, whose lands were intertwined.
exp.14:3:
It says that the southern boundary of the land of Judah continued to a place called Azmon, then reached the "stream of Egypt" (a dry watercourse that many identify with the Wadi el-Arish), and from there turned west. The word "boundary" means border, and "south" is the direction referred to here. It ends by saying: "This shall be your south coast."

The passage describes how the promised land was divided among the tribes of Israel after the conquest led by Joshua. Here the limits of Judah are traced. These details show that God kept his promise to his people in a concrete and orderly way.

God is interested in the details of our lives. You can trust that his promises are real and not vague. Today, thank him for something specific he has given you.
exp.8:2:
This verse says that the people of Gibeon found out what Joshua had done to Jericho and to Ai. The word "inhabitants" is what the verse uses for those who lived in the town, and the word "heard" shows that news of Israel's victories had already spread across the land.

The narrator of the book describes what happened after the conquests. While other Canaanite kings joined together to fight against Israel, Gibeon took a different path: deception. The verses that follow say they pretended to be travelers from a distant land in order to make a peace agreement. Their reaction grew out of the fear caused by what they had heard.

For today: what we hear about God and his works moves the heart. The Gibeonites acted with lies, and that is not an example to copy. But it reminds us that ignoring God is not an option. When we hear his truth, let us respond with humility and sincerity, not with cunning or pride.
exp.8:19:
Here the princes of Israel say they will let the Gibeonites live. The reason is that they had made an oath in the name of Jehovah, and they fear that God's wrath will fall upon them if they break it.

The phrase "lest wrath be upon us" is the same as "so that wrath may not come upon us."

The Gibeonites had pretended to come from a distant land in order to make a covenant with Israel. The leaders swore an oath without consulting God, and the congregation grew angry when they discovered the deception. The princes speak here to defend their decision: although it was a mistake, the oath made before God carried weight. Afterward, the Gibeonites became woodcutters and water carriers.

For today: let us think carefully and pray before we promise something. And once we have given our word, let us strive to keep it with honesty, taking the name of God seriously.
exp.18:17:
The explanation says that the territory of the tribe of Issachar included several cities, among them Jezreel, Chesulloth and Shunem. The word "border" here means the area or boundary assigned, and the phrase "toward Jezreel" marks the direction of that boundary. These are names of places that form part of a longer list.

The narrator of the book of Joshua describes how the promised land was divided among the tribes of Israel. After Zebulun, the fourth lot came out for Issachar. This list of cities shows that God kept his promise to give each family a specific place. Who exactly wrote the book is not known with certainty; tradition links it to Joshua.

God is interested in the specifics of our lives: places, families and names. Just as each tribe received its share, you too have a place and a task that God has entrusted to you. Today you can take care of what has been given to you with gratitude, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.14:18:
Achsah says to her father Caleb: "Give me a blessing." By this she means an extra gift. She reminds him that the land he gave her is dry, a land of little water. For this reason she also asks for springs of water. Caleb gives her the upper springs and the lower springs.

Achsah is the daughter of Caleb and the wife of Othniel. Caleb had promised his daughter in marriage to whoever conquered Kiriath-sepher. The southern land, the Negev, was arid, and without water it was not useful for planting or raising livestock. That is why she approaches her father with respect and a clear request.

We can ask God with confidence for what we truly need, as a daughter asks her father. Achsah does not complain or stay silent: she asks with humility and practical sense. God invites us to bring our needs to him with sincerity.
exp.1:9:
Rahab, the woman of Jericho, tells the two Israelite spies that in her city everyone already knows what God did for his people. She speaks of how the Lord dried up the water of the Red Sea when they came out of Egypt, and of the defeat of Sihon and Og, kings of the Amorites on the other side of the Jordan. The word "destroyed" means that they were completely overcome.

Rahab speaks in secret, at night, on the flat roof of her house, where she had hidden the spies. She explains why she believes: the news of what God did filled all the people of the region with fear. That is why she asks for mercy for her family.

Today, faith can be born by hearing what God has done. Rahab did not see the miracles, but she believed what she heard and acted on it. Remembering and telling of God's works can awaken trust in others, and in us when we doubt.
exp.8:3:
The verse says that the Gibeonites used cunning. They made themselves pass for ambassadors from a distant country. They loaded their donkeys with old sacks and old wine skins, torn and patched, so as to appear that they had made a very long journey. "They did work wilily" describes deceiving with clever cunning.

The one who narrates is the author of the book of Joshua. The kings of Canaan joined together to fight against Israel, but the people of Gibeon, when they heard what had happened at Jericho and at Ai, became afraid. They chose to deceive in order to save their lives and to obtain an alliance with Israel.

For today: appearances can deceive, even sincere people. Before making important decisions, it is wise to pray, ask God, and examine the facts calmly. Later in the chapter we see that Israel did not consult the Lord, and that brought consequences.
exp.9:11:
Joshua speaks to God and, in front of all the people, orders the sun to stop over Gibeon and the moon over the valley of Aijalon. "Amorites" is the name of a people of Canaan. "Spake to the Lord" means that he prayed to God. The Bible says that God heard that request.

Joshua is the leader of Israel after Moses. The Amorite kings attacked Gibeon, an ally of Israel, and Joshua went to defend it. God was already giving the victory with great confusion and with hailstones. Joshua asks for more time to finish the battle. Scholars understand in several ways how this miracle happened, and the text does not explain it in detail.

We can pray boldly for what God has already promised us, trusting that he hears us. Let us ask with humility, and remember that the victory depends on God, not only on our own effort.
exp.9:9:
This verse tells that God himself threw the Amorite armies into confusion when Israel attacked them at Gibeon. It was a great defeat, and the Israelites pursued them along the road that goes up to Beth-horon, striking them down as far as Azekah and Makkedah. The phrase "discomfited" means that God filled them with confusion and panic, and the word "slew" simply means that he struck them down.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Israel had made a covenant with the Gibeonites, and five Amorite kings attacked them because of it. Joshua marched all night to help them, and God had promised him victory. The text credits the triumph to God, not only to Israel's strength.

For today: when you face something bigger than you, take the step of obedience that is yours to take, as Joshua did when he marched through the night, and trust that God is the one who gives the outcome.
exp.14:8:
This verse continues describing the northern border of Judah. The line goes down from the top of the hill toward the spring of the waters of Nephtoah, reaches the cities of mount Ephron, and then turns to Baalah, which is Kirjath-jearim. The border is drawn in a winding way across the land.

The book of Joshua tells how the promised land was divided among the tribes of Israel. Here the narrator lists specific places to mark the territory of Judah. It is not known with certainty where all of these places were; some are identified with more confidence than others.

For today: God keeps his promises with real and concrete details. You can trust that he also cares for the details of your life, even the ones that seem small, and receive with gratitude what he has given you.
exp.20:9:
This verse says that the first lot, that is, the first drawing of cities for the Levites, fell to the descendants of Aaron. They belonged to the family of Kohath, within the tribe of Levi. The word "lot" refers to what is distributed by drawing, and "was" is the form of the verb used here.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel divided the promised land. The Levites did not receive a territory of their own, but cities scattered among the other tribes, just as the LORD commanded through Moses. The narrator makes clear that the drawing was carried out in an orderly way. The descendants of Aaron, the priests, received the first cities, in the region of Judah and Simeon.

God cares for those who serve others, and He arranges things with order and justice. Today we can generously support those who devote themselves to teaching and caring for the spiritual life of the community, and trust that God also provides for us.
exp.14:51:
This verse names only three places: Arab, Dumah, and Eshean. They are part of a longer list of towns in the hill country of Judah. Today it is not known for certain where they were exactly, and scholars do not agree on their location.

The book of Joshua tells how the promised land was divided among the tribes of Israel. Here the narrator, who cannot be identified with certainty, lists in detail what fell to the tribe of Judah. Lists like this served to record that God was keeping what he had promised his people.

For today: God remembers even the small places that almost no one recalls. If sometimes you feel your life goes unnoticed, remember that to God your name and your place matter, and that he is faithful in the details.
exp.6:1:
This verse tells that Joshua sent men from Jericho to Ai, a city near Beth-aven, to the east of Bethel. He asked them to view the land, that is, to explore it and observe how it was. They went and looked it over.

The narrator reports what Joshua, the leader of Israel, did right after the victory at Jericho. But the verse before reveals something Joshua did not know: Achan had taken things that God had forbidden, and for that reason God was angry. Joshua planned with good judgment, but without knowing that there was a hidden sin among the people. The spies came back confident, and the attack ended in defeat.

Planning well is good, but it is not enough. Before taking an important step, it is wise to pray and ask God to show us what we cannot see, even in our own hearts.
exp.23:20:
What it says: The people of Israel answer Joshua firmly: "No, but we will serve the Lord." That is, they reject his warning that they will not be able to, and they declare that whatever happens, they will follow God. The word "but" here means "on the contrary" or "rather."

Context: Joshua, now old, gathers the tribes at Shechem to renew the covenant with God. He warns them that serving the Lord, the holy and jealous God, is serious and not an emotional impulse. His warning seeks to make their commitment sincere. Afterward, Joshua asks them to put away the foreign gods, which shows that there were still idols among them.

For today: Saying "I will serve God" is easy; living it requires daily decisions. Ask God for help and examine what things are taking the place of Him in your heart, so that you may set them aside with humility.
exp.15:6:
This verse continues the boundary of the territory of Ephraim. From Janohah, the line goes down to Ataroth and Naarath, reaches Jericho, and ends at the Jordan River. "Reaches" means that it arrives at that place, and "ends at" means that it stops there. Today it is not known with certainty where all these places were.

The book of Joshua tells how Canaan was divided among the tribes of Israel after the conquest. The narrator is anonymous, although tradition links him to Joshua. He describes these boundaries in detail to make clear that each family received its inheritance, according to the promise God had made to them.

God is concerned with the concrete and the everyday, not only with the great. Each tribe had its appointed place. Today we can be thankful for what God has entrusted to us, whether much or little, and care for it faithfully, without envying what belongs to others.
exp.14:40:
This verse ends a list of cities: Gederoth, Beth-dagon, Naamah, and Makkedah. The text says there are sixteen cities with their villages, that is, the smaller towns that depended on each city. It is worth noting that fewer than sixteen names appear in the list, and scholars explain this in different ways, with no certain answer.

This is not a speech by a character; it is the account in the book of Joshua. Here it describes how the promised land was divided among the tribes of Israel. These cities belong to the tribe of Judah, in the lowland region, toward the west. God was fulfilling the promise he made to Abraham and his descendants.

For today: God keeps his promises in detail, even in small and little-known places. If he cares for every city and every village, he also cares for your everyday life. Trust that not one of his promises is forgotten.
exp.14:56:
This verse closes a list of towns in the hill country of Judah. It names Cain, Gibeah, and Timnah, and says they are ten cities with their villages, that is, with the small settlements that depended on them. With these three, the group of ten that began with Maon and Carmel is complete.

Here the account of Joshua describes how the promised land was divided among the tribes of Israel. Judah received a large territory, and its towns are listed by region. This Gibeah is not the one in Benjamin, and this Carmel is not the famous mountain; they are places in Judah. Today the location of all of them is not known with certainty.

God is interested in details, and he keeps his promises with real names and real places. If he cared for every small village, he also cares for your everyday life. Trust that no part of your story goes unnoticed by him.
exp.3:8:
This verse tells that Joshua set up another group of twelve stones, this time inside the Jordan River, right where the priests carrying the ark of the covenant had stood. The words "to this day" show that the writer wrote at a time when the memorial could still be seen, or at least was still well remembered. Some scholars think it was under the water; the Bible does not make this clear.

The people of Israel had just crossed the Jordan on dry ground, thanks to a miracle from God. Earlier, twelve men took twelve stones out of the river, one for each tribe, to set up a reminder in the camp. Here the narrator adds this second memorial, so that no one would forget what God had done.

Today we can do something similar: write in a notebook the times God helped us. When doubts come, rereading it will strengthen our faith.
exp.18:40:
This verse begins to list the towns that the tribe of Dan received as its inheritance. It says that their territory included Zorah, Eshtaol, and Ir-shemesh. The word "boundary" refers to the territory or its limits, and "inheritance" is the land received as a family's property. The old spellings and forms are the ones written in the verse above.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua describes the division of the promised land among the twelve tribes. After Naphtali, the seventh lot fell to Dan. The lists of towns were important because they showed that God was keeping what he had promised to Abraham and his descendants. Ir-shemesh is often understood to mean "city of the sun," and some scholars think the name may reflect a place with earlier Canaanite history.

For today: God pays attention to the specific and cares for every detail of our lives. We can trust that he has a place and a purpose for us, and live with gratitude for what he has given us.
exp.20:4:
He says that the rest of the descendants of Kohath, a group of the Levites, received ten cities by lot. Those cities were in the territories of Ephraim, Dan, and the half tribe of Manasseh. "Cities" here means towns or settlements, and "by lot" means they were divided by casting lots, like a drawing.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua speaks. He tells how Israel did what the LORD had commanded: the Levites did not receive a territory of their own, but cities scattered among the other tribes, with their pasturelands around them. In this way they could serve and teach the people everywhere.

For today: God cares for those who serve others, and the people responded with generosity. We can support with gratitude those who teach and serve us in the faith, and gladly share what God has given us.
exp.14:7:
This verse follows the line of Judah's northern border. The boundary goes up through the valley of the son of Hinnom, along the south side where the Jebusites lived, and the text names it as Jerusalem. Then it goes up to the top of the mountain that lies to the west of that valley, at the end of the valley of the giants, toward the north.

Joshua 15 describes how the promised land was divided among the tribes. The narrator, whom tradition often associates with Joshua, records the boundaries carefully so that each tribe would know what had been given to it. The Jebusites were still living in Jerusalem (v. 63), which shows that the conquest was not yet complete.

For today: God attends to the details and keeps his promises. You can trust that he also has a place and a purpose for you, and that it is yours to receive with gratitude and to live faithfully where he has placed you.
exp.5:26:
It says that God was with Joshua, meaning he accompanied him and gave him success in what he did. For that reason his fame spread throughout the whole country. The word "was" here is the older form of the verb, and the phrase about the news spreading means that the report became known and was passed along everywhere.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Joshua, closing the account of the fall of Jericho. Earlier it is told that Rahab, who had protected the messengers, was saved, and that Joshua made a vow against anyone who would rebuild the city. This verse sums up that the true secret of Joshua was the presence of God, not only his own ability.

For today: before wishing for success or recognition, seek to be close to God. Ask him each day to accompany you in your work, your family and your decisions, and trust that his presence is worth more than any fame.
exp.5:21:
Joshua orders the two men who had scouted the land to go into the house of Rahab, the prostitute, and bring her out with everything that belongs to her. He tells them to do this just as they promised her before. The quoted phrases in the source are not part of the verse your reader sees, so they are left out here; the verse itself says "as ye sware unto her," meaning as they had sworn an oath to her.

Joshua speaks as the leader of Israel right after the walls of Jericho fell. Years earlier, Rahab had hidden the spies (Joshua 2), and they swore to protect her and her family. Now, in the middle of the destruction, Joshua makes sure that promise is kept.

For today: keep what we promise, even when it is hard or inconvenient. God is faithful, and those who follow Him should guard their word, especially toward those who trusted them. Rahab also reminds us that God welcomes anyone who trusts in Him, regardless of their past.
exp.18:5:
This verse closes the first list of cities given to the tribe of Simeon. It names two more places, Beth-lebaoth and Sharuhen, and says that in total there were thirteen cities together with their villages, that is, with the small towns that depended on them.

Here no character speaks; the book of Joshua recounts how the promised land was divided among the tribes. Simeon received its portion within the territory of Judah (Joshua 19:1), in the south. These lists served as a record that God was keeping what he had promised to his people. Some place names are hard to locate today.

For today: God cares even for the small details, and he knows you by name too. Trust that your place and your calling matter, even when they seem modest or little seen.
exp.18:19:
This verse is part of a list of towns: Rabbith, Kishion, and Abez. These are three towns named without any further detail. They belong to the territory that the tribe of Issachar received. Today it is not known for certain where each one was located, and scholars disagree about their exact position.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel divided the promised land among the tribes. Here the narrator, whom tradition associates with Joshua although the book does not say so clearly, records the portion that fell to Issachar, its fourth share. Lists like this kept track of the boundaries so that each family would know its inheritance and care for it. It was a way of showing that God kept his promise to Abraham.

God notices the small things. Even little-known towns are written in his Word. You also count for him, even when no one else takes notice of you. Trust that he keeps what he promises.
exp.17:16:
This verse continues describing the northern border of the tribe of Benjamin. From the spring of Rogel, the boundary turns northward and passes through En-shemesh, then past Geliloth, which lies opposite the ascent of Adummim, and goes down to the stone of Bohan, a son of Reuben.

Context: Joshua divides the promised land by lot among the tribes that still had no inheritance. The text is a list of boundaries, written so that each family would clearly know what had been given to it. Who Bohan was, and why a stone bore his name, is not known for certain.

For today: God cares about the concrete details of his people's lives. If he took care that each family knew its place, he also knows you and cares for you. Trust that your portion and your path are not unknown to him.
exp.7:32:
This verse describes how the whole people were arranged for a solemn ceremony. All of Israel was standing on both sides of the ark of the covenant, facing the Levitical priests who carried it. The officers were the ones in charge of organizing the people. The foreigners and the native-born were standing together: half of them facing Mount Gerizim and the other half facing Mount Ebal. This is what Moses had commanded, so that a blessing would first be pronounced over the people.

The narrator tells what Joshua did after entering Canaan. He followed the instructions of Deuteronomy 27 and 28: he built an altar, wrote the law on stones, and gathered everyone to renew the covenant with God.

For today: God invites us to hear his Word together, without leaving anyone out. We can do the same today if we read the Bible with our family or our church, and if we receive with humility both his promises and his warnings.
exp.12:27:
This verse closes the list of territories that the tribe of Gad received east of the Jordan River. It says that those cities, together with their villages (that is, small nearby towns or settlements), were the inheritance of each family of Gad. The word "inheritance" refers to the land that belonged to them as a permanent possession.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel divided up the promised land. The narrator summarizes what Moses had already assigned to Gad, Reuben, and half the tribe of Manasseh, before Israel crossed the Jordan. Those lands were part of what Israel had taken from King Sihon.

For today: God keeps what He promises, even in the details. We can trust that He cares for us in the small and everyday things as well. Today you can thank Him for something specific He has given you, such as your home, your family, or your work.
exp.20:14:
This verse continues the list of cities that were given to the descendants of Aaron. Here Holon and Debir are named, each "with its pasturelands." The pasturelands were the grazing land on the outskirts of the city, where the Levites could keep their livestock. In other versions, Holon appears as Holon.

The account is told by the narrator of the book of Joshua. It explains how Israel carried out what God commanded through Moses. The tribe of Levi did not receive a territory of its own, so the other tribes gave it cities to live in among them and to serve the people in spiritual matters. These cities were located in the territory of Judah and Simeon.

Today we can learn that God cares for those who serve in his work, and that it falls to us to help. Think of a pastor, a teacher, or a missionary you know, and look for a concrete way to support them with your time, your prayer, or your financial help.
exp.7:13:
This verse tells how the king of Ai saw Israel near the city and rose up very early. He went out with all the men of the city to fight in the open plain, at the appointed time. The explanation of the quoted words "hasted" and "liers in ambush" has been left out, since the verse above already makes their meaning clear. The king did not know that there were Israelite soldiers hidden behind his city.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua speaks. Israel had been defeated earlier at Ai because of Achan's sin. Now God gave Joshua and the people a plan to win. The king trusted what he could see, but he did not see the plan that God had already prepared.

For today: we do not always see everything that is happening. The king felt safe with incomplete information. Before deciding something important, ask God for wisdom, listen to counsel, and do not rush to trust only appearances.
exp.15:3:
This verse says that the two sons of Joseph, Manasseh and Ephraim, received their inheritance in the promised land. The word "inheritance" here names the share of land each group was given. Although they are named together as the sons of Joseph, each of them formed their own tribe.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel divided the land of Canaan after entering it. The narrator describes the boundaries of each territory in detail. This verse closes the general description of Joseph's portion and prepares the way for what follows, the border of Ephraim. Tradition attributes the book to Joshua or to writers close to him, though there is no complete certainty.

For today: God keeps his promises, even when they take generations. You can trust that he does not forget what he has promised, and receive with gratitude what he gives you, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.5:11:
This verse tells that Joshua rose early, on the second day of God's plan for Jericho, and that the priests took up the ark of the Lord again. The ark was the sacred chest that symbolized God's presence with his people. Rising early shows readiness and obedience.

It is a narrative scene. God had given Joshua a strange strategy for taking Jericho: to march around the city in silence, one circuit each day. Joshua does not argue or change the plan; he simply carries on, just as God had directed.

For today: obedience to God is often lived out in what is repeated and simple, even when we do not yet see results. You can begin your day with faithfulness in what God has asked of you, trusting that he is at work even when everything still looks the same.
exp.7:31:
This verse says that Joshua wrote a copy of the law of Moses on stones. He did it in the sight of all the people of Israel. The word "copy" here means a second writing of that law, taken from the book Moses had already written.

After conquering Jericho and Ai, Joshua led the people to Mount Ebal to carry out what Moses had commanded in Deuteronomy. He built an altar, offered sacrifices, and wrote the law on stones. Then all the people heard the blessings and the curses of the law. It is not known for certain whether the stones were the ones from the altar or others, and scholars understand this in different ways.

Today we can learn that God's Word should be in plain sight and at the center of life. You could choose one verse, copy it by hand, and put it where you will see it every day.
exp.21:22:
Here the tribes from the other side of the Jordan make a solemn oath. They say that if they built that altar to turn away from following the Lord, or to offer burnt offerings, grain offerings or sacrifices of peace on it, then let the Lord himself call them to account.

The sons of Reuben, Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh are speaking. The other Israelites had accused them of rebellion for setting up an altar by the Jordan, since there was supposed to be only one altar for sacrifices, in the place where the sanctuary stood. They answer by calling God as their witness. Afterward they explain that the altar was a reminder for their descendants, not a rival place of worship.

For today: when someone misreads your intentions, do not defend yourself in anger. Speak with sincerity, stand before God and explain calmly. And if you are doubtful about others, ask before you condemn.
exp.1:18:
It says that whoever goes out of Rahab's house during the conquest of Jericho will be responsible for their own death, and the spies will not be guilty. But if anyone stays inside the house, the spies take on the responsibility: if someone lays a hand on them, their blood will fall on the spies' heads.

The two spies of Israel are speaking. Rahab hid them and helped them escape, and they promise to save her and her family. They set clear conditions: the red cord in the window, the family gathered inside the house, and Rahab's silence about the agreement.

For today: the salvation God offers is generous, but it asks us to trust and obey. Rahab believed and acted, and her family was protected because they stayed where the promise was. We can ask ourselves whether we are trusting what God has said, or whether we are still looking for safety by other paths.
exp.2:13:
The explanation says that the people of Israel left their tents, where they had been camped, to cross the Jordan River. The priests went at the front, carrying the ark of the covenant, the sacred chest that represented God's presence and his covenant with Israel. The sentence is left open because the account continues in the following verse.

Context: Joshua is the leader of Israel after the death of Moses. God had given him instructions to enter the promised land. The river was swollen, as the text says, at the time of the harvest. The priests were to take the first step, and only then would God hold back the waters. The people moved forward trusting in that promise.

For today: Sometimes God asks us to take the first step before we see the full solution. We can move forward in obedience, putting God at the front of our decisions, and trust that he goes with us.
exp.23:32:
It says that Eleazar, the son of Aaron, died; he had served as priest in Israel. They buried him in "the hill that pertained to his son Phinehas," that is, in the hill that belonged to his son Phinehas, in the hill country of Ephraim. The word "hill" in this verse means a hill or a small rise of land.

Here no character speaks; it is the narrator of the book, who closes the story. The death of Joshua and the burial of Joseph have already been told. Now the death of the priest Eleazar is recorded, the one who had helped divide the land. So one generation of leaders comes to an end. Some think Phinehas later became priest, though this verse only says he received that hill.

For today: leaders pass away, but God remains faithful. Give thanks to those who taught you the faith and, with God's help, serve him steadily so that others will do the same.
exp.17:13:
This verse continues describing the border of the tribe of Benjamin. The line turns toward the sea side (the Mediterranean, to the west), runs south to the hill that lies in front of Lower Beth-horon, and ends at Kirjath-baal, which is Kirjath-jearim, a city that belonged to Judah. With this, the western boundary is closed.

Here no character speaks in a discourse; instead, the account records how the land was divided. Joshua had already led the conquest, and now each tribe was receiving its inheritance. Exact places are noted to prevent disputes and to show that God's promise to Israel was being fulfilled.

For today: God is concerned with what is concrete and orderly. We can trust that He cares for the details of our lives, and also learn to respect boundaries and what God has given to each person.
exp.18:43:
This verse names three more cities that were given to the tribe of Dan as their inheritance: Eltekeh, Gibbethon, and Baalath. It is part of a long list of towns.

The book of Joshua tells how the promised land was divided among the tribes of Israel. Here the narrator, whom tradition associates with Joshua, though no one knows for certain who wrote it, lists the cities of Dan. Lists like this showed that God was keeping his promise to Abraham to give a land to his people. Where some of these places were exactly is not certain today.

For today: God pays attention to the small things. He names each city one by one, and so he reminds us that he cares for every detail of our lives. You can thank him today for a specific blessing, even if it seems small, and trust that he keeps what he promises.
exp.14:4:
This verse describes the eastern border of the land that fell to the tribe of Judah. That border was the Salt Sea (today called the Dead Sea), up to the point where the Jordan River flows into it. From that point, the northern border began at the bay of the sea that reaches into the land, like a tongue.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel divided the promised land among the tribes. The text does not give a particular speaker here; it is a narrative record of the borders. They are described carefully because the land was a promise from God, and each family needed to know what its inheritance was.

For today: God cares about the specific and the everyday. Just as he gave each tribe a defined place, he also looks after you in small details. Trust that your place and your portion are in his hands.
exp.21:11:
When the people of Israel heard about this, they learned that the tribes on the other side of the Jordan had built an altar, and the whole nation gathered together at Shiloh, where the tabernacle stood. They intended to go up and make war against them.

The account is told by the author of the book of Joshua. The Israelites thought their brothers had turned away from God, since there should be only one altar for offering sacrifices. They feared that judgment would fall on everyone again, as it had happened before. However, they did not yet know the reason for the altar. Afterward they sent messengers to ask.

For today: before reacting with anger or judging someone, let us seek the truth with humility. Zeal for God is good, but it should be accompanied by sincere questions, patience, and a desire for reconciliation.
exp.8:11:
Here the Gibeonites say that the bread they took from their houses was hot, that is, freshly baked, on the day they set out on their journey. Now, they say, they see it dry and covered with mold. With this they want to prove that they come from very far away. "Behold" means "here it is." "Mouldy" means covered with mold.

The speakers are the Gibeonites, who live nearby, but they pretend to come from a distant land. They fear dying as Jericho and Ai did, so they prepare a deception to secure an alliance with Israel. They use old bread, torn wineskins, and worn clothing as their "proofs."

For today: appearances can be convincing, but they do not always tell the truth. The Israelites looked at the evidence and did not consult the Lord. Before deciding something important, it is wise to pray, seek God's guidance in His Word, and not trust only what we see or what others tell us.
exp.11:6:
This verse begins the list of the kings that Joshua and the Israelites defeated on the west side of the Jordan River. The region runs from Baal-gad, in the valley of Lebanon, in the north, to the mount Halak, near Seir, in the south. Striking them means that they defeated them. The portions assigned to each tribe were the allotments, and Joshua gave that land to them as an inheritance.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, who summarizes the conquests. Earlier he mentions what Moses did on the east side of the Jordan; now he presents what Joshua accomplished on the west. The list shows that God fulfilled his promise to give the land to Israel.

God is faithful to his promises, even when they take time. It is worth keeping a record of what He has done in your life, to remember it and to trust Him when you doubt.
exp.10:6:
This verse tells how Joshua advanced with all his fighting men and attacked the northern allied kings suddenly, while they were camped by the waters of Merom. The verse says they fell upon the enemy by surprise.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. A large coalition of Canaanite kings, with many horses and chariots, had joined together to fight against Israel. God had already told Joshua not to be afraid, because the next day he would hand them over. Joshua did not wait in fear: he obeyed and acted with confidence in that promise.

For today: when God has given you a clear word in the Bible, do not let fear paralyze you. Trust Him and take the step of obedience that is yours to take, even when the problem seems bigger than you.
exp.21:1:
Here Joshua tells these tribes that they kept everything Moses, the servant of the Lord, commanded them, and that they also obeyed him in everything he asked of them.

Joshua speaks after the conquest of Canaan. Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh had received land east of the Jordan, but they had promised to help their brothers in the war. Now that the other tribes were already at rest, Joshua acknowledges their faithfulness before sending them back to their homes.

For today: constant obedience deserves to be recognized. Try to keep your commitments through to the end, and when someone is faithful, encourage them and thank them with sincere words.
exp.10:22:
This verse sums up the conquest of Canaan. It says that Joshua took the land just as God had commanded Moses. Then he divided it among the tribes of Israel as their inheritance, according to their families. "Rested from war" means that the land had a time of peace, without major battles.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel entered the promised land after the death of Moses. Here the narrator gives a summary of the earlier campaigns, which included the Anakim, a people of great stature. It is a summary: later in the same book it says that land still remained to be possessed, so "the whole land" is understood as overall control of the region, not every corner of it.

God keeps what He promises, although sometimes He takes His time and His people pass through struggles. We can trust His promises and also obey Him step by step, waiting for Him to finish what He began. And when a time of rest comes, let us give Him thanks.
exp.22:13:
Joshua says he is about to die, that he is going the way of all the earth. He asks the people to acknowledge, with all their hearts and all their souls, that God fulfilled every promise He made to them. The phrase "are come to pass unto you" means "have been fulfilled for you." Not one good word failed.

Joshua, now an old man, speaks in his farewell to Israel. After the conquest, he reminds them of God's faithfulness so that they will not turn away from Him. Both before and after this verse he warns that if they mix with the neighboring peoples and worship their gods, they will lose the land. His argument is that God fulfilled the good things and will also fulfill His warnings.

For today: remember the times God has been faithful to you. Write them down and thank Him. That trust will help you obey Him and resist whatever pulls you away from Him.
exp.7:0:
God tells Joshua not to be afraid or lose heart. He orders him to take his whole army and go up to attack the city of Ai. He assures him that he has already given into his hand the king, the people, the city, and the land. "Lose heart" means to lose courage; "men of war" are the soldiers.

The Lord, the God of Israel, speaks to Joshua, who was leading the people after Moses. Earlier, Israel had been defeated at Ai because of Achan's hidden sin (chapter 7). With that problem dealt with, God gives him encouragement and a plan again. He then gives him a strategy: prepare an ambush.

For today: after a failure or a fault, God invites the one who repents to rise up again. His promise does not remove the need for effort: Joshua was to trust, and also to plan and act with wisdom.
exp.7:16:
This verse says that all the men of Ai and Bethel went out to pursue Israel. Because they went after them, they left the city unprotected, with its gates open. The phrase about "making themselves seem defeated" means that Joshua and his people pretended to be beaten.

The book of Joshua tells what happened after Israel's first defeat at Ai, which was caused by the sin of Achan. With the people now in order, God gave Joshua a plan: an ambush. The people of Ai thought they would win again and became overconfident. It is not known exactly where Bethel stood in this battle or how many men it had; the text only says that it helped.

Today we can learn that self-confidence can leave us without defense. When we believe we already know everything, we lower our guard. Let us ask God for humility and attentiveness so that we do not neglect what we must protect.
exp.6:11:
God says that Israel will not be able to stand against its enemies and will flee before them. The reason is that the people have become something set apart for destruction, a thing devoted to God that brings a curse if it is kept. God adds that he will not continue with them unless they destroy the devoted thing that is among them.

The Lord speaks to Joshua, who lay prostrate after the defeat at Ai. A man had taken items from Jericho that God had commanded to be set apart, and he hid them. His sin affected the whole community, because Israel acted as one people under the covenant. For this reason God calls for the camp to be purified.

For today: if there is something we know displeases God and we hide it, let us not keep making excuses. Let us confess it and leave it behind, trusting that God forgives and restores whoever returns to him with sincerity.
exp.11:23:
The explanation says that the king of Tirzah was the last in the list of defeated kings, and that there were thirty-one kings in total. Each king is counted one by one. Tirzah was a city in the north of Canaan.

The book of Joshua is a historical narrative; no speaker is identified in this verse, but the narrator closes a summary. Earlier, the text recounts Israel's conquests under Joshua. This list reminds the reader that God kept his promise to give the land to his people. Some names in the list are translated in different ways, and scholars are not sure of their exact meaning.

For today: God takes care of the details and keeps what he promises, even when it takes time. Write down the times God has helped you, one by one, as in this list. That strengthens your confidence when you face new challenges.
exp.14:15:
Caleb makes a proposal: whoever attacks the city of Kirjath-sepher and captures it will receive his daughter Achsah as his wife. The words "smite" and "take" in the verse show that the reward is for striking down the city and taking it, and the phrase "to him will I give ... to wife" means that he would give her to him in marriage.

Caleb, one of Israel's faithful spies, speaks here in his old age while the tribe of Judah receives its inheritance. He had already driven out the giants from Hebron and now wants to take Debir. His offer was a way of encouraging others to take part in the conquest. In that culture, parents often arranged marriages, and the Bible only records what happened without presenting it as a model for all times.

For today: Caleb trusted God and encouraged others to move forward with courage. We can ask ourselves what difficult task God is asking of us, and whom we can encourage to serve with faith.
exp.9:26:
It says that at evening, when the sun was going down, Joshua gave the order to take down from the trees the bodies of the five kings who had been defeated. They threw them into the cave where the kings had earlier hidden, and they closed the mouth of the cave with great stones. The trees on which the bodies had been hung are the wooden posts or trunks where they were displayed, and the stones that stayed in place were still there when the account was written down.

This is part of the story of the conquest of Canaan. The narrator tells how Joshua acted against the kings who attacked Gibeon. Taking the bodies down before nightfall follows the law in Deuteronomy 21:22-23, which asked that a body not be left hanging overnight. The stones served as a reminder of what had happened.

For today: God cares about the details of justice and order, and he wants us to obey his Word even in difficult moments. We can ask ourselves whether we faithfully do what God asks of us, including in small things.
exp.14:41:
This verse names three towns of the tribe of Judah: Libnah, Ether, and Ashan. It is part of a list of places in the lowlands, called the Shephelah, to the west of the hill country of Judah. The ancient names may sound strange to us, but they were real places where families lived.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel received the promised land. Here the narrator, traditionally associated with Joshua, though this cannot be affirmed, carefully lists the territory of each tribe. This list forms a group of nine towns with their villages. Recording the names showed that God was fulfilling what He had promised to Abraham and his descendants.

For today: God pays attention to the concrete, to every place and every person. Nothing He gives is forgotten. You can trust that He knows the details of your life and keeps His promises, even when you do not yet see them fully. Thank Him today for something specific He has given you.
exp.2:11:
It says that Joshua orders the choosing of twelve men, one from each tribe of Israel. The word "take" in the verse means to choose or select. It does not yet explain what they will be for, but this becomes clear later: in chapter 4, each of them takes a stone from the Jordan as a memorial.

Joshua is speaking, the leader who followed Moses. The people are about to cross the Jordan River to enter the promised land. Joshua has just announced that God, present with them through the ark, will open the way. Choosing one representative from each tribe shows that the whole nation takes part and that God's work belongs to everyone.

For today: God often accomplishes his purposes by involving his people. Ask yourself what small but concrete responsibility you can take on in your church or family, trusting that God goes ahead of you.
exp.21:25:
Here the children of Reuben and Gad explain why they built an altar beside the Jordan. They say they decided to build it, but not to offer burnt offerings (offerings burned up completely) or any other sacrifices. That altar was not meant for worshiping apart from the rest of Israel.

The speakers are the tribes that had settled east of the Jordan. The other tribes thought they had rebelled against God and nearly went to war with them. For this reason these tribes make their motives clear: they wanted their descendants never to be cut off from faith in the LORD. The altar would be only a reminder, a witness.

For today: before judging someone's actions, it is wise to ask about and listen to their reasons. Many conflicts are avoided through a sincere and humble conversation.
exp.20:29:
This verse continues the list of cities that the tribe of Asher gave to the Levites. Two are named here: Mishal and Abdon. The word "suburbs" refers to the pasture lands around each city, where the Levites could keep their livestock. The following verse adds Helkath and Rehob, to make four cities in all.

The book of Joshua tells how the promised land was divided. The Levites did not receive a territory of their own, because their inheritance was to serve God. So each tribe gave them cities to live in among the people. It is thought that the account aims to show that Israel carried out what had been commanded through Moses.

For today: God cares for those who serve others, and he wants his people to support them generously. We can ask ourselves how to support our pastor, teacher, or missionary, through prayer, time, or practical help.
exp.9:29:
This verse tells how God gave the city of Libnah, along with its king, into the hands of Israel. The Israelites attacked it "with the edge of the sword," that is, they destroyed it in battle, leaving no survivors. They treated its king the same way they had treated the king of Jericho, who also died.

It is part of the account of Joshua's conquests in Canaan. The author presents these victories as the work of the Lord, and repeats similar phrases for each city. Many understand this within the promise God made to Abraham about the land, and within judgment on peoples whom God regarded as deeply corrupt. These passages are difficult, and scholars interpret them in various ways, especially because of the language of total destruction.

For today: the passage reminds us that victory comes from God, not only from our own strength. We can face our challenges with humility, trusting in his help and not in our pride.
exp.16:3:
Here it is told that the five daughters of Zelophehad came before the priest Eleazar, Joshua, and the leaders. They reminded them that God had commanded Moses to give them an inheritance. Leaders of the people is what the word "princes" in the verse means. Joshua gave them land among their father's brothers, just as God had said.

The one speaking is the narrator, who records the words of these women. Their father died without sons, and normally only men received land. Years earlier, they had made this request to Moses (Numbers 27), and God approved their petition. Now, already in the promised land, they ask that it be fulfilled.

For today: God keeps what he promises, and he invites us to ask with respect and confidence for what he has already said. He also teaches us to value and listen to those who ask for justice with humility.
exp.2:14:
This verse tells that the priests who carried the ark came to the Jordan River and dipped their feet at the water's edge. It notes that in those days, the time of the harvest, the river used to overflow its banks.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Joshua, recounting the moment when Israel enters the promised land. God had said that the waters would stop when the priests stepped into the water. The mention of the overflowing is meant to highlight that the crossing was difficult and that only God could open the way.

For today: sometimes God asks us to take the first step of faith before we see the solution. Obey in what he has already shown you, even when the obstacle seems enormous, and trust that he goes with you.
exp.0:4:
This verse says that no one will be able to successfully oppose Joshua during all his life. God promises to be with him just as he was with Moses. The words "I will not fail thee, nor forsake thee" mean that God will not abandon him or leave him alone.

God speaks shortly after the death of Moses. Joshua must now lead Israel to enter the promised land. God reminds him of the promise made to Moses and encourages him before a great and difficult task. The promise of God's presence is tied to the call to obey his law.

For today: when you face a responsibility that is bigger than you, remember that God does not ask you to move forward alone. His company sustains you, and you can respond with obedience and trust, taking one step at a time.
exp.10:20:
The verse tells that Joshua destroyed the Anakims, descendants of Anak, a people known for their great stature. They lived in the mountain regions, in Hebron, Debir, Anab and other areas. Joshua put an end to them and to their cities.

The narrator of the book recounts how Israel took the promised land. The Anakims were the "giants" who had frightened the spies in the time of Moses. Here it is shown that God did what he had said. The conquest is a difficult theme, and scholars interpret it in different ways.

Today, this passage reminds us that God is faithful to his promises, even when the obstacles seem enormous. We can face our fears by trusting in him, without using violence as an example.
exp.5:19:
The explanation says that the people shouted loudly when the priests blew the trumpets, and the wall of Jericho came down. The phrase about the shout means that they raised a great shout. The rams' horns are the trumpets made from ram's horn. The wall fell flat, completely. Then each person went into the city straight ahead from where they stood, and they took it.

The narrator tells what happened after Israel obeyed God's instructions: marching around the city for seven days. Earlier, Joshua had warned them not to take anything set apart as devoted, that is, belonging to God and to his judgment. The passage is also hard: the destruction of Jericho is presented as judgment, and Christians have interpreted it in various ways. Even so, Rahab was protected because of her faith.

Today, we can trust God and obey him even when his way seems strange, knowing that the victory comes from him.
exp.22:2:
Joshua reminds the Israelites of what they themselves saw with their own eyes: God defeated the peoples of Canaan before them. The word "nations" here means the peoples or nations of the land. And the phrase "fought for you" means that the victory was not only the strength of Israel's army, but the work of God on their behalf.

Joshua speaks as an old man, after years of conquest and rest. He gathers the leaders of Israel to give them a final message before he dies. He wants them to remember God's faithfulness and to keep trusting Him and obeying Him, because some peoples still remained in the land and the challenge continued.

For today: when you face a difficulty, call to mind the times God helped you before. Write them down or tell them to someone. Remembering His past faithfulness strengthens confidence for the present and encourages you to keep obeying Him, without depending only on your own strength.
exp.2:4:
Joshua tells the people to sanctify themselves, that is, to set themselves apart for God and prepare themselves inwardly and outwardly. The reason is that the next day the Lord would do wonders, that is, extraordinary miracles, among them. The word "sanctify" here is a command that means to consecrate yourselves.

Joshua speaks as the leader of Israel, who is about to cross the Jordan River into the promised land. They had already been told that the ark of the covenant would go ahead, and that they should keep their distance so they could see the way clearly, since they had never passed that way before.
