This preparation shows that the people were to approach God with respect and reverence. The Bible does not detail here exactly what that sanctification consisted of.

For today: before expecting God to work in our lives, we can prepare ourselves with humility, prayer, and repentance. Letting go of what gets in our way helps us see and receive what He wants to do.
exp.18:9:
This verse says that the third lot came up for the tribe of Zebulun, according to their families. The border of their territory reached as far as a place called Sarid. The word "lot" here refers to the drawing by which the land was distributed. "Border" means boundary or limit, and "inheritance" is the land received as a family's portion.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel received the promised land. The narrator describes, tribe by tribe, the division that was made at Shiloh after the conquest. Each boundary is detailed because each family needed to know with certainty what God had given them. The exact location of Sarid is not known with complete certainty.

God cares about the details of your life. Just as he gave each tribe its place, he has a place and a purpose for you. Trust what he has given you and do not envy the portion of others.
exp.17:19:
This verse says that the Jordan River marked the boundary on the east side, that is, the eastern edge, of the territory of the tribe of Benjamin. With this, the description of its borders is complete. "Boundary" means limit or border, and the land received as an inheritance is what is meant by the portion given. "According to their families" means the land was divided by the clans of the tribe.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua summarizes the division of the promised land. Joshua directed the process, and the land was assigned by lot before God at Shiloh. The text closes the borders of Benjamin and then lists its cities. It shows that God fulfilled, with order and detail, what he had promised his people.

For today: God cares about the details of your life and gives you a concrete place. Instead of comparing your inheritance with that of others, thank him for what he has entrusted to you and be faithful in it.
exp.2:8:
Joshua invites the Israelites to come close and listen carefully to what God has to say to them. The phrase "come here" in the original is rendered in the verse as "Come hither," and the name of the Lord is the LORD, the God they serve. This is not just a talk from Joshua: he wants them to hear God's own words.

Joshua speaks as the new leader after the death of Moses. The people are about to cross the Jordan River to enter the promised land. God had just told Joshua that he would be with him as he had been with Moses. Now Joshua gathers the people to explain what God will do, to strengthen their trust before a very difficult step.

For today: before taking a big step in life, stop and draw close to God to listen. Read his Word and pray calmly. He encourages and guides those who listen to him.
exp.11:15:
This verse is part of a list of kings. It says there was one king in Makkedah and one in Beth–el, and that each of them was defeated. The word "one" is repeated as in a count: one, one, one. Today we would write "Beth–el" as "Bethel."

The book of Joshua tells how Israel entered the promised land. Here the author, whom tradition often links to Joshua though this is not certain, summarizes the victories west of the Jordan. There are thirty-one kings in total. The list reminds us that God fulfilled what He had promised His people, even though each city had its own story.

For today: God remembers every name, even those that seem small to us. If today you feel that your life is only a detail in a long list, remember that God keeps His promises step by step. Give thanks for a recent small victory and trust that He is still at work.
exp.23:6:
This verse recalls that, when the Israelites cried out to God, he put darkness between them and the Egyptians. Then he brought the sea upon the Egyptians and covered them. The sea in question is the Red Sea. After that, the people lived for many days in the wilderness.

Here God speaks through Joshua, at the assembly in Shechem. Joshua goes over the story of deliverance to remind the people how much God has done for them. With that memory in view, he asks them to decide whom they will serve.

For today: when you are in trouble, cry out to God and remember how he has helped you before. Remembering his faithfulness in the past strengthens trust and gratitude, and encourages you to obey him today.
exp.2:7:
God tells Joshua to command the priests who carry the ark of the covenant (the sacred chest that represented God's presence and his covenant with Israel) to do the following: when they have come to the edge of the Jordan River, they are to stop there, standing in the water.

The one speaking is God, and Joshua passes on the order. Israel was about to enter the promised land, and the Jordan was an obstacle. God wanted to show that he would be with Joshua as he had been with Moses. The priests went ahead of the people, leading them.

Today, sometimes God asks us to take a step of faith before we see the solution. The priests had to get their feet wet first. We can obey what God shows us today, trusting that he will open the way.
exp.9:28:
It says that Joshua and all the people of Israel went out from Makkedah and headed to Libnah, a Canaanite city. There they began to fight against it. The word "á" is an old way of spelling "a," and "pasó" here means that he moved from one place to another.

This is a historical account, not a speech. The narrator tells how Joshua advanced through the south of Canaan, city by city, after the victory at Makkedah. The book presents these campaigns as part of God's fulfillment of His promise to give the land to Israel. These passages of war are difficult, and Christians understand them in different ways.

For today: Joshua did not stop after a victory, but continued with the task God had given him. We can learn to persevere faithfully in what God entrusts to us, without resting on the achievements of the past.
exp.12:0:
He says that Joshua was already an elderly man, well advanced in years. Then God spoke to him and reminded him of his age, but also told him that a great deal of land still remained to be taken and settled. The phrase "stricken in years" is an old way of saying that he was very advanced in age. "Possessed" means taking the land and settling in it.

The Lord (God) speaks to Joshua, the leader who succeeded Moses. They had already won many battles and divided a good part of the promised land, but some areas were still left, such as those of the Philistines, which the following verses list. God reminds him of this so that the work is not left half-finished and what remains is divided.

For today: God does not forget what still needs to be done in our lives, even when we have already come a long way. We can be thankful for what has been achieved, but keep trusting that He guides us toward what lies ahead, regardless of our age.
exp.20:26:
This verse says that the children of Gershon, a family of the Levites, received two cities from the half tribe of Manasseh, east of the Jordan: Golan, in the region of Bashan, and Beeshterah. Golan was also a city of refuge for the one who had killed another person. The pasture lands around the city, where the Levites could keep their animals, are the suburbs mentioned in the verse. A city is what the verse calls each of these places.

The account comes from the book of Joshua. When Israel divided the land, the tribes gave cities to the Levites, who had no territory of their own, as commanded through Moses. The cities of refuge protected the one who had killed someone unintentionally, until his case was made clear (Numbers 35).

Today we can learn to be a safe place: to listen with patience, to seek justice, and to offer mercy. We can also support with generosity those who serve God and others.
exp.16:9:
This verse describes the boundaries of the lands given to the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh. Ephraim lay to the south and Manasseh to the north, and the Mediterranean Sea was their common border toward the west. To the north, Manasseh reached as far as the land of Asher, and to the east, as far as that of Issachar.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel received the promised land. Here the narrator, whom tradition associates with Joshua though this cannot be known with certainty, explains each border in detail. This showed that God was keeping his promise to the descendants of Joseph, and every family knew what belonged to it.

For today: God cares for the concrete and for each person. Just as he gave each tribe its place, he has a place and a calling for you. Trust in what he has given you, and faithfully manage your own portion: your family, your work, and your community.
exp.0:7:
The explanation says that the Law of God must not depart from Joshua's lips. He is to repeat it and think about it day and night, so that he may obey it. The promise is that in this way his way will prosper and he will have good success.

God speaks to Joshua after the death of Moses. Joshua must lead Israel into the promised land, a task that caused fear. God asks him for courage, but the basis of that courage is remaining faithful to his Word. Prosperity here is linked to obedience and to God's presence, not to a formula for getting rich.

For today: set aside a few minutes each day to read a passage of the Bible, repeat it in your mind throughout the day, and ask yourself what concrete step of obedience it asks of you.
exp.9:39:
The verse sums up Joshua's campaigns in the south of Canaan. It says that he struck the country of the hills, of the south, of the lowlands and of the slopes, along with their kings. The phrase "he left none remaining" is a way of speaking common in the war accounts of that time, and everything is presented as the fulfillment of what God had commanded.

The narrator of Joshua closes here a series of victories: Hebron, Libnah, Debir and other cities. The text insists that it was God who fought for Israel. These passages are difficult, and scholars debate how much is language of total victory and how much is literal destruction. It is worth reading them alongside the rest of the Bible, which also shows mercy, as in the case of Rahab.

For today: when a task seems impossible to us, let us remember that God sustains those who obey him, and let us seek his guidance before acting.
exp.19:0:
This verse says that God spoke to Joshua. It is the introduction to a command. The word "spake" means the same as "said," and the verse is the opening of an instruction. The Lord is the name of God in this translation.

The one speaking is God, and Joshua is the leader who succeeded Moses. The people were already settled in the promised land. God reminds him of something he had commanded earlier through Moses: setting apart cities of refuge. There, a person who had killed someone without intending to could flee, so as not to become the victim of unjust revenge while his case was examined.

Today we can learn that God cares for both justice and mercy. He does not want punishment to be handed out without thought, nor the harm to be ignored. We can imitate him by being patient before we judge, and by offering help and protection to someone who has fallen into a mistake without any bad intent.
exp.18:12:
The boundary of the tribe of Zebulun continues its course eastward, passing by Gath-hepher and Ittah-kazin, and reaches Rimmon, which goes around to Neah.

This passage belongs to the division of the promised land, which Joshua directs after entering Canaan. The text is not a speech but a description of boundaries. Places are named so that each tribe would clearly know its inheritance. Today the exact location of some of these sites is not known with certainty.

For today: God keeps his promises and attends to the details, even those that seem small to us. You can trust that he also cares for your own particular life, your home, your work, and your path. Today give thanks to God for what he has given you, and faithfully manage what he has entrusted to you.
exp.18:18:
This verse continues a list of towns within the territory that fell to the tribe of Issachar: Hapharaim, Shion, and Anaharath. In this version the names appear with older spellings (Hapharaim, Anaarath). We do not know for certain where each place was; some are placed in the northern part of Israel, but scholars do not fully agree.

There is no character speaking in the first person here. The book of Joshua narrates how the promised land was divided by lot among the tribes. This list, part of the fourth lot, serves as a record of borders and towns. It showed each family where it was to live, as a fulfillment of God's promise to his people.

For today: God attends to the concrete and to every detail of your life. Even though these names may seem distant to us, they remind us that He keeps what He promises and gives each person a place. Give thanks today for what you have received and care for it faithfully.
exp.6:3:
This verse tells that about three thousand men of Israel went up to attack the city of Ai, but they turned and fled before its inhabitants. The phrase "fled before" means they escaped from them, defeated.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Joshua had sent spies, and they advised sending only a few soldiers, thinking Ai was small and that it was not necessary to wear out the whole people. However, Joshua did not seek God at this step. The chapter later explains that Israel had sinned, for Achan took things that God had forbidden at Jericho (Joshua 7:1). That is why the defeat came.

For today: a past victory does not guarantee the next one. Before deciding, even when something seems easy, let us seek God in prayer and examine our hearts with humility.
exp.1:22:
The two spies, who had been hidden in the mountain, returned. They came down from there, crossed the river, and reached Joshua, son of Nun. They told him everything that had happened to them. The two words "returning" and "men" are the same as the ones in the verse above, and "happened" is simply what the verse says they reported.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Joshua had sent these two men to explore the land, especially Jericho. Rahab protected them, and they stayed hidden for three days until the pursuit ended. Now they complete their task: they give an account to the one who sent them. Their report, which follows in the next verse, encourages Joshua.

For today: when God guides us in a task, it is good to return with honesty and tell what we have lived through, both the hard and the good. We can also do this in prayer, remembering how God cared for us along the way, and that strengthens our trust for the next step.
exp.6:9:
God tells Joshua to get up. Joshua was lying on the ground, face down, and God asks him why he is still like this. The word for this posture, the one that was quoted, refers to throwing oneself down on the ground as a sign of grief or humility.

The Lord speaks. Israel had just been defeated at Ai, a small city. Joshua tore his clothes, prayed in anguish, and was worried about the name of God. But God explains to him that the cause of the defeat was not a lack of power, but the hidden sin among the people: someone had taken things that God had set apart for himself.

Praying in pain is good, but sometimes God calls us to act. When something goes wrong for us, in addition to grieving, it is wise to examine our hearts honestly, acknowledge what is wrong, and obey God with determination.
exp.0:16:
The people promise to obey Joshua just as they obeyed Moses. They set a condition or wish: that the LORD, the God of Joshua, be with him as he was with Moses. The words "Á" and "fué" are old spellings, and the sentence that explained them has been removed.

The tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh speak together with the people, answering Joshua. Moses had already died, and Joshua was the new leader. They were about to cross the Jordan to enter the promised land. Their answer confirms that they accept his leadership. Some interpreters see in their words sincere support; others note that they also seek security in the midst of change.

Today we can respect and support those who guide us, but above all pray that God will be with them. Good leadership needs the presence of God, and our obedience should be sincere and steady.
exp.18:44:
This verse is part of a list of towns that the tribe of Dan received as its inheritance: Jehud, Bene-berak, and Gath-rimmon. These are simply the names of towns within its territory. "Territory" means the land or boundary assigned to them.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua speaks, recording how the promised land was divided among the tribes of Israel, as God had arranged. The lists show that the promise made to Abraham was being fulfilled in a concrete way. The following text says that Dan lacked enough territory and then took Leshem, calling it Dan. About the exact location of several of these towns, scholars do not always agree.

For today: God keeps His promises even in the small details. If we trust Him, we can be thankful for what He gives us and move forward in faith when we feel that something is lacking.
exp.0:0:
This verse says that, after Moses died, the servant of the LORD, God spoke to Joshua, the son of Nun. Joshua had been Moses' assistant, his close helper and attendant. The verse uses the word "came to pass" to mean "happened," and in it we see Moses' minister, that is, his assistant and close servant.

Here the narrator tells us that Israel was at a time of change. Moses, the great leader who brought them out of Egypt, was no longer there. Then, in the verses that follow, God himself speaks and tells Joshua to rise and lead the people toward the promised land. God does not leave his people without direction.

For today: when a season ends or someone who guided us is gone, God is still there. We can be faithful in small things, as Joshua was in serving Moses, and listen to God to take the next step.
exp.17:20:
This verse begins the list of cities given to the tribe of Benjamin, divided by families. It names Jericho, Beth-hoglah, and the valley of Keziz. Some think Keziz was the name of a city in a valley, but its exact location is not certain.

After describing the boundaries of the territory, the account names the specific cities. Joshua was dividing the promised land among the tribes that had not yet received their share, and the narrator records the names so that each family would know what its inheritance was. Jericho, the city that fell in chapter 6, now forms part of that inheritance.

God keeps his promises with real details: places, names, and families. Just as each tribe received its share, you too can trust that God cares for what you need. Give thanks for what he has given you, and avoid comparing yourself with others.
exp.19:4:
It says that if the nearest relative of the dead man pursues the one who caused the death, the leaders of the city of refuge must not hand that person over. The reason is that the man killed his neighbour unintentionally, by mistake or accident, and he had not held any hostility toward him before. "The avenger of blood" was the close relative appointed to take revenge for the blood.

God speaks to Joshua, and through him to the people of Israel, now settled in the promised land. He commands that cities of refuge be set apart to protect the one who kills without intention, while a fair judgment is made. In this way personal revenge was prevented from spilling more innocent blood.

Today it reminds us that justice needs truth, calm, and evidence before condemning anyone. Before judging someone or reacting in anger, let us listen to their story and distinguish between a mistake and a bad intention.
exp.20:1:
The explanation says that the heads of the Levite families went to Shiloh, in the land of Canaan, and reminded everyone of a command from God given through Moses: that cities be given to them to live in. "Cities" are towns or settlements, and the grazing lands around them, where they kept their livestock, are what the verse calls the suburbs; the livestock themselves are what the explanation calls their cattle.

The Levite leaders speak before the priest Eleazar, Joshua, and the heads of the tribes. The Levites did not receive a territory of their own like the other tribes, since their inheritance was to serve God. That is why they now ask, respectfully, that what God had already commanded be carried out.

For today: when God has promised something, we can ask for it with confidence and with respect, remembering his word. And those of us who have more, like the tribes of Israel, can help generously those who serve God and others.
exp.20:15:
This verse closes the list of towns that were given to the priests, the descendants of Aaron. It names Ain, Juttah and Beth-shemesh, and adds up to nine cities from Judah and Simeon. "Suburbs" refers to the towns themselves and the open land around them, used for livestock.

The account is told by the narrator of Joshua. The Levites did not receive their own territory, because their inheritance was to serve God. For that reason the people gave them cities within each tribe, as commanded in Numbers 35. In some parallel texts, such as 1 Chronicles 6, there are small differences in the names, for example Ashan instead of Ain.

For today: God cares for those who serve in spiritual work, and his people share in that care. We can ask ourselves how to support, through prayer, time or concrete help, those who teach and serve in our church.
exp.7:33:
Joshua reads aloud all of God's law, leaving nothing out: both the blessings, which promise good to those who obey, and the curses, which warn of the consequences of disobedience. The phrase "according to all that is written in the book" means "in agreement with" what is written in the book.

Israel had just entered the promised land, and Joshua leads the people to renew the covenant on Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, as Moses had commanded (Deuteronomy 27). Everyone was present: leaders, women, children, and foreigners. The account is narrative, and it emphasizes that Joshua obeyed faithfully.

For today: God speaks to us in his complete Word, not only in what comforts us. You could read the Bible regularly, including the difficult parts, and share it with your family, so that everyone may know and trust God.
exp.23:28:
This verse tells us that Joshua, son of Nun, died at the age of one hundred and ten. He is called "the servant of the Lord," a title of great honor. Before this, that title was given only to Moses. The words "after these things" refer to what had just happened, and "the Lord" is the name of God.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, not Joshua. Joshua had just said goodbye to the people. He had renewed the covenant with them, set up a stone as a witness to their promise to serve God, and sent them back to their lands. With the death of this leader the book comes to an end. It is not known for certain who wrote it, and it is thought that someone added this ending later.

For today: Joshua is remembered for his faithfulness, not his fame. We can ask God that, at the end of our lives, our family and those who knew us will remember us as people who served him steadily.
exp.1:5:
This verse tells us that Rahab had brought the two spies up to the roof of her house, which was flat. There she hid them under stalks of flax that had been dried and piled up, ready to be worked. She put them there so that no one would see them.

It is the narrator who explains what Rahab had done. She had just told the messengers of the king of Jericho that the men had already left, but in fact she had them hidden. She did it because she had heard what God had done for Israel and she recognized his power. Her lie is a difficult point: the Bible records it, but does not present it as an example to copy, and there is discussion about how it should be understood.

For today: Rahab acted in faith, even though she was a person with a questionable past. God can use anyone who trusts in him. Let us ask him for courage to act in faith and, at the same time, in truth.
exp.20:36:
This verse follows a list of cities that Israel gave to the Levites. Kedemoth and Mephaath, together with their suburbs (the pasture lands around each city), were two of the four cities taken from the territory of Reuben. Here "cities" means towns or settlements.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua speaks. After dividing the land, Israel carries out what God commanded through Moses: the Levites would not receive a territory of their own, but cities scattered among all the tribes. In this way they could teach the law and serve the whole people. The list shows that each tribe contributed its share.

For today: God cares for those who serve others, and invites us to do so with generosity. We can support pastors, teachers, and missionaries with offerings, time, or kindness, so that they can devote themselves to teaching and caring for people.
exp.9:38:
The explanation says that Joshua and the Israelites conquered the city of Debir, together with its king and its towns. The word "towns" here refers to small villages, and the phrase "they put them to the sword" means they killed them with the sword. The text adds that they did to Debir the same thing they had already done to Hebron and Libnah.

This is part of the account of the conquest of Canaan. The narrator summarizes the campaigns in the south and says that Joshua was acting according to the command of the LORD. It is a difficult passage, and scholars understand it in different ways: some see a judgment on peoples who were deeply corrupt, while others think the language of "utterly destroying" is a typical way of speaking about war in that time.

For today: this text is not a model for using violence. It invites us to take seriously the holiness of God and to ask him for wisdom to read hard passages in the light of Christ, who calls us to love even our enemies.
exp.9:1:
It says that King Adonizedek and his people were very afraid. The reason is that Gibeon was not a small village but a great city, like those that had kings, greater than Ai, and with mighty men for war.

The narrator tells how Jerusalem reacted when it learned that Joshua had defeated Jericho and Ai, and that Gibeon had made an alliance with Israel. The Gibeonites had made a treaty of peace through deception, but Israel kept it. For Adonizedek, losing a city so strong was a threat, and that is why he called other kings to attack it.

For today: fear can lead us to react with anger or violence toward what we cannot control. When something frightens us, it is wise to stop and trust in God, instead of acting out of fear.
exp.22:4:
This verse says that God himself will drive out the peoples who still remain in the land, expelling them from before Israel, and that the people will take possession of their lands, just as God had promised. The words "will drive out" and "will expel" mean to force out, and "will possess" means they will receive those lands as their own.

Joshua speaks as an old man, near the end of his life. He gathers the leaders of Israel and reminds them that God has fought for them. He assures them that God will finish the work, but right away he calls them to faithfulness to the law of Moses and not to mix themselves with the gods of those nations.

For today: God keeps what he promises, and that trust sustains us in what we do not yet see finished. But the promise also calls for obedience. Today you can rest in the fact that God is still at work in your life, and at the same time choose faithfully, day by day, not to let other things take the place that belongs to him.
exp.21:4:
Joshua asks the men of Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh to take diligent care to obey what Moses taught them. That is: to love God, to follow all his ways, to keep his commandments, to cleave to him (that is, to stay close to him, joined to him), and to serve him with all their heart and all their soul. To "charge" means to command or to make known with authority.

Joshua speaks as the leader of Israel after Moses. These tribes had helped conquer the land west of the Jordan, and now it was time for them to return to their families and possessions on the other side of the river. Before sending them off, he commends their faithfulness and blesses them. He reminds them that what matters most is not the land, but their loyalty to God.

Today, rest or success should not draw us away from God. When you finish a difficult season, nurture your closeness to him: pray, read his Word, and serve him sincerely in everyday life.
exp.12:28:
This verse says that Moses gave land to the half tribe of Manasseh. Each family within that half tribe received its share, according to its clan. The words "gave" and "possession" in the verse are the English equivalents of the phrases used in the original wording, so the reader may compare them directly with the text. "Inheritance" means the land that is received and passed down to one's children.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel settled in the promised land. Here the narrator recalls what Moses had already done before he died: giving land east of the Jordan to Reuben, Gad, and the half tribe of Manasseh. This is done to make clear that those territories were rightfully theirs, and that each family had its place. The following verses give the boundaries in detail.

God cares for each family, not only for the large groups. Today we can remember that He knows your place and your need. Trust in His provision, and be thankful for what He has given you, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.5:17:
Joshua warns the people to beware of the "accursed thing," an old word meaning something set apart and given entirely to God for destruction. He orders them not to touch or take any of it, because if they did, the camp of Israel would fall under the same judgment and be brought into trouble and distress.

Joshua speaks just before the fall of Jericho. God is handing the city over to them, and it was to be devoted to God with no one keeping any plunder. Only Rahab and her household would be saved, because she had protected the messengers. The gold, the silver, and the metals would go into the treasury of the Lord.

For today: when God gives us a victory, we should recognize that it belongs to him and not take advantage of it in secret. Obedience, even in small things, protects our lives and those around us.
exp.17:27:
This verse ends the list of towns that the tribe of Benjamin received. It names Zelah, Eleph, Jebusi (which is Jerusalem), Gibeath and Kirjath. In total there are fourteen cities with their villages, that is, the small settlements that depended on them. The word "inheritance" means the land received as a possession passed down, and "according to their families" means that it was divided by clans.

It is part of the account in which Joshua divides the promised land among the tribes, casting lots at Shiloh. The author does not speak here in the first person; he simply records in detail the territory of Benjamin. That Jebusi appears in the list does not mean it had already been conquered; according to other passages, it took a long time before it was taken.

For today: God attends to the details of his promise, and every family had its place. Trust that he also has a place and a purpose for you, even when it is sometimes hard to see.
exp.12:14:
This verse says that Moses gave land to the tribe of Reuben, and that he did so according to their families, that is, giving each clan its share.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel takes possession of the promised land. Here the account pauses on the territory east of the Jordan, which Moses had already distributed before he died. Joshua, now old, is commanded to divide the rest. The author recalls this allotment to make clear that each tribe had its place, and that the tribe of Levi received no land because its inheritance was to serve God.

God cares for each family and each person, and gives each one a place and a task. Instead of comparing your portion with that of others, you can give thanks for what God has entrusted to you today and manage it faithfully.
exp.13:10:
It says that Caleb, at eighty-five years old, feels as strong as he did at forty, when Moses sent him to explore the land. It says that his strength remains the same both for war and for "going out and coming in," a phrase that means moving about, working, and carrying on daily life.

The one speaking is Caleb, before Joshua, at the division of the promised land. He recalls the promise Moses made to him for having followed God wholeheartedly. Forty-five years have passed. Caleb credits his life to the LORD and does not rely on himself; that is why he asks for the mountain where the Anakim live, knowing he needs God's help.

For today: faith does not retire. Even as the years pass, we can keep serving God with what we have, trusting his promises and asking him for strength for new challenges, rather than only remembering the past.
exp.18:39:
It says that the seventh and last lot of the land division fell to the tribe of Dan, distributed among their families. "Lot" means the drawing by which each territory was assigned. "Inheritance" is the land received as a heritage. "According to their families" indicates that the land was divided among the clans of the tribe.

The narrator of the book of Joshua tells how Canaan was divided among the tribes of Israel. Joshua and the priest Eleazar directed the drawing of lots, which was done before God at Shiloh. With Naphtali the list of the sixth tribe ends and that of Dan begins, the last one in this section. Later it is mentioned that Dan had difficulty taking possession of its territory, although this verse only opens its list.

Today we can remember that everything we receive comes from God's hand, even what comes "in last place." Trusting in his provision helps us live with gratitude and without envy.
exp.12:17:
This verse is part of a list of towns: Jahazah, Kedemoth and Mephaath. These are names of places east of the Jordan River. The words "And... and... and..." simply link the names together in one long enumeration.

Here the account describes the territory that Moses assigned to the tribe of Reuben, according to the book of Joshua. The narrator wants to record real places and their boundaries. Lists like this showed that God was keeping his promise to give land to his people. Little is known about Jahazah and Mephaath; their exact location is uncertain. Kedemoth appears later as a Levitical city, but that is stated in other passages.

For today: God pays attention to the small and the specific. Just as he did not forget the names of little-known towns, he does not forget yours or your everyday details. Trust that God keeps his promises, even when you cannot see the whole picture.
exp.5:9:
Here Joshua orders the Israelites to keep complete silence as they march around Jericho. They could not shout, raise their voices, or speak any word until the day he gave them the signal. Only then were they to shout.

Joshua speaks as the leader of the people, following the instructions God had given him for taking Jericho. While the priests blew the horns (trumpets made from ram's horns) and the ark went at the front, the people simply walked in silence. This helped everyone keep their eyes on God and not on their own voices or their doubts.

There are moments when trusting God means staying quiet, obeying, and waiting. Before we complain or say too much, we can stop, pray, and wait for the Lord's direction.
exp.6:18:
Joshua speaks to Achan with both kindness and firmness. He asks him to acknowledge the greatness of God, to give Him honor, and to say honestly what he did, without hiding anything. Giving glory means recognizing that God is just and worthy of honor. Hiding something means keeping it covered or concealed. The names Achan and Achar refer to the same person.

Israel had been defeated at Ai because someone took things that God had forbidden to be taken from Jericho. Through a casting of lots, God pointed out the tribe, the family, and the household of Achan. Joshua, as the leader of the people, addresses him as "my son" and gives him the opportunity to confess. The following text shows that Achan admits his sin.

For today: when we have failed, hiding sin harms us from within. Confessing it honestly to God, and to whomever it concerns, is a way of honoring Him and opens the path to restoration.
exp.20:19:
This verse says that the remaining families of the descendants of Kohath, from the tribe of Levi, received cities by lot within the territory of the tribe of Ephraim. The cities were towns for dwelling, along with the pasture lands around them, and the lot was the way the land was divided.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua tells how Israel, now settled in the land, carried out the command to give the Levites cities to live in, since they did not receive a territory of their own. Earlier the priests, descendants of Aaron, had been assigned their cities, and now the portion for the rest of the Kohathites is given. Among those cities was Shechem, a city of refuge.

For today: God cares for those who serve others, and his people should do the same. We can support with generosity and gratitude those who dedicate their lives to teaching and spiritually caring for the community.
exp.9:0:
He was told three things: Joshua had taken Ai and utterly destroyed it, which means he had wiped the city out and left it in ruins. He had done to Ai and its king just what he had done to Jericho and its king. And the people of Gibeon had made peace with Israel and were living among them.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua speaks. He tells how the kings of Canaan reacted to Israel's advance. Adoni-zedek is alarmed because Gibeon, a large city, was no longer on his side. The text that follows says they were greatly afraid, and that he looked for allies among other kings.

For today: fear can lead us to react with alliances and human plans, without asking what God wants. When something troubles us, let us pray first, ask for wisdom, and act with humility.
exp.21:24:
The explanation says that the Jordan River became a border between the tribes on the east side (Reuben and Gad) and those on the west. The speakers fear that one day the children of the western tribes might say to their children, "you have no part in the Lord," and so lead them away from the faith. The word "border" here means a dividing line, and "fearing the Lord" in this verse means honoring Him and serving Him.

The speakers are Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, who lived east of the Jordan. They had built a great altar, and the other tribes thought it was a rebellion and were preparing for war. They explain that the altar was not meant for sacrifice, but as a witness that they too belonged to the people of God.

Today we can make sure that no one is left outside the family of faith because of distance, differences, or misunderstandings. Before judging, it is wise to listen. And to our children we can leave clear signs that God is theirs too.
exp.10:18:
It says that, of all the cities of Canaan, only one made peace with Israel: Gibeon, inhabited by the Hivites. The word that means "except" is used here, and all the other cities were taken by war.

The writer of Joshua summarizes years of military campaigns. Gibeon had made a covenant with Israel through a deception (Joshua 9), and Joshua honored it. The following verse explains the resistance of the other peoples as something God allowed. It is a hard passage, and scholars interpret it in various ways.

For today: Gibeon recognized who God was and sought peace instead of resisting. We can learn to approach God with humility rather than stubbornness, trusting that his mercy remains open to anyone who seeks him.
exp.14:54:
This verse names four cities of the tribe of Judah: Maon, Carmel, Ziph, and Juttah. It is part of a longer list of towns in the mountainous region of the south.

Here the speaker is not a character but the narrator of the book of Joshua. After the conquest, the land is divided among the tribes, and the places are recorded in detail. It was like an official register of what God was giving to each family. This group of cities joins the previous one, which numbered nine, and the next one, which numbers ten. Some of these places reappear later in the story of David, but that is another account.

For today: God pays attention to the specific and to every place among his people. Nothing of yours is too small for him. Pray for your neighborhood and your town, naming them with affection, and trust that God cares for them.
exp.23:23:
The explanation says that the people of Israel answer Joshua with a firm promise: they will serve the Lord, their God, and will do whatever he says. "Will serve" means they will worship him and live for him. "Will obey his voice" means they will listen to his word and put it into practice.

Joshua is now an old man and is gathered with the tribes at Shechem, near the end of his life. He has reminded them of everything God did for them and has challenged them to choose whom they will serve. He asked them to put away the foreign gods. This answer leads to a covenant that same day. The Bible later shows that they did not always keep what they promised.

For today: saying that we love God is a good beginning, but it must be accompanied by concrete obedience. Ask God to show you what "foreign gods" (things that take his place) you should put away, and take a step today.
exp.9:15:
The five kings who had attacked Gibeon fled from the battlefield and took refuge in a cave in Makkedah. Today we would write "was" in place of the older form. Makkedah was a Canaanite city, although its exact location is not known with certainty.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Some understand that this verse tells what happened during the battle, before Israel returned to Gilgal, and that the story is picked up again with more detail. The kings were seeking to save themselves, but God was already fighting for Israel, and the victory was his.

When a person hides from the consequences of their actions, they do not manage to escape them. It is better to trust God and ask him for help to face honestly what we need to correct.
exp.4:9:
The explanation says that the people of Israel camped in Gilgal and kept the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month, at evening, in the plains of Jericho. The phrase "they set up camp" means that they established their camp.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Israel had just crossed the Jordan and circumcised the males, as a sign of their covenant with God. Now they remember how God delivered them from Egypt. The Passover was the memorial of that deliverance (Exodus 12). They were near Jericho, in enemy territory, and yet they stopped to worship. Shortly afterward the manna ceased.

For today: before you face your battles, pause to remember and give thanks for what God has already done for you. That strengthens confidence for the next step.
exp.20:3:
It says that when the cities were divided among the Levites, the lot first fell to the family of Kohath. Within that clan, the descendants of Aaron, who were the priests, received thirteen cities in the territories of Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin. Cities and towns are what the verse calls "cities," and the open land around them, used for grazing, is the pasture land that belonged to each city. The lot was a method of drawing lots to divide the land.

The leaders of the Levites approached Joshua and the leaders at Shiloh, reminding them that God had commanded through Moses that they be given cities. The Levites did not receive a territory of their own like the other tribes, so they would live scattered among all Israel, serving the people in spiritual matters.

God takes care of those who serve others, and we can do so as well. Today we can generously support pastors, teachers, and missionaries, and make sure that those who dedicate their lives to teaching the Word have what they need to live with dignity.
exp.13:13:
It says that Hebron became the inheritance of Caleb, son of Jephunneh the Kenezite, and that it remained his "unto this day." The reason given is that he "wholly followed" the Lord, that is, he followed him completely, without leaving his obedience half-done.

The speaker here is the narrator of the book. Caleb was already about 85 years old and asked Joshua for the hill country that God had promised him decades earlier. The Anakim lived there, a people feared for their strength. Caleb trusted that God would be with him. Joshua blessed him and gave him Hebron. This verse sums up why that land belonged to him.

For today: steady faithfulness is valued before God. Keep trusting Him and obeying Him, even when the years pass or the challenge seems enormous.
exp.14:19:
This verse says that what follows is the portion of land that fell to the tribe of Judah, divided according to their families. "Inheritance" means property that is received and passed down from one generation to the next. A "tribe" is a large group of families descended from a common ancestor, in this case Judah.

Here no character is speaking; it is the narrator of the book of Joshua. It closes the story of Achsah, the daughter of Caleb, who asked for springs of water in addition to her dry land, and it leads into the list of Judah's cities. Joshua recounts how God kept His promise to give the land to His people.

For today: God keeps what He promises, and He does so with detail and care for each family. We can trust that He does not forget us. And, like Achsah, we can ask Him with confidence not only for the basics, but also for what we need so that life can bear fruit.
exp.17:8:
The chosen men went out and traveled through the land. They sketched and described it city by city, divided into seven parts, and wrote it down in a book. Then they returned with Joshua to the camp at Shiloh.

The one who narrates is the author of the book of Joshua. Seven tribes had not yet received their inheritance, and Joshua asked them to organize themselves. He sent representatives to make a written report, so that the land could be divided in an orderly way before the Lord, by means of lots. Shiloh was the place where the tabernacle stood.

God gives us promises, but often he expects us to act with order and effort. Before deciding something important, it is wise to observe, plan, and put things in writing, and then bring them before God with trust and humility.
exp.20:12:
This verse tells that the descendants of Aaron, who were the priests, were given Hebron, a city of refuge for someone who killed another person without meaning to, and also Libnah. The term "suburbs" refers to the open pasture lands around a city, used for livestock.

It is part of the list of cities that Israel gave to the Levites, because they did not receive a territory of their own like the other tribes. The account is narrative, not a speech. The preceding verses explain that Hebron was given to the priests, but its fields and villages already belonged to Caleb, who had received them earlier as an inheritance.

For today: God cares that there are places of mercy and justice. We can ask ourselves how to be a refuge for others, by listening with patience, protecting the vulnerable, and offering a second chance, without ignoring truth or justice.
exp.20:6:
This verse says that the descendants of Merari, one of the three groups of the Levites, received twelve cities by their families. These cities came out of the territories of Reuben, Gad and Zebulun. The word "cities" here refers to towns or settlements, and the phrase "by lot" means that they were divided by casting lots, a method that left the decision in God's hands.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel divided the promised land. The Levites did not receive a territory of their own, because their task was to serve God and teach his people. For this reason God commanded, through Moses, that each tribe should give them cities to live in among everyone. The narrator records the division carefully, to show that God fulfilled what he had commanded.

For today: just as Israel supported the Levites, we can generously support those who serve in the church, and also make sure that no one among us is left without a place.
exp.14:57:
It says that Halhul, Beth-zur, and Gedor are three more cities in the list of the territory of the tribe of Judah. Here another group of towns in the hill country begins. The phrase "with their villages," which appears in the nearby verses, refers to the small settlements that surrounded each city.

Context: there is no character speaking; it is the account of Joshua, describing how the promised land was divided among the tribes. This list of cities of Judah serves as a record of what each family received. It shows that God kept his promise to give the land to Israel, and that the division was orderly and written down.

For today: although they are only names, God remembers them one by one. That teaches us that he knows the places and the people that seem small to us. Today you can thank him for keeping his promises and trust that he has you in mind.
exp.0:6:
It says that Joshua must be strong and very courageous, but with a clear purpose: to carefully obey all the law that Moses gave him. He must not turn aside "to the right hand or to the left," that is, neither to the right nor to the left. Being "prosperous" means that things will go well for him in whatever he undertakes.

God speaks to Joshua after the death of Moses. Joshua must lead the people of Israel into the promised land. It was a huge task and it was frightening. So God promises to be with him, as he was with Moses, and asks that his courage rest on obedience to his word.

For today: courage is not only facing dangers, but also following God's word when it is hard. This week, choose a pending decision and ask yourself what the Bible teaches about it. Then act with confidence, knowing that God is with you.
exp.7:10:
It says that all the soldiers who were with Joshua went up and drew near to the city of Ai. They pitched camp on its north side, and a valley lay between the army and the city. The phrase about "the people of war" refers to the soldiers, and "pitched the camp" means that they set up camp.

The narrator describes how Joshua begins the second attack against Ai. Earlier, Israel had been defeated there because of Achan's sin (chapter 7). Now, with the relationship with God restored, Joshua follows the plan God gave him: an ambush. While the army camps in plain view, another group waits hidden to the west.

For today: after a failure, God allows us to try again, but with obedience and a good plan. Put in order whatever you need to correct, ask Him for direction, and take the step with patience.
exp.20:22:
It says that the tribe of Dan handed over two cities to the Levites: Eltekeh and Gibbethon. Each one came with its pasturelands, that is, the grazing fields around the town where the livestock were kept. In this passage, the word for town is used for a city.

The narrator of the book of Joshua tells how each tribe gave cities to the Levites, following what God had commanded through Moses. The Levites did not receive a territory of their own, since they served God in worship and teaching. For that reason they lived scattered among all the tribes.

Today we can learn to support with generosity and gratitude those who serve in the church, and to make sure they have what they need to live. Think of one concrete way to support a teacher, pastor, or servant in your community this week.
exp.13:12:
This verse tells that Joshua blessed Caleb, son of Jephunneh, and gave him the city of Hebron as an inheritance. "Blessed" here means that he asked God's favor on him. An "inheritance" is the land received as permanent property for a family.

Caleb had just spoken to Joshua. He was about eighty-five years old, but he felt strong and asked for the mountain that God had promised years earlier, when he and Joshua spied out the land. The Anakites lived there, a people of great size who dwelt in fortified cities. Caleb did not trust in himself, but in the Lord being with him. Joshua, as leader of the people, recognizes his faith and confirms the promise.

For today: steadfast faith is precious to God. We can keep trusting his promises even when the years pass or difficulties seem enormous, asking him for strength to obey him with our whole heart.
exp.3:14:
It says that God spoke to Joshua. The name of God in the Old Testament is "the Lord," and the phrase introduces an instruction that comes right after it. It is a short phrase that leads straight into the command.

Here the one speaking is God, and he speaks to Joshua, the leader of Israel after Moses. The people had already crossed the Jordan River by a miracle. God had just exalted Joshua in the sight of all Israel, and now he gives him the order that the priests carrying the ark should come up out of the river. God directs every step, even the details.

For today: God still guides those who listen to him. Before taking the next step, take a moment to pray and read the Bible. He does not only help us begin; he also shows us when and how to go on.
exp.22:11:
The explanation says that if the Israelites turn away from God and join themselves to the peoples who remain in the land, making marriages with them and living in close company with them, there will be consequences. The quoted phrase that means "draw near to or join themselves to" is set aside, and the words that mean "make agreements or covenants" and "go in unto them" are explained as close, familiar dealings with those people.

Joshua, now an old man, speaks in his farewell to Israel. He reminds them that God fought for them and calls them to love him. The warning is that mixing with those peoples would lead them to follow their gods, and that would take them away from the promised land.

For today: let us take care with the influences closest to us, such as friendships, a spouse, and habits, because they shape our hearts. This is not about looking down on people, but about keeping our faithfulness to God and asking him for wisdom to choose well.
exp.7:19:
They says the men of Ai looked behind them and saw the smoke of their city rising into the sky. They realized they were trapped and had no way to escape in any direction. The Israelites who had pretended to flee toward the wilderness turned around and attacked them.

It is part of the account of the conquest of Ai. Earlier, Israel had been defeated there because of the sin of Achan. Once that was dealt with, God gave Joshua a strategy: an ambush. The narrator recounts how God kept his promise to hand the city over. Some readers point out that this is a text about ancient warfare, and it is best read within its historical context.

When God leads, his plan may seem strange at first, but it has a purpose. Trusting and obeying step by step, with patience, helps us see his faithfulness.
exp.7:24:
The verse says that on that day twelve thousand people died, men and women together, and that all of them were people of Ai.

This account is narrated by the author of the book of Joshua. Ai had already defeated Israel before, because of the sin of Achan. Now, after the people repented, God gave Joshua the strategy of an ambush. This conquest is part of the entry into Canaan, and the book presents it as the fulfillment of God's word. Scholars discuss how to understand the number and the severity of these events, and it is a difficult passage that is best read with humility.

For today: the earlier defeat showed that obedience matters. When we fail, God invites us to acknowledge the mistake, return to Him, and move forward trusting in His guidance.
exp.8:25:
This verse says that Joshua kept his word and protected the Gibeonites. He saved them from the power of the Israelites, so they were not killed.

The Gibeonites had tricked Israel into making a peace agreement, pretending to come from far away. When the deception was discovered, they confessed that they had been afraid of dying. Joshua had sworn in the name of the LORD, and for that reason he did not kill them, although he made them work cutting wood and carrying water for the altar. Some see here a punishment for the deception, and others also see mercy.

God expects us to be faithful to our word, even when it costs us or when we have been deceived. Before we make a commitment, it is wise to pray and seek advice, so that we decide with wisdom.
exp.17:24:
This verse is part of a list of towns. It names Gibeon, Ramah, and Beeroth, which were places in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin. They were real places, with their houses, families, and fields.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel received the promised land. Here the narrator, whom tradition associates with Joshua though no one knows for certain who wrote it, describes how the territory was divided among the tribes that had not yet received their portion. Lists like this served to record that each family had an assigned place.

For today: God pays attention to the concrete and to every detail. If He saw to it that every town had its place, He also knows your home, your work, and your situation. Trust that you are not a number to Him, and give thanks today for the place where He has put you.
exp.22:15:
It says that if the people of Israel break the covenant God commanded them and go to serve and worship other gods, God's anger will be kindled against them. The word for "transgressed" means to break or violate; the phrase "other peoples' gods" refers to the gods of other nations; and the wording that says "they will be taken away or destroyed" from the land refers to being removed from the land and perishing.

Joshua, now old and near the end of his life, speaks and gathers Israel together. He reminds them that God fulfilled all of his good promises. Because of this, they should also take his warnings seriously. God had given them the land, and living in it depended on faithfully keeping the covenant.

For today: God is faithful, and that invites a sincere response. Today we can ask ourselves what things are taking the place of God in our hearts, such as money or success, and with gratitude put him first again.
exp.12:2:
It says that part of the land still left to be taken went from Sihor, a river or stream near Egypt, up to the territory of Ekron, to the north. That land was counted as Canaanite. There were the five lords of the Philistines: Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron. The Avites are also mentioned. The phrase "which is counted" means "it is considered" or "it is regarded as."

God speaks, reminding Joshua, now old, that a great deal of land still remained to be possessed. Israel had received great victories, but the task was not finished. God lists the territories still pending before the inheritance is divided among the tribes. Scholars debate exactly where Sihor was, but the general meaning is clear.

For today: even though we may have grown a great deal in faith, there are always areas where God wants to keep working in us. Do not be discouraged by what remains; keep trusting and walking with Him step by step.
exp.13:4:
This verse says that the children of Israel divided the land of Canaan just as the Lord had commanded Moses. The word "division" here refers to the sharing out of the land among the tribes. In other words, they did not do it their own way, but followed the instructions God had already given.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua is summarizing how the division was carried out. It is explained earlier that two and a half tribes already had land on the east side of the Jordan, and that the Levites received no territory, but cities to live in and pasture land for their animals. Because Joseph had two tribes, Manasseh and Ephraim, the total number of tribes remained twelve. Soon, Caleb will come to Joshua to claim the promise that the Lord made to him.

For today: obey God in the big things and in the practical things. Before deciding how to divide money, time, or responsibilities, we can seek what the Word teaches and act with justice and faithfulness.
exp.18:0:
It says that the second lot, that is, the second portion of land distributed by casting lots in this part of the division, fell to the tribe of Simeon, according to their families. Their inheritance lay within the territory of Judah. The word "inheritance" refers to land received as a family possession, and "lot" was the means by which the land was assigned.

Here no character speaks; the narrator of the book of Joshua tells how the promised land was divided after the conquest. Judah had already received its large territory, and then Simeon received cities within that area. Some believe Judah had more land than it needed, and that is why it was shared. That is a common explanation, not something the text states directly.

God cares for each family and gives it a place. It also reminds us to be generous: to share what we have with others, without thinking that everything belongs only to us.
exp.22:3:
Here Joshua says that God, through the casting of lots, has already divided among the tribes of Israel the whole land: both the territories of the nations already defeated and those of the nations that still remained. The word "lot" means a drawing by lot, and "the great sea" is the Mediterranean Sea, to the west. An "inheritance" is a gift that is received and passed on to one's children.

Joshua, now an old man, speaks before the leaders of Israel. He wants to remind them that God fought for them and that the work of fully taking possession of the land is not yet finished. For this reason he encourages them to keep trusting God and to obey the law of Moses.

For today: God gives us many blessings, but sometimes we fail to receive them with faith and faithfulness. Remember what He has already done for you, and let that give you courage to obey Him today.
exp.17:26:
This verse is part of a list of towns. It names three more towns that the tribe of Benjamin received: Rekem, Irpeel, and Taralah. We know almost nothing about them; the Bible mentions them only here, and their exact location is uncertain.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua describes how the promised land was divided among the tribes of Israel. Benjamin received an area between Judah and Ephraim. This list of towns served as a kind of land deed: it showed what belonged to each family and brought order and security to everyone.

For today: God pays attention to the small things. Although these towns hardly have any fame, they were written down in his Word. If you feel overlooked, remember that God keeps his promises and knows your place and your name.
exp.17:23:
This verse continues the list of towns belonging to the tribe of Benjamin. It names Chephar-haammonai, Ophni, and Gaba, and closes this first section by saying there are twelve cities with their villages, that is, the small settlements that surrounded each city. The names sound strange today, and for some of them we do not know for certain where they were located.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel divided the promised land among the tribes. Here the narrator, who writes in a simple and orderly way, records the boundaries and the cities that fell to Benjamin. The purpose is to make clear that God kept his promise to give each tribe an inheritance.

For today: God remembers every detail, even small and little-known places. If he cared for every village, he also cares for your everyday life and your matters that seem minor. Trust that nothing of yours goes unnoticed by him.
exp.14:49:
This verse is part of a list of towns. It names three more places in the hill country of Judah: Anab, Eshtemoh, and Anim. They were in the high ground of the south, near Debir. Today some scholars believe a few of these places can be located in southern Judea, but not all of them agree on the exact location.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel received the promised land. Here the narrator describes the territory of the tribe of Judah, divided according to its families. These lists served to record that God kept his promise to Abraham and to his people. Each name recalled a real place where specific families would live.

For today: God does not overlook the details or the small places. If you feel unimportant today, remember that God cares for each person and each home. Trust that he does what he promises, and give thanks for what he has given you.
exp.15:1:
This verse continues tracing the border of the territory of the tribe of Joseph. The line goes out from Bethel, reaches Luz, and continues to the border of the Archites, at Ataroth. "Boundary" means the edge or limit, and "goes out" means the line keeps running or extends. Luz was the old name of Bethel (Genesis 28:19), but here they seem to be named separately. Some believe they were two nearby places, and this is not known for certain.

The narrator of the book of Joshua describes how the promised land was divided among the tribes after the conquest. These lists of places show that God kept, with precision, what He had promised to His people.

For today: God cares about the details of your life, even the ones that seem small. Trust that He is faithful, and give thanks for the place and the concrete blessings He has given you.
exp.14:27:
This verse names three more towns in the list of cities belonging to the tribe of Judah, in the southern region called the Negev. Hazar-shual means something like "the fox's courtyard." Beer-sheba is the well-known town at the far southern edge of the land. Bizjothjah appears only here, and its exact location is not certain.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel received the promised land. Here the narrator, traditionally associated with Joshua, though others see the hand of later editors, lists the towns assigned to each tribe. Lists like this served to make clear who lived in each territory and to remind the reader that the land was a fulfilled gift from God.

God cares about the concrete and everyday: places with names, families with homes. Even sites that are little remembered matter to Him. If you feel small or unknown, remember that God knows you by name and has given you a place. Care with gratitude for the space He has entrusted to you today.
exp.8:13:
They say the Israelites tasted the bread and the provisions of the Gibeonites to check their story, but they did not seek God's counsel. "Provisions for the journey" were the food for the trip, and "the mouth of the LORD" means what God says, his direction. They acted on what they saw, without asking for his guidance.

The Gibeonites lived nearby, but they pretended to come from a distant land because they feared Israel would destroy them. They used dry bread, torn wineskins and worn clothing as deception. Joshua and the leaders trusted appearances and made a covenant with an oath. Three days later they discovered the truth.

Before deciding something important, let us pray and seek the voice of God in his Word, even when everything seems clear. Our eyes and our experience can fail, but God sees everything. Asking him for wisdom keeps us from errors that later cost us dearly.
exp.3:0:
It says that when all the people had finished crossing the Jordan River, God spoke to Joshua. The word "Lord" is the name of God in this older translation, and "spake unto Joshua" means "spoke to Joshua." The important detail is that God speaks right as the crossing ends.

Joshua is the new leader after the death of Moses. God had just stopped the waters of the Jordan so the people could enter the promised land. Now He gives him instructions to set up twelve stones, one for each tribe, as a reminder of what He did.

For today: when God helps you through a difficulty, do not forget it right away. Find a simple way to remember it, such as writing it in a notebook or telling it to your children or friends, so that your faith and the faith of others may be strengthened.
exp.11:0:
This verse opens a list of the kings whom Israel defeated east of the Jordan River. It also marks the boundaries of the land they took there: from the Arnon stream in the south to Mount Hermon in the north, including the whole eastern plain, also called the Arabah.

The words "smote" and "possessed" appear in the verse above. "Smote" means they struck them down in battle, and "possessed" means they took and kept that land.

The book of Joshua does not say who wrote this section; the text reads like a report that summarizes the victories. Here the account looks back at the conquests made under Moses, before going over Joshua's conquests west of the Jordan. Its purpose is to remember what God had already accomplished.

For today: remember the times God has sustained you. Writing down those victories, great or small, strengthens confidence to face what lies ahead.
exp.14:38:
This verse names three cities of Judah: Lachish, Bozkath, and Eglon. They are part of a long list of towns. Eglon is another city, distinct from a king with the same name.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel received the promised land. Here the narrator, traditionally associated with Joshua, though no one knows with certainty who wrote it, details the territory of the tribe of Judah, by cities and regions. This group belongs to the lowland region, the Shephelah. Lachish and Eglon appear earlier as cities that had been defeated. The list shows that God's promise was fulfilled in a concrete way.

For today: God keeps his promises with real details, and he forgets no one. If he remembered every small town, he also remembers you. Trust his faithfulness, even in what seems small or little noticed.
exp.21:0:
Joshua 22:1 tells us that Joshua gathered three groups from Israel: the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half tribe of Manasseh. The phrase is left open, and what Joshua says to them comes in the next verse.

These tribes had received their land east of the Jordan River, and Moses had asked them to help their brothers conquer Canaan before returning home (Numbers 32). Now the conquest had moved forward, and Joshua, the leader of Israel, gathers them to recognize their faithfulness and send them back to their families.

For today: value and acknowledge with sincere words those who have been faithful to their commitments. You too can keep what you have promised, even when it costs time and effort, knowing that God sees that steadiness.
exp.2:0:
It says that Joshua got up early, and he and all of Israel left the place called Shittim and came to the bank of the Jordan River. There they camped and waited before crossing. Here "lodged" means that they stopped to spend the night and wait. "Passed over" means "crossed over."

It is a narrative account, not a speech. Moses had died, and Joshua was now leading the people toward the promised land. The Jordan was a great obstacle, and the verse does not say here how they would cross it. Before taking the step, Israel came to the edge of the river and waited for God's instructions, which come in the verses that follow.

Joshua began early and with determination, but he also knew how to wait. When God calls us to something difficult, we can take the first step of obedience and then stop to seek him in prayer before deciding how to go on.
exp.1:10:
When we heard these things, the people of Jericho were left without courage. Their hearts melted with fear, and no one had any more bravery left in the face of Israel. Rahab recognizes that the God of Israel rules in heaven above and on the earth below, that is, over everything.

The one speaking is Rahab, a woman of Jericho, to the two spies whom Joshua sent. She had heard how God dried up the Red Sea and gave victory over the kings Sihon and Og. Because of this she believes and asks them for mercy for her family.

For today: when you feel fear or uncertainty, remember that God is sovereign over all. Rahab made a decision of faith based on what she knew of Him, and today we too can trust God and respond to Him.
exp.23:26:
Joshua tells all the people that this great stone will be a witness between them and God. He imagines that the stone has heard all that the Lord spoke to them. Therefore, if one day the people turn away, the stone will be there as a witness against them. The phrase "lest ye deny your God" means "so that you are not false to your God," that is, so that they do not promise one thing to God and then do another.

Joshua, now an old man, has just renewed the covenant with Israel at Shechem. The people had promised to serve only the Lord. Joshua wrote the words in the book of the law and set up the stone as a visible reminder. Soon after, he died.

For today: our promises to God matter. It is wise to have concrete reminders, such as a written verse, a prayer journal, or a special date, that help us to be faithful and sincere with Him.
exp.16:17:
It says the hill country, now covered with forest, will belong to the house of Joseph. They will have to clear it in order to live there, and their borders will reach as far as they manage to occupy. It also promises that they will drive out the Canaanites, even though these have chariots of iron (war chariots with iron parts) and even though they are strong.

Joshua speaks. The tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh complained that their territory was small and that the Canaanites of the valley had iron chariots, which were frightening. Joshua answers them that, being a numerous and strong people, they must make an effort: clear the hill and fight. He shows them confidence, but also asks them for hard work and courage.

For today: God sometimes gives us opportunities that seem difficult, like a forest to be cleared. Instead of complaining or fearing obstacles, we can take the first step with effort and trust in God.
exp.19:8:
This verse sums up the purpose of the six cities of refuge. They were for all the children of Israel and also for the stranger who lived among them. If someone killed a person at unawares, that is, by mistake or without intent, he could flee there. There he would not be killed by the avenger of blood, the relative seeking to avenge the death. He had to remain until he stood before the congregation, the assembly that would judge him.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel settles in the land. Here the narrator closes the list of cities, fulfilling what God commanded through Moses (Numbers 35). The purpose was to protect life and also justice: an accident was not punished the same way as a murder.

Today we can learn not to judge in haste. Before condemning someone, it is wise to listen, to distinguish between error and wickedness, and to offer mercy along with justice.
exp.7:27:
It says that Joshua set fire to the city of Ai and left it as a heap of ruins forever. "Burnt" means set on fire; "made it an heap" means that he turned it into a heap; "desolation" means completely destroyed; and "unto this day" indicates that, when the book was written, the ruins could still be seen.

The narrator of the book tells what Joshua did after defeating Ai. Earlier, Israel had failed there because of the sin of Achan (chapter 7). Now, by obeying God, Israel wins. The destruction is understood as a judgment of God on the peoples of Canaan. It is a difficult topic, and scholars explain it in different ways.

For today: God takes sin seriously and also rewards obedience. If there is something in your life that you have hidden or neglected, bring it honestly before God. He forgives and gives strength to move forward with a clean conscience.
exp.10:17:
This verse says that Joshua fought for a long time against the kings of that land. The conquest was not quick. "Made war" means he was engaged in battle, and "a long time" points to several years, although the text does not give the exact number.

It is part of the account in the book of Joshua, which tells how Israel entered Canaan after the death of Moses. The author summarizes the campaigns in the north and in the south. The passage that follows explains that all of this happened by the hand of the LORD, according to what he had commanded Moses. It is a difficult theme, and many Christians read it carefully, within the context of its time and of God's judgment.

For today: God keeps his promises, but often it takes time. If you are waiting for an answer or a victory, do not be discouraged by the delay. Remain faithful and steadfast each day.
exp.14:33:
This verse continues a list of towns of the tribe of Judah in the lowland region: Zanoah, Engannim, Tappuah, and Enam. These are names of places, not of people.

The narrator of the book tells how the promised land was divided among the tribes of Israel. Joshua led this division, and the list shows that God was fulfilling what he had promised his people centuries before. Each town was recorded with care.

For today: if God took care to record even the small towns, he also knows you by name and is interested in the details of your life. Trust that his promises are kept, even when they seem slow or seem small.
exp.22:10:
Joshua 23:11 says: "Take good heed therefore unto yourselves, that ye love the Lord your God."

Joshua, now old and near the end of his life, speaks to Israel as he gathers them to say farewell. He reminds them that God gave them victories over strong nations. For this reason he calls them to faithfulness. He warns that if they mix with the nations that remained and adopt their way of life, they will lose the blessing of the land.

For today: let us not take love for God for granted. Let us care for it as something alive, through prayer and reading his Word. It is also wise to guard the influences that shape us most, so that they do not draw us away from him little by little.
exp.18:38:
This verse closes the list for the tribe of Naphtali. "Inheritance" is the land received as a possession, and "villages" are the small towns that surrounded each city. It says that each family of the tribe received its share, with its cities and surrounding areas.

The book of Joshua tells how Israel divided the promised land, tribe by tribe, by lot. The narrator, whom tradition often associates with Joshua, though this is not known for certain, ends here the portion of Naphtali, the sixth lot, and then continues with Dan. All of this shows that God fulfilled what he had promised to the patriarchs.

For today: God keeps his promises with attention to detail and forgets no one. You can trust that he also cares for your life and your family. Give thanks for what he has already given you and manage with faithfulness the share you have been given.
exp.4:5:
The explanation says that Israel walked forty years in the wilderness, until all the men of war who had come out of Egypt had died. They died because they did not obey the Lord, and for that reason He swore they would not see the promised land. The phrase "were consumed" means they gradually passed away until none were left. "A land that floweth with milk and honey" describes a fertile and abundant land.

Here the narrator of the book of Joshua explains why Joshua circumcised those born in the wilderness. That generation had not received the sign of the covenant on the journey. Now, at Gilgal, before the conquest, the people were renewed as the people of God. The text does not give more detail about why they had not been circumcised earlier.
