For today: obedience to God matters, and disobedience has consequences. But God was faithful to His promise and brought the new generation into the land. Today we can listen to His voice with confidence and obey Him without delay.
exp.2:15:
When the priests carrying the ark touched the water, the Jordan River stopped. The water coming down from above stood still "in a heap," very far away, near a city called Adam. The water flowing down toward the Salt Sea (the Dead Sea) ran out and was cut off. In this way the people crossed over opposite Jericho. "Zaretan" is a place whose exact location is not known for certain.

This is the account of the narrator of the book of Joshua. Israel, led by Joshua, was entering the promised land. The Jordan was overflowing with the spring harvest, so crossing it was impossible for them. God opened the way when the priests obeyed and took the first step of faith.

For today: God often opens the way after we take the step of obedience. We do not always see everything resolved beforehand, but we can trust and move forward with what He has already asked of us.
exp.8:6:
The men of Israel answer the Hivites, who were a people of Canaan. They say to them that perhaps they live nearby, in the middle of the land that Israel is receiving. Then they ask how they could make a covenant (a pact or agreement of peace) with them. The word "perhaps" here expresses doubt and suspicion.

The Gibeonites, called Hivites here, came to Gilgal wearing old clothes, patched shoes, and dry bread, so as to appear that they had come from very far away. They wanted to save their lives. Israel had been commanded not to make a covenant with the peoples of Canaan, so its leaders are right to doubt. However, the account shows that they later did not consult God (v. 14).

For today: when something looks very convincing, it is wise to stop, pray, and ask God before deciding. Appearances can deceive, and haste or confidence in our own judgment can lead us into mistakes that last a long time.
exp.2:9:
Joshua tells the people that they are going to see a sign: the living God is with them, and he will drive out from the land the seven peoples who lived there. The phrase "drive out from before you" means that he will force them out. The word "know" means they will find out by experience. "Living God" sets him apart from idols, which do not act. The names are the peoples of Canaan: the Canaanites, Hittites, Hivites, Perizzites, Girgashites, Amorites, and Jebusites.

Joshua speaks to Israel just before they cross the Jordan River, which was probably swollen. Moses had already died, and Joshua was leading the people toward the promised land. The priests would carry the ark of the covenant, a symbol of God's presence, and Joshua wanted them to trust that God was leading them. How the driving out of these peoples should be understood is a matter some scholars debate.

Today we can remember that God is not a distant idea but is present and active. When you face a difficult step, take the next step of obedience, trusting that he goes with you.
exp.16:1:
The verse says that the rest of Manasseh's descendants also received their share of the land, divided by families. Six clans are named: Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Hepher and Shemida. The word "lot" does not mean good or bad luck, but the portion of land assigned by casting lots. The phrase "male children" indicates that the list follows the line of the men.

This is part of Joshua's account of the division of Canaan. The narrator explains that Manasseh had two groups: the family of Machir, which had already received land east of the Jordan, and these other clans, which receive their portion to the west. With this he prepares the story of the daughters of Zelophehad.

For today: God cares for every family, even those that almost no one mentions. You too have a place and a calling. Be thankful for what God has given you and serve Him faithfully there.
exp.9:5:
The people of Gibeon sent a message to Joshua, who was in the camp at Gilgal. They ask him: "Do not abandon your servants; come up quickly to rescue us and help us." The phrase "Do not slack your hand" in this verse means "do not stand idle." The word "quickly" in the verse means "fast." Five Amorite kings had joined together against them.

The ones speaking are the Gibeonites, who had shortly before made a peace agreement with Israel. Now the neighboring kings are attacking them for having allied themselves with Joshua. That is why they ask for the help promised in that agreement. Joshua responds, and God assures him of victory.

For today: when you are in trouble, do not keep silent or isolate yourself. Ask for help with humility, from God and from people you trust. And if someone asks you for help and it is within your power, help them without delay.
exp.5:3:
This verse gives precise instructions for taking Jericho. Seven priests would go before the ark carrying seven trumpets made of rams' horns. On the seventh day, the people would march around the city seven times while the priests blew the trumpets. The instruction is addressed to the whole people.

The one speaking is the LORD, giving instructions to Joshua. God had already declared that he was handing Jericho into their hands, so the victory was a promise, not merely a military plan. The ark, which represented God's presence, went at the front. The method was unusual, and it shows that the victory would come from God and not from Israel's own strength.

Today we can learn that obeying God step by step, even when his way seems strange or slow, is trusting that he keeps what he promises. Ask yourself: what simple act of obedience is he asking of you today?
exp.23:21:
Joshua tells the people that they themselves are witnesses to their own choice. They have chosen the Lord, that is, God, to serve him. And the people confirm it: "We are witnesses." The phrases that the explanation glosses as "you" and "you have chosen for yourselves" are not part of the verse your reader sees, so they are left out here.

Joshua, now old, gathers the tribes of Israel at Shechem to renew the covenant with God. He reminds them of what God has done for them and warns that abandoning him would bring serious consequences. When the people promise faithfulness, Joshua makes them see that their words carry weight and that they will be held responsible for them.

For today: our promises to God are not empty words. Think of a decision of faith you have made, and look for one concrete step this week to carry it out, perhaps by sharing it with someone who can help you stay firm.
exp.20:38:
The explanation says the tribe of Gad gave the Levites two more cities: Heshbon and Jazer, each with its pasturelands, which were the grazing fields around the city where the Levites could keep their livestock. With these two, there are four cities from Gad. The word for the pasturelands is not part of this verse's wording, so it is simply described here as the grazing fields around each city.

There is no speaker addressing us directly; this is Joshua's account of how the cities were divided. The Levites did not receive territory of their own, but cities scattered among all the tribes. These cities belonged to the descendants of Merari, one of the Levite clans. In this way they could teach God's law and serve the people throughout Israel.

For today: God cared for those who devoted themselves to serving him, and the people responded with generosity. We can ask ourselves how we might support, with our time, prayer, or resources, those who teach and serve in our church.
exp.7:11:
This verse says that Joshua chose about five thousand men and hid them in an ambush, that is, in a secret place from which to attack by surprise. He set them between the cities of Beth-el and Ai, on the west side of Ai.

Israel had been defeated at Ai because of Achan's sin. Once the people had been cleansed, God gave Joshua a plan: to attack the city with a trap. While the main part of the army showed itself to the north, these men waited hidden to the west. There are differences between this passage and verse 3, which mentions thirty thousand men, and scholars explain this in several ways.

For today: after a fall, God gives us another opportunity. Following his direction with patience and preparation, without rushing, usually brings better results than acting on impulse.

sum.6: Israel loses the battle at Ai because Achan took forbidden things from Jericho and hid them. God explains to Joshua that there is sin among the people. Achan is found out, confesses, and is punished, and in this way the sin is removed from the midst of Israel. The text teaches that hidden sin affects everyone.
sum.14: This chapter describes the land allotted to the tribe of Judah: its borders and its many towns. Caleb receives Hebron, drives out the giants, and gives his daughter Achsah in marriage to Othniel, who captures Debir. At the end, Judah was unable to drive out the Jebusites from Jerusalem.
sum.10: Jabin, king of Hazor, gathered many kings from the north to fight against Israel. But God told Joshua not to be afraid. Israel won the battle, burned Hazor, and took the land, following what God had commanded Moses. The chapter shows that God keeps his word, and in the end the land rests from war.
sum.11: This chapter gives a list of the kings that Israel defeated. First come Sihon and Og, who were beaten east of the Jordan under Moses. Then come thirty-one kings of Canaan, who were beaten west of the Jordan under Joshua. It shows that God gave his people the promised land, and that these victories are remembered by specific names.
sum.0: After the death of Moses, God commands Joshua to lead the people across the Jordan and take possession of the promised land. He promises to be with him, and tells him to be strong and courageous and to meditate on the law day and night. Joshua prepares the people, and the tribes on the other side of the Jordan promise to obey him.
sum.19: God told Joshua that Israel should set apart cities of refuge, so that anyone who killed someone by accident could flee there, be heard by the elders, and live safely away from the avenger. There he would wait for his trial and stay until the death of the high priest. Six cities were chosen, on both sides of the Jordan, and they were also for the foreigner.
sum.2: Joshua leads the people to the Jordan and orders them to consecrate themselves and to follow the ark at a distance. When the priests carrying it step into the water, the river stops, and all Israel crosses on dry ground. In this way God shows that he is with them and with Joshua, just as he had been with Moses.
sum.18: In Joshua 19, the rest of the land is divided by lot among Simeon, Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Dan, with their cities and borders. The people of Dan, lacking territory, conquer Leshem and name it Dan. In the end, Joshua receives the city he asked for, according to the word of the LORD, and the division is completed at Shiloh.
sum.21: Joshua sends off the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, commending them for their faithfulness and encouraging them to love and serve God. When they build an altar beside the Jordan, the other Israelites fear a rebellion and prepare for war. But once the builders explain that it was only meant as a witness, the conflict is avoided, and everyone praises God.
sum.8: The kings of the region joined forces to fight against Israel, but the Gibeonites tricked Joshua with old clothes and moldy bread so they could make a treaty. Israel did not consult God, and they had to keep their oath. The Gibeonites survived, but they became woodcutters and water carriers for the altar.
sum.1: Joshua sends two spies to Jericho, and Rahab hides them and deceives the king's men, because she believes that Jehovah is the God of heaven and earth. She asks that they save her family, and they promise to do so if she ties a red cord in her window. The spies return and report that the land is afraid.
sum.16: Manasseh receives its land, and the five daughters of Zelophehad receive an inheritance, just as the LORD had commanded Moses. Some Canaanites still remain in several cities because the Israelites did not drive them out completely. The descendants of Joseph ask for more land, and Joshua encourages them to clear the forest and trust that they will be able to win.
sum.23: At Shechem, Joshua gathers Israel together and reminds them of everything God did for them, from Abraham all the way to the land he promised. He invites them to choose whom they will serve, and the people promise to serve the LORD, while Joshua declares, "As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD." Then they make a covenant, and Joshua dies.
sum.9: Five Amorite kings attacked Gibeon because it had made peace with Israel, and Joshua defended the city, trusting in God's promise. God gave the victory with hailstones and by making the sun stand still. Then Joshua defeated the kings and conquered the cities of the south, since the text says that God was fighting for Israel.
sum.3: After crossing the Jordan, God tells Joshua to have twelve men, one from each tribe, take twelve stones out of the river and set them up in the camp at Gilgal. These stones will serve as a reminder for the people of Israel. In this way, their descendants will know that God dried up the Jordan and that his hand is strong.
sum.22: Joshua, now very old, gathers the leaders of Israel and reminds them that God fought for them and gave them the land. He encourages them to obey the law of Moses, to love only the LORD, and not to mix with the gods or the marriages of the nations that remain. He warns them that if they turn away, they will lose the land.
sum.4: The kings of Canaan were filled with fear when they heard that God had dried up the Jordan. Joshua circumcised the new generation, Israel celebrated the Passover at Gilgal, and the manna stopped once they began eating the produce of the land. Then Joshua met the Commander of the army of the LORD and worshiped him.
sum.13: Israel begins dividing the land of Canaan among the tribes by lot, as God had commanded through Moses, and the Levites receive cities instead of a territory of their own. Caleb, now 85 years old and still strong, asks for the mountain that God had promised him, and Joshua blesses him and gives him Hebron, because he had followed God faithfully.
sum.20: The Levites asked for the towns that God had commanded through Moses, and Israel gave them forty-eight towns with their pasturelands, spread among all the tribes, including six cities of refuge for those who had killed someone. The chapter ends by saying that God gave the land and the rest He had promised, and that not one of His good promises had failed.
sum.7: God tells Joshua not to be afraid and gives him victory over Ai through an ambush. This time Israel takes the plunder. Afterward, Joshua builds an altar on Mount Ebal, writes the law on stones, and reads to the whole people the blessings and curses, showing the importance of obeying God's word.
sum.12: The LORD tells Joshua, who is now old, that a great deal of land still remains to be taken, and He commands him to divide the territory among the nine and a half tribes of Manasseh. The chapter recalls the lands east of the Jordan that Moses had given to Reuben, Gad, and the other half-tribe of Manasseh. The tribe of Levi received no land, because the LORD Himself was their inheritance.
sum.17: Israel gathered at Shiloh and set up the tent of meeting there. Joshua rebuked the seven tribes that had not yet taken possession of their land, and he sent three men from each tribe to survey the land and describe it. Then he cast lots before the LORD, and the first portion went to Benjamin, whose boundaries and cities are set out in detail.
sum.15: Joshua 16 describes the territory allotted to the descendants of Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh, and gives a detailed account of the boundaries of Ephraim's land. Some of Ephraim's cities were located within the territory of Manasseh. However, they did not drive out the Canaanites from Gezer, who remained there as tribute-paying subjects, and this shows an incomplete obedience.
sum.5: God tells Joshua that Jericho will fall if the people march around the city with the ark for seven days, and on the seventh day they shout at the sound of the trumpets. And so it happens: the wall collapses and the city is destroyed, but Rahab and her family are saved because she had protected the spies. The chapter shows the obedience and faithfulness of God.
